exp40v2-sol.wireframe:
Wireframes, mockups, prototypes

Discovery & Design › Solution Design & Prototyping. What is the lowest-fidelity artefact that answers the question I hold? The argument here is that the familiar answer — low fidelity is cheaper — has stopped being true, and that two harder justifications are all that survive.

1. Two decisions, five weeks apart

Bengaluru, 3 February 2026. Deeksha Gangolli, vice-president of product at Firki Health, had a release train leaving on 14 February and a redesigned flow she did not trust. Firki's Android app helped people with type-2 diabetes track and reorder medication; 11.2 lakh had registered and 2,60,000 were monthly active. The flow ran from a dosage change prescribed at a clinic to a reorder arriving at the door.

The baseline was precise, because Firki instrumented it. In January 2026, 1,48,000 of the 2,60,000 monthly active users opened the refill card at least once. Of those 1,48,000, 16,872 completed a refill within 30 days of their own first open — 11.4 per cent, on the denominator that matters for anything inside the flow: card-openers, not actives. The window is per user, so the cohort closed only in mid-February. At ₹84 each, the flow earned ₹14.17 lakh. Devanshi Gokarn, her designer, had a redesign she believed in; of the 16 Firki had shipped since early 2024, four measurably reduced the primary metric, a base rate of 25 per cent. The decision was not whether to test but what to build. Devanshi wanted four days for a mockup, twenty-two frames with real copy. Dakshita Govekar, the engineering lead, wanted nine days to put a coded prototype on handsets, suspecting latency rather than layout.

Pune, 9 March 2026. Durvesh Gondhalekar, head of product at Fitrat Devices, had a harder version of the same question and a date he could not move. Fitrat built the Frostline: a 200-litre chilled milk collection unit for village dairy co-operative societies, with a weighing bridge, a milk analyser and a five-inch resistive touch console. The operator, usually the society secretary, entered a member number, confirmed the weight and fat reading, and printed a slip. The console had been redesigned. Bezel tooling locked on 27 April 2026, forty-nine days away, and a federation order for 4,200 units at ₹58,400 each — ₹24.53 crore — carried a delivery penalty of 0.5 per cent of order value a week, capped at five per cent.

Durvesh's team had built an elegant console simulator that ran on a tablet. Dhanya Guruprasad, who ran field research, said it was useless. Collection at the median society began at 05:10 and had to finish before the chilling truck left at 06:45; 220 members poured in that window; the operator's hands were wet and often gloved; ambient light at 05:10 in February was close to nothing. A tablet on a Pune desk at two in the afternoon answered none of the questions that would decide whether the Frostline 2 worked.

Both decisions turn on one judgement, and it is not "use low fidelity". It is a judgement about which properties must be real for the answer to be trustworthy.

2. The idea, and the four schools that disagree about it

Define the terms, because usage has drifted. A wireframe represents structure while withholding surface: layout, hierarchy, labels and flow, without typography, colour or imagery. A mockup represents surface at near-final quality while withholding behaviour. A prototype represents behaviour — something responds, so a task can be attempted. Not three points on one line, then, but three subsets of the product's properties, each chosen so that what you did not build cannot be mistaken for what you did.

The lineages explain the confusion. "Wireframe" comes from computer graphics, where a wireframe render showed edges without surfaces. "Mockup" comes from manufacturing: aircraft programmes of the 1930s and 1940s built full-scale wooden cockpit mock-ups and reviewed them with pilots, because moving a lever in wood cost nothing and moving it in aluminium cost a production line. "Prototype" is the engineer's first article. The practice entered software through its first argument with itself: by the mid-1980s Barry Boehm's UCLA experiment had found that teams which prototyped first produced smaller, more usable products with less coherent architecture. Fred Brooks wrote in 1975 that one should plan to throw one away, then withdrew it twenty years later — an admission that the throwaway assumption was an artefact of what throwing away then cost. Four schools hold genuinely different positions, best put as propositions each would and would not sign.

The usability-engineering school treats the artefact as an instrument for measuring task performance. It signs: iteration count matters more than participant count, and polish is a cost with no diagnostic return. It will not sign: a prototype's purpose is to establish whether anyone wants the thing. Its canonical move, Marc Rettig's 1994 argument for paper prototypes, was not mainly about money: polish suppresses criticism, because reviewers stop telling you the architecture is wrong once the thing looks finished.

The sketching school, in Bill Buxton's formulation, holds that sketches and prototypes are different species. A sketch suggests, and its ambiguity is a feature, because it invites proposal rather than approval; a prototype describes. It signs: fidelity should lag commitment. It will not sign: every artefact needs a decision rule first — the generative work it cares about is what you cannot pre-register.

The experiment school treats the artefact as a demand instrument. It signs: an artefact built without a pre-stated decision rule is theatre, and an MVP is a learning vehicle, not a small product. It will emphatically not sign low fidelity is a virtue: if the question is willingness to pay, polish is part of the treatment, not a confound, and a grey box under-reports intent for reasons unrelated to the product itself.

The engineering-prototype school, strongest in hardware, classifies prototypes as analytical or physical and focused or comprehensive, and sets fidelity by the risk being retired, often physical rather than human. It signs: when failure modes are coupled, a comprehensive physical prototype is irreplaceable, and a focused one can mislead because the interaction between subsystems is the risk. It will not sign throwaway is cheaper: in its world the prototype is also the specification, the test fixture and the regulatory record.

3. Mechanics: four dials, of which two are usually set by accident

Expert practice begins before any tool opens, with a sentence of the form I believe X; if X is false I will do Y instead of Z. No Y that differs from Z, no question — and the artefact is decoration. Then four independent dials get set. Visual fidelity is how finished the surface looks; breadth is how much is covered; interaction depth is how much really responds, and on what data. And the dial almost nobody sets on purpose: context realism — device, lighting, hour, time pressure. It decided Fitrat's case, and is invisible in any ladder drawn as one axis.

The second-order effect most practitioners miss is that each dial trades one confound for another. Raise visual fidelity and you stop under-measuring desirability but start suppressing structural critique. Raise breadth and you remove out-of-context judgement but add fatigue and a halo from the first screens. Stub the interaction and you remove imagined latency but introduce suspiciously clean data. No setting has zero confounds; the skill is naming the one you accepted.

The formal treatment is a value-of-information calculation. Severity is stated once and held common across harm classes: a regression costing 2,960 completed refills in a 30-day window, worth 2,960 × ₹84 = ₹2,48,640. For the copy and friction classes that is two points of conversion among the 1,48,000 who open the card — 13,912 completions instead of 16,872. The entry-point class cannot sit on that denominator, because somebody who never finds the card never becomes an opener; there the same severity means about 25,965 fewer openers out of the 2,60,000 actives, at 11.4 per cent. Holding severity common across mechanisms is an assumption every EVI below inherits.

Her first pass used six weeks as the detect-and-roll-back window. ₹2,48,640 is a 30-day figure, so the daily rate is ₹8,288 and 42 days is an exposure of ₹3.48 lakh. Count in days: a four-week "month" and a calendar month differ by eight per cent here. The base was wrong anyway — the metric needs 30 days per user before a cohort can be read, and the one comparable regression took eleven weeks to attribute. Seventy-seven days at ₹8,288 is ₹6.38 lakh, nearly double, and enough to change the recommendation rather than sharpen it.

At the wrong exposure every rung loses money even at marginal cost, and a disciplined manager reading that column tests nothing. At the corrected exposure the wireframe clears its ₹24,000 by ₹8,407. The mockup's cost hides a second wrong base: of its ₹57,600, about ₹44,000 would be spent whatever the research plan said, because the mockup is also the build specification Dakshita's engineers work from. Charging the full ₹57,600 to the diagnostic decision is the exposure mistake in reverse — a cost attributed to a decision that did not cause it. At a marginal ₹13,600 it clears ₹18,817 by ₹5,217, but that rests wholly on the ₹44,000, which is stipulated rather than measured: it breaks even only if ₹38,783 of it, 67 per cent, is genuinely reusable. The treatment is asymmetric too — the wireframe's fourteen frames feed the twenty-two and earn no reuse credit, understating its ₹8,407. Two wrong bases, in opposite directions, moved the recommendation from test nothing to build the wireframe and the mockup, not the prototype. A fidelity decision is a capital-allocation decision, and those are wrecked more often by bad denominators than by bad multiplication.

4. When it applies, stated as testable claims

"Pick the lowest fidelity that answers your question" rests on four claims, each failing somewhere.

One: fidelity and cost rise together. True for thirty years, now substantially false. A mature component library makes a high-fidelity mockup nearly as cheap as a wireframe — Devanshi's twenty-two frames cost six person-days against two and a half for fourteen grey-box frames, a ratio of 2.4, not the ten or twenty the classical argument assumed. Generative tooling goes further still. Where this fails, only the measurement and commitment arguments remain. For Durvesh it holds absolutely: ₹6,000 of foam-core against an ₹11.60 lakh dawn pilot is a ratio of 193.

Two: the question is known before the artefact is built. When it is, the advice is plainly right. When it is not, the sketching school's objection bites: the artefact's job is to generate the question, and you cannot pick a fidelity for a question you do not have. Durvesh's foam-core panel was built in that mode and produced the question that mattered, about gloves.

Three: the answer does not depend on what you faked. This fails most often and most expensively, and it is the whole of Dhanya's objection. The tablet simulator faked the panel technology — capacitive rather than resistive, so a gloved finger behaves quite differently — plus the light, the hour and the queue, each load-bearing.

Four: climbing a rung later is cheap. Cheap in software, brutal across an irreversibility date. After 27 April, changing tap-target geometry means a re-tool at ₹37.50 lakh plus eleven weeks, and eleven weeks hits the five per cent penalty cap on ₹24.53 crore, ₹1.23 crore: ₹1.60 crore against a ₹2.24 lakh rig. Where this fails the instruction inverts — not the lowest fidelity that answers the question but the highest reachable before the date, scheduled backwards.

And where the idea actively misleads: when the question is desire rather than performance, low fidelity does not under-measure the answer, it measures something else. A grey-box wireframe of a premium service tests as cheap-looking, and the team reads positioning out of an artefact containing none. If the question is "will anyone pay", the lowest fidelity that answers it is high.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

In a two-sided marketplace no single-sided artefact answers the real question, because the product is liquidity and liquidity cannot be drawn. The right low-fidelity instrument is a Wizard of Oz on the supply side: a human doing by hand what the matching engine will later do. That answers whether the demand-side experience is acceptable and nothing about whether it scales — and teams report the first as the second.

In regulated contexts fidelity changes the governance path, not just the cost. Firki's mockup carries real dosage-titration copy, which is clinical content; showing it to patients needs a sign-off adding nine days the grey-box rung does not incur. In medical devices the usability engineering file is itself a deliverable, so an unrecorded session is not cheap but unusable — and the cheap rung is sometimes slower, because the expensive one was already on the compliance calendar.

In hardware plus software the failure modes couple. A focused prototype of the console answers tap accuracy but not what happens when the compressor cycles and the panel sweats, because that is an interaction between subsystems. The risk lives in the seams, and focused prototypes are blind to seams by construction.

In AI-native products output varies, so a deterministic click-through showing one good output misrepresents the product worse than a grey box would. The expert move is to prototype the distribution: show three sampled outputs including a poor one, and make the recovery path part of the artefact. A human playing the model answers "is a good output useful" and nothing about "can the model reliably produce one".

At the organisational seams a mockup becomes a promise: a frame built from design-system components may depend on one that exists in the design file and not in the Android codebase, so the mockup's cost stops predicting the build's. Mature companies say they prototype at the lowest useful fidelity; what they do is keep a standing design system and produce mockups by default, because the mockup is at once review currency, handoff specification and marketing asset. That is not indiscipline — most of its cost is owed anyway, and the diagnostic question gets answered by something cheap beside it. Teams that believe the rhetoric build low-fidelity artefacts in addition to the mockups they were always going to build: the most expensive way to be virtuous.

6. Nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The dials are independent, and nearly everyone treats them as one. The tell is a team that says "let's go higher fidelity" and raises all four together — colour, screens, behaviour, and the session moved from field to office — so that when the result changes nothing can be attributed. An expert raises one dial per round and says which. The related tell is a review whose comments move from "should the refill live here at all" to "the chip should be eight pixels lower" within minutes of the artefact looking finished: detail-level comments are what people produce once they have inferred, from the surface, that structure is now closed.

Context realism is a dial, usually set to zero by accident. The tell is a readout naming participants and tasks but not the hour, device, network or lighting. Fitrat's 2023 sessions ran at two in the afternoon on a laptop with dry hands; nothing flagged it, because the readout had no field for it. The obvious reading treats context as nice-to-have; in operational products it is often the dominant term, and low context realism answers a question nobody asked.

Rounds, not participants, are the scarce resource — and which is scarce flips between consumer and enterprise. The tell is a consumer team running one twelve-person study while an enterprise team runs five five-person rounds; both have it backwards. Firki recruits five refill users in two days for ₹6,000 and runs three rounds in ten days, so low fidelity is efficient. Fitrat needs federation permission and a dawn visit: twenty-three days and about ₹64,000 a round, which over forty-nine days to tooling lock permits two rounds. The obvious reading — enterprise should iterate more cheaply — inverts: when rounds are scarce, each must carry more questions, pushing fidelity up.

What you build, you defend. The tell is a team that cannot say what evidence would make them abandon an artefact they spent two weeks on, and a review where the mockup's author also summarises the findings. The countermeasure is procedural: write the rule first, have someone who did not build it run the sessions, discard it visibly once it has answered. The obvious reading treats this as a discipline problem cured by seniority; it is structural, and seniority makes it worse.

7. Product type and company stage — including where the difference is not real

Start with where the differences are not real. Writing the question and the decision rule before choosing the artefact is identical across consumer, enterprise, platform, hardware and AI products; so is the four-dial decomposition, and so is the detection arithmetic. Anyone claiming their domain is special here is usually arguing for the right to skip the question.

The real differences reduce to three variables: the cost and latency of participant access, the location of irreversibility, and whether the question concerns performance or desire. Consumer products have cheap participants, frequent releases and no irreversibility date, so low fidelity with many rounds is near optimal — though consumer questions run to desire, where polish is the treatment. B2B and enterprise have expensive participants mediated by account relationships, with irreversibility in the contract rather than the code; the rational response is fewer, broader, higher-fidelity rounds, and a willingness to prototype the administrative surface, where enterprise products actually fail and which never appears in a wireframe. Platforms cannot be prototyped from one side; the dial that matters is data realism. Hardware inverts the advice outright.

By stage, what shifts is what is scarce. A pre-product-market-fit team has no users and no instrumentation, so artefacts substitute for data and low fidelity plus ten conversations is the best instrument available. At Firki's scale it inverts: with 1,48,000 card-openers a month and a 5 per cent release channel, the instrumented release is the more valid instrument for a behavioural question — dearer than any prototype at ₹2,97,600 on Table 2, and right anyway, because validity rather than cost is scarce. Prototyping then belongs to what instrumentation cannot reach: comprehension, intent, and flows that do not yet exist.

8. Three worked examples

8.1 Firki: cheap artefact, bought answer

The grey-box round ran on 5 and 6 February with five recruited refill users: four located the refill entry unaided inside twenty seconds, the fifth after a prompt — one failure, inside the four-of-five rule. The latency question Deeksha refused to buy with a prototype. She spent one person-day, ₹9,600, instrumenting the live refill card and read the real 95th-percentile response across 1,48,000 monthly openers rather than five simulated ones. The prototype would have cost ₹1,34,400 for a five-person estimate of what the live system reports exactly for ₹9,600. Expertise is not only choosing a lower rung; it is noticing the answer lies off the ladder.

8.2 Fitrat: the number no mockup could produce

Dhanya's telemetry from eleven instrumented societies in November 2025 gave a mean handling time of 24.5 seconds per pourer — the mean, because a session total is a sum and handling times are right-skewed enough that a median would understate it. At the median society by pourer count, 220 pourers consume 220 × 24.5 = 5,390 seconds, or 89.8 minutes inside a 95-minute window from 05:10 to the truck's 06:45 departure. Slack is 5.17 minutes — 310 seconds over 220 pourers, so 1.41 seconds per pourer is the entire budget. The redesigned confirm step added 3.5 seconds: 220 × 28.0 = 6,160 seconds, 102.7 minutes, ending 7.7 minutes after the truck has gone.

Then the base correction, which is why this example is here. The median society was the wrong unit. At Ambegaon, tightest of the eleven, 243 pourers run inside a 101-minute window: 243 × 24.5 = 5,953.5 seconds, 99.2 minutes, leaving 1.78 minutes of slack — 106.5 seconds over 243 pourers, or 0.44 seconds per pourer. The governing constraint is three times tighter than the median implied, and the redesign exceeds it eightfold. A rule written against the median passes a console that fails where failure is most visible to the federation. No artefact of any fidelity catches that; only the right denominator does.

8.3 Where it failed: Fitrat's 2023 console, and the ratio that caused the next mistake

The Frostline 1 console was validated in 2023 with a high-fidelity rendered simulation on a 13-inch laptop at the Pune office, at two in the afternoon, with ten participants recruited from inside the building. Visual fidelity near maximum, interaction depth high, context realism approximately zero. The sessions went well. In the field, of 1,840 service tickets logged in FY25, 312 — 17.0 per cent — were console mis-entry, repeat weighing or slip reprint. Recovery was a retrofit: a raised-ridge bezel plus firmware across the 2,640 units installed, at ₹1,480 each, or ₹39.07 lakh.

The post-mortem framed this as ₹39.07 lakh of retrofit against a ₹2.24 lakh rig: a 17.4-fold return. The denominator was wrong. Catching it in 2023 would still have cost ₹6.80 lakh of bezel redesign and a re-run of ingress and EMC testing, so the comparison is ₹39.07 lakh ÷ ₹9.04 lakh = 4.32. It is tempting to cut the numerator too: 84 of the 312 tickets, 26.9 per cent, were slip-printer jams that no console rig detects, apparently leaving 228 of 312 — 73.1 per cent — and ₹28.55 lakh. That proration is wrong. The retrofit was one fixed programme, a bezel and a firmware build shipped to all 2,640 units; its cost does not fall because a quarter of the tickets had another cause. A fixed cost cannot be apportioned by a ratio of causes.

The recommendation survives — 4.32 times is an excellent return — but the inflated figure did real damage, because the 17-fold number was the one that circulated. Through 2024 Fitrat built rigs for questions a foam-core panel or a telemetry query would have answered, spending roughly ₹14 lakh on fixtures that changed no decision. A correct decision justified by an exaggerated ratio produces an over-correction next time, harder to see because it looks like rigour.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Fidelity creep without a question
The artefact gains screens and polish with no new question attached. Early sign: frame count rising faster than the question list. Diagnostic: "which frame answers which question?" Cost: 22 frames grown to 40 is five extra person-days, ₹48,000, buying agreement rather than evidence.
Testing in the wrong context
Fitrat's 2023 case exactly. Early sign: the readout has no field for device, hour, light or hands. Diagnostic: "name every condition of real use we did not reproduce." Cost: ₹39.07 lakh of retrofit, plus the ₹14 lakh over-correction after it.
Reading preference as behaviour
Participants say they would use it; the team records adoption evidence. Early sign: findings quoted rather than counted. Diagnostic: "what did they do, and how many of how many?" Cost: ₹6.38 lakh per regression of historical size, found eleven weeks late.
Under-powered rounds treated as clearance
A five-person round with no problems found is reported as a pass. Early sign: "no issues" without naming the incidence the round could detect. Diagnostic: "what is the smallest problem this round catches two times in three?" — from Table 1, p ≈ 0.20 (exactly 0.197). Cost: a 5 per cent blocker runs to ₹70,896 a month.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does fidelity change the findings? The sceptical position is empirically grounded: controlled comparisons of paper against computer prototypes have repeatedly found similar sets and numbers of usability problems, implying polish is a cost with no diagnostic return. The opposing position accepts that and restricts it: those studies measured task performance, and fidelity changes which classes surface, affecting stated preference, trust and desirability even where error counts hold. For the sceptics to be wrong, a decision must be shown to have turned on a class appearing only at high fidelity. For the restrictors to be wrong, high-fidelity rounds would have to surface no class absent from low-fidelity rounds — which almost no team tests.

Five participants, or a measured sample? The classical model says discovery follows 1 − (1 − p)n with p near a third, making five participants sufficient and more of them wasteful relative to another round. The opposing camp, drawing on large-site studies where five users found a small minority of problems, argues the model assumes one homogeneous p and independent participants, where real incidence is heterogeneous, so five users sample the common problems and nothing else. Both are right about different distributions, which is why the discipline that matters is stating the incidence your round can detect rather than defending a number. The classical position fails whenever problems are mostly rare and segment-specific.

Does the artefact corrupt the decision? One camp holds that polish creates commitment: effort is sunk, authorship public, stakeholders ratify what looks finished, so fidelity should stay low until the decision is made. The other holds the reverse — ambiguity corrupts decisions, because each reviewer silently fills the gaps with a private assumption and the team mistakes silence for consensus, discovering the disagreement in code. Both describe real pathologies, and what separates them is organisational: with weak decision rights, low fidelity manufactures false consensus; with strong authorship norms, high fidelity manufactures escalation. The prescription depends on a fact about the company — unsatisfying and, as far as the field has established, correct.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this recites the ladder. Someone who has internalised it writes the question and the decision rule before opening a tool, and abandons artefacts whose answers would change nothing. They set one dial at a time. They separate diagnostic from production cost before comparing anything. They name the accepted confound, in a sentence beginning "this round cannot tell us". They schedule backwards from irreversibility dates. And they look off the ladder first: the surest signature of expertise is a manager who answers a fidelity question by pointing at the funnel or the support queue.

12. The decisions

Deeksha shipped on 14 February. She built the grey-box wireframe for ₹24,000, pre-registered to pass only if at least four of five users found the refill entry unaided within twenty seconds; the high-fidelity mockup, built regardless as the build specification, its diagnostic use confined to dosage-copy comprehension and its nine-day clinical review started on day one so it could not become the critical path; and a ₹9,600 production probe for latency, under a rule that the release holds if the live 95th-percentile response exceeds 1,400 milliseconds. She did not build the prototype.

Durvesh committed ₹2.24 lakh to the rig — 3D-printed bezel, real resistive panel, driven by a laptop — and killed the ₹48,000 tablet simulator, whose capacitive panel made its central finding uninterpretable. He moved the dawn pilot three weeks earlier by hand-assembling six units rather than waiting for pre-production, because the cycle-time question can only be answered at a society at 05:10, before firmware freeze. The rule he wrote was Dhanya's: no more than 0.44 seconds added per pourer at Ambegaon, failing which the confirm step is removed rather than redesigned.

Discussion questions

  1. Deeksha priced the mockup's diagnostic cost at ₹13,600 by subtracting the ₹44,000 she would have spent anyway. Durvesh could argue the same about the rig, whose bezel geometry feeds the tooling file. Should he? What separates a legitimate production-versus-diagnostic split from a device for approving what you already wanted to build?
  2. The corrected retrofit ratio was 4.32, not 17.4, and the recommendation survived. Suppose it were 0.8. What should Durvesh do with a rig that is the only instrument able to answer a question whose expected value does not cover its cost, seven weeks before an irreversible tooling lock?
  3. Firki's trust-and-price harm class has caused no regressions in sixteen shipments, but its 95 per cent upper bound is 20.6 per cent, not zero. Is confining the mockup to copy comprehension defensible, or has Deeksha used a small denominator to avoid the question she least wants answered?
