Tells you whether the question is performance or desire — the fork that sets the visual dial.
Value proposition statement
Makes the claim under test falsifiable, so a mockup is judged against it, not taste.
Concept → feedback → iterate
Rounds, not artefacts, produce learning.
case20v1-sol.wireframe:
Nirmiti Supply: The Reorder Screen

A case on choosing the lowest fidelity that answers the question

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 19 October 2026, Amudha Hemachandran sat in Nirmiti Supply's Pune office with a calendar open and a problem that fitted into three lines. The board would meet on Friday, 6 November, two days before Diwali. It expected a recommendation on the redesigned "repeat order" experience in the company's dealer app. Amudha, the group product manager, had to tell her team by Friday, 23 October which kind of prototype to build, because the build would start the following Monday.

Three kinds were on the table, and they differed by a factor of more than twenty in cost. She did not yet know which question the board actually needed answered. That, she suspected, was the real decision.

2. Company background

Nirmiti Supply, founded in Pune in 2019, sells electrical and plumbing hardware to independent dealers: the shop that stocks switches, wires, pipes and fittings for the local electrician. Nirmiti buys from manufacturers and distributors, delivers within two days, and offers dealers thirty days of credit. Its app, available in Marathi, Kannada, Tamil, Telugu and Hindi, carries a catalogue of about 18,000 items and takes payment by UPI or against credit. In September 2026 it had 4,800 active dealers across Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Telangana.

The competition is crowded. Udaan and Jumbotail are broad business-to-business marketplaces; Moglix and OfBusiness are strong in industrial supplies. Nirmiti's argument is narrower: deep stock in one category, regional-language screens, and field representatives who visit each dealer about once a fortnight. Most dealers are comfortable with WhatsApp and UPI. Many are less comfortable with a long, English-influenced catalogue.

3. The situation

Nirmiti's dealers fall into two habits. Of the 4,800 active in September, 2,160 placed their orders through the app and 2,640 sent them by WhatsApp message or call to their field representative, who keyed them in. The 2,640 are 55 per cent of the base; the 2,160 are 45 per cent. Representative logs showed that the WhatsApp group averaged three orders a month each, or 7,920 orders, and that each one cost roughly ₹45 in representative time to key and confirm. That is ₹3,56,400, about ₹3.56 lakh a month.

Between 5 and 9 October, Amudha's researcher interviewed 40 dealers drawn from the WhatsApp group, all of whom had been asked why they did not reorder in the app. Exhibit 1 sets out what they said. The interviews are a sample of the WhatsApp group, not a count of it, and each dealer gave one main reason.

Exhibit 1: Main reason given for not reordering in the app (40 WhatsApp-ordering dealers, interviewed 5 to 9 October 2026)
Main reasonDealersShare of 40
Could not find the "repeat last order" list1435%
Prefer dealing with the representative (relationship, credit haggling)1230%
Item names not in their own language or trade shorthand820%
Other615%
Total40100%

Source: Nirmiti research notes. One main reason per dealer, coded by the researcher. Shares are of the 40 interviewed, not of all 2,640 WhatsApp-ordering dealers.

The team was spread across time zones. Alamelu Hanumanthu, the senior designer in Berlin, had already sketched a new repeat-order screen. Ananthi Harinarayanan, the sales head in New Jersey, was on calls with distributors at what was late evening in Pune. Aruna Haribabu, the data scientist in Toronto, had the event logs. The engineering team in Bengaluru was waiting for a start signal. Berlin was three and a half hours behind Pune, and from 25 October, when European clocks went back, it would be four and a half. New Jersey and Toronto were nine and a half hours behind until 1 November.

4. The people

Alamelu Hanumanthu, senior designer, Berlin. She wants to test the layout on paper first. Her view is that findability, the main reason for 14 of the 40 dealers interviewed, is a layout problem, and that polished screens invite dealers to critique colours rather than the flow.

Ananthi Harinarayanan, sales head, New Jersey. She wants something she can show to a large distributor and to the board: a working demo. She worries that sketches will look unserious next to Udaan's app. She also argues the board will not fund what it cannot see running.

Aruna Haribabu, data scientist, Toronto. She wants a coded prototype wired to real catalogue data, so that she can measure time to first reorder and drop-off by step. She regards interview counts as thin.

Amudha Hemachandran, group product manager, Pune. She owns the decision and the board recommendation.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1, above, tells Amudha that the top two reasons together cover 26 of the 40 dealers interviewed, but of different kinds. Findability can be tested with a layout. The relationship with the representative cannot be fixed by any screen, and a prototype of any polish will not tell her how many dealers hold that view across the whole base.

Exhibit 2: The three prototype routes
OptionWorking daysCost (₹ lakh)Ready byCan answer
A. Paper wireframes, tested with 12 dealers in Pune, Coimbatore and Hyderabad51.2Fri 30 OctCan dealers find and use the repeat list, and do the labels read clearly in Marathi, Tamil and Telugu?
B. Clickable mockup of 14 screens124.5Tue 10 NovFlow, wording and a demo for distributors
C. Coded prototype on live catalogue4028.0Fri 18 DecSpeed, error rates, drop-off by step

Source: Nirmiti design and engineering estimates, 16 October 2026. Costs include internal time at loaded rates and dealer travel and incentives. Ready-by dates assume a Monday 26 October start; working days exclude weekends only, and festival holidays are not deducted.

Exhibit 2 and the calendar in Exhibit 3 show a hard fact. Only Option A reports before the board meets on 6 November. Option B lands four days after it, and Option C in the week before Christmas, well after the festive restocking that matters most to dealers. Amudha also did a sum on the prize. If a better screen moved 1,000 of the 2,640 WhatsApp dealers to the app, at three orders a month and ₹45 a keyed order, Nirmiti would save ₹1,35,000 a month, or ₹1.35 lakh. Option C at ₹28 lakh would then take about 21 months to repay in representative time alone. That figure ignores faster orders and fewer errors, and the ₹28 lakh is a prototype cost, not the production build that would deliver the saving, but it showed her that a heavy build needed a better argument than savings.

Exhibit 3: Time scale 10 pixels per calendar day from 19 October (x = 40 + 10 × days elapsed). Bars start Monday 26 October. Diwali falls on Sunday 8 November.

6. The options

Option A: paper wireframes. Alamelu draws the repeat-order flow as five hand-sized screens in the dealers' own languages. A researcher and a field representative show them to 12 dealers, four each in Pune, Coimbatore and Hyderabad, asking each to "reorder what you bought last month". The upside is speed and cost: ₹1.2 lakh and a result by 30 October. The cost is that it shows nothing of speed or real catalogue behaviour, and Ananthi has nothing to demonstrate.

Option B: a clickable mockup. Fourteen designed screens linked in Figma, for ₹4.5 lakh. It tests wording and flow in more detail and gives Ananthi her demo. It would arrive four days after the board.

Option C: a coded prototype. Engineers in Bengaluru build a working reorder flow on the live catalogue for ₹28 lakh, which gives Aruna real timings. It answers the most questions, and answers them last.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly is the question the board will need answered on 6 November, and what is the question the team needs answered before building anything?
  2. From Exhibit 1, which of the four reasons can a screen fix, and which can no prototype of any fidelity address?
  3. For each option in Exhibit 2, what could the result show that would change what Nirmiti does next? What could it not show?
  4. If you chose Option A, what result, set before the test, would count as success, and what would you do with each outcome?

8. A note for the learner

This topic frames the decision with one question: what is the lowest-fidelity artefact that answers my current question? Fidelity is not quality. A prototype is a learning vehicle, and its fidelity should rise only when the question being asked cannot be answered at the level below. Wireframes test structure and findability. Mockups test look, wording and perceived credibility. Coded prototypes test behaviour, speed and data. Each step up multiplies cost and delays the next decision.

A well-reasoned answer names the current question and rejects options that answer a different one. Here the current question is narrow: can a dealer find and use the repeat list? It is not "will the app win dealers from the representative", which only a live rollout can settle.

One defensible path is Option A, with a decision rule written on 23 October. If at least 9 of the 12 dealers (75 per cent) find the repeat list and complete a reorder unaided in under a minute, proceed to Option B with Alamelu's layout, and let Ananthi demo that. If 6 or fewer do, the layout is wrong and a second paper round costs about a week by the team's own estimate, far less than discovering it inside a ₹28 lakh build. Results of 7 or 8 are ambiguous, and Amudha should say in advance that she will run a second paper round of six dealers.

The reasoning has limits that a careful student states. Twelve dealers can show a gross failure but not a small difference, and they were chosen in three cities, not sampled from four states. Paper cannot show that the redesign moves the 2,640 dealers (55 per cent of the base) who order through representatives. The 12 of 40 interviewed dealers who prefer the relationship may never move, and the board should hear that. Aruna's data needs are real, but they belong to a later question, once the layout is settled, and Option C then becomes a sensible investment because it will test something specific. Ananthi's concern about credibility is also real; the answer is to show the board the dealers' reactions to the paper test, which is evidence, not decoration, and to promise Option B's demo within days of the result.
case40v1-sol.wireframe:
Indian School of Business · Case 40 · Discovery & Design

Paravai Technologies: Thirty Design-Days Before Deepavali

Coimbatore, Sunday 18 October 2026

1. The night before

The last power-loom lorry had gone down Avinashi Road by eleven, and Bavithra Irudayaraj was still at the kitchen table in Saibaba Colony with two laptops open. On the left, the interactive prototype of Seller Desk 2.0: forty-one screens, every one pixel-complete, walked through in July by ninety-six knitwear sellers, most of whom pronounced it nalla irukku. On the right, the August field funnel from the same product, built and shipped, in the sellers' own sheds: twenty-eight of two hundred and forty invited sellers had published a live SKU.

Tomorrow, Monday 19 October, she had a nine o'clock with Bhoopathi Illindala, who had hired her nineteen months ago, and at six in the evening a flight to Dubai for Tuesday's design-acceptance workshop with Pareen Retail Group. Between them she had to say what Paravai would do with the thirty design-days before Friday 6 November, the last working day before the Tiruppur units closed for Deepavali on Sunday 8 November.

Paravai had spent seventy-five design-days and ₹43.70 lakh on five artefacts of Seller Desk 2.0, and the two cheapest had told her something the two high-fidelity ones had not. She did not know whether that was a lesson about fidelity, about who the user was, or about a research design nobody had written down.

2. Paravai, 2017–2026

Paravai Technologies Private Limited was founded in Coimbatore in 2017 by Bhoopathi Illindala, whose family ran a sixty-machine compacting unit in Tiruppur. The first product, still called Floor internally, tracked cut-to-pack progress against a purchase order; by 2021 it ran in some nine hundred units at ₹1,500 a month.

Two decisions from that period shaped October 2026. The first was the design system, built in 2022 and known as the kit: good work, built entirely as desktop-width Figma components, because the paying product then was a desktop dashboard. Mobile variants were scoped twice and deferred twice, so any mobile mockup had to be hand-assembled — three times the cost of a desktop screen, on Beulah Irlapati's own estimate.

The second was the master services agreement of March 2024 with Pareen Retail Group, a Dubai value-apparel chain, which carried Paravai from ₹9 crore to ₹52.80 crore of annual recurring revenue in the two and a half years since. Schedule 4, conceded in the last fortnight of negotiation, is titled Design Acceptance: every Buyer Portal release must be preceded by an interactive, pixel-complete prototype covering one hundred per cent of changed screens, reviewed at Pareen's offices and signed by its sourcing director. A release without one carries a fee credit of two per cent of that month's fees. Nobody objected.

3. The industry

By 2026 the Tiruppur knitwear cluster — some ₹45,000 crore of apparel a year, mostly export — sat at the junction of three forces none of its units had asked for. GST e-invoicing had reached units above the ₹5 crore turnover threshold, so what had been WhatsApp photographs became structured filings. ONDC made it possible to list a size-set catalogue on an open network rather than inside one marketplace, with its own apparel attributes: size, colour, HSN code and a scannable identifier per size-set. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act put obligations around the PAN, GST and bank details an onboarding flow collects, including a consent notice in the seller's language.

Zoho and Freshworks had normalised the idea that serious software is built in Tamil Nadu and sold globally, and Zoho's Coimbatore presence meant Paravai competed for their engineers. Pulari Commerce Cloud of Bengaluru was giving its catalogue app away, and Paravai's sellers already sold through Flipkart, Meesho and Myntra. Paravai's pitch was that it was the one system a unit needed on both sides of the order; its exposure was that half its revenue came from buyers who could switch and half from sellers who could stop paying ₹20,000 a year.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

Seller Desk 2.0 began in February 2026 with a defensible observation: of roughly 9,400 paying units only a minority ever published a catalogue, and Baladitya Irungovel's buyers kept asking for depth Paravai could not supply. The kick-off framed the programme as a redesign — the onboarding flow was ugly, eleven screens long and desktop-first.

In March, Bavithra ran what she thought of as a warm-up: four design-days, ₹38,000 out of pocket, eleven sellers in Tiruppur and Palladam, a paper flow on A4 sheets and a Wizard-of-Oz in which a Paravai associate on a WhatsApp thread played the system. Nine of the eleven did not do size-set scanning themselves; a sourcing agent or the buyer's QC did. It was filed: eleven people, no screens, and in the March review Beulah's objection prevailed that a sample that size could not redirect a roadmap.

Through April and May the team built in the kit: thirty-four design-days, forty-one pixel-complete screens, walked through at Pareen's Dubai offices on 21–22 May alongside the Buyer Portal acceptance set, the travel being already paid for. In June they became an interactive prototype, and between 1 and 10 July ninety-six sellers were taken through it in Paravai's Tiruppur office, on a company handset, over office Wi-Fi, a facilitator beside them. In Beulah's deck, Exhibit 2 read as a clean result.

The build reached the field as an instrumented beta on Monday 10 August and ran to Monday 31 August; Exhibit 3 is what it showed. Sellers were not on Wi-Fi: the GST lookup, pre-filled in the prototype, took nine to forty seconds on a shared 4G connection under corrugated roofing. Field staff reported the scanner, simulated in the prototype by a tap-to-advance hotspot, failing under fabric-shed lighting; fifty-eight of the ninety-one sellers who reached that step never got past it. And Bhavadharini Idupulapati's log analysis from Toronto, circulated on Friday 18 September, found that on the old app in July 2026, 2,972 of the 4,186 SKUs published (71.0 per cent) came from accounts her heuristic flagged as agent logins — what the eleven sellers had said in March.

5. The people

Bavithra Irudayaraj, VP Product, Coimbatore. Position: the July study answered a question nobody asked. Incentive: she owns the activation number, and signed off the July research design. Not saying: she agreed with Beulah's objection to the March note.

Bhoopathi Illindala, co-founder and CEO, Coimbatore. Position: ship before Deepavali; a January Series B needs a seller-side curve. Incentive: he conceded Schedule 4 himself. Not saying: Punnai Capital has twice asked whether seller revenue is a business or a distribution cost.

Beulah Irlapati, Head of Design, Berlin. Position: the thirty remaining design-days belong in mobile kit variants, since every mockup is overpriced until they exist. Incentive: her team is measured on acceptance workshops. Not saying: she has conceded privately that the July prototype was unfit for the barcode question, and it was her deck that put 89.4 per cent before the board.

Bharadwaj Iragavarapu, VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Position: nothing is left to design; instrument the real app and let the field speak. Incentive: 118 build-days are sunk. Not saying: the offline queue he promised shipped with a known defect.

Bagavathi Ilamparuthi, principal engineer, Pune. Position: the scanner problem is optics and lighting, not interface. Incentive: he proposed an external vision SDK in June and was refused. Not saying: Porul Vision Systems, his preferred vendor, has offered a pilot at an undisclosed price.

Bhavadharini Idupulapati, senior data scientist, Toronto. Position: decide who the user is before choosing a fidelity. Incentive: she regards hers as the only work here that has reframed anything. Not saying: her agent flag is a heuristic over device and session patterns, never validated against a real seller, and she has twice declined to put an error bar on it.

Baladitya Irungovel, Head of Enterprise Sales, New Jersey. Position: a pixel-complete prototype of the compliance-dossier module must exist by Thursday 29 October for Pomona Sourcing. Incentive: a ₹9.60 crore three-year term sheet, ₹3.20 crore a year. Not saying: he has already shown Pomona three screens from the May kit set.

Basavaraj Ilavarasan, Director of Customer Success, Singapore. Position: do not release a flow that can leave SKUs in draft; his team absorbs every incomplete listing as a four-a.m. ticket. Incentive: ticket volume per account is his metric. Not saying: his team has done the Pareen size-set data by hand since June.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 puts 55 of the 75 design-days (73.3 per cent) into the two high-fidelity artefacts and 13 of the 75 (17.3 per cent) into the two low-fidelity ones. Exhibit 4's two panels describe the same team. Exhibit 3 records no reason for any drop.

7. Voices

“Mean step completion 89.4 per cent. The flow is understood. The remaining risk is engineering.”

Beulah Irlapati, slide 4, July research summary, 13 July

“Beulah, 89.4 is the average of six numbers. Forty-seven people out of ninety-six got to the end. Both are in your own table on slide 9.”

Bhavadharini Idupulapati, reply-all, 14 July, 11.04 p.m. Toronto

“We did not test the scanner. We tested a photograph of a label with a hotspot on it. Please stop quoting 68.4 at me as if a camera was involved.”

Bagavathi Ilamparuthi, #seller-desk channel, 2 September

“Madam, scanning-ellam agent paathukkuvaanga. I only tell him the lot number. Why should I take photo of barcode in my own godown?”

Seller 7, Palladam, Wizard-of-Oz transcript, 5 March

“I am not asking for perfect. I am asking for a number I can put on a slide in January. Thirty days of design is thirty days. Spend them on something a customer sees.”

Bhoopathi Illindala to Bavithra Irudayaraj, Friday 16 October

8. The options, as Bavithra sees them tonight

One: release to all 9,400 units before Deepavali, the size-set step made skippable. Bhoopathi gets his curve. But ONDC's apparel attributes mean a skipped size-set leaves the SKU in draft, so what grows is installs, not catalogue, and Basavaraj's team becomes the scanner.

Two: hold the release and spend the thirty design-days on low-fidelity field work. Paper and the Wizard-of-Oz, in sheds, with agents present. It costs almost nothing, and in March it changed the question rather than the answer. It also slips release into late November and concedes the June–July work was mis-specified.

Three: split the base. Release to a 1,200-unit Tiruppur cohort, keep the other 8,200 on the old app, instrument heavily. Bharadwaj's preference. It answers nothing Exhibit 3 has not, unless the instrumentation records who is holding the phone, which nobody has scoped.

Four: buy the problem. Licence Porul Vision Systems' scanning SDK at ₹1.10 crore a year, ₹9.17 lakh a month. Bagavathi's route: it treats the barcode step as a technical defect, and spends ₹1.10 crore to avoid asking whether the step belongs in the seller's hands.

Five: build mobile variants of the kit. Beulah's route. It lowers the price of every future mockup and produces no learning in a quarter that will consume mockups anyway.

All five answer the question how much fidelity, and when. Bavithra has written on her printout, and shown nobody, a sixth line: that the March eleven and Bhavadharini's 71.0 per cent point at a different question — whether Seller Desk is a product for sellers or an instrument operated by agents on their behalf — and that the artefact answering it is a service run by hand in two towns, not a screen. She has no budget line for a thing with no screens in it, and the sixth line rests on eleven interviews and an unvalidated heuristic.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Capacity between Monday 19 October and Friday 6 November is 15 working days across four designers, or 60 design-days. Beulah has committed 22 to the Buyer Portal Release 12 acceptance set and 8 to the Pomona demo, leaving 30. The Dubai workshop is Tuesday 20 October, Pomona's demo Thursday 29 October, and the cluster closes for Deepavali on Sunday 8 November.

Money is not binding: Exhibit 5's ₹38.60 crore of cash and 19.8 months of runway leave room for the SDK, the field work or both. Contract is. Pareen's 9 October email asserts that seller catalogue screens fall inside Schedule 4 — which, if conceded, makes every seller-side release dependent on a pixel-complete prototype and a Dubai signature. Paravai's counsel in Chennai is split. Regulation binds differently: the DPDP consent notice must be in the seller's chosen language and the kit has no mobile Tamil component, so a compliant consent screen costs design-days out of the same thirty. And Bhoopathi has told the board that Seller Desk 2.0 ships in FY27.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. For each artefact in Exhibit 1, name the question it could have answered and the question Paravai asked it. Where do the two diverge most expensively?
  2. Exhibit 2 reports 89.4 and 49.0 from one table. What belongs on slide 4, and what denominator belongs beside it?
  3. Exhibit 2's step 4 and Exhibit 3's barcode step are both completion rates among those who reached the step: 54 of the 79 who reached it (68.4 per cent) and 33 of the 91 who reached it (36.3 per cent). What can and cannot be inferred from the gap?
  4. Panel A and Panel B of Exhibit 4 are both correct. Which would you have shown the board, and what does the answer imply about who gets to define discovery?
  5. Schedule 4 was conceded to win Paravai's anchor account. Was it a mistake? If Paravai must live with it, what decision rule about fidelity belongs in the next contract it signs, and who enforces it?
  6. It is nine o'clock on Monday 19 October. What does Bavithra do with the thirty design-days, what does she stop doing, and what does she tell the board about the 71.0 per cent, given that she agreed in March with the objection that buried it?

At half past midnight Bavithra tapped through the onboarding once more in the dark kitchen, and every field still filled itself in. Somewhere in Palladam a man who was not the seller would open a shed at six; at six in the evening she would be on a plane to a room where another set of pixel-complete screens would be approved by people who had never been there. She had the cash and the thirty days. She did not have a question she trusted.

Paravai Technologies, Pareen Retail Group, Pulari Commerce Cloud, Pomona Sourcing, Porul Vision Systems, Punnai Capital and all individuals here are fictitious; named brands and institutions are market context only.
exp20v2-sol.wireframe:
Wireframes, mockups, prototypes

The lowest-fidelity artefact that answers the question you have today.

1. The fourteen-week proposal

On Monday, 8 June 2026, Chirag Dalvi, the product manager responsible for Foyer, opened the quarterly planning document at Fanoos Home Interiors in Pune with one line already circled in red. Foyer is the company's planning tool: a homeowner enters a room, picks a layout for a modular kitchen or wardrobe, receives a price estimate and, if interested, requests a visit from a human designer. Colm Doyle, who ran the contract engineering team in Dublin that built most of Foyer, had proposed the largest item in the quarter: a three-dimensional room configurator, fourteen weeks of work at ₹96 lakh, which would let a customer drag cabinets around a rendering of her own room. Chandana Dabholkar, the founder, liked it because rivals such as Livspace and HomeLane already showed three-dimensional renders.

Dalvi had the funnel numbers open beside it. In an average month Foyer recorded 12,000 planner starts. Of these, 9,600 chose a layout (80 per cent of starts), 4,800 reached the price estimate (50 per cent of those who chose a layout), and 1,440 requested a designer visit (30 per cent of those who saw a price). The largest single leak by volume lay between choosing a layout and seeing a price: 4,800 people. The proposal rested on a belief that those people left because they could not picture the result in their own homes. Nobody had asked them.

What was at stake is easy to state. If the belief was right, the configurator would pay for itself in about three months of operation. If it was wrong, Fanoos would spend ₹96 lakh and fourteen weeks of its only mobile team building an excellent answer to a question its customers were not asking, and the actual cause of the leak would sit untouched until the following year. Dalvi's design lead, Charulata Deodhar, offered a different proposition: before anyone wrote code, spend eleven working days and under ₹2 lakh to find out which question was the real one. This page follows that proposition.

Foyer's monthly funnel as Dalvi saw it. Each rate uses the previous row as its base.
Funnel stepPeopleShare of previous step
Started the planner12,000n/a
Chose a layout9,60080%
Saw a price estimate4,80050%
Requested a designer visit1,44030%

2. The idea

Three words are routinely used as if they were interchangeable, and the confusion is the root of most wasted effort. A wireframe is a drawing of a screen in which only structure is decided: what appears, in what order, with what emphasis, usually in grey boxes and placeholder text. A mockup is a static picture of a screen with the visual design applied: colour, typography, real images, real wording. A prototype is any artefact a person can interact with, so that you can watch what they do rather than hear what they say. A prototype can be a stack of paper sketches that a colleague swaps by hand, a set of linked wireframes on a laptop, or working code on a real phone. The first two words describe what is drawn; the third describes whether it responds.

Underneath all three sits a single property called fidelity: how closely the artefact resembles the finished product. High fidelity is not one thing, as section 5 will show, but the practical rule is that each step up in fidelity costs several times more than the one below. The problem the practice was invented to solve is old. Software teams learned in the 1980s and 1990s that discovering a wrong screen after coding it cost many multiples of discovering it on paper. Marc Rettig's 1994 article "Prototyping for Tiny Fingers" made the argument for deliberately rough prototypes to the software profession, Carolyn Snyder's 2003 book on paper prototyping turned it into a method, and Bill Buxton's 2007 book on sketching argued that sketches are cheap precisely so that they can be wrong.

Deodhar condensed this into the sentence Dalvi repeated in the planning meeting: build the cheapest thing that can be wrong in the way you are worried about. The sentence is useful because it is operational. It does not say that rough is good or that polish is bad. It says that every artefact is a test of a specific worry, and that you should stop climbing the cost ladder the moment the artefact is capable of failing the test.

3. How it actually works

Deodhar's process had eight steps, three of which practitioners usually leave implicit. The first is to write the worry as a question about behaviour, not about taste. "Do customers like the layout screen?" cannot fail. "Of eight people who abandoned Foyer after choosing a layout, how many name the inability to see their own room as their first reason for stopping?" can. The second step, one of the implicit ones, is to write the decision rule before testing: which result leads to which action. Dalvi and Deodhar agreed that if five or more of eight participants, coded by their first point of stalling, named the missing view of their own room, they would recommend the configurator. Fewer than five and it would be set aside. Writing the threshold in advance matters because afterwards almost any result can be narrated as support.

Third, pick the lowest rung that can fail the question. The question concerned where people stop and why, which depends on the order and content of screens, not on shading or animation, so paper was enough. Fourth, build only the path being tested: six sketched screens from layout choice to price. Fifth, recruit from the population that has the problem: Deodhar drew eight people from the 4,800 monthly abandoners and paid each a ₹1,500 voucher (₹12,000 in all), with the other ₹6,000 of the ₹18,000 budget going to printing, a room and a freelance sketcher. Sixth, give tasks rather than ask for opinions: "get a price for your kitchen", while Deodhar sat as the "computer", swapping paper screens as the participant tapped. Seventh, tally each participant's first stall point against the rule. Eighth, climb a rung, change the design, or stop, and record why.

4. A worked example, line by line

Start with what the configurator was worth if the belief were true. Dalvi's proposal assumed that the configurator would lift visit requests as a share of planner starts from 12 per cent to 15 per cent (equivalently, holding 4,800 price-viewers fixed, from 30 to 37.5 per cent of those who see a price). At 12,000 starts a month, 12 per cent is 1,440 requests and 15 per cent is 1,800, a gain of 360. Foyer's finance partner supplied two figures: 22 per cent of visits become orders, and each order contributes ₹38,000 after the cost of the visit. Applying the 22 per cent to each request, expected contribution per request is 0.22 × ₹38,000 = ₹8,360. This is a simplifying assumption: a request that never becomes a visit lowers the true figure, and with it the gain and the delay cost below. The monthly gain is 360 × ₹8,360 = ₹30,09,600, or about ₹30.1 lakh. On a ₹96 lakh build that pays back in 96 ÷ 30.1 = 3.2 months of operation if the belief is true, which starts only after the 14-week build (about 3.2 months), so roughly 6.4 months from the start of work.

Now price the alternative. The paper round costs ₹18,000 and three working days; a clickable wireframe round to test whatever the paper round suggests costs ₹1.4 lakh and eight working days. Together: ₹1.58 lakh and eleven working days, which is about half of a 22-working-day month. Compare that with the cost of being wrong. We need two assumptions, and both are assumptions, not data: the team's honest chance that the belief is wrong, which Dalvi set at 40 per cent after asking three colleagues, and the share of wrong beliefs the rough tests would actually catch, which we set at one half, since small samples miss things.

Net value of testing first, in ₹ lakh, relative to building at once. Formulas in the last column. Test cost 1.58; build cost 96; monthly gain if the belief is true 30.1; delay of half a month costs 15.05 when the belief is true and nothing when it is false.
LineFirst pass: P(wrong) = 40%Second pass: P(wrong) = 5%How computed
Build cost avoided19.202.40P × 0.5 × 96
Test cost1.581.580.18 + 1.40
Expected delay cost9.0314.30(1 − P) × 15.05
Net value of testing first+8.59−13.48avoided − test − delay

On the first pass the figures favour testing: 19.20 − 1.58 − 9.03 = +8.59 lakh. Now change one input, the team's confidence. If Dalvi had been 95 per cent sure, so that P(wrong) is 5 per cent, the avoided cost shrinks to 0.05 × 0.5 × 96 = 2.40, while the expected delay grows to 0.95 × 15.05 = 14.30. The net becomes 2.40 − 1.58 − 14.30 = −13.48 lakh, and the right answer reverses: build. Setting the net to zero, 48P = 1.58 + 15.05(1 − P), gives a break-even P of about 26 per cent. If you believe your idea is wrong more than about a quarter of the time, test first; below that, the delay costs more than the insurance. Testing does not always win; the answer depends on stated inputs.

The paper round ran on 16 and 17 June. Deodhar coded each participant's first stall point: the first screen at which they stopped, hesitated for ten seconds or asked a question.

First stall point, eight participants, paper round. The categories are mutually exclusive, so the counts sum to the number of participants.
First stall pointParticipants
Asked to see the result in their own room2
Could not enter room dimensions (did not know them)5
Wanted to speak to a person before going further1
Total8

Two of eight asked for their own room; the rule required five. Five of eight stalled earlier, at a screen that demanded exact dimensions in feet and inches, which most had never measured. The configurator would not have reached these people, because it also needs the dimensions before it can draw the room. Eight people give direction, not a rate: the finding is not that 62.5 per cent of all abandoners stall on dimensions, only that a leading cause existed that nobody had named.

5. Five nuances a learner must become aware of

Fidelity is three dials, not one

Visual fidelity (how finished it looks), interaction fidelity (how it responds) and content fidelity (whether the words and data are real) move independently. Foyer's paper round had almost no visual fidelity and zero interaction fidelity, yet used the real wording of the dimension screen, and that content fidelity was what exposed the problem. A beautiful mockup with placeholder text such as "Lorem ipsum, your price here" would have hidden it.

Polish changes what people tell you

A finished-looking screen invites comments on colour, icon choice and spacing, because those are the things visibly open to comment. A rough sketch invites comments on structure and flow, which is usually the question.

A prototype is not a minimum viable product

A prototype is built to be thrown away and to answer a question; a minimum viable product, in the sense the best programmes teach, is a learning vehicle with a clear decision rule, delivered to real users in real use. The prototype asks "should we build this?"; the product asks "do people keep using it?".

What low fidelity cannot tell you

Paper cannot tell you whether a 3D render will load in under three seconds on a ₹9,000 Android phone, whether a gesture feels natural, or how a screen behaves with real, messy data such as a room with a slanted wall. Where the worry is performance, feel or data realism, the lowest fidelity that answers the question is a high one.

Watch behaviour, not opinion, and ask who was in the room

"Would you use this?" is answered kindly and unreliably; a task such as "get a price", followed by silence, produces evidence. A facilitator who says "you can tap here" has answered the question for the participant, and a result from the wrong participants answers a different question altogether.

6. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products such as Foyer, user and buyer are the same person and recruiting is easy, so rough rounds are cheap; the danger is testing on friends. In B2B products, the person who uses the software is often not the person who buys it, participants are scarce, and a wireframe must be walked through with several roles. Fidelity decisions are also governed by workflow realism: an accountant will not tolerate a prototype whose numbers do not reconcile. In marketplaces, there are two sides, and a prototype has to be tested on each; a wireframe that delights sellers may frighten buyers, and the artefact must show what each side sees of the other.

Company stage matters too. An early-stage company has few engineers, so even a modest build is expensive relative to its runway, and paper is nearly always correct. A large company has a different pressure: governance. Prototypes get reviewed by legal, brand and platform teams, who pull the work upward in fidelity before the question has been answered. The remedy is to label the artefact "a test of one question" and keep review forums apart from learning sessions.

7. Common mistakes

Polishing before the question exists. From outside, you see a team that has a gorgeous mockup and a long list of unanswered doubts about it. The underlying misunderstanding is that fidelity signals seriousness. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask the team to complete the sentence "this artefact will show us whether ___", and to notice if the blank is empty.

Testing taste instead of behaviour. The symptom is a research summary that reads "users liked it" and a launch that disappoints. The misunderstanding is treating approval as evidence of intention. The diagnostic is to read the session script: if every question begins with "what do you think", there was no task.

No decision rule. The symptom is a debrief that ends with "interesting; let's do another round". The misunderstanding is that testing produces decisions on its own. The diagnostic takes ten seconds: find the document that states what result would have changed the plan, dated before the session.

8. What good looks like

The same Monday, handled well, looks much as it did. The product manager writes the question in behavioural terms, sets a rule such as five of eight before any session, prices two rounds at ₹1.58 lakh and eleven working days, and tests only on people who have the problem. The script uses real wording and hands over tasks. The result is tallied against the rule written beforehand, the debrief names what the evidence cannot say (eight people are a direction, not a rate), and it ends in a decision with a date.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

On 18 June Dalvi told the planning meeting that the configurator would not be built in the quarter. The tally was 2 against a threshold of 5, and the leading stall was a dimensions field the configurator would have made no easier. Deodhar built a clickable wireframe offering size bands in place of exact dimensions (for instance, "a standard L-shaped kitchen in a two-bedroom flat"), to be tested in the second round at ₹1.4 lakh and eight working days. The configurator was not killed; it moved to a list of ideas to revisit if size-band users later said they could not picture the result. Dalvi's reasoning was that the paper round had cost ₹18,000, about 0.19 per cent of the build, and that both planned rounds together (₹1.58 lakh) would come to about 1.6 per cent of ₹96 lakh. It had moved the team from a plausible guess to an observed leading cause among first stalls, though the test is silent on whether the five who stalled at dimensions would later have wanted a view of their own room.

Three topics follow naturally. Storyboarding, the predecessor, argues that screens come after the story; here, the story was "a person who does not know her room's dimensions wants a price". Usability testing and prototype testing teach how to run the sessions Deodhar ran: how many people, how to code a stall, how not to lead. AI-generated prototypes change the cost of rungs 2 and 3, and the central skill, picking the rung that can fail your question, becomes more valuable rather than less when climbing is nearly free.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of the last feature your organisation built: what was the cheapest artefact that could have shown it to be wrong, and why was it not made? Second, in your own product, which question are you currently answering with a high-fidelity artefact that a sketch could answer, and which one are you answering with a sketch that, honestly, only code can?
case40v1-sol.storyboard:
Ilakku Technologies (A)

Twelve Panels in Besant Nagar

A product leader in Chennai has a redesigned claim flow, a demonstration that charmed two American insurers, and four panels of a story nobody has ever watched.

1. The night before

It was a little after eleven on Thursday, 22 October 2026, and the north-east monsoon had settled over Besant Nagar with the steadiness of a thing that intends to stay. Revathy Balasubramanian, Vice-President of Product at Ilakku Technologies, had cleared her dining table. On the left, her laptop, open on the Project Inai prototype: four screens, a progress ribbon, a photograph tray that slid up like a drawer. On the right, the board pack she owed Raghuram Bhaskaran by Friday noon. Between them, taped to the cupboard door, twelve hand-drawn panels of a delivery rider's night after a collision at the Ambattur signal.

Rithika Bhimavarapu had drawn them in Berlin in May, and four were blank but for a time and a question mark. Panels five to eight: nine-forty in the evening to half past midnight. Nobody at Ilakku knew what happened in those three hours, and for five months nobody had thought it mattered, because the product did not appear in them.

On Monday 26 October, Revathy had to tell a board that had already been told the new flow was in field trial what Ilakku would do with it. She had ₹192.30 lakh spent on Inai, a ninety-day change-control clock, a Dubai renewal whose notice window opens on 1 December, two American proposals due on 13 November, and a quarter of telemetry that had arrived on 5 October and refused to agree with the usability test she had designed herself in July.

2. The company, and the agreement that still binds it

Ilakku Technologies Private Limited was founded in Guindy in 2019 by Raghuram Bhaskaran, a former general-insurance operations manager, and two engineers from his motor-claims team. The idea was narrow and good: claims on commercial two-wheelers were small and numerous but handled as though they were large and rare. A rider earning ₹980 a day could lose six days of work — ₹5,880 — waiting for a surveyor. Ilakku would put intimation, photographs and survey scheduling into one Android app and sell it as a cost line, not a feature.

In February 2024 that ambition met its most consequential decision (Figure 1). Indravan General Insurance, a mid-sized private insurer with a fast-growing two-wheeler book, offered to co-develop. It put in ₹6.00 crore, took exclusivity in the Indian commercial two-wheeler line until 31 March 2027, and — the clause nobody argued about — reserved written approval over any change to a screen that captures claim-intimation data, with a review window of up to ninety days. Ilakku's engineers read it as a formality. It was not: a change filed on Monday 26 October 2026 could not be live before 24 January 2027, after Deepavali on 8 November and after Pongal, the two weeks when delivery volumes, and collisions, peak.

The second constraint was quieter and self-inflicted. The app that shipped in September 2024 was offline-first, right for patchy networks, and single-login — one claim, one device, one identity. Ramprasad Bandaru, who designed that store in Pune, had said for a year that it could not hold two actors on one claim without a re-architecture he priced at fourteen engineer-months.

3. The industry

India's quick-commerce boom had put an enormous, young, informal two-wheeler fleet on the road. Zomato, Swiggy, Zepto, Blinkit, Flipkart and Amazon India moved parcels through fleet partners who owned the rider relationship and — critically for Ilakku — employed the supervisors who knew when a bike went down. Hero, Honda, TVS and Bajaj supplied most of the machines.

Regulation shaped the edges. IRDAI's pressure on settlement turnaround gave Indravan a reason to care about survey scheduling. The Motor Vehicles Act meant any third-party or injury claim needed a police report, which is a queue and not a screen. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 made the photograph tray a liability too: an accident photograph holds number plates and faces, and Ilakku's consent notice was written for the rider, not the people in the frame.

Ilakku's foreign exposure ran two ways. Iltizaam Fleet Services LLC, a Dubai last-mile operator, had piloted since November 2025 — company bikes, hub shifts, an on-site workshop, and an insurer that would not accept an intimation without a police report number. And Rakesh Boddupalli in New Jersey had found that American fleet insurers would take a meeting on the Inai demonstration alone.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Project Inai began in April 2026 after Indravan's claims head complained that photographs were being rejected and surveys rescheduled. The diagnosis inside Ilakku was unanimous: the screens were bad. Rithika disagreed with the diagnosis without disagreeing with the work. She asked for six weeks to draw the rider's night as panels before anyone drew a screen: Ilakku's 2023 journey map showed stages rather than moments, and nobody could say what a rider does at ten at night with a bent fork and a parcel. The compromise was that both would happen at once — Rithika would draw, Bengaluru would build.

She drew from six rider conversations — two in Chennai, four on video — and submitted twelve panels on 29 May 2026 (Exhibit 5). Five to eight she left blank, with the times written in and nothing else: her two Chennai riders had told her flatly contradictory things about that stretch, and she would not average two people.

Meanwhile the prototype became beautiful. In June, Raghuram showed it to a board member. In July, Revathy ran a usability test in Guindy (Exhibit 3): twenty riders, eighteen completing the four-step intimation unaided, a median of two minutes forty-one seconds. In August, Rakesh opened two American conversations on the strength of the same screens, and Rajalakshmi Balasundaram reported that Ravikiran Bhogaraju in Dubai had asked why a rider would ever be standing next to a garage.

Then on 5 October, Roopa Bommireddy pulled the quarter's telemetry from the live 2024 app — not the prototype — for 1 July to 30 September 2026 (Exhibits 2 and 4). Four beliefs came apart. Riders were not the people filing: 428 of 1,284 app intimations began on a rider's own login — 33.3 per cent. The photograph step was not a tray problem: 509 of 821 abandoned sessions ended on that screen — 62.0 per cent. The intimation was not happening at the roadside: the median gap between logged incident and first app action was six hours fifty minutes. And the ninety-per-cent figure quoted since July came from charged handsets on office Wi-Fi between eleven and four, with eight photographs already in the gallery. Nobody had any observation of what the rider does in panels five to eight — the hours in which, read with any imagination, the claim is decided.

5. The people

Revathy Balasubramanian, 38 — VP Product, Chennai
Position: nobody can choose until somebody watches the three unwatched hours. Incentive: Inai shipping is her promotion case and she owns the Indravan renewal. Not saying: the board pack she is drafting still carries the ninety-per-cent line.
Raghuram Bhaskaran, 51 — co-founder and CEO, Chennai
Position: ship the Inai screens, file the change request Monday, keep the American story alive. Incentive: a Series B conversation is open. Not saying: he told a board member in June the prototype was in field trial, and the pack has repeated it twice.
Rithika Bhimavarapu, 34 — Principal Designer, Berlin
Position: draw the whole night, blank panels included, then decide what to build. Incentive: her panels are the most-cited artefact in the company and she wants a design function. Not saying: her two Chennai interviews contradicted each other, and she was never funded to travel.
Ramprasad Bandaru, 44 — Director of Engineering, Pune
Position: drawings do not change a data model; the fourteen-engineer-month re-architecture is the only work that makes a supervisor-first flow possible. Incentive: he has lost two engineers this year. Not saying: the single-login store is his own 2024 design.
Roopa Bommireddy, 36 — Staff Data Scientist, Toronto
Position: the field and the test measured different things, and panels five to eight were never measured. Incentive: she is judged on the metrics layer. She says openly that only 706 of the 6,420 supervisor logs — 11.0 per cent — were audited by hand, and that 38 of 706 were misclassified, 5.4 per cent. Not saying: she twice asked for the quarter's rate to be left out of the board pack.
Rajalakshmi Balasundaram, 41 — Customer Success, Singapore (APAC and Gulf)
Position: Dubai needs a different sequence; one product promised to both markets is how Ilakku loses the renewal. Incentive: her pay is weighted to gross retention. Not saying: she has shown Iltizaam a mock of a hub flow that exists in no backlog.
Rakesh Boddupalli, 47 — Head of Sales, North America, New Jersey
Position: ship what was demonstrated. Incentive: his commission accelerates above ₹400 lakh of new annual contract value. Not saying: both prospects asked chiefly about a workers'-compensation journey the product does not touch.
Ravikiran Bhogaraju, 45 — Head of Operations, Iltizaam Fleet Services, Dubai
Position: he wants a police-report field and a hub-workshop sequence; the garage panel means nothing to him. Incentive: his measure is downtime hours. Not saying: his supervisors have been intimating on paper since August.

6. Exhibits

Neither American prospect has seen the product on a live claim, and the Gulf item rides on the Iltizaam renewal at risk above.

7. Voices

"Ninety per cent of riders can complete the flow unaided. That is the sentence for the board."

Raghuram Bhaskaran, product review, 8 October 2026

"Ninety per cent of the twenty who turned up. We recruited twenty-four. Every one held a charged phone in an air-conditioned room with the photographs already in the gallery. I wrote that card; it is my fault it reads like a finding."

Revathy Balasubramanian, replying in the same meeting

"We are losing half the claims — 3,210 of 6,420, look at it."

Raghuram, internal chat, 6 October

"That denominator is punctures and breakdowns. Against insurable events it is 3,210 of 3,860 intimated, 83.2 per cent — and the classifier that produced the 3,860 was audited on 706 logs with thirty-eight errors in them. We do not know that rate to better than a few hundred claims."

Roopa Bommireddy, replying from Toronto

"The field data proves the new tray works — ninety-five per cent completed that step."

Ramprasad Bandaru, engineering stand-up, 12 October

"The 95 per cent is the prototype in a room; the 62 per cent is the live app in the rain. Not the same measure over the same split: one is step completion under supervision, the other a share of abandonments."

Roopa, same thread

"The American pipeline is 540 against the 972 we have recognised — more than half the company, unsigned."

Rakesh Boddupalli, forecast call, 9 October

"Your 540 is twelve months and the 972 is six. Against the twelve-month contracted base it is 540 of 1,944 — 27.8 per cent. Your 540 of 972 is 55.6 per cent, and it is the wrong comparison."

Roopa, on the same call

"One rider told me he slept at the tea shop; the other said his supervisor sent a tempo. Both are true and they are different products. Somebody has to sit there at eleven at night."

Rithika Bhimavarapu, email to Revathy, 19 October

8. The options, as Revathy currently frames them

A. Ship Inai. File the change request Monday, accept 24 January 2027, keep the board narrative intact. The cost is that what ships was validated under conditions Exhibit 4 says do not occur: 362 of 1,284 submitted intimations — 28.2 per cent — began with the battery below a fifth of charge.

B. Pause and go and look. Six weeks of observation in Chennai, Coimbatore and Madurai between ten at night and two in the morning, to fill panels five to eight, then redraw. The cost is the 13 November proposals, probably the Deepavali quarter, and Raghuram unsaying something to the board.

C. Build for the supervisor. Fund Ramprasad's fourteen engineer-months at a blended ₹2.40 lakh per engineer-month (Bengaluru ₹2.70 lakh, Pune ₹2.10 lakh, in equal measure), which is ₹33.60 lakh, so one claim can hold a rider, a supervisor and a garage. The telemetry supports it: 856 of 1,284 app intimations already begin on a supervisor's login. But that is evidence of who files, not that filing is where the value sits.

D. Split the product. An India sequence and a Gulf sequence, as Rajalakshmi wants. Indravan's exclusivity is India-only, so the Gulf is clear; the cost is two surfaces on one team that has lost two people this year.

All four assume the deliverable is a screen flow belonging to Ilakku. None asks whether the rider should have an app at all, whether the intimation belongs in the WhatsApp thread the supervisor already lives in, whether the ₹4,000 the garage wants at half past nine is the product, or whether a call-centre-and-field-agent operation would serve Indravan better. The framing also treats the four as exclusive, when the ninety-day clock and six weeks of observation could run at once. And it treats Exhibit 5 as a finding: three of twelve panels hold a product, 25.0 per cent — damning until Roopa points out it is 3 of the 8 drawn panels — 37.5 per cent — and that four blanks are not a gap but an absence of data.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets on Monday 26 October 2026; papers are due Friday noon. Cash at 30 September 2026 was ₹9.40 crore against a net burn of ₹1.15 crore a month, which is 8.2 months — into the first week of June 2027. Project Inai has consumed ₹192.30 lakh: 54 engineer-months at ₹2.40 lakh, which is ₹129.60 lakh, plus Rithika's six months at ₹10.45 lakh a month — €11,000 at ₹95 to the euro — which is ₹62.70 lakh. Her month costs 4.35 times an Indian engineer's, a ratio nobody on the board has asked about and everyone in Pune has noticed.

Indravan's ninety-day window is not negotiable before exclusivity lapses on 31 March 2027. Iltizaam's renewal notice window opens on Tuesday 1 December 2026, and Ravikiran has asked for a police-report field that does not exist. The American proposals are due Friday 13 November. The DPDP exposure on third-party faces has no owner. Against contracted revenue of ₹1,944 lakh for the year (Exhibit 7), the ₹180 fee covers ₹304 of cost (Exhibit 6), so every accepted app intimation loses ₹124 — ₹1.59 lakh across last quarter's 1,284 if all were accepted, and ₹3.98 lakh had all 3,210 come through the app.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What did the July test in Exhibit 3 measure, and what did it not? Write the sentence Ilakku may honestly say about it.
  2. Do Exhibits 3 and 4 contradict each other on the photograph step? State each figure's measure, base and population first.
  3. Are Rithika's four blank panels Ilakku's largest risk or an invitation to invent? How would you decide, and what would you spend?
  4. Exhibit 5 puts the product in three panels. What would make three the right number, and what would make it a diagnosis?
  5. Unit economics on an app intimation are negative and immaterial; contract revenue is material. Which should govern Monday, and what does that imply about what the product is for?
  6. It is Monday morning, 26 October. What do you do, in what order, with whose time and money — and what do you say to a board twice told the flow is in field trial?

At half past midnight Revathy took panel seven off the cupboard door and held it under the lamp. A time, a question mark, and Rithika's handwriting in the corner: who pays for the bike tonight? On the laptop the prototype waited at step one, ribbon empty, tray tucked out of sight. Outside, a rider went past the gate in the rain with a bag on his back, and Revathy did not know whether he was on his way to a drop or on his way home, and that difference was the whole case.
case20v1-sol.storyboard:
Haritha Krishi: Forty-Two Screens Before One Story

A decision case on storyboarding, Hyderabad, October 2026

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 26 October 2026, Pavan Arunachalam, head of product at Haritha Krishi, stood at the whiteboard in the company's Madhapur office in Hyderabad and counted what was on it. There were forty-two screens, printed from Figma and taped up in rows, a complete flow for a new feature called Harvest-Pay, which would let a farmer buy seed and fertiliser on credit and repay it automatically when the crop was sold. Beside the printouts hung six sheets of A3 paper with stick figures on them, drawn on Thursday by a field team in a Guntur village.

Engineering in Pune held a six-week sprint slot starting Monday, 2 November. If Pavan did not confirm the scope by Friday, 30 October, the slot would pass to another team and the next opening was Monday, 16 November. He had five working days to decide whether to build the forty-two screens.

2. Company background

Haritha Krishi, founded in 2018 in Hyderabad, sells seed, fertiliser and crop-protection products to smallholder farmers in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, mainly growers of chilli, cotton and maize on two to five acres. Orders reach the company through 420 field agents, called Krishi Mitras, who sit with the farmer, take the order on a phone app and arrange delivery from a district warehouse. In the year to March 2026 the company handled input sales worth ₹212 crore across 1,85,000 registered farmers.

DeHaat and BigHaat are better funded, and AgroStar sells through its own app. Farmers also buy from the village input dealer, who sells on credit and is repaid after harvest. Haritha has no lending licence, so Harvest-Pay would run through a partner NBFC that follows the RBI's digital lending guidelines. Repayment would be deducted from the sale proceeds when the farmer sold the crop to one of Haritha's buyers at the Khammam or Enumamula mandi, with the farmer's consent recorded under the DPDP Act. Padmaja Alluri, the co-founder and chief executive, wanted the pilot live early in the rabi season, accepting that even the earliest build would reach farmers in December.

3. The situation

The forty-two screens were the product of eleven weeks of work. Paula Ahrens, a designer in Berlin, had built them from a requirements document, and the work had cost ₹9 lakh so far. Berlin is four and a half hours behind Hyderabad in winter, so most of her exchange with Pavan had been comments on the files. Earlier in October twelve Krishi Mitras tried the click-through, and eleven completed it without help.

The paper test had been Priya Arigela's idea. Priya runs field operations from Guntur and distrusts any design a farmer has not seen. Without telling the design team, she had her agents draw the story as six panels and talk it through with thirty farmers, ten each in villages near Guntur, Khammam and Warangal. Exhibit 1 shows what happened. At the fourth panel, which showed the repayment being deducted when the crop was sold to Haritha's buyer, the group thinned sharply.

Exhibit 1: Paper storyboard test, 30 farmers, three districts
PanelSceneReachedUnderstoodWould go on
1Farmer needs seed before sowing303030
2Krishi Mitra offers credit on the app302927
3Credit limit and amount shown272625
4Repayment deducted when crop is sold to Haritha25229
5Crop sold at the mandi998
6Receipt and loan closed888

Source: field notes, Guntur team, 22 October 2026. "Reached" is the number who said yes at the previous panel. Farmers were chosen by Krishi Mitras from villages where they already work, so the sample is not random. "Would go on" is stated intention, not behaviour.

Eight of thirty farmers, about 27 per cent, would have gone from panel one to panel six. Of the twenty-five who reached panel four, sixteen stopped there. Priya's notes gave the reasons: eleven said they already sell to a local commission agent, an aadhatiya, who advances them cash each season and expects the crop in return; three wanted to pick the buyer and the price on the day; two feared how much would be deducted. Eleven, three and two make sixteen. The forty-two screens contained no screen for a farmer who sells elsewhere.

4. The people

Padmaja Alluri, chief executive, Hyderabad. She has promised the board 600 farmers on Harvest-Pay by March, which Pavan reads as 600 completing a full cycle, though the wording was loose. She sees every week of delay as lost season.

Prasanna Ayyadurai, engineering lead, Pune. His team is booked and the specification looks complete to him. He worries that a changed flow would cost the slot.

Paula Ahrens, designer, Berlin. She is proud of the flow and a little hurt that a paper sketch overtook it.

Priya Arigela, head of field operations, Guntur. She believes the aadhatiya, not the app, decides whether a farmer takes credit, and says a design that ignores him will fail however polished it is.

5. The options

Pavan saw three distinct courses. The first was to confirm the forty-two screens and build, treating the paper test as a small, unrepresentative sample. Engineering would cost ₹38 lakh and the pilot would be ready on Friday, 11 December. The second was to pause for two weeks, forfeiting the slot, redraw panels four and five so that they allowed a farmer to repay from a sale to anyone, then re-run the storyboard with thirty new farmers and amend the screens only where the story changed. The third was to leave the story alone and test the existing click-through with thirty farmers, which would use work already paid for but also forfeit the slot. Exhibit 2 sets out cost and timing.

Exhibit 2: The three options compared
