A. Build the 42 screens038Fri 11 DecOnly what the pilot shows, after the money is spent
B. Redraw and retest the story3.338 (ceiling)Fri 25 DecWhether a story that allows sale elsewhere survives farmers
C. Test the click-through2.138Fri 25 DecWhether farmers can operate the screens

Option B cost: ₹1.2 lakh redesign plus ₹2.1 lakh field work, total ₹3.3 lakh. Engineering for B is a ceiling because a revised flow may need fewer screens. Option A figures are Prasanna's estimate. B and C both start their field work on 2 November, finish before the next slot opens on Monday, 16 November, and build for six weeks from then, so each is two weeks behind A. Option C is field work alone: the same thirty farmers at ₹2.1 lakh, with no redesign.

Exhibit 3 draws the same test: each bar is the number of farmers, out of thirty, who would go on after that panel, at four pixels per farmer.

Exhibit 3: Where the story breaks. Source: Exhibit 1, "Would go on" column.

6. What Pavan knew, and what he did not

Exhibit 1 pointed to a specific gap. On Pavan's reading, Padmaja's target was 600 completed cycles. Haritha planned to invite 1,500 into the pilot, so 40 per cent of them had to complete. The paper test gave 8 of 30, about 27 per cent, which on 1,500 invitees would deliver 400, and a stated intention usually flatters what people later do. Had she meant only farmers who took credit, 25 of 30 would suffice and the bar is easily met, so he meant to ask which she meant, and whether a loan closing after the crop sale fits inside March. Against that, the sample came from villages near existing agents, and the thirty farmers had seen sketches rather than a working product.

Pavan could not tell from thirty farmers whether the redrawn story would lift the figure to 40 per cent, only that the old story lost sixteen of twenty-five at one panel. Priya argued that a ₹38 lakh pilot was an expensive way to learn what a ₹3.3 lakh sketch session might show first.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Read Exhibit 1 panel by panel. Where does the story fail, and why could eleven positive Krishi Mitra tests not show it?
  2. What assumption about the farmer's behaviour did the forty-two screens contain, and which panel exposes it?
  3. Using Exhibit 2, what does each option tell Pavan, and when? Which cost is recoverable if the idea is wrong?
  4. Padmaja needs 600 farmers by March. What decision rule should Pavan set, in advance, for continuing, changing or stopping?

8. A note for the learner

Storyboarding draws the experience as panels before screens, so that the sequence of a person's day can be judged before anyone argues about buttons. The forty-two screens answered the question "can an agent operate this?" and the panels answered "will a farmer take part?". A click-through cannot easily ask the second question because it contains no path for someone who sells elsewhere.

A well-reasoned answer separates the two questions, names what each option can and cannot answer, and sets the test result that would change the decision before the test is run. One defensible path is Option B. It costs ₹3.3 lakh against ₹38 lakh of engineering, delays the pilot by two weeks, and aims at the panel where sixteen farmers left. Set the rule in advance: build only if at least 12 of 30 new farmers, chosen by someone other than the agents, would go all the way through. That is 40 per cent, the rate needed for 600 of 1,500 on Pavan's reading. Treat it as necessary, not sufficient: intention flatters, and 12 of 30 is imprecise, so a pass licenses building and is not a forecast. If fewer do, the next conversation is about the aadhatiya, not about screens.

Option B has limits, and they should be stated. Thirty farmers cannot show a rate to within a few points, and stated intention is not behaviour. The retest cannot say whether Haritha can displace the commission agent's advance, only whether a story that does not require it is worth building. Option A is not foolish; it is the choice if the fortnight the slot loss costs is worth more than the learning. Option C is the weakest, because it loses the same fortnight as B and buys certainty about usability when usability was never the doubt. Paula's screens are not wasted under B; those behind panels one to three stay.
exp20v2-sol.storyboard:
Storyboarding

Drawing the experience as panels before drawing screens

1. A Monday in Pune

On Monday, 5 October 2026, Parnika Kasbekar, head of product at Nirvik Care, opened a spreadsheet that had been approved the previous Friday. Nirvik Care, a Pune start-up, sells a medication service to adult children abroad whose parents remain in India. A smart pillbox sits on the parent's breakfast table; a companion app tells the child whether the morning tablets were taken. The company had promised 40 pilot families by 30 November; the design sprint began on 19 October.

The spreadsheet allotted design lead Pranesh Kodgire 90 hours to produce 18 finished screens, at an internal rate of ₹1,800 an hour, or ₹1,62,000. Parnika hesitated for a specific reason: three of the four flows the team had built screens-first in the previous year had needed large rework after the first pilot. The three that failed had each looked coherent screen by screen, and each failed in a moment no single screen contained.

Her decision was whether to spend 12 further hours first, drawing the experience as eight small pictures and letting outsiders react before any screen existed. The cost was a delay and some engineering suspicion that this was theatre. The risk of skipping it was ₹72,000 of rework on a schedule with no slack.

2. The idea

A storyboard is a sequence of drawn panels that shows one person, in one place, using the product to get something done, with the product's role visible but not detailed. Each panel captures one moment; the sequence carries cause and effect. Its purpose is to let a team and its customers judge an experience as a story before anyone commits to interface design.

The technique comes from film animation. Story artists at the Walt Disney studio in the early 1930s, usually credited to Webb Smith, pinned scene sketches on a wall so the plot could be judged and cut before expensive animation began. Interaction designers borrowed the method later, and by the 1990s it was a standard way to show how a design fitted into a person's day. It solves an old problem: screens are drawn from the product's point of view, while value is experienced from the person's.

It sits between two neighbouring tools. A customer journey map (a table of the stages a customer passes through, with their actions and feelings at each) describes life as it is. A storyboard is that journey with the product inserted. It takes its input from the concept and elevator pitch, and hands its output to wireframes (rough, unstyled layouts of screens), mockups and prototypes. Parnika's sentence: "We are going to find out what is wrong with the story while it costs us twelve hours, not forty."

3. How it actually works

There are five steps, and practitioners usually leave the first and last implicit. The first is to choose the moment of value: the single job the customer wants done, stated as an outcome. For Nirvik Care it was "Prasad Kharkar in Toronto knows by breakfast in Pune that his mother Padma has taken her tablets, without calling her." Every panel must serve that sentence.

The second step is to name the character and the setting. Padma is 74, lives alone in Pune, and uses WhatsApp but dislikes unfamiliar apps. Prasad is 46 and checks his phone at 9:45 in the evening, Toronto time. A storyboard about "a user" collapses into generalities; one about Padma forces specific questions about her patience.

The third is to list the beats in order, from trigger to outcome. The fourth is to draw each beat as one panel with a one-sentence caption, including at least one beat in which the product does nothing, because that is where real life intrudes. The fifth is to put the strip in front of people who were not in the room, ask each of them what happens next at every panel, and record where they disagree with the story. Figure 1 shows the eight panels Parnika's team drew.

Panels 1 to 4 describe a morning that already works: the pillbox prompts, Padma takes the tablets, the lid sensor records it. Panel 5 adds the planned confirmation step, and from there the story deteriorates. The flaw was never in a button. It was the assumption that a 74-year-old would perform an extra task to prove a deed the hardware had already witnessed.

4. A worked example

On Friday, 9 October, researcher Oorjita Kamtekar showed the strip, one panel at a time, to 12 parents aged 65 or over in Pune, asking at each panel, "What would you do now?" At panel 5, 9 of the 12 said they would not open the phone to confirm. All 12 parents saw the strip, so 9 of 12 is 75 per cent. Three said they would comply, though two added that they would probably forget.

The money follows from where each flaw is found. Pranesh estimated that the confirmation step ran through screens 7 to 14 of the 18, which is 8 screens, each needing 5 hours of rework: 40 hours, or ₹72,000. If the flaw were found on the storyboard, the fix meant redrawing panels 5 to 8: four panels at 1.5 hours each, 6 hours, or ₹10,800. Drawing the original eight panels cost 12 hours, or ₹21,600.

Table 1. Cost of the two sequences when the confirmation flaw exists (rate ₹1,800 per hour)
Path and activityHoursCost (₹)
Screens first: build 18 screens (18 × 5 h)901,62,000
Screens first: rework 8 screens (8 × 5 h)4072,000
Total, screens first1302,34,000
Storyboard first: draw 8 panels (8 × 1.5 h)1221,600
Storyboard first: redraw 4 panels (4 × 1.5 h)610,800
Storyboard first: build 18 screens (18 × 5 h)901,62,000
Total, storyboard first1081,94,400

Simplification: the corrected design is assumed to need the same 18 screens on both paths. Rework hours are Pranesh Kodgire's estimate, not a measurement. It also assumes the storyboard test always exposes a real flaw.

The difference is ₹39,600, or 22 hours at ₹1,800. Figure 2 draws the totals to one scale.

Now change one input. Suppose the strip had contained no flaw. Storyboard-first would then cost ₹21,600 plus ₹1,62,000, or ₹1,83,600, against ₹1,62,000 for screens first: a loss of ₹21,600, the price of insurance that paid nothing. If the flaw exists, storyboarding saves ₹72,000 less ₹10,800, or ₹61,200, relative to rework. Break-even is the probability p at which p × ₹61,200 equals ₹21,600, which is 35.3 per cent. Nirvik Care's own history was three flawed flows out of four, or 75 per cent; at that rate the expected gain is 0.75 × ₹61,200 − ₹21,600, or ₹24,300. The sample of four is thin, but far above threshold.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

A storyboard is not a journey map

A journey map describes stages, actions and emotions across a relationship with a company, often averaged over many customers. A storyboard is one person on one occasion with the product present. The map says where the pain is; the storyboard shows what the product does about it.

It is not a user flow or a wireframe

A user flow is a diagram of screens and the transitions between them. It records what the system does. A storyboard records what the person does, feels and has to remember, including time spent away from any screen. If a panel could be replaced by a screenshot, the story has gone.

Fidelity should be low on purpose

Stick figures are a feature. Polished art invites comments about colour and polish, while rough art invites comments about the plot. Pranesh's 1.5 hours per panel is near the upper limit; a panel that takes half a day has become a deliverable.

The character must be specific

"A busy professional" cannot be wrong, and therefore cannot be tested. Padma at 74, with a lid she opens by habit, can be wrong in ways a reviewer will notice.

Show what the product does not do

Panel 4 contains no screen and no action beyond a sensor reading. That emptiness showed the problem was already solved, which made panel 5 look redundant.

The author cannot test it

The person who drew the strip fills gaps from memory without noticing. Only a viewer who was absent from the planning can report that panel 5 is confusing. Hence the question "what would you do now?" rather than "do you like it?".

What it cannot tell you

A storyboard cannot show whether a button is findable or whether anyone will pay. Stated intentions are cheap: the three parents who said they would comply may still forget. Usability needs a prototype; willingness to pay needs an offer.

Questions to ask before relying on one

Whose day is this, and how many of them did we see? What did viewers do, as against say? What decision will this strip change, and what result would change it?

6. Across product types and company stages

In a consumer product, the main risk is the context of use: noise, children, a low battery, a shared phone. In a B2B product, the character is usually a buyer and a user, so the strip needs two rows; drawing only the user hides the person who can veto the sale. In a marketplace, there are at least two sides, and a storyboard must show the moment each side experiences the other: a seller photographs a product and a buyer, hours later, sees the result. Such strips often reveal a timing gap between the sides.

Company stage changes the audience more than the method. An early-stage team uses the strip to test an idea with a handful of customers, as Parnika's twelve parents show. A large company also uses it to align legal, support and engineering. Larger firms risk turning the strip into a signed-off document; keep it disposable.

7. Common mistakes

Screens in disguise

Symptom: reviewers debate button labels in the first five minutes. Misunderstanding: that a storyboard is a cheap mockup. Diagnostic: cover the interface sketches; if the story no longer makes sense, the panels were not carrying it.

The happy path only

Symptom: every reviewer nods and nobody argues. Misunderstanding: that the strip should sell the concept. Diagnostic: add one panel in which something goes wrong, and see whether the team knows what the product does next.

Drawn after the decision

Symptom: the strip is dated after the specification and matches it exactly. Misunderstanding: that the point is documentation. Diagnostic: ask what changed because of the strip; if nothing, it was ceremony.

Reviewed by friends

Symptom: unanimous approval from colleagues and no field contact. Misunderstanding: that any reader is a valid test. Diagnostic: count viewers who belong to the character's group; if zero, the strip is untested.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Parnika's week looks like this. The strip is drawn in two days by designer and researcher together, on paper. It is tested within days with a dozen people from the character's real world, each asked what happens next, and the tally is written on the strip: 9 of 12 at panel 5. The team removes the confirmation step, redraws panels 5 to 8 so that the lid sensor, not the parent, confirms the dose. Engineers read the strip before the sprint. The strip was a conversation, and it changed the plan.

9. What Parnika decided, and what comes next

On Monday, 12 October, Parnika approved the redrawn strip and released Pranesh's 90 hours to build the 18 screens against it. She had paid ₹32,400 for the strip and its repair, and avoided ₹72,000 of rework. Her reasoning on 5 October rested on a prior flaw rate of 75 per cent (three of four earlier flows) against a break-even of 35.3 per cent; by 12 October the test had replaced the prior. Had fewer than about one earlier flow in three failed, she would have skipped the strip.

Next come wireframes, mockups and prototypes, which turn the approved story into things a person can touch, and the loop of concept, feedback and iteration, which treats each prototype as a question with a decision rule. The storyboard is the loop's first and cheapest turn.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of a product you have shipped or used: which moment of the customer's day sat entirely outside every screen, and what would a panel there have shown? Second, if a storyboard test returned 5 of 12 customers rejecting a step, with the break-even figure from Table 1 unchanged, what else would you need to know before acting?
exp40v2-sol.storyboard:
Storyboarding

Drawing the experience as panels before any screens exist

1. Two boards, sixteen days apart

On Tuesday, 15 September 2026, Pramita Khasnis laid ten sheets of A4 along a table in Pune. Khasnis runs product at Navgati Freight Systems, which sells dispatch software to forty-six road-freight operators. Her design lead, Prathamesh Khadilkar, had drawn the sheets on Friday, 11 September. Their subject was not a screen but a shift: Pakhi Kalbag, a dispatcher at Niyam Roadlines, handing a truck to a relay driver outside Nashik.

A decision was due at the board meeting on Tuesday, 20 October: whether to commission the handoff module. Purnendu Karmarkar, the engineering director, had costed it at fourteen engineer-weeks at ₹1.1 lakh each, fully loaded — ₹15.4 lakh against a roadmap with no slack. Three competent people in the room disagreed about what happened at a relay point. None had been to one.

Sixteen days later, on Thursday, 1 October, Oditi Kanhere met the same problem in another form in Bengaluru. Kanhere co-founded Nazariya Tutor, a CBSE-aligned mathematics tutor on WhatsApp with 31,000 weekly active students in Classes 9 and 10. The feature awaiting a launch decision on Monday, 26 October was called Explain it again differently. She could not draw a panel of what the tutor says, because what it says is a draw from a distribution. Her ML lead, Pushkaraj Kudtarkar, had just evaluated 400 sampled questions; 40 answers were wrong.

A storyboard's value is not that it depicts an experience; depiction is cheap and the author controls it. Its value is that it localises disagreement onto a few moments that can then be tested for a fraction of what building costs. Alignment is a by-product.

2. The idea, and the four positions it divides

A storyboard is an ordered sequence of panels, each showing one moment in a named person's experience from that person's point of view, with the product present but undetailed, and with what the product does not control — the other people, the noise, the clock — drawn in. The sequence carries cause and effect across elapsed time.

Four phrases do the work. Named person: a board about "the user" cannot be falsified, because nobody can say it is untrue of them. Point of view: screens are drawn from the vantage where the system is the protagonist, panels from the one where the product is a minor character. Undetailed: once a panel holds a button, the review becomes an argument about the button. What the product does not control: where most failures live, and where no screen flow can put them.

The technique exploits a cost asymmetry. At the Walt Disney studio in the early 1930s a minute of finished animation cost weeks and a scene sketch cost minutes, so the story department moved every editing decision upstream of the expensive step. Software inherited the asymmetry but moved the expensive end to building and selling; Khasnis's ₹15.4 lakh is the modern form of a week of inked cels. What the field has never settled is what the board is for.

The narrative-first school descends from Carroll's scenario-based design and Cooper's personas, and has its commercial form in the product narrative written before any code. It signs: a team that cannot narrate what happens before and after a panel does not know what it is building. It will not sign that a board is a user-interface artefact, or that panels should hold screens.

The evidence-first school treats the board as a rendering of assumptions: each panel is a claim with an owner, a confidence and a test. It signs: a panel nobody has observed is a hypothesis and must be labelled one. It will not sign that a shared, beautiful story is progress.

The build-to-learn sceptics object that any panel can be drawn to work, because the author chooses the room, the mood and the outcome. They sign: a storyboard cannot be wrong in a way that hurts its author. They will not sign that panels de-risk a build.

The service-systems school, running from Lynn Shostack's 1984 service blueprint through contextual design's sequence models, objects to the form itself. Paritosh Kelusker, a service designer Navgati had used before, put it to Khasnis plainly: a one-actor board is a lie of composition, because freight value is made by four actors across a line of visibility, and one point of view hides the handoff where the experience breaks.

3. Mechanics in depth

Expert practice has a spine, and it is not "draw the flow". It has six slots and is filled from the end backwards.

Three steps are routinely left implicit. The first is to write the decision rule before drawing: what would the board have to show for the team not to build this? Khasnis wrote hers on the back of panel one — if the dispatcher's problem is the phone call and not the record, we build nothing. The second is to write each caption as a sentence with a named subject and an active verb: "driver details are confirmed" has hidden its actor; "Pakhi phones the second driver to check he is at the dhaba" has not. The third is to allocate the gaps, because elapsed time is invisible in a screen flow and is where patience is spent.

The quantitative treatment is the critique round. Khadilkar's board went to nine reviewers on 15 September: four from Navgati, three dispatchers from customer operators, and two long-haul drivers. Each read the strip in silence, then placed up to three marks, one per panel at most, on panels they did not believe. Disbelief was asked for rather than preference, which clusters on the panels people find interesting.

Panel (abbreviated caption)Disbelief marks
1 Pakhi opens the shift board at 06:200
2 She reads last night's exception list1
3 She sees the relay truck is 40 minutes out3
4 She confirms the second driver is at the relay point8
5 She reassigns the trip in the system2
6 The outgoing driver signs off on the handheld1
7 The truck leaves the relay point0
8 She logs why the handoff ran late5
9 Her supervisor reviews the shift at 14:003
10 Next morning she starts with a cleaner list2
Total marks placed25

Nine reviewers, three marks each: 27 available, 25 placed.

Read the exhibit for concentration, not totals. Panels 4 and 8 hold 13 of the 25 marks placed — 52 per cent. Panel 4 alone was marked by 8 of the 9 reviewers, 88.9 per cent, and both drivers marked it. That is the whole output: not a story, but two coordinates. The other eight carry 12 marks between them.

Cost of the critique roundHoursAt ₹2,600/hour
Khadilkar, drawing and redrawing11₹28,600
Nine reviewers, two hours each18₹46,800
Total29₹75,400

Set ₹75,400 against the ₹15.4 lakh build and the ratio is 20.4 to one. That ratio is the usual case made for storyboarding, and it is the wrong one: the board does not substitute for the build. The honest comparison is second-order. Panel 4 can be checked by three ride-alongs at a relay point, costed at ₹1.8 lakh; panel 8 by two days of call-log review at ₹0.6 lakh. Together ₹2.4 lakh, or ₹3.15 lakh with the round's own ₹75,400 added; ₹15.4 lakh divided by ₹3.15 lakh is 4.9, and by ₹2.4 lakh alone 6.4. The board converted a ₹15.4 lakh exposure into a ₹3.15 lakh purchase of information.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are worth stating as claims a team can fail. A board that fails three of the five should not be drawn.

ClaimNavgatiNazariya
Spans more than one setting or actorHolds: control room, cab, relayPartly: parent often present
The dispute is what happens, not how it looksHolds: three accounts of one relayFails: only the output is disputed
Being wrong is expensive in the buildHolds: ₹15.4 lakh, no slackHolds: eval work, reputation
Value accrues across hours or daysHolds: tomorrow's shiftHolds: a test score in March
Someone can name a real person and dayHolds: Pakhi Kalbag, that MondayHolds: transcripts on file

Three situations make the technique actively misleading rather than merely wasteful. The first is the single-step utility — a toll tag, a QR scan, a toggle: the honest board is two panels, so the team invents a third and fourth, and the invented drama is then designed for. The second is a product whose binding constraint is feasibility, where weeks go into drawing an experience the system cannot produce and realism hides the impossibility. The third, and the commonest, is a board drawn from no observation: panels confer authority in proportion to their craft, so a well-drawn fiction reads as a finding — what Kanhere calls laundering.

5. Hard edges

At the seams the single-protagonist form fails in ways that matter. Kelusker's objection is strongest in two-sided products, where the standard error is to draw the supply board as a mirror of the demand board. They are not mirrors: they share one panel.

In regulated products the awkward panel is the one nobody wants to draw. A consent notice under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, or a key-fact statement of the kind the Reserve Bank of India requires in digital lending, is a real moment costing real seconds, yet it is routinely drawn with the protagonist already past it. The expert move is to draw it at the same size as the turn.

Hardware-plus-software changes the timing rather than the method. Tooling freezes months before software does, so the board is frozen earlier and read as a commitment instead of a sketch, and the first panels are not in the product at all but in a corridor, where the carton still sits unopened. Here the no-screens rule is suspended deliberately: for a physical product the object is the context, and a rendered photograph of it is not interface detail.

AI-native products are the genuinely hard case. A panel asserts an output; a model samples one. Drawing the modal answer and reviewing it is the oldest form of demo fraud, committed in good faith. Kanhere drew three strips at the same moment in the student's day, one per outcome class, reviewed in proportion to frequency.

Nazariya offline evaluation, 400 sampled questions, closed 1 Oct 2026QuestionsShare
Correct and pitched at the student's level26867.0%
Correct but pitched too high9223.0%
Wrong4010.0%
Total400100.0%

A student at the median asks 12 questions a week. At a wrong-answer rate of 40/400 = 0.10, that student meets 12 × 0.10 = 1.2 wrong answers a week, and, if questions are independent draws at that rate, the chance of at least one in the first week is 1 − 0.9012 = 1 − 0.282 = 0.718. The strip drawn last was the one most students would live in their first week: panel counts follow frequencies.

How mature companies handle this is less impressive than what they say. The published practice is a canonical board in every specification's header, re-reviewed whenever a panel changes. The observed practice is that boards decay from kickoff, because the artefact that survives is the one that gates something. Boards that gate a budget release live; boards that inspire die by the second sprint.

6. Nine things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Captions before pictures. The competent practitioner draws and then captions; the expert writes the sentences, reorders them until the story holds, and draws last. The tell is a board whose captions could be deleted without loss — a flow diagram with illustrations. Drawing first commits the team to a composition before anyone has agreed what happens.

The protagonist has a name and a date. Experts will not start without one real person and one real recent day. The tell is "the user" in a caption, or a protagonist whose age is given as a range. The objection that one person is a sample of one misreads the purpose: the board is a specification of what evidence would be about.

Panels are state changes, not steps. The diagnostic is whether two adjacent panels can be swapped without the story becoming false. If they can, they are steps, and steps belong in a flow. Khadilkar's first draft had fourteen panels; four were swappable, and merging them let the critique round concentrate.

Somebody pays in panel five. Every board needs a panel where the protagonist pays — in minutes, money, effort or social risk, such as telephoning a colleague and appearing not to trust him. The tell is a board where the product is free. Navgati's panel 4 was a cost panel in disguise.

There is a second person in the frame. Experts notice when every panel holds exactly one human, because almost no consequential decision is made alone. A second figure can be decorative, so the test is whether that person ever changes the outcome. In Nazariya's boards a parent appears in four panels and influences two.

Gaps carry the elapsed time. Panels are drawn the same size; the gaps are not. Navgati's first seven gaps run 5, 10, 40, 3, 95, 2 and 8 minutes, 163 in all, and the largest three carry 145 of the 163, or 89.0 per cent. The experience is mostly waiting, and the module touched none of it.

Draw the strip you hope is rare. A board every reviewer enjoys has failed. Experts draw the failure branch as its own strip at full size; the novice tell is recovery appearing as a parenthesis in a caption. Nazariya's 0.718 shows why: an event at 10 per cent per question is the common case over a week.

The decision rule precedes the drawing. Ask a team what the board would have to show for them not to build the thing. Experts have that written down before the first panel; competent practitioners produce it after review, which is to say they produce a rationalisation. Skip it and the board can only confirm.

Roughness is a signal. Experts keep boards visibly unfinished — pencil, the wrong grey, a crossing-out left in — because polish instructs reviewers to admire rather than object. The tell is a board set in the brand typeface. But rough boards are easy to ignore, and an ignored board gates nothing.

7. What actually changes by product type and stage

Less changes than the literature implies. The spine, caption-first drafting, the state-change rule and the disbelief critique are invariant; adapting them for a segment usually weakens them. Four differences are real. In B2B the protagonist is not the buyer, so the user's day and the buyer's quarter have different after-states, and enterprise work needs a third strip for the administrator's first week after procurement. In marketplaces the shared panel of Figure 5 is the whole game, and the board must show the empty state. In hardware the board is a commitment device, frozen by tooling lead times. In AI products the panel asserts what the system cannot promise.

Stage changes function more than form. At seed the board substitutes for a specification and takes an hour; at Navgati's stage it holds a cross-squad story together; at scale it competes with the roadmap and becomes theatre unless wired to a gate. Kanhere drew her board to decide; Khasnis drew hers to find out who disagreed.

8. Three boards with numbers, one of them a wreck

Nivaran Elder Care, which sends caregivers to older people living alone, drew an eleven-panel board of a home visit in August 2026. Most disbelief landed on panel 6, the handover note, which the board showed being read by a family member. Oshma Kagal, its product lead, shadowed 36 visits: in 23 of the 36 no family member was at home, 63.9 per cent.

Nakshewala Interiors, which sells modular kitchens, used a board to find a sequencing error rather than an interface one. Priyal Khanvilkar's board put design approval after the advance payment, as the business then worked, and made the nineteen-day wait between measurement and approval visible. Approval moved before the advance.

Nakshewala Interiors: orders cancelled after advanceOrdersCancelledRate
Quarter to 31 March 2026, approval after advance4206315.0%
Quarter to 30 June 2026, approval before advance390112.8%

63 of the 420 orders is 15.0 per cent; 11 of the 390 is 2.8 per cent — the same measure over the same split. Cancellations counted within 45 days of the advance, so both windows closed by 14 August 2026.

The wreck is instructive because the board was excellent. Nabhya Pay storyboarded a merchant-settlement product across twelve panels in 2024, showing a shop owner checking settlement at 9 pm after closing, and built it from July 2024 to March 2025 for ₹2.6 crore. Prabuddha Kirpekar, who drew the board, had based it on three interviews, two of them with merchants' accountants rather than merchants; his composite protagonist had no Tuesday. Ninety days after launch, 180 of the 1,400 merchants onboarded before March 2025 had used it, 12.9 per cent. The team re-storyboarded with the accountant as protagonist and found that 14 of the 22 merchants re-interviewed, 63.6 per cent, said the accountant held the phone. Re-pointing roles, permissions and notifications took eleven weeks and ₹41 lakh; ninety days after the September 2025 relaunch 602 of the same 1,400 merchants, 43.0 per cent, were using it.

9. Failure modes and how they announce themselves

Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost if late
Fiction launderingCraft rises, observation stays nilWhose Tuesday was this?A full build, as at Nabhya Pay
Screens in panelsA button argument in ten minutesCover the screens — does it parse?The story freezes around an unchosen interface
Golden-path boardAll pleased; no failure stripWhat does the tenth user see?Churn absorbs the branch
The orphaned seamTwo boards, no handoffWhich panel is on both?A product that works on each side alone
Decay after kickoffA premise changes, no re-reviewWhat changed under panel 4?Building to an abandoned story
Board as theatreBranded; gates nothingWhat budget does this unlock?The method is discredited internally

A board's authority and its evidentiary basis move independently, and the gap is invisible from inside. Every diagnostic above asks about provenance rather than content — which is why asking "where did panel 4 come from?" works and asking "is this right?" does not.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

One point of view, or swimlanes. Kelusker's school rests on real evidence: in service businesses failures cluster at handoffs, and a one-protagonist board cannot show both sides of a handoff without lying about one. The narrative school rests on evidence just as real — blueprints are read by nobody outside the team that drew them, and an unread document cannot localise disagreement. For the blueprint school to be wrong, a one-actor board plus one shared panel would have to catch the same seam failures as a four-lane blueprint. Figure 5 is that bet, untested at scale.

Build risk, or only organisational risk. The sceptics' evidence is that storyboarded products fail at roughly the rate of unstoryboarded ones, and that the author's control over the panels makes the method unfalsifiable. The reply is that the board was never a risk-reduction device but a disagreement-localising one, and the risk reduction belongs to the tests it points at — which concedes most of their claim. For them to be wrong, boards would have to change which tests teams run.

Can a learned system be storyboarded. Kanhere's three strips are one position. The other, held by people building agentic products, is that the unit of design has moved from the panel to the policy: what the system does is a function it learned, not a sequence an author chose, so drawing panels of a policy produces false confidence. Kudtarkar holds a version of this view inside Nazariya. For it to be wrong, outcome classes would have to be stable enough that a strip drawn against last month's distribution still describes next month's — an empirical question about drift, and the honest answer in October 2026 is that nobody knows.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the technique produces a board and asks whether people like it. Someone who has internalised it treats it as an instrument with a reading. They write the decision rule first and show it to a sceptic. They ask for disbelief, not approval, and they count. They leave panels alone when nobody doubts them — the discipline that turns a ten-panel board into a two-test plan. And they throw the board away once the disputed panels have been tested, because a board that survives its critique round is furniture.

12. The two decisions

Khasnis will go to the 20 October board without the handoff module. She is asking instead for ₹2.4 lakh and three weeks to test panels 4 and 8, on the stated rule that if the dispatcher's real problem is the phone call rather than the record, Navgati builds nothing. The board has not given her the answer; it has shown her that eight of her nine reviewers disbelieved the same panel, and that she was about to spend ₹15.4 lakh on a premise most of them did not share.

Kanhere will launch Explain it again differently on 26 October under two conditions. The strips produced the first: the wrong-answer strip becomes a requirement, a one-tap way for a student to mark an answer wrong and have it re-queued. The evaluation table set the second: the mis-pitched class, 23.0 per cent in the 400-question sample, must fall below 10 per cent on the next sample before the feature enters the default flow. Phalguni Kashikar, her research lead, has the task nobody had done: sitting in four homes with the parent present.

Discussion questions

  1. Khasnis's round cost ₹75,400 and redirected ₹15.4 lakh. If the ride-alongs confirm panel 4 exactly as drawn, was it worth running — and what did Navgati buy?
  2. Kelusker says the board hid the relay seam, yet the disbelief landed on panel 4 anyway. Does that vindicate the one-actor board, or did nine reviewers do a blueprint's work by hand?
  3. If drift makes Nazariya's outcome classes unstable month to month, what is left of the storyboard for an AI-native product?

13. Going deeper

Concept and elevator pitch — the sentence every panel must serve. Customer journey mapping — the life the board inserts a product into. Writing a solution hypothesis — turns a disbelieved panel into a testable claim. Ideation: brainstorming, Crazy 8s, HMW — alternative turns a board can stage cheaply. Value Proposition Canvas and Value proposition statement — discipline the cost panel. Wireframes, mockups, prototypes — the expensive step the board protects. Concept → feedback → iterate — the cycle the critique round serves. AI-generated prototypes — collapse the cost of rendering a panel, raising the laundering risk. What an MVP is — the two-test plan, not the small product.
case20v1-sol.hypothesis:
Gullak Ledger: A Hypothesis Worth Testing

A teaching case on writing a solution hypothesis

1. Opening

On Thursday, 15 October 2026, Lishita Raichura, Director of Product at Gullak Ledger Technologies, sat in the company's Indiranagar office in Bengaluru with a blank slide titled "Collections: decision." The board's product review was on Tuesday, 20 October. By then she had to commit the company either to a five-month build costing ₹1.4 crore, or to something much smaller whose purpose was to find out whether the big build deserved to exist.

The problem was not in doubt: Gullak's distributors were paid late. What was missing was a sentence beginning "We believe". Nobody had written down, in one testable line, what would fix it.

2. Company background

Gullak Ledger Technologies, founded in Bengaluru in 2019, sells a GST invoicing, e-way bill and ledger app to sub-stockists and small wholesalers, mostly FMCG distributors supplying kirana shops in cities such as Pune, Indore, Lucknow and Coimbatore. At the end of September 2026 it had 62,000 paying subscribers at ₹3,600 a year, annual recurring revenue of ₹22.32 crore.

The market is crowded. Vyapar and Zoho Books compete on invoicing, Tally remains the default for older accountants, and Khatabook and OkCredit own the habit of recording what a shopkeeper owes. Payment rails are not Gullak's to own: UPI, run by NPCI, carries the money, and PhonePe, Razorpay and Paytm already offer collection links. Gullak's edge is that it holds the invoice, the due date and the retailer's phone number in one place.

3. The situation

In July and August 2026 the product team studied 36 distributors who had agreed to share payment data. Exhibit 1 shows what happened to their 1,240 credit invoices. The team fixed one definition and used it everywhere: an invoice counts as on time if it is paid in full within 7 calendar days after its due date. By that definition 682 invoices, 55.0 per cent, were on time. The other 558, 45.0 per cent, were not, and they carried ₹10.63 crore of the ₹19.37 crore invoiced.

Exhibit 1: When 1,240 invoices were paid (36 distributors, invoices due 1 July to 31 August 2026)
Payment timingInvoicesShare of invoices (%)Value (₹ lakh)
Paid by due date40232.4482
1 to 7 days late28022.6392
8 to 30 days late36129.1650
More than 30 days late19715.9413
Total1,240100.01,937

On time = paid within 7 days after the due date (first two rows: 402 + 280 = 682). Shares are of invoice count, not value. ₹1,937 lakh = ₹19.37 crore.

The people closest to the problem saw it differently. Lipsa Rudrangi, who leads customer success from Singapore, reported that distributors rarely chased because chasing a kirana owner before Diwali risked losing the account to a rival wholesaler. A contract designer in Berlin, who had drafted early reminder screens, warned that a message that sounded like a demand would be deleted. A Dubai trading house that bought spices through one Gullak distributor paid in dirhams by bank transfer, a reminder that a UPI link would not serve every payer.

In September the team ran a quick trial. Six friendly distributors sent WhatsApp reminders with a UPI link on 150 invoices; 96 were paid on time, 64.0 per cent. Several executives took this as proof. Exhibit 2 shows why Lalan Rathod, the data scientist in Toronto, did not.

Exhibit 2: The September trial against two possible baselines
PopulationPeriod (invoices due)DistributorsInvoicesOn timeOn-time rate (%)
All 36 data-sharing distributors, no remindersJul to Aug361,24068255.0

On time = paid within 7 days after the due date in every row. The six trial distributors are included in the 36. Rates are on-time invoices divided by invoices in that row.

Comparing 64.0 with 55.0 suggests a nine-point gain. But the six were already better payers than the group: 60.8 per cent on their own earlier invoices. Against their own history the gain is 3.2 points, on 150 invoices, in a different month. Rathod added that on 150 invoices the plausible range around 64.0 per cent runs from about 56.3 to 71.7, which contains the 70 per cent the sales team was quoting.

4. The people

Lishita Raichura (Bengaluru) owns the decision. She wants to avoid spending ₹1.4 crore on a belief nobody has written down.

Lokesh Rangachari, head of engineering in Pune, has six engineers idle after the last release and a design for a complete collections suite: reminders, UPI AutoPay mandates, a retailer payment score and a dashboard. He wants to build it once and properly, and distrusts "throwaway" prototypes.

Lochan Rustogi, head of sales from New Jersey, hears distributors asking for "something to make shops pay" and wants a launch before the festive season. He told the board that reminders "will take on-time payments to seventy per cent."

Lalan Rathod (Toronto) wants a stated threshold and a control group before anyone commits money. He joins Bengaluru's 9.30 a.m. calls at midnight Toronto time.

5. Exhibits and the proposed test

Raichura and Rathod drafted three versions of the hypothesis, shown in Exhibit 3. Only the third could be proved wrong.

Exhibit 3: Three drafts of the solution hypothesis
DraftWordingCustomer named?Job named?Measurable pass mark?
1"Reminders will improve cash flow."NoNoNo
2"We believe WhatsApp reminders will reduce late payment for distributors."Yes, looselyNoNo, "reduce" has no number
3"We believe a WhatsApp reminder sequence with a one-tap UPI link, sent from the distributor's own business number 2 days before the due date, on it, and 3 and 6 days after, will solve late payment by shopkeepers for small FMCG distributors while doing the job of getting paid without souring the relationship. Pass: at least 70.0% of treated invoices paid within 7 days after the due date, at least 10 points above control."YesYesYes: 70.0% and a 10-point gap

The last reminder (day +6) falls inside the 7-day outcome window so that a payment it prompts can still count.

Draft 3 fixes the outcome window at 7 days after the due date, the same as in Exhibits 1 and 2, so every later figure uses one population and one definition. Exhibit 4 places the test on the calendar. Diwali falls on Sunday, 8 November, and shopkeepers settle accounts unusually fast in the weeks before it, which is why a control group is needed: festive cash would lift both arms, and only the difference is attributable to the reminders.

Exhibit 4: Scale 14 px per day from 15 October (x = 40). The last invoice due on 22 November reaches the end of its 7-day window on 29 November.

The proposed test enrols the 36 data-sharing distributors: 24 receive the sequence, 12 do not. Rathod expects roughly 370 treated and 190 control invoices, about 560 in all, due between 26 October and 22 November. The cost is ₹9.0 lakh: ₹4.8 lakh engineering, ₹2.4 lakh operations and support, ₹0.6 lakh messaging and onboarding of 24 business numbers, and ₹1.2 lakh for a review of retailer consent under the DPDP Act, since each shopkeeper's phone number becomes personal data in a message flow.

6. The options

Option A: Build the full collections suite. Rangachari's team builds reminders, AutoPay mandates and the payment score for all 62,000 subscribers, delivered by March 2027 for ₹1.4 crore (₹140 lakh). The upside is a complete product. The cost is that the 70 per cent belief stays untested until the money is spent.

Option B: Test the written hypothesis. Run Draft 3 as a 24-versus-12 test from 26 October, with the decision rule agreed in advance. The upside is a verdict on 30 November for ₹9.0 lakh, about 6.4 per cent of Option A. The cost is a month's delay, a manually operated prototype that is not a product, and the chance that Rustogi's festive launch window is missed.

Option C: Offer working capital instead. Partner with an NBFC so distributors can borrow against unpaid invoices, accepting lateness and financing it. The upside is quick revenue share. The cost is a different concept for a different problem: it finances lateness rather than reducing it, and ties Gullak's brand to credit losses.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, what is the correct baseline against which the September trial should be judged, and what does the trial actually show?
  2. Take Draft 2 and Draft 3. Which element of the "We believe" template does each fill, and which does Draft 2 leave empty? Why does the 7-day window matter to every figure that follows?
  3. Why does the test in Exhibit 4 need a control arm in a Diwali month? What would you conclude if both arms reached 72 per cent?
  4. Which option would you take to the board on 20 October, and what result on 30 November would make you stop, refine or build?

8. A note for the learner

A solution hypothesis turns "we should build reminders" into a claim that can fail. The template, "We believe [concept] will solve [problem] for [customer] while doing [job]", forces four choices, and a fifth, the pass mark, makes the claim testable. Raichura's difficulty was a missing shared definition of success, not a lack of ideas.

A well-reasoned answer begins by fixing the outcome: paid within 7 days after the due date, over invoices from distributors like these. It then checks that every comparison uses the same population. The September trial's honest reading is a 3.2-point gain on 150 invoices, which is neither a proof nor a refutation.

One defensible path is Option B. Approve the ₹9.0 lakh test and write the rule before the data arrives: if treated reaches at least 70.0 per cent and exceeds control by at least 10 points, and at least 18 of 24 treated distributors (75 per cent) keep the sequence switched on, scope Option A from the tested pieces. If treated falls short of 70.0 but beats control by 10 points or more, refine the message and window. If the gap is below 10 points, drop the concept and revisit Option C as a fresh hypothesis. Option A commits ₹140 lakh to a belief; Option B spends ₹9.0 lakh to learn whether it is true. The Dubai payer shows why "customer" must be specific: this hypothesis concerns UPI-paying kirana retailers only.
exp40v2-sol.hypothesis:
Writing a solution hypothesis

A validated problem is not an instruction to build. Between the two sits one sentence — we believe this concept will solve this problem for this customer while they do this job — and what separates a disciplined team from a busy one is how it is written and retired.

1Two desks, one sentence

On Thursday, 20 August 2026, Elakkiya Dharmalingam sat with a slide she did not want to present. She is Director of Product at Ullekh Systems, a Bengaluru firm whose warranty-claims software serves eleven appliance and HVAC makers and their 2,480 authorised service franchises. Franchises file claims after a repair, manufacturers audit them, and for the quarter ended 30 June 2026 a quarter came back unpaid, leaving the franchise out of pocket for the part.

In early July the slide had read, in the chief executive's words, cut first-pass rejections by a third. Farhad Doongaji, her engineering counterpart, had priced the build — nine months, ₹2.4 crore — then asked by what mechanism, and worth how much.

A thousand kilometres away, on Tuesday, 22 September 2026, Fali Dinshaw had the opposite problem. He is VP Product at Uchcharan Labs in Pune, whose spoken-English app serves first-job aspirants with Hindi, Marathi or Telugu as a first language. Of 9.4 lakh installs to 31 May 2026, 12.0 per cent of new users completed eight practice sessions within twenty-one days, 6.8 per cent were active on day 30, and 2.1 per cent paid within ninety days. His team had run a clean randomised test, won it, and were watching a number fall.

Elakkiya had a mechanism and almost no statistical power; Fali had abundant power and no mechanism he could name. Falsifiability is a property of the sentence, not of the sample size. Power buys precision on a link already named; it cannot supply the link.

2The idea, and who disagrees about it

A solution hypothesis is a conditional causal claim, written before the work, in the form we believe [concept] will solve [problem] for [customer] while doing [job], together with the observation that would retire it. The concept names a mechanism, not an artefact — "the serial is captured before the technician leaves the site", not "a camera screen". The problem is a quantity with a stated base and date. The customer is whoever must change behaviour, often not whoever pays. The job clause is a scope limit, and a hypothesis without one cannot be wrong anywhere.

Two traditions met late here. The scientific one runs from Popper — a claim earns standing by what would refute it — through Chamberlin's 1890 plea for multiple working hypotheses to Platt's 1964 strong inference, which asks for the experiment that discriminates between rivals. The industrial one runs through Deming's plan-do-check-act and the Toyota A3, where the word is countermeasure: provisional, attached to a measured gap. Blank, Ries, Thomke, Kohavi and Torres industrialised the join: the MVP became a learning vehicle rather than a small product. All of it answers one failure: teams turned a validated problem straight into a backlog, so the causal claim was never written down.

3Mechanics in depth

Expert practice is less about phrasing than decomposition. Elakkiya wrote the concept as a chain of separately observable links, each owned by a different party, with priors taken from data she already held. Her hypothesis: capturing the part's serial number by camera at the job site, queued offline, will remove serial-related rejections for franchise technicians while they close a repair visit. The technician opens the app at the job (p₁, telemetry); having opened it, completes the capture (p₂, flow instrumentation); the claim clears first-pass audit (p₃, the audit log).

Multiplying, 0.70 × 0.60 = 0.42, and 0.42 × 0.85 = 0.357. The addressable slice is the 9,960 serial-caused rejections in Exhibit 3, so the concept's own arithmetic predicted 9,960 × 0.357 = 3,556 claims a quarter. Subtracting from 24,910 leaves 21,354 rejections on the same 99,300 claims filed — 21.5 per cent against 25.1 today, a drop of 3.6 percentage points, not a third. Multiplying honestly killed the slogan before money was spent: the first second-order effect of the sentence is to move the argument from the demo to the priors.

The step usually left implicit is choosing which link to test, since testing the link you are already confident about buys nothing. Elakkiya's widest prior was p₂, also the only link inside Ullekh's own software, so she scoped a five-week concierge test on 40 franchises in Account A, 13 July to 16 August 2026, at ₹18 lakh. Sample size came from precision, not significance: estimating a proportion near 0.70 to within ±5 points at 95 per cent confidence needs 1.96² × 0.70 × 0.30 ÷ 0.05² = 3.8416 × 0.21 ÷ 0.0025 = 323 visits, so her floor was 325.

The threshold, derived rather than chosen. Build if true: ₹2.4 crore. Three-year contribution if true: ₹11 crore. Prior that the chain holds: 0.40. Build blind: 0.40 × 11 − 2.4 = ₹2.0 crore expected. Test, build only on a pass: 0.40 × (11 − 2.4) − 0.18 = 3.44 − 0.18 = ₹3.26 crore. Value of resolving the uncertainty = 0.60 × 2.4 = ₹1.44 crore; against an ₹18 lakh test, 8.0 to 1. The 0.40 is the probability the chain's priors hold, not the 0.357 it predicts if they do — different quantities.

Fali's equivalent runs through power, not precision. At 80 per cent power and 5 per cent two-sided significance, with baseline 12.0 and target 18.0 per cent, the sample per arm is 2 × (1.96 + 0.84)² × p̄(1 − p̄) ÷ δ², where p̄ = (0.12 + 0.18) ÷ 2 = 0.15, so p̄(1 − p̄) = 0.1275 and δ² = 0.06² = 0.0036. Then 2 × 7.84 = 15.68, 15.68 × 0.1275 = 1.9992, and 1.9992 ÷ 0.0036 = 555.3, so 556 per arm. Fali had 9,400 eligible new installs, 4,700 per arm. Holding p̄(1 − p̄) at that same 0.1275, his detectable effect was √(1.9992 ÷ 4,700) = √0.00042536 = 0.0206, about 2 percentage points, and 4,700 ÷ 556 is roughly eight and a half times the sample he needed for a question he had not made falsifiable. That 2 points covers the overall effect only: inside a quartile of 1,175 the formula gives √(1.9992 ÷ 1,175) = 0.0412, about 4 points, so Exhibit 4's Q3 gap of 0.6 is noise.

4When it applies, and when it misleads

Three conditions, each checkable. First, the outcome is caused through links you can observe separately. Elakkiya passes: telemetry, instrumentation and an audit log read three parties. Fali fails, because "progress feels legible" is not an observation. Second, the cost of being wrong exceeds the cheapest decisive test by a margin that survives scepticism about the test. Elakkiya passes at 8.0 to 1; Fali's test is nearly free, so the condition is trivially satisfied and uninformative — a sign his constraint lies elsewhere. Third, the party who must change behaviour receives the benefit, or you have named the transfer. Elakkiya's technician bears the effort while the franchise owner receives the cash, and that transfer was unnamed.

The idea misleads where value depends on network scale, since a small honest test measures a different product and yields a number anyway, and where preference is endogenous to exposure, so the first test measures familiarity. Both bound the scope; neither licenses skipping the sentence.

5Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Elakkiya's chain crosses three organisations, and the link she can least afford to be wrong about is the one she does not own: p₁ sits in a technician's habits, employed by a franchise; p₂ in Ullekh's code; p₃ in a clause of a manufacturer's audit manual. Platform and two-sided settings are worse: the hypothesis must say which side moves first, since a change rational for supply and irrational for demand nets to nothing. In regulated products the seam is a dated external gate: a medical device's screening workflow cannot be tested on patients before approval, so the testable version is narrower than the belief. In hardware it is irreversible tooling — once the mould is cut, the hypothesis has been answered by committee. AI-native products are non-stationary: a hypothesis true against one model version can be false against its successor, so the honest form carries a tolerance clause and an expiry.

Mature companies say they resolve this with a hypothesis review board. What they mostly do is quieter: a leader walks the chain, finds the link a counterparty owns, and spends capital moving it rather than building around it, as Ullekh did at 9.2 per cent of the build.

6Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The chain multiplies, so the slogan always loses. Tell-tale sign: one conversion rate quoted with no intermediate links. Links at 0.70, 0.60 and 0.85 sound like confidence and arrive at 0.357. The obvious reading, that the team is pessimistic, is wrong: the pessimism is arithmetic.

Falsifiability lives in the verb. Tell-tale sign: a hypothesis whose verb is "understands", "trusts" or "feels". Fali's first draft had learners "feel their progress". The obvious reading is that this needs better metrics; it needs a different sentence, since no metric measures that clause.

The decision rule belongs on the interval, not the point. Tell-tale sign: a point estimate just under a round threshold while the room argues about whether to call it. Elakkiya's p₂ came in at 85 of 208 app-opens, 40.9 per cent, against a floor of 45. With 0.409 × 0.591 = 0.241719, divided by 208 = 0.00116211, square root 0.0341, times 1.96 = 6.7 points, the interval runs 34.2 to 47.6 per cent and contains the floor.

Mind the base, and the date it was measured. Tell-tale sign: a share-of-reasons quoted as a share-of-population, as in Exhibit 3. The obvious reading is a rounding quibble; it is a factor of four here, and at Ushma below it reverses a purchase decision.

The weakest link is usually owned by someone else. Tell-tale sign: the link with the widest prior is a counterparty's rule, not your code. Experts test it first by asking the counterparty, which most teams skip.

Heterogeneity can invert the sign. Tell-tale sign: a positive average beside a plausible mechanism by which the same feature discourages part of the population. In Exhibit 4, "it works, with room to improve for weaker users" is backwards: it works for some because of the mechanism that harms others.

The job clause is the scope limit. Tell-tale sign: a hypothesis with no "while doing" clause, which cannot be wrong anywhere and so cannot be right anywhere in particular. "At the job site, before leaving" made Elakkiya's claim testable; at end-of-day reconciliation it is a different hypothesis.

A failed hypothesis retires a mechanism, not a concept — and the kill is cheap only if the successor was named first. Tell-tale sign: a kill meeting that ends with no named next hypothesis, which is how teams learn that discipline is punished. Elakkiya's August readout retired technician-side capture, not the belief behind it.

7How this differs by product type and stage

The real differences are about what is scarce. In consumer products randomisation is cheap and mechanism identification is hard, so the discipline shifts to writing a sentence a test can refute and pre-registering subgroups. In B2B and enterprise the reverse holds: mechanism is legible because you can watch ten users work, but power is absent and buyer and user differ, so the sentence must name both — Eshna Dhebar, who runs Ullekh's manufacturer accounts, insisted it name the audit clerk as well as the technician, which is how the successor hypothesis came to exist. In platforms it must state which side moves first; in hardware it must be answerable before tooling; in AI products the mechanism drifts.

By stage: before product-market fit the hypothesis is the unit of work and killing one is progress. At growth stage it competes with a roadmap already promised to customers, and pre-commitment's real function is political cover for an unwelcome answer. At scale it touches several teams' metrics. What does not change — worth saying plainly, since frameworks sold by segment imply otherwise — is the sentence's structure, the multiplication of the chain, and deciding on the interval.

8Three worked examples

Ullekh, and the hypothesis on the wrong side of the seam. The test closed on 16 August with 325 logged visits. The app was opened at 208 of them, 64.0 per cent against a prior of 0.70; capture was completed in 85 of those 208, 40.9 per cent against 0.60. Carrying the observed links at four decimals, 0.64 × 0.4087 = 0.2616, and 0.2616 × 0.85 = 0.2224, so 9,960 × 0.2224 = 2,215 rejections removed a quarter. That leaves 22,695 on 99,300 claims filed, 22.9 per cent — 2.2 points for ₹2.4 crore. The successor hypothesis, written in July and tested between 1 and 19 September with the audit teams of Accounts A and B, was that the rule could accept a photograph of the rating plate instead of a typed serial. It cleared 5,171 of those two accounts' 8,340 serial-caused rejections, 62.0 per cent. Account C's chiller terms cannot accept a photograph, so the projection is 24,910 − 5,171 = 19,739, or 19.9 per cent: 5.2 points, for a ₹22 lakh build.

Uchcharan, and the test that was won and lost. Fali's hypothesis was that replaying a learner's own first recorded session beside today's, with a single diff score, would make progress legible and sustain practice. Randomised across 9,400 installs from 1 to 21 June 2026; since the metric is eight sessions within twenty-one days of install, the last window closed 12 July and the readout waited until 13 July. Treatment activation came in at 724 of 4,700, 15.4 per cent, against 564 of 4,700, 12.0 per cent, in control — a 3.4-point lift, well outside the 2.1-point detectable effect. The team shipped to all users on 15 July. On 22 September, ninety days after the last install, paid conversion came in at 75 of 4,700, 1.6 per cent, against 94 of 4,700, 2.0 per cent, in control, and day-30 retention at 306 against 315, or 6.5 against 6.7 per cent. Section 1's 2.1 and 6.8 are the pre-June all-install baseline, a different population and not the comparator here. Freny Dalwai had pre-registered a split by first-week improvement.

The mechanism was honest, and that was the problem. For learners who were improving, a visible diff was encouragement; for the slowest quartile it was a weekly reminder that three weeks of effort had produced nothing measurable, and 47 fewer of them reached eight sessions. The recovery split the hypothesis in two: legible progress sustains practice when progress is real; where it is not, legibility must arrive with a changed practice plan. A second arm took installs from 20 July to 9 August, closed its last window on 30 August and read out on 31 August, pairing the replay with an automatic plan change below a set improvement threshold. Q4 recovered to 120 of 1,175, 10.2 per cent; Q1 held at 295 of 1,175, 25.1 per cent; overall 791 of 4,700, 16.8 per cent — 4.8 points above the June control arm, the average of 9.1, 7.0, 2.0 and 1.2. The feature had shipped to everyone on 15 July, so no concurrent control existed and that 4.8 carries six weeks of seasonality.

Ushma Thermal Devices, and the base that reversed a decision. Fahim Dhamnaskar's Pune firm builds modular cold rooms for mandi traders. The hypothesis: a two-tonne room at ₹4.6 lakh will be bought by traders moving at least 1.5 tonnes of leafy produce a day, because spoilage exceeds the instalment. A trader moving 1,800 kg a day at ₹22 a kilogram with 11 per cent spoilage loses 198 kg, ₹4,356 a day, ₹1,13,256 across 26 trading days, against an instalment of ₹12,570 a month on ₹4.6 lakh at 14 per cent reducing balance, compounded monthly over 48 months. But the 11 per cent was measured across the whole mandi chain, and only 4 of those points occur after produce reaches the stall, which is all a stall-side room can touch. Addressable spoilage is 72 kg a day, ₹1,584 a day, ₹41,184 a month — of which the trader bears 27 per cent, the rest falling on farmers under consignment. That is ₹11,120 against ₹12,570: false by ₹1,450 a month. The base was wrong, not the arithmetic.

9Failure modes and their early warnings

The decorative hypothesis announces itself when nobody can name a result that would stop the build; ask "what number, stated now, would make us not ship this?" Caught late, it costs the whole build. Base error appears as a share-of-reasons used as a share-of-population; ask "what is the denominator, and when was it measured?" Caught late it inverts the business case, as at Ushma. Proxy capture appears as a moved headline with a still chain; ask which link moved, and which instrument says so. Timing error appears when a readout precedes the close of the metric's window — Uchcharan's twenty-one-day activation could not be read on 24 June, which is why the arm waited until 13 July; ask for the window's close date, not the calendar.

10Where experts genuinely disagree

The first live disagreement is when the number goes in. The falsificationist position is that a threshold written after the data is not a threshold; it rests on the ease with which teams rationalise ambiguous results, and would be wrong if pre-committed numbers systematically mis-specified the thing worth measuring — which is what happened to Fali in June. The generative position is that early numbers formalise ignorance, and that two or three prototypes compared against each other teach more than one measured against a figure invented in advance; it would be wrong if prototype judgements tracked taste rather than later outcomes.

The second is whether a hypothesis may survive its first refutation. The conviction school argues that in new categories the first test samples a population that has not had the experience, so a negative result is weak evidence; it would be wrong if preference were mostly stable under exposure. Elakkiya's case is not an instance: she retired a mechanism, not a concept. The third is the unit of analysis — one hypothesis tested carefully, after Platt, or several compared, after Chamberlin — turning on whether your constraint is instrumentation or imagination. A fourth is unsettled: whether AI-native products can hold a stable hypothesis when the model changes under the test. And a cost no school owns: making falsifiability a condition of funding biases a portfolio towards instrumentable ideas.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks for the denominator before the conclusion, and writes the chain before the pitch, bringing the multiplied number rather than the stage that flatters it. They refuse to test the link they are already sure about, and hunt for the one in someone else's rule book. They argue about the interval, not the point. They name the successor hypothesis before the kill meeting. And when their own test wins, they ask which subgroup paid for the average.

12The decisions, and three questions

On Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Elakkiya recommended stopping the ₹2.4 crore technician-side build and shipping the ₹22 lakh audit-rule change: a projected 5.2 points against 2.2, at 9.2 per cent of the cost. She kept serial capture alive as a smaller hypothesis scoped to Account C, because the August interval of 34.2 to 47.6 per cent contained her floor: unproven rather than disproven. Fali did not ship the replay as a global default. He gated it on the plan-change intervention, rewrote the hypothesis with a job clause and a heterogeneity clause, and held ninety-day paid conversion as the decision metric, because the metric he could read first had already misled him once.

  1. Elakkiya set her floor on p₂ at 45 per cent and observed 40.9, interval 34.2 to 47.6. Should the floor have been written on the lower bound, and at what cost in sample size?
  2. Fali's June test was statistically valid and commercially harmful. Which clause of his hypothesis, rewritten, would have made the Q4 result predictable?
  3. Ullekh's cheapest intervention lay in a counterparty's rule book. What does that imply for how a product organisation allocates discovery effort?

13Going deeper

Validating a problem hypothesis
Supplies the quantity and base the chain must move.
What an MVP is
The vehicle that tests one link, defined by its decision rule.
PRD structure
Where the surviving hypothesis and its thresholds become a commitment.
Ideation: brainstorming, Crazy 8s, HMW
Generates the rival hypotheses strong inference needs.
Concept and elevator pitch
Compresses the hypothesis, exposing a mechanism never named.
Value Proposition Canvas
Makes the customer and job clauses explicit, catching incidence errors.
Value proposition statement
What the hypothesis becomes if it survives: an assertion.
Storyboarding
Makes p₁ and p₂ visible as moments, where implausible priors show.
Wireframes, mockups, prototypes
The instruments that test a link cheaply.
case40v1-sol.hypothesis:
Raahdari Technologies: The Trip Ledger That Nobody Closed

A pilot ended one owner above its own stop line: a verdict on the product, or on the sentence written in May?

1. Baner, Pune — Sunday night, 18 October 2026

The air-conditioning had been switched to the weekend setting, so Anagha Ghaisas worked with the glass door propped open. The board of Raahdari Technologies Private Limited would meet at nine-thirty the next morning, Monday 19 October 2026, at Nariman Point and on video. Her item was ₹1.13 crore to take the trip ledger from 180 truck owners to 2,000 in the January–March quarter.

Taped to the whiteboard was the sheet she had written on Monday 11 May 2026, before a line of the product existed.

Pinned to the wall, 11 May 2026

We believe an automatic trip ledger — assembled from FASTag toll crossings, UPI diesel payments and a two-tap driver confirmation — will remove per-trip margin blindness for owners of two to eight trucks, while they are doing the job of deciding which loads to accept next week.

We will have been right if, in the cohort onboarded in June 2026, at least 60 per cent of owners are ledger-active in both month 2 and month 3 of their ninety-day window, the 90 days after that owner's onboarding. An owner is ledger-active in a month if, for at least 80 per cent of that month's completed trips, the trip is closed in the app — diesel, driver advance, tolls and freight receipt all entered — within five days of unloading. A trip exists if FASTag or GPS says it happened, not if the app says so. Between 35 and 60 per cent we revise and rerun. Below 35 per cent we stop.

The cohort closed on Saturday 12 September 2026, when the last of the 180 windows ran out. Sixty-four owners were ledger-active in both months: 35.6 per cent, one owner above the line below which she had written that they would stop.

2. The company, and the contract that owns the roadmap

Adwait Gosavi founded Raahdari in 2019 with a trip-sheet app sold to the transport commission agents of Bhosari. It made little money and taught him one thing: the agents, not the owners, decided which loads moved. By 2022 the company had drifted upmarket into visibility software for freight forwarders.

The decision that still shapes every week of engineering was taken on Friday 15 November 2024: a three-year agreement with Rizq Global DMCC, a Jebel Ali forwarder. It runs to 31 December 2027 at ₹3.6 crore a year, carries a 99.5 per cent uptime commitment and a schedule of committed features. Eleven of Raahdari's 28 engineers — 39.3 per cent — sit inside that schedule and cannot be moved without Rizq's consent. In the year to 31 March 2026 it billed ₹8.66 crore: Rizq alone ₹3.6 crore, or 41.6 per cent; other forwarders ₹3.10 crore; and 4,100 small owners on the legacy ₹399-a-month app, ₹1.96 crore.

The trip ledger was the attempt to go back down-market with something that could not be done on paper, at ₹299 a month — a cut Ashima Ginwala has never accepted.

3. The industry

India's road freight market is enormous, fragmented and, where Raahdari operates, almost entirely unbanked. Owners of two to eight trucks hold the bulk of the national fleet, buy diesel on credit, pay drivers in cash advances, and discover their margin, if at all, when the commission agent settles the month. Around them sit well-funded platforms: BlackBuck, built on FASTag and fuel for exactly this segment; Porter and Vahak in load matching; Delhivery and the Tata and Mahindra captive networks higher up; and Raasta Freight Technologies of Gurugram, which gives a trip ledger away free.

Public infrastructure makes the product possible: NPCI's FASTag rails across the NHAI toll network make a truck's movement observable, UPI a diesel payment, the GST e-way bill the consignment. Regulation makes it hard. Under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending framework a sourcing fee must be paid by the lender and not the borrower, and any default-loss guarantee must be funded — Rangoli Finserv, the NBFC Raahdari is negotiating with, has asked verbally for a guarantee it cannot post. Nor is the exposure only Indian: Rizq's payments are in dirhams, and the United States pipeline runs from Edison, New Jersey (Figure B), where Arvind Gulvady sells to shippers with no notion of a commission agent.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Discovery began in January 2026 with field work in Nagpur, Raipur and Durg (Figure A). In April the team surveyed 412 owners on the problem hypothesis: that owners cannot tell which trips lose money and so accept loads that destroy margin. The headline looked decisive: of the 389 actually asked, 276, or 71.0 per cent, could not name a loss-making trip from the previous month. But 23 of the 412 were never asked, the script skipping owners who employed a full-time accountant — precisely those most likely to have answered. Over all 412 approached the share is 276 of 412, or 67.0 per cent — a floor, since it credits all 23 with the answer the team's own reasoning says they were least likely to give.

The solution hypothesis was written on 11 May. Three prototype-and-critique rounds followed between 18 and 29 May: an evening WhatsApp questionnaire, dropped after Anneliese Gerlach pointed out that it made the owner the data-entry clerk; a driver-side two-tap confirmation; and the FASTag-and-UPI build. Onboarding ran 1–14 June: 318 approached, 212 agreed, 180 completed, running 684 trucks (Exhibit 1).

On Monday 31 August Anagha circulated an interim read. Month 2 had closed for every owner by 13 August: the month-2 share was 96 of 180, or 53.3 per cent, and the memo said twice that month 3 was still running for most of the cohort. By mid-September it was the company's number, in Arvind's deck and a note to Rukmavati Partners. The outcome the sheet defined, ledger-active in both months, is 64 of 180, or 35.6 per cent. Both are correct. Only one is the test.

The second error was larger. Exhibit 2 shows how long trips took to close: of the 10,800 trips the cohort ran in months 2 and 3, 4,644 — 43.0 per cent — closed within five days, and a further 3,456 closed late but within thirty days, so 8,100, or 75.0 per cent, closed within thirty. Thirty days is Rangoli's threshold, not Raahdari's: it pools an owner's months 2–3 trips and lends if 70 per cent or more of them closed inside it.

On Tuesday 14 July Ashima's business case made the same move on the only figure then available. Month 3 had not begun for anyone and month 2 only for the earliest onboarded, so she had the 1,240 trips closed at all by 11 July, of which 930 — 75.0 per cent — closed within thirty days: a share of closed trips, which she applied to owners. 135 of 180 would qualify at ₹1,400 per owner-month, or ₹1,89,000 a month. Rangoli's tier memo of 2 October, Exhibit 5, settles it: at owner level, pooling each owner's months 2–3 trips, 104 of 180 — 57.8 per cent — reach 70 per cent, and 104 at ₹1,400 is ₹1,45,600 a month — a shortfall of ₹43,400 a month, ₹5.21 lakh a year. Nothing was mis-multiplied; the population was wrong. The same substitution sits in the Series A plan, which assumes 12,000 owners by March 2028 at 75 per cent qualification: 9,000 qualifiers at ₹1,400 a month is ₹15.12 crore a year. At 57.8 per cent, 6,936 qualifiers is ₹11.65 crore — ₹3.47 crore less. Avneet Gill has written that neither belongs in a plan: the 57.8 per cent came from field staff who visited each owner twice and called weekly, at the cost in Exhibit 3.

From 14 to 22 September, exit interviews reached 142 of the 180; Exhibit 4 is the finding nobody has absorbed. Fifty-eight of 142, 40.8 per cent, said the app told them which trips lose money. Seventy-one, exactly half, said they used it mainly to settle with the driver: the advance, the diesel, what was owed the next morning. The sheet names the job as deciding which loads to accept next week. Half the owners reached describe a job that happens at six in the morning, with a driver in the doorway.

5. The people

Anagha Ghaisas, Vice-President, Product, Pune
Wrote the 11 May sheet and insisted on the stop line; her credibility rests on having pre-committed to it. Not saying: the clause naming the job was chosen in forty seconds and never tested.
Adwait Gosavi, co-founder and Chief Executive, Pune
Wants the money approved: 180 owners settles nothing, and Raasta Freight's free ledger closes the window by March. Not saying: the Series A conversation he opened in September used the 53.3 per cent.
Ashima Ginwala, Chief Financial Officer, Pune
Found her own July error and reported it on 5 October, which has made her the most trusted and most cautious person in the room. Argues for adopting Rangoli's thirty-day rule outright: a paying counterparty settles against it. Not saying: such a ledger is worth nothing to the owner himself.
Amogh Gondhalekar, Vice-President, Engineering, Bengaluru
Will support anything that spares the reconciliation service, built for five-day settlement. Not saying: the two-tap confirmation he shipped fires at 11 p.m. India time, when drivers have no network.
Anneliese Gerlach, Principal Designer, Berlin
On a contract expiring 31 December 2026 at €95,000, ₹93.10 lakh at ₹98 to the euro. Has argued since May that the ledger was designed for an owner at a desk on a Sunday. Not saying: a European client has approached her.
Avneet Gill, Lead Data Scientist, Toronto
Costs CAD 165,000, about ₹1.06 crore a year at ₹64 to the dollar — two and a half times a Bengaluru hire at ₹42 lakh. The only person who has written down that the pilot forecasts nothing, the cohort having been recruited rather than sampled. Not saying: she is the most expensive line in the budget.
Arvind Gulvady, Senior Vice-President, Enterprise Sales, Edison, New Jersey
Carries the enterprise book and is indifferent to a ledger that funds nothing he sells. Not saying: Rizq has asked what happens to its roadmap if the SMB business is scaled.
