6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“The five-day rule is not a product requirement. We chose it because reconciliation holds state for twelve days. Relax it to ten and half this argument goes.” — Amogh Gondhalekar, 7 October

“Then we are measuring a filing cabinet, not a ledger. He does not need to know in ten days what he lost. He needs to know before he hands over the next advance.” — Anagha Ghaisas, same meeting

“Thirty days and five days are not two views of one thing, and neither are trips and owners. In July I had a share of closed trips, and I spent it as a share of owners. That it was 75 per cent then and 75 per cent now is luck, not corroboration.” — Ashima Ginwala, email to the board, 5 October

“Can we stop asking which number to use and ask who the user is. I watched nineteen owners. Not one opened the app on a Sunday; fourteen opened it between 5.40 and 7.10 in the morning, with a driver waiting. We wrote a hypothesis about a planning job and built one for a settlement job.” — Anneliese Gerlach, 9 October

“Nineteen owners out of 180. I cannot put that in a plan. And again: this cohort was not sampled, it was recruited, and every owner had someone call them weekly for a month. The 57.8 per cent is about our field team.” — Avneet Gill, reply, 9 October

“The calls landed on my budget, not my plan. And let me say the rest. My agents closed trips for owners — I do not know how many. When an owner would not do it on day four, the agent did it on day five so the account would not fall out of the pilot. That is inside the 43.0 per cent.” — Audrey Goh, 13 October

“Saheb, the diesel and the advance I know now. Which load is good, my agent in Nagpur tells me, as he has for eleven years. Your app I open when Avadh brings the truck in.” — Ankush Gedam, Ramdhan Roadlines, Nagpur, six trucks

8. The options as Anagha sees them

One: rewrite the hypothesis around settlement. Replace the planning job with the driver-settlement job, strip the app to what works at 6 a.m. on one bar of signal, retest in January. Cheap in engineering, expensive in narrative: it concedes the survey validated a problem the product does not solve.

Two: keep the hypothesis and fix the funnel. Treat 35.6 per cent as a delivery failure, not a hypothesis failure — better onboarding, a driver app that fires at 7 p.m. — and rerun the test. Except that Exhibit 3 shows onboarding already cost ₹5,640 against a plan of ₹2,350: the lever is more of what overspent.

Three: adopt the thirty-day definition. Take Rangoli's rule as the product's outcome, report 57.8 per cent, bank ₹1,45,600 a month and build towards the credit line. It makes the next twelve months solvable, and hands the definition of success to a counterparty whose term sheet is unsigned and whose fee structure is untested against the RBI's.

Four: scale and let the data decide. Onboard 2,000 owners by March and settle it with volume. Adwait's preference. At the pilot's unit cost, 2,000 × ₹5,640 = ₹1.13 crore, about six weeks of net burn — and what would be scaled is the version Gerlach says is used for a job it was not designed for.

All four accept the same frame: that the choice is which threshold to score against. Nobody has written a hypothesis about the driver, who does the two taps and owns none of the outcome, or about the commission agent, who has decided Ankush Gedam's loads for eleven years. And no option carries what the 11 May sheet carried: a population, a window, and a number at which the team agrees to be wrong.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets on Monday and will not reconvene before 14 December. Cash at 30 September 2026 was ₹9.4 crore against net burn of ₹78 lakh a month; at that rate the balance is exhausted in the first week of October 2027. Rukmavati Partners' term sheet is conditional on a December data room. The Rizq contract runs to 31 December 2027, holds 11 of the 28 engineers, and its December release cannot slip. Rangoli's term sheet is unsigned, its guarantee demand unfunded; driver location and wage data sits under the DPDP Act, so the settlement flow Gerlach wants carries the heaviest consent burden. And Diwali is three weeks away, so January is the earliest clean cohort — which does not report until April.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Restate the 11 May sheet in your own words. What population, window and threshold does it commit to, and which does the 35.6 per cent result test?
  2. Exhibit 2 reports 43.0 per cent of trips closed within five days; Exhibit 1 reports 35.6 per cent of owners passing the test. What would you need to relate them, and what does Goh's remark do to both?
  3. Ginwala's July paper multiplied correctly and concluded wrongly. Describe the error in one sentence without a number. Where else on these pages does it survive uncorrected?
  4. Gill says the pilot forecasts nothing. If she is right, what was it for, and what would a cohort have to look like for its rate to belong in a plan?
  5. Exhibit 4 suggests the app is used for a job the sheet does not name. Does that make the hypothesis false, incomplete, or badly worded — and does it change what Raahdari should build, or only what it writes down?
  6. It is Monday morning. Anagha has fifty minutes and one slide. What does she recommend, what does she say about her own stop line, and what does she promise to know by 14 December?

At half past eleven she took the sheet down and read it again. It was still a good sentence: it named a believer, a mechanism, a customer and a job, and a population, a window and a number, so that nobody could argue afterwards about what would have counted. The trouble was that it had been answered: sixty-four of 180, one of them a man whose truck had sat nine days at a check post.

She put the sheet face up and opened a blank page beside it. At the top she wrote We believe, then sat a long time writing nothing else, because she could not decide whether the next word was an owner, or a driver, or an agent in Nagpur — and because whichever she chose, somebody would ask what number would make her give it up.
exp20v2-sol.hypothesis:
Writing a Solution Hypothesis

Discovery and Design, Solution Design and Prototyping. The question: can I state what we believe will solve the problem in a way that can be tested?

1. The meeting on 12 May

On Tuesday, 12 May 2026, Eshika Dhamdhere, head of product at Ujaas Payables in Coimbatore, faced a room of six colleagues and a blank whiteboard. Ujaas sold invoicing software to knitwear manufacturers in Tiruppur, most of them units with ten to forty machines. Her team had spent nine weeks establishing that these owners issued invoices on thirty-day terms, and buyers paid on average 38 days after the due date. Owners borrowed against the gap at roughly 18 per cent a year. The problem was validated, meaning interviews and payment records had shown it real, frequent and costly.

What the room wanted now was a product. The engineering lead, Faizan Dabke, had eleven candidate features, from reminders to a buyer credit-scoring dashboard, each with an advocate. The quarter's engineering budget was about ₹46 lakh, enough for one serious bet, and a wrong choice would surface only in November, after the money was spent.

Dhamdhere did not ask which feature was best. She asked a smaller question: could anyone in the room write down, in one sentence, what they believed would solve the problem, in a form that about ten weeks of evidence could prove wrong? Nobody could.

2. The idea

A solution hypothesis is a falsifiable statement of the form: we believe this concept will solve this problem for this customer while doing this job. A hypothesis is a claim that evidence can contradict. A concept is a described way of solving the problem, rich enough to be tested but not yet a finished product. The customer is a specific kind of person, not a market. The job is the underlying task the customer is trying to get done, a term from the jobs-to-be-done tradition associated with Clayton Christensen and Tony Ulwick in the 1990s and 2000s.

The template descends from Steve Blank's customer development work in the early 2000s and Eric Ries's The Lean Startup (2011). It answers a recurring failure: teams agreed on a problem, jumped to building, and found that "we all agreed" meant five private pictures of the solution.

Each slot closes an escape from refutation. "A reminder tool" without the customer could succeed with large exporters and fail with small units, and the team would call it a success. Without the job, a resented reminder would count as working. The decision rule at the bottom is not part of the classic template, but the best programmes add it, because a sentence without a stated threshold can be read afterwards as confirmed whatever happens.

Dhamdhere's repeatable sentence: "We will not build anything until we can say what result would make us stop."

3. How it works

The mechanics have seven steps; practitioners usually leave steps 3 and 4 implicit.

Step 1 supplies the input: a validated problem. Step 2 is the sentence. Dhamdhere's team wrote six candidates in forty minutes; five were unfalsifiable. "We believe automation will help owners get paid faster" fails because no result would contradict it.

Step 3 is the implicit one. Every concept rests on several assumptions: that buyers read WhatsApp, that owners will let a tool message their buyers, that a payment link shortens delay rather than merely making it easier to pay when buyers intend to anyway. The riskiest assumption is the one that would most damage the concept if wrong and about which least is known. For Ujaas it was that buyers pay sooner when reminded by a payment link, since the others could be fixed later.

Step 4 fixes the decision rule: the results that mean ship, revise or stop, written before any data arrives. Step 5 is the cheapest test that can produce them; step 6 reads it against the rule; step 7 acts, and revising means changing one slot of the sentence.

4. A worked example

Ujaas's cheapest test was not software. For the invoices that 40 consenting units issued in June 2026, a team member sent the reminders by hand from a shared phone, each with a UPI pay link, so the stated assumption was tested. Each unit issued 24 invoices between Monday 1 June and Tuesday 30 June, and Faizan Dabke's script randomly assigned 12 of each unit's invoices to receive reminders and 12 to serve as a control. That gives 40 × 12 = 480 invoices per arm. The outcome measure was the share of invoices in an arm paid within seven days of the due date. The last due date was Thursday 30 July, so the last measurement closed on Thursday 6 August, and the readout was on Monday 10 August.

The decision rule had two parts. First, the economics. An average invoice was ₹1,80,000. A converted invoice is paid at most 7 days late, so it saves at most 31 of the 38 days; the 38 is an average over all invoices, including those already paid on time. At 18 per cent a year, 31 days of financing on ₹1,80,000 is ₹1,80,000 × 0.18 × 31 / 365, about ₹2,752. Reminders cost an estimated ₹150 per reminded invoice. Break-even lift is therefore 150 / 2,752, about 5.5 percentage points. The team set the bar just above it: scale if the lower end of the 95 per cent confidence interval (95 per cent of intervals built this way contain the true lift) was at least 6 points.

Table 1. First pass. Denominator: 480 invoices in each arm.
LineReminder armControl arm
Invoices in arm480480
Paid within 7 days of due date216144
On-time rate45.0%30.0%
Lift (45.0 minus 30.0)15.0 points

This is the simple two-proportion version, treating invoices as independent although they cluster in 40 units. The standard error, which measures how much the lift would wobble from sample to sample, is the square root of (0.45 × 0.55 / 480 + 0.30 × 0.70 / 480). That is the square root of (0.000516 + 0.000438), or 0.0309. Multiplying by 1.96 gives a margin of 6.05 points, so the interval runs from 8.9 to 21.1 points. The lower end clears 6, so the rule says scale. At 15 points, the saving is 0.15 × ₹2,752 = ₹413 per invoice, less ₹150, a net ₹263.

Second pass, one input changed. Suppose the reminder arm had 192 on-time payments, 40.0 per cent, and the control stayed at 144. The lift is 10.0 points, which exceeds 6, and a careless reader would ship. But the standard error becomes the square root of (0.40 × 0.60 / 480 + 0.000438), or 0.0306, the margin 6.0 points, and the interval 4.0 to 16.0. The lower end is below 6, and indeed below the 5.5 break-even. Net value at the point estimate is ₹275 less ₹150, ₹125 per invoice, but a loss cannot be ruled out. The rule says revise, probably by testing longer or on more units.

The same idea and a respectable point estimate lead to opposite decisions once uncertainty is counted.

5. Nuances

Hypothesis versus feature request

"Build reminders" is an instruction. A hypothesis says what will change for whom if reminders are built, and so can be wrong. The quick test: if no outcome could embarrass the statement, it is a plan.

Solution versus problem hypothesis

A problem hypothesis says owners suffer from late payment. A solution hypothesis says this concept will relieve it. Evidence for the first is no evidence for the second; owners can suffer real pain and still reject every remedy offered.

The concept is not the product

The test used a human with a phone. A concept describes a mechanism, and the hypothesis survives changes of technology while the mechanism holds.

Customer specificity cuts both ways

Naming "owners of 10 to 40 machine units" lets the result be trusted for that group, and nothing more. Too narrow, and the result concerns a market too small to matter; too broad, and nobody can interpret it.

Jobs versus features

The job is "chase buyers without damaging the relationship", not "send messages". Elumalai Dhandapani, who ran a 22-machine unit in Tiruppur, told the team he feared a robotic message more than a late payment. A hypothesis ignoring the job would have missed that.

Statistical weight is not proof of value

A significant lift says the reminder worked in June, in this sample, with a human sender. It does not say buyers will tolerate automation.

Confused with a forecast

A forecast predicts a number; a hypothesis commits to a decision. "We expect 15 points" is a forecast. "Below 6 at the lower bound, we revise" is a hypothesis with consequences.

What it cannot tell you

It cannot generate the idea, cannot say whether the problem deserved solving, and cannot value anything outside the stated slots. A newcomer should ask: what would I do differently if this were false? If the answer is nothing, the hypothesis is decoration.

6. Across product types and company sizes

Table 2. How the four slots shift by context.
ContextWhat changesTypical evidence
ConsumerCustomer is broad, so segment first; the job is often emotionalBehaviour of hundreds or thousands of users in days
B2BBuyer, user and payer differ; a sentence may need two customersA handful of accounts, commitments such as signed pilots
MarketplaceTwo sides, so two hypotheses that depend on each otherSupply and demand tested in one narrow city or category

Consumer volume permits fast quantitative tests, but "everyone" is not a customer. In B2B, as at Ujaas, samples are small, so the rule must lean on commitments more than statistics. In a marketplace, each side's willingness depends on the other, so the hypothesis must name which side is seeded first.

Size matters too. An early-stage company can test a concept with a phone and a spreadsheet. A large company has more data but more people with different pictures of the solution, so the written sentence works as a coordination device.

7. Common mistakes

Table 3. Symptoms, misunderstandings and diagnostics.
MistakeSymptom from outsideMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Solution disguised as a problemThe "problem" slot names a missing featureDescribing absence of the solution as painDelete the concept; does the problem still read as a hardship?
Unfalsifiable wordingEveryone nods; no number appearsVague agreement equals alignmentAsk: what result makes us stop?
Threshold set after the dataThe bar moves toward the resultThe rule is a formalityCheck the document's timestamp against the data's
Testing the easiest assumptionLots of green results, no change in planConfusing activity with learningRank assumptions on damage and uncertainty

When a team writes "owners lack a reminder tool", the sentence has already assumed its answer. The cure is the deletion test in the table. The third is corrosive: the threshold drifts until the result passes, and the organisation learns that tests decorate decisions already made.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the 12 May meeting ends with one sentence on the whiteboard and a number beside it. The team has ranked its assumptions, chosen the riskiest, and agreed that a manual test costing about ₹72,000 (480 reminded invoices at ₹150) and ten weeks is cheaper than any build. Faizan Dabke is asked not what to build but what the test needs, and the answer is a randomisation script.

9. Closing

On Monday 10 August, Dhamdhere saw the first-pass result and followed the rule. She approved reminders as the quarter's bet, but limited the first release to the 40 pilot units plus 60 more, and wrote a second, narrower hypothesis: that automated messages, not human-sent ones, would hold the lift. She also asked that Dhandapani's concern about robotic tone be tested explicitly. Had the second-pass numbers arrived, she would have extended the test, because the interval could not exclude a loss.

To go further, read about what an MVP is. A minimum viable product is best seen as a vehicle for learning with a decision rule attached, so the sentence you have just learned to write becomes its specification. After that, study how a product requirements document is structured, since it carries the sentence forward to engineers.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of a feature currently on your team's roadmap: what result, specifically, would make you remove it, and has anyone written that down? Second, if the customer slot in your own hypothesis were narrowed by half, would your confidence in the result rise or fall, and what would that tell you about the market you are really serving?
case40v1-sol.ideation:
Saptak Systems: 118 Ideas, Three Pilots and One Quarter to Spend

Saptak Systems, Samaa Health Group, Sampriti Path Labs, Saroja Diagnostics and Samvaad Field Cloud are fictional; the market, regulators and brands around them are real.

1. Sunday night, Koramangala

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 18 October 2026, Bhuvana Hombarde was still in Saptak Systems' Koramangala office, photographing a wall. It held 118 index cards in five columns, one for each “how might we” question written in September. Nine carried a red dot; three of the nine carried a second dot, in blue, for the pilots that had closed a week earlier. The other 109 carried nothing, which Bhuvana had begun to find the uncomfortable part.

At half past nine next morning, Monday, 19 October, she had to tell Saptak's build-commit meeting what the fourteen working weeks to end-January would carry, and on Friday, 30 October tell the board the same in one slide. On 31 March 2027 a clause in Saptak's contract with Samaa Health Group of Dubai would measure one number — home blood-collection visits completed on the first attempt — and either leave Saptak's largest contract intact or take ₹14.70 lakh of credits out of it.

All three pilots had worked. That was the problem. They worked by amounts that could not be told apart, in three Indian cities, on a metric written into a contract for a city in another country — and the idea the panel scored highest had never been built.

2. Saptak Systems, 2017–2026

Saptak was founded in Bengaluru in 2017 by Bharti Hoskote, a pathology-chain operations head, and Bikram Hundekari, who had written routing software in Pune. The product was unglamorous: dispatch for home sample collection, in which a phlebotomist rides to a flat in Gomti Nagar or RS Puram and gets the sample to a laboratory inside a cold-chain window. By 30 September 2026 Saptak had ₹41.50 crore of annual recurring revenue, nine laboratory-chain clients and 198 employees: 126 in Bengaluru, 48 in Pune, nine in Singapore, six in New Jersey, four in Dubai, three in Toronto, two in Berlin.

One decision shaped everything after. On Friday, 18 March 2022, to win its first large contract, Saptak agreed to run dispatch through the client's own Android application rather than ship its own phlebotomist app. The architecture was a cage: Saptak owned the booking flow, the dispatch engine and the patient's messages, but not the screen in the phlebotomist's hand. Changes to that screen entered the client's release train, six to fourteen weeks long, and Saptak's view of field work came from nine differently instrumented apps.

3. The industry

Indian diagnostics in 2026 was consolidating and price-competitive. Dr Lal PathLabs, Metropolis Healthcare, Thyrocare and Redcliffe Labs competed on test menus and turnaround; Tata 1mg, PharmEasy and Apollo 24|7 competed for the patient's first click. None sold what Saptak sold: its real competitors were each client's own chief technology officer and Samvaad Field Cloud, a Hyderabad start-up that took two mid-sized chains in 2025.

Three regulatory facts bore on it. NABL accreditation governed the sample chain and ICMR guidance who could draw blood, and where. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governed consent for every message sent to an Indian patient, and Saptak's consent ledger was an unfinished obligation, not an asset. Samaa's visits sat in the United Arab Emirates under Federal Decree-Law 45 of 2021, which Dubai read differently from the way Bengaluru read the DPDP Act.

The force nobody regulated was expectation: a patient who could watch a Zepto rider approach on a map did not accept a four-hour window and a call that might not come. Byron Hauser, selling into American laboratory networks from New Jersey, wanted a live technician ETA to demonstrate and had none.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In mid-2026 Saptak did something it had never done properly: it validated the problem first. Between 15 June and 3 July two product managers ran 96 patient interviews in Lucknow, Indore and Coimbatore, and 41 ride-alongs. In the July–September 2026 quarter the platform scheduled 12,40,000 home collection visits and completed 9,79,600 of them on the first attempt — 79.0 per cent. Each of the remaining 2,60,400 cost a laboratory about ₹126 to recover — ₹74 of time and travel, ₹31 of consumables and cold chain, ₹21 of call-centre work — and a third never converted. A September survey asked patients why; the apps' logs told another story (Exhibits 6a and 6b).

From Monday, 14 to Wednesday, 16 September, Brinda Hansoti flew from Berlin to run a three-day divergence sprint: five “how might we” questions, three rounds of Crazy 8s in Bengaluru, a parallel engineering room in Pune, a field workshop with thirteen phlebotomists in Indore, an asynchronous wall for Berlin, and one call Singapore and Dubai could join. It produced 162 raw ideas, de-duplicated to 118 (Exhibits 1 and 2; Illustrations 1 and 2). An eleven-person panel scored them and shortlisted nine (Exhibit 3). Three were piloted from Monday, 21 September to Sunday, 11 October, data cut Wednesday, 14 October (Exhibit 4, Illustration 3).

Four things believed in September were no longer believed on 18 October. Bikram's estimate for the two-hour slot window had been 52 person-weeks in September, 71 in early October and 88 at the cut. The Indore micro-hub had been staffed, at the client's initiative, with two hand-picked seniors. Bo Hanley could not get pin-code controls in Coimbatore and matched on district. And the self-collection kit's regulatory impossibility, ranked third by the panel, rested on an assertion in a slide, not on any approach to CDSCO or NABL.

5. The people

Bhuvana Hombarde, VP Product, Bengaluru, owns the commitment. She believes the validation but suspects the nine shortlisted ideas sample one room's taste, not the 118. Her bonus rides on the Samaa gate; she has not said she thinks it measures the wrong thing.

Bharti Hoskote, co-founder and chief executive, wants two board sentences: Saptak holds Samaa, and Saptak ships discovery fast. She is indifferent between the pilots and will not say so.

Bikram Hundekari, co-founder and chief technology officer, Pune, argues for the two-hour slot window: the one candidate a competitor cannot copy in a quarter. He has not volunteered that his estimate rose from 52 to 88 person-weeks in five weeks, nor that routing needs a screen he cannot control.

Brinda Hansoti, principal designer, Berlin, facilitated the sprint and wants a second round of divergence on the six untested ideas; her retainer turns on design outcomes. She has not mentioned that she set the Crazy 8s rounds for 10:00–13:00 India time: 06:30 in Berlin, 12:30 in Singapore, half past midnight in Toronto and New Jersey.

Bo Hanley, data scientist, Toronto, wrote the pilot analysis and will not sign a ranking. He slept through the sprint and wrote up six ideas afterwards, none shortlisted. He wants decisions made on measurement.

Bhakti Huilgol, head of customer success, Singapore, argues for the micro-hub: no code, the laboratories' operations heads asked for it, and it can start in November. Measured on Asian-account retention, she knows the Indore hub ran with hand-picked staff, and has told Bo, not Bhuvana.

Bhaumik Hirapara, finance head, keeps pointing out that Exhibit 5's rework saving is the laboratories' money while the rollout cost is Saptak's. He wants the cheapest route to 88.0 per cent in Dubai and, with the Series C data room open, no new recurring cost.

Byron Hauser, SVP Sales, New Jersey, wants the live ETA because he can demonstrate it. He has not said that the prospect he cites asked for SMS reminders, a different build, or that his quota excludes Samaa.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Eighty-eight person-weeks buys the only thing on that wall a competitor cannot ship in a quarter. The rest is messaging.”Bikram Hundekari, engineering channel, 15 October
“We have ₹87.60 lakh left after the pilots — enough for the ETA and the micro-hub. Give me the ETA and I have a reference logo by February.”Byron Hauser, email to Bhuvana, 16 October
“Two corrections. The pilots were charged to the second-quarter innovation line and are sunk; this budget is intact at ₹110.00 lakh, less ₹18.50 lakh for the consent ledger: ₹91.50 lakh. And the ₹10.71 crore of rework avoided in Exhibit 5 is our clients' money. Ours is the ₹14.70 lakh of credits if Dubai misses the gate.”Bhaumik Hirapara, reply, 16 October
“Someone's sheet divides year-one completions by pilot cost and gets 64,952 per lakh for the micro-hub against 47,412 for the ETA. That compares a rollout outcome with a three-week test bill; the micro-hub's year-one cost is ₹94.18 lakh. Divide like with like.”Bo Hanley, note of 17 October
“Pilot A measured consented patients. Multiply 6.5 points by 71.3 per cent coverage and the platform expectation is 4.63 points; for Samaa, at 84.0 per cent, 5.46 — though that borrows an Indian consent figure for Dubai and assumes unconsented patients gain nothing. The gate asks 6.6. All three intervals overlap, so I cannot tell you B beats A, or A beats C.”Bo Hanley, same note
“The Indore hub ran with Bhanupriya Halkude and one other senior. Of course it looked good. Put a new joiner on it in December.”Bhakti Huilgol, client call notes, 13 October
“Three days, five questions, one of which never got a round. H4 has fourteen ideas and we tested none. If a self-collection kit works for the routine panels, the first-attempt metric stops mattering for that volume. We did not diverge; we converged in a room with a view of Hosur Road.”Brinda Hansoti, voice note from Berlin, 17 October
“We will read 88.0 per cent for January to March on our own visits. I understand you have evidence from Uttar Pradesh. We do not schedule in Uttar Pradesh.”Bilal Haddad, COO, Samaa Health Group, 9 October

8. The options as Bhuvana sees them

Option 1: ship A alone. ₹44.05 lakh of Saptak's money, 40 person-weeks, no change to any phlebotomist screen, live by mid-January. Byron gets his demonstration. But the 6.5 points were measured on consented patients in Lucknow, and the gate is in Dubai.

Option 2: ship B alone. ₹69.70 lakh and 88 person-weeks, on an estimate that has moved twice. The highest point estimate, +7.0 points, and the only candidate Bikram considers defensible. It needs a change inside client release trains of six to fourteen weeks, putting the Samaa quarter at the mercy of someone else's roadmap, and its control was matched by district.

Option 3: ship C, and spend the engineering quarter elsewhere. ₹2.92 lakh of Saptak's money and no code. It asks three laboratory partners to absorb ₹91.26 lakh a year no contract obliges, on a result from two hand-picked phlebotomists in one city.

Option 4: refuse the shortlist. Four weeks of fresh divergence on H3, H4 and the six untested ideas, then build in January. It forfeits the Samaa quarter and the ₹14.70 lakh, and Bharti cannot take it to the board.

All four share two unwritten assumptions. The first is that the objective is first-attempt completion, because that is the number in the Samaa clause — although Bo Hanley's appendix shows completion within forty-eight hours at 96.2 per cent in the Lucknow treatment arm against 95.4 per cent in its control, a gap of 0.8 points with an interval of ±0.8 that just reaches zero: not distinguishable from zero, but not excluded. The second is that the choice set is the nine. The gate is narrow: Samaa's 36,500 visits out of the quarter's 12,40,000 are 2.9 per cent of platform volume, while its ₹4.90 crore of recurring revenue is 11.8 per cent of Saptak's ₹41.50 crore.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Money: ₹110.00 lakh of discretionary product spend for 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027, less ₹18.50 lakh for the DPDP consent ledger, leaving ₹91.50 lakh. A and B together would cost ₹113.75 lakh and cannot both be funded.

People: 140 assignable person-weeks in the fourteen working weeks to 30 January, after Diwali week from 8 November — six engineers in Bengaluru at ₹0.62 lakh a person-week, three in Pune at ₹0.58 lakh, half of Brinda's time at ₹1.95 lakh and half of Bo's at ₹1.70 lakh: ₹101.99 lakh if every week is used. The nine shortlisted ideas need 334 person-weeks.

Regulation and contract: no message to an Indian patient without a consent record; no change to sample handling without NABL comfort; no self-collection device without a CDSCO view nobody has sought; and a Samaa clause measuring Dubai visits from 1 January to 31 March 2027 against 88.0 per cent, from 81.4 per cent today, a figure Samaa reports and Saptak cannot audit, with ₹14.70 lakh of credits behind it.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What did the September sprint produce — 162 ideas, 118, nine, or three? Which belongs on Bhuvana's board slide, and why?
  2. Exhibits 6a and 6b bear on the same 420 visits over bases of 286 and 420, and disagree. What can Saptak conclude about why first attempts fail, and what would it measure instead?
  3. Exhibit 5 ranks the pilots two ways, and row A changes rank with the base chosen. Which denominator belongs with which decision?
  4. The panel's highest-scored idea was never piloted; the piloted ones ranked second, fifth and eighth. Does Exhibit 4 tell you anything about the six untested ideas?
  5. Suppose the pilot results are real and transferable. Does any take Samaa from 81.4 to 88.0 per cent by 31 March 2027? If not, what follows?
  6. It is Monday morning, 19 October. What does Bhuvana commit the fourteen weeks to, whom must she disappoint, and what three sentences does she give the board on 30 October, including what she does not know?

11. Later that night

Bhuvana turned off the lights and left the wall lit by her phone. The nine red dots sat two to a column except in H4's, which had one. That column, about not travelling at all, held fourteen cards, and she could not remember a minute of argument about them. She thought about Brinda's room with a view of Hosur Road, about Bilal Haddad's sentence that Samaa did not schedule in Uttar Pradesh, and about the cheapest thing she had tested being the costliest to run.

Her laptop showed a half-written slide titled Build commit, Q3 FY27, with one bullet: We ran the process. Here is what we learned. She had not decided the second bullet. At twenty past midnight she wrote three option names on a sticky note, pocketed it and went down to the car park without choosing.
exp20v2-sol.ideation:
Ideation: Diverging Before Converging

Brainstorming, Crazy 8s and "How might we" questions, and the test for having generated enough options.

1. A slot with one idea in it

On Monday 9 March 2026, Gunita Fadnis, head of product at Vaikhari Kitchens, had a decision due on Thursday 12 March. Vaikhari sells weekday-lunch subscriptions in Bengaluru and Hyderabad, cooked in two kitchens and delivered by bike. The engineering roadmap held one open six-week slot, from 13 April, with six engineers. Harshil Fakhri, the chief executive, wanted it filled by Thali Remix, a recipe-refresh feature inspired by his own cooking, which would cost ₹26 lakh to build.

The problem was not in dispute. Of the 9,300 subscribers active on 1 October 2025, 1,240 (13.3 per cent) had lapsed, meaning thirty days without an order, by 31 December. At an average ₹3,500 a month, that was ₹43.4 lakh of monthly billings. Hemlin Fidai, the researcher based in Singapore, had interviewed 60 lapsed subscribers between 12 January and 20 February. She asked all 60 why they stopped, and 41 of them (68.3 per cent) said the meals had begun to feel repetitive by about the third week.

Fadnis's worry was narrower than whether Thali Remix was good. It was the first answer anyone had proposed, and nobody had proposed a different one. If she committed the slot and the feature failed to move lapses, the next free slot fell in June, and another quarter of lapses would pass first. She needed a defensible answer to a question that sounds soft: have we generated enough alternatives to be allowed to choose?

The figure shows why she was uneasy. A team that starts converging at the left edge, with one option, is not choosing; it is ratifying. The rest of this page explains how to widen the band deliberately, how to tell when it is wide enough, and what the band cannot do for you.

2. The idea

Ideation is the deliberate production of many candidate solutions to a problem already shown to matter, before any of them is chosen. It exists to correct a habit: teams treat the first workable answer as the answer, because it arrives early, carries its proposer's authority and feels like progress. Three tools, each guarding a different part of the process, sit under the heading.

ToolWhat it isOrigin
BrainstormingA group session producing options under a rule of deferred judgementAlex Osborn, an advertising executive at BBDO; described in Applied Imagination (1953)
Crazy 8sEight rough sketches of eight different ideas, one minute each, drawn aloneAssociated with Jake Knapp at Google and Google Ventures; set out in Sprint (2016)
How might we (HMW)A question that frames a problem so that it invites answers without containing oneUsually credited to Min Basadur at Procter & Gamble in the 1970s; spread by IDEO and Stanford's d.school

The sentence Fadnis could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: "Before we pick, we owe the decision options that differ in mechanism, not just in wording." The last phrase carries the weight. Ten variations on a recipe card are one idea, ten times.

3. How it actually works

Fadnis ran the session on Tuesday 10 March with six people: herself, Hetansh Fatnani (design lead), Gulbahar Faldu (operations, Hyderabad kitchen), Fidai on video from Singapore, and two engineers. Five steps, two of which are usually left implicit.

Frame the question. A "how might we" question has three working words: "how" assumes a solution exists, "might" licenses ideas that may fail, "we" makes the answer shared. Too broad ("HMW fix retention") yields slogans; too narrow ("HMW add a recipe card to the box") smuggles in the answer. Fadnis wrote: "How might we make the fifteenth lunch feel as considered as the first?" Fifteen is five weekdays across three weeks, taken from Fidai's interviews.

Sketch alone, against the clock. Each person folds a sheet into eight panels and fills one panel per minute for eight minutes, a different idea in each. The clock forces past the obvious first idea, which is the point.

Share and cluster. Sheets go on the wall. The group merges duplicates and groups what remains by mechanism, meaning the way an idea is supposed to change behaviour. Check coverage is the implicit step: count distinct ideas and mechanisms, and ask whether new sketches are still opening new mechanisms. Narrow comes last, by dot vote, with each person holding three dots.

4. A worked example

Six people at 8 sketches each produced 48. After merging duplicates, 36 distinct ideas remained. They fell into six mechanisms:

MechanismDistinct ideasDots (of 18)
Menu variety and rotation97
Schedule flexibility (skip, swap, pause)85
Portion, price and bundle62
Social and office ordering52
Delivery timing and packaging41
Taste personalisation41
Total3618

Variety held 9 of 36 ideas (25 per cent) but drew 7 of 18 dots (38.9 per cent): the room's attention ran ahead of its supply, as it does when the chief executive's idea is in the category. Eighteen dots is six voters times three.

This is the answer to Fadnis's question. Raw idea count was still climbing: sketches 6 to 8 added 12 distinct ideas, taking the total from 24 to 36. Mechanisms were not: the sixth appeared at the fifth sketch, and the last three rounds opened none. So the team had enough breadth to converge, even though it had not exhausted its ideas.

Convergence then used a rough expected-value screen. Retained subscribers equal the 1,240 who lapsed in the quarter to December, times the share of them an idea reaches, times the share of those it saves. Cost is the cost to build and run the full feature. The 70 per cent reach for concept A rounds up Fidai's 68.3 per cent who cited repetition; the other reach and save rates are the team's judgement, which is why the table is a screen and not a forecast. The 60 interviewees were 4.8 per cent of the 1,240, so the 70 per cent assumes they speak for the rest.

ConceptReachSave rateRetainedCost (₹ lakh)Retained per ₹ lakh
A: regional menu weeks (variety)70%10%86.8421.7
B: swap-a-meal (flexibility)45%15%83.799.3
C: office group ordering (social)20%30%74.4145.3

Second pass, one input changed. Suppose a cheap fake-door test shows A's save rate is 4 per cent, not 10. Retained falls to 1,240 times 0.70 times 0.04, or 34.7, and retained per lakh to 8.7. B, at 9.3, now leads. With B at its assumed 15 per cent, A beats B only if its save rate exceeds 4.3 per cent (B's 9.3 per lakh times A's ₹4 lakh is 37.2 retained, divided by 868 reachable). The leader flips on one input nobody has measured. That is the argument for generating across mechanisms: the runner-up was a different mechanism, so the flip had somewhere to land.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Quantity is a means, not the measure

Osborn's slogan was that quantity breeds quality, and Figure 3 shows the mild truth in it: more sketches produced more ideas. But the count that matters is distinct mechanisms. Forty-eight variants of one mechanism leaves the decision exactly as narrow as one. The tension is real, and the resolution is to count mechanisms.

Groups talking can produce less than people writing

Michael Diehl and Wolfgang Stroebe's 1987 experiments found that people brainstorming aloud in groups generated fewer ideas than the same number of people working alone and pooled afterwards. One cause is production blocking: only one person can speak, so others wait and forget. Hence silent sketching first, discussion second.

It diverges from a validated problem

Ideation multiplies answers; it does not check the question. Had Fidai's 41 of 60 been 8 of 60, forty-eight sketches would have been polished answers to a minor complaint.

Crazy 8s suits some questions better than others

Sketching favours interface, flow and packaging ideas. Pricing, policy and operating-model ideas are awkward to draw, so the sheet quietly under-samples them. Notice what your format cannot produce.

An HMW is not a requirement, and not a goal

"HMW increase retention by 5 per cent" is a target. "HMW add Thali Remix" is a solution. A useful HMW names a person, a moment and a tension, and leaves the mechanism open.

It cannot tell you which idea works

The reach and save rates above are guesses, and the screen merely arranges them. Only a test, with a decision rule written beforehand, converts a guess into evidence. A clustered wall and a dot vote measure enthusiasm.

Questions to ask before relying on it

Who was in the room, and whose perspective was missing, such as delivery riders or the kitchen? Which constraint did everyone silently accept? Would the winner survive a change in its least certain input, as A would not have if its save rate were 4 per cent?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

SettingWhat changes
ConsumerCheap, fast tests are available, so ideation can run weekly and the dot vote can be provisional.
B2BThe buyer, user and payer differ; sketches must name which of them an idea serves, and customer interviews replace fake doors.
MarketplaceEvery idea has two sides; a rider-side fix can damage the customer side, so each sketch must state both.
Early-stageThree people can run it in an hour; the risk is that the founder's idea anchors the rest.
Large companyMore voices and dependencies; the risk is a polished process that produces many ideas inside one inherited mechanism.

Vaikhari sits between categories: a consumer subscription with a supply side (two kitchens). Gulbahar Faldu's presence mattered because several sketches changed what a kitchen can prepare, and only she could say at what cost.

7. Common mistakes

MistakeSymptom from outsideMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Aloud firstIdeas cluster around the first one spokenDiscussion equals generationCompare distinct counts to raw counts: a low ratio signals anchoring
Counting ideas"We had 60 ideas" but one mechanismVolume equals breadthSort the wall by mechanism and count the piles
Voting before testingThe founder's category wins the dotsPopularity equals evidenceAsk what number would change the ranking

In Vaikhari's case the second symptom was visible on Monday: Thali Remix was one mechanism, and every suggestion made that Monday was a variant of it.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Thursday's decision looks like this. The question is framed as an HMW and agreed in writing. Six people sketch alone for eight minutes. The wall is sorted by mechanism, coverage is plotted as in Figure 3, and the team notes that mechanisms stopped appearing. The shortlist contains at least two ideas of different mechanisms. Each carries the number most likely to be wrong, and the decision to proceed is tied to a test with a threshold agreed beforehand. Nobody leaves believing that the best idea has been found; they leave believing that the cheapest wrong choice has been ruled out.

9. Closing

On Thursday 12 March, Fadnis told Fakhri she would not commit the slot to Thali Remix, which belonged to the variety mechanism (concept A's category). She proposed instead two parallel two-week fake-door tests, one for A and one for B, each measuring reach and save rate, with a rule written beforehand: build whichever shows the higher measured retained subscribers per ₹ lakh of build cost (₹4 lakh for A, ₹9 lakh for B).

Her reasoning was the page's argument in short: diverge until new mechanisms stop appearing, converge on a shortlist that spans mechanisms, and let a measured number decide. What to learn next is "Generating and comparing solution alternatives," which supplies better ways to compare than a dot vote, and then design sprints, which place Crazy 8s inside a week of prototype, test and critique.

Two questions to sit with. First, in the last decision you made, how many alternatives differed in mechanism rather than wording? Second, what single unmeasured number would flip your current favourite, and what is the cheapest way to measure it?
exp40v2-sol.ideation:
Ideation: brainstorming, Crazy 8s, and How Might We

Generating enough alternatives before converging on one — what the practice is, what the evidence says, and where competent practitioners disagree.

1. Two decisions

On Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Harshada Fozdar had ninety minutes of her team's calendar and no good way to spend it. Fozdar is group product manager at Vidura Credit Systems, a Bengaluru firm whose collections software runs inside eleven non-banking financial companies. Discovery had closed on a problem she trusted: of 4,800 field-collection visits allocated in August 2026 and all since closed, 1,488 ended without contact with the borrower — 31 per cent. The agents' explanation was mundane: nobody is home, and the app offers nothing to do next. A board paper was due on Tuesday, 3 November 2026, and Vidura's chief technology officer had named the answer: a route optimiser.

Her difficulty was not that the route optimiser was wrong, but that it was the only candidate anyone had articulated. Eighteen months earlier the same room had converged in one meeting on a dialler integration that shipped, worked and moved nothing.

Two days later, on Thursday, 8 October 2026, Gandhar Falnikar had a different problem in Pune. Falnikar heads product at Vartul Devices, which sells a ₹11,900 connected room air purifier direct to Indian households and has 38,000 units in the field. Of the 22,000 units ever connected to the companion app, 10,120 were running a filter past its rated life — 46 per cent. He wrote in every memo that this is measured over connected units only, and that the 16,000 never connected are a different, probably worse population. Tooling for the next housing revision freezes on Monday, 16 November 2026: if the answer involved geometry he had barely six weeks.

Both faced the question this topic exists to answer: have I generated enough alternatives before converging on one? Neither could answer it by introspection, and the standard answer — hold a brainstorm — has the widest gap between folklore and evidence in product practice.

2. The idea, and five camps

Ideation, stated precisely, is the deliberate production of structurally distinct candidate solutions to an already-validated problem, under a rule that defers selection until generation is finished. Each qualifier is load-bearing, and each is usually dropped. Without a validated problem, ideation is a well-facilitated argument about preferences. Without structural distinctness, fifty sticky notes can be one idea at fifty fidelities. Without deferral, the first legible proposal anchors the room and everything after it is commentary.

Alex Osborn published Applied Imagination in 1953 with four rules — defer judgement, pursue quantity, welcome wild ideas, build on others — aimed at advertising teams that settled on the first presentable campaign. Min Basadur later added that the hard part is problem-finding, and gave the field the form How might we…, whose grammar concedes that the answer is plural. Michael Diehl and Wolfgang Stroebe then established that face-to-face groups produce fewer and worse ideas than the same people alone, for three reasons: production blocking, evaluation apprehension and social loafing. Karan Girotra, Christian Terwiesch and Karl Ulrich showed in 2010 that the fix is structural — individuals generate alone, then the group builds and screens — and that this hybrid beats the pure group on both idea count and best-idea quality. Crazy 8s, eight sketches in eight minutes, reached product teams through the design-sprint format, a fourth tradition: constraint, not permission, produces divergence. Engineers got there first: Toyota's set-based concurrent engineering carried several designs deep into development and narrowed late.

Those traditions do not agree. The facilitation school signs: the binding constraint is premature convergence, and a facilitator relieves it; it will not sign that a group out-produces the same people alone. The structural school signs: sequence and artefact determine output; it will not sign that the room is where ideas come from. The constraint school signs: eight minutes and eight boxes beat a free day; it will not sign that more time yields more options. The reframing school signs: most poor ideation is competent ideation against a badly framed question; it will not sign that volume is the metric. The options school signs: the count worth generating is a function of option cost and value variance; it will not sign that divergence is intrinsically good. A sixth position, held by operators, signs none of it: ideas are not scarce, willingness to kill is.

3. Mechanics, and the arithmetic

Expert practice begins before the session, with an input contract. Discovery at Vidura closed on Friday, 27 June 2025; on Wednesday, 9 July 2025 Fozdar ran ninety minutes with five people and spent the first twenty testing the question rather than generating ideas. A How Might We has an altitude, and altitude is testable: she wrote three versions of the question, ran a six-minute silent round on each with the same five people, and had two raters cluster the output into families. Two proposals share a family if killing either on principle would kill the other.

The broad question produced the most ideas and the worst ratio: 44 ideas across 4 families, 11.0 each, nearly all restatements of nudge, discount, penalty and call. The narrow question produced 12 ideas in 2 families, having already chosen the solution. The mid-altitude question produced 36 ideas — eight fewer than the broad one — across 9 families, more than twice the broad question's 4. Fozdar's rule follows: a question is at the right altitude when five people produce five structurally different solutions in the first three minutes of a six-minute round, none of them the obvious one.

With the question fixed, generation was hybrid: six minutes of silent solo writing, a Crazy 8s round of eight concepts in eight minutes, then a round-robin in which people could only extend somebody else's sketch. Three rounds of eight, twenty-four in all, each scored with one forward estimate — the additional annual recovery, in ₹ lakh, the team believed it would produce. These are forecasts, not measurements.

The sums are 140 + 230 + 254 = 624, so the mean across twenty-four ideas is 624 ÷ 24 = ₹26.0 lakh. The median is ₹22 lakh: the twelfth and thirteenth sorted values are both 22. A mean above the median is the signature of right skew, and the skew is the whole quantitative case for divergence, because a team takes away the maximum, not the average. The best of the first eight was 31; of the first sixteen, 61; of all twenty-four, 73. Ideas nine to sixteen added 61 − 31 = 30; seventeen to twenty-four added 73 − 61 = 12. The three best — 73, 61 and 52 — sum to 186, which is 186 of the 624 lakh of estimated value, or 29.8 per cent.

Two second-order effects are visible in the picture and invisible in the room. The build-on round carried both the largest sum (254) and the best single idea (73): the group's value is recombination, not generation. And the curve is a staircase with long flat stretches, so a team that stops when ideas stop feeling new stops on a plateau — ideas seventeen to twenty-two added nothing, then idea twenty-three added 12.

4. Conditions you can test

Four conditions make wide divergence worth its cost, and each can be checked.

C1. The problem is validated and its evidence is physically on the table.
Fozdar passes: 1,488 failed visits out of 4,800. Falnikar passes with his own caveat — the 46 per cent is over 22,000 connected units, not all 38,000.
C2. The value distribution is right-skewed and the tail is unpredictable.
Vidura's exhibit shows both halves: mean 26.0 against median 22, and the winner arriving twenty-third. Vartul is weaker: for a filter-life problem the plausible families are few.
C3. Generating an option costs far less than testing one.
True in both, by very different ratios.
C4. A selection rule exists before generation starts.
Fozdar had one. Falnikar did not, and his tooling freeze was quietly doing the selecting.

Where is the idea actively misleading? When a single hard requirement dominates — a regulatory deadline, one mandated integration — the solution space is a point and divergence manufactures false choice. When the space is already enumerated by physics or a platform's affordances, generation is transcription. And when the real constraint is unwillingness to kill, ideation only fills a queue nobody may empty.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product companies hit a seam: an idea from one team is often a feature request on another's roadmap, so the output is a set of negotiations, not options. The honest handling, which few companies describe publicly, is to run ideation twice — once unconstrained, once with the platform team present — and treat the difference as organisational cost.

Two-sided businesses break single-score scoring. At Vaanya Fresh, a produce marketplace, every idea has two value estimates that often have opposite signs: a scheme lifting buyer conversion by shortening the delivery promise pushes cost onto the grower. One ₹ lakh column hides the trade; the fix is two columns and an exchange rate set before the session. Regulated products make compliance a generator rather than a filter, because “how might we satisfy this rule and still…” is productive.

Hardware-plus-software is Falnikar's case, and the seam runs along the tooling calendar: sort candidates by whether they touch geometry, since those that do must clear the freeze date. AI-native products are the newest edge: when behaviour is learned rather than specified, many “different” ideas are the same intervention on one prompt or retrieval step, so distinctness is defined over the mechanism, not the visible feature.

6. Nine expert distinctions

The clustering is the vote. When a facilitator groups the stickies and the room nods, convergence has happened under cover of tidying up. The tell is that nobody argues about the cluster names. Grouping looks administrative, but the taxonomy decides which ideas look like duplicates and which look singular — and singularity attracts votes.

Idea count is hygiene; family count is divergence. Experts walk past a wall of sixty stickies and count families. The tell is a board where every idea shares a verb — remind, notify, alert, nudge — one family in four coats. More stickies mean more divergence only if variety and quantity share a mechanism.

Altitude is testable, not a matter of taste. A question is too low when the first three ideas differ only in parameters, too high when they are abstractions. The tell is a room going quiet for the wrong reason: at low altitude people are bored, at high altitude lost. Both need opposite corrections.

Dot voting selects for legibility. The idea easiest to explain in nine seconds wins, and explicability correlates with familiarity, which correlates with having been tried. The tell is a winner nobody needs to ask a question about. Experts score against the decision rule, keeping the dots as a read on mood.

Idea laundering. An existing roadmap item re-enters the session as a fresh sticky and acquires the legitimacy of having been generated. The tell is an idea arriving fully specified, with an estimate and an owner, where everything else is a fragment. It looks like the hardest thinking in the room; it is a pre-filtered option set.

The kill log is the asset. Rejected ideas without recorded reasons return every planning cycle, and the cost is not the rework but the teaching that nothing is ever decided. The tell is the same proposal in consecutive quarters with no new evidence. Experts record the reason, not the verdict: a reason can expire.

Fund the runner-up thinly. When the spread between first and second is small relative to its own uncertainty — Vidura's 73 and 61 are within a fifth of each other — a two-week version of the second idea is cheap insurance. The tell is a team that cannot name its runner-up: the option set collapsed to one unnoticed.

The room is the distribution you sample from. Adding a field collection agent to Fozdar's session does not raise the average idea; it changes the tail, because that person's ideas come from a different distribution. The tell is a set of options that all live on a screen, in a business whose problem happens on a doorstep.

Crazy 8s is an abandonment exercise. Its value is not the eight sketches but the forced release of the first at sixty seconds, before it can be defended. The tell of failure is eight boxes holding one idea at eight fidelities. Eight minutes is not too little time; it is the mechanism.

7. Product type and stage

What does not change: the mechanics of a silent round, a Crazy 8s sheet and a family count are identical in consumer, B2B, enterprise, platform, hardware and AI products. What changes is the cost of a tested option, who must be in the room, and the gate after generation.

In consumer products the option is cheap to test and the population large enough to measure, so divergence is limited mainly by release risk. In enterprise software the test is expensive in another currency — a customer's patience — so expert teams generate widely and test with surrogates: clickable mockups and a named account's reaction, not a shipped flag. In platforms and marketplaces divergence must be scored on two sides, and an idea excellent for one side is not a candidate until the exchange rate is stated. In hardware the asymmetry is numeric: Exhibit 3's 16.0 against 2.0 means one Vartul option costs eight Vidura options, which argues for surrogate tests rather than fewer ideas, since ₹4.2 lakh of choice work screens seven concepts for roughly a quarter of one soft tool. In AI products generation is nearly free and selection is the whole problem.

Stage matters less than people claim, with one exception. A pre-product-market-fit team should diverge on the problem rather than the solution, and most of its apparent ideation failures are discovery failures; a scaled team's constraint is the kill log. The exception: a large installed base raises option costs with every release, making cheap surrogates progressively more valuable.

8. Three worked rounds

Vidura, July 2025 to September 2026. Idea 23 — a doorstep-failure flow converting a missed visit into a scheduled self-service payment link, from the build-on round — was estimated at ₹73 lakh of additional annual recovery. It shipped on Friday, 26 September 2025. Over the twelve months from 1 October 2025 to 30 September 2026 it produced a measured ₹58 lakh, which is 58 of the 73 lakh estimated, or 79 per cent. Only idea 23 was built, so the ranking is untested; what the exhibit can show is the level, and landing a fifth short of estimate is the normal condition of ideation scores — the reason a decision rule should rank rather than threshold.

Vartul, October 2026. Falnikar's round produced six families, four of which touched geometry — a filter door, an indicator ring, a cartridge keyed so the wrong filter will not seat, a louvre redesign — and two of which did not: an app-side consumption model and a filter subscription. Tooling all four geometry options would have cost 4 × 16.0 = ₹64 lakh, two-thirds of the ₹96 lakh quarterly exploration budget. Lead time ruled them out independently: the six-week tooled lead of Exhibit 3 is 42 days against the 39 between 8 October and 16 November. The ₹4.2 lakh choice study across seven concepts, at ₹0.6 lakh each, ranked the subscription first.

Vinyas Labs, February to May 2026 — the failure. Gunisha Fakira's team, building a document-extraction copilot in Hyderabad, generated 412 ideas in one afternoon on Tuesday, 17 February 2026 with model assistance. Scoring them on four criteria with three scorers meant 412 × 4 × 3 = 4,944 judgements; at forty seconds each that is 197,760 seconds, or 54.9 hours, about 18.3 hours per scorer. Twelve weeks passed and nothing shipped. Worse, when the same two raters applied one taxonomy to both sets, the 412 ideas resolved to 9 families while the team's 31 hand-written ideas from January resolved to 7: 13.3 times the volume bought two families. The recovery, from Tuesday, 12 May 2026, was a cap of forty candidates and a rule written before generation.

9. Failure modes and warnings

Every early warning in that table is structural and visible before money is spent; every cost lands weeks later. That is why experts spend their scepticism on the session's inputs — the question, the rule, the attendance list, the option price.

10. Where experts disagree

Does the group add anything? The structural camp points at four decades of replicated productivity loss and says the group's only legitimate roles are recombination and screening. Steelmanned, the opposing position is not that groups generate more but that they generate ideas no individual would reach, because the stimulus set differs — and Vidura's exhibit supports it, since the best idea came from the build-on round. For the structural camp to be wrong, the hybrid's advantage would have to come mainly from the group phase, which the 2010 experiments do not separate.

Frame or options? The reframing camp holds that altitude choice dominates everything downstream, and Exhibit 1's 9 families against 4 is its evidence. The options camp replies that reframing is unfalsifiable in practice — the counterfactual question cannot be run — and that a wide enough option set contains the reframe anyway. For the reframing camp to be wrong, mid-altitude and broad questions would have to produce equal family counts with ideas held constant.

Has generative AI dissolved the problem? One camp observes that the marginal cost of an option has gone to roughly zero and concludes that selection is now the whole discipline. The other points at Vinyas Labs: 412 ideas, 9 families, a collapse in structural diversity because the generator samples from one distribution. The first camp's strongest version concedes the homogenisation and calls it a prompting problem; it would be wrong if family counts stayed flat under that treatment.

Should you ideate at all? The operator position — ideas are not scarce, decisions are — is the strongest sceptical argument: it predicts the Vinyas failure precisely. Its weakness is that it cannot explain the Vidura staircase, where idea twenty-three was worth 12 more than the best of the first sixteen and was in nobody's head beforehand.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this differs from someone who has studied it in four observable ways. They spend more time on the question than on the session, and will cancel a workshop whose problem has no base attached. They count families rather than ideas, out loud, in the room. They can state the price of one tested option without looking it up, and treat lowering it as a product investment. And they write the decision rule before generation, which exposes who will not accept the result.

12. What each decided

Fozdar did not hold the ninety-minute workshop on 6 October 2026. She spent the first session on altitude, found that the route optimiser was one of three ideas in a single family — all assuming the problem is where the agent goes, not what happens when nobody answers — and reconvened with two field agents present. Her board paper on 3 November 2026 recommends the top-ranked idea plus a thin two-week runner-up, both priced.

Falnikar separated his six families by whether they touched geometry, spent ₹4.2 lakh on the choice study rather than ₹16 lakh on one tooled variant, and will let the 16 November 2026 freeze pass with the housing unchanged. His 46 per cent, he noted, is a statistic about connected units; what the 16,000 unconnected units do is next quarter's discovery problem.

  1. Vidura's best idea arrived twenty-third of twenty-four, and ideas seventeen to twenty-two added nothing. On what principle would you decide, in advance, where to stop?
  2. Falnikar's 46 per cent is measured over 22,000 connected units out of 38,000. Should that change the ideation round, the discovery before it, or neither?
  3. Vinyas Labs got 9 families from 412 ideas, and 7 from its earlier 31. Cap the ideas, change the generator, or change what is scored?

13. Going deeper

Validating a problem hypothesis
Supplies C1; no figure has a base without it.
'How might we' questions
The altitude lever of Exhibit 1.
Writing a solution hypothesis
Makes a surviving family falsifiable.
Generating and comparing solution alternatives
The convergence half.
Concept and elevator pitch
Legibility as an asset, not a bias.
Design sprints
The container around Crazy 8s.
Value Proposition Canvas
Forces families apart up front.
Value proposition statement
Does the family survive one sentence?
Storyboarding
Exposes what a sketch hides.
Wireframes, mockups, prototypes
Where option cost is set, and lowered.
AI-generated prototypes
Section 10's question: cheap, correlated.
case20v1-sol.ideation:
Hastakala Living: Eight Sketches, Three Tests, One Friday

A teaching case on ideation, with a note for the learner

1. Opening

On the evening of Thursday, 15 October 2026, Manjari Sastry, head of product at Hastakala Living, sat in the company's Baner office in Pune with a spreadsheet that had arrived forty minutes earlier. For three days, 12,000 past customers had been shown one of three ideas for getting them to buy a second set of bed linen, and the reservations were in. By Friday, 23 October, Manjari had to tell the founder, Mitali Sanghvi, how the fourth-quarter product-build allocation of ₹50 lakh would be spent. The engineering teams in Bengaluru and Pune were due to start on Monday, 26 October.

She held a measured leader, a founder's favourite that was not the leader, and a worry that the team had stopped generating options too early.

2. Company background

Hastakala Living, founded in Pune in 2018, sells cotton and handloom-weave bed linen and table linen to urban households. Revenue for FY2025-26 was ₹86 crore, of which 38 per cent came through its own website and the rest through Amazon.in and Flipkart. Competitors range from Bombay Dyeing to Fabindia, IKEA India and marketplace private labels. It has had 1,10,000 customers, of whom 90,000 have consented to email under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

The business has one stubborn weakness. Of the 31,200 customers who bought for the first time in 2025, 2,808 had bought again by 15 October 2026, a repeat rate to date of 9.0 per cent. Customers acquired late in 2025 have not yet had a full twelve months, so this is a lower bound on the twelve-month rate.

3. The situation

Manjari's team did not begin with solutions. In August it interviewed 48 customers from the 2025 cohort who had not bought again, drawn from the 28,392 non-repeaters, and asked each for the main reason. Exhibit 1 sets out the answers. The sample is small, so Manjari treats it as a map of reasons, not a measure of their size.

On Tuesday, 6 October, the team met for a "how might we" session, framed as: how might we make the second set an easy yes for someone who already owns a first set they like? It began at 6:00 pm in Pune: 2:30 pm in Berlin, 8:30 am in Toronto, 8:30 pm in Singapore. Six people drew eight rough sketches each in the Crazy 8s format, 48 in all, then clustered them and voted with three dots each, 18 dots in total. Exhibit 2 shows the result.

Between 12 and 14 October the team then ran a fake-door test. From the 90,000 consented customers it drew 12,000 at random, split them into three random cells of 4,000, and emailed each cell one concept page with a button to reserve a place. Only three of the five shortlisted ideas were tested; those could be mocked up in a week. The gifting bundle and the price-match guarantee have no behavioural data at all.

The vote and the test disagreed. Subscription took the most dots, 6 of 18, but Match-my-set drew the most reservations, 92 against 64. Malhar Sapra, the data scientist, computed the gaps from Exhibit 2. Match-my-set over the reminder, 92 against 48, is a gap of 3.75 standard errors and unlikely to be chance. Match-my-set over subscription is 2.26 standard errors, suggestive but from a single test. Subscription over the reminder, 64 against 48, is 1.52, which the data cannot separate from noise.

Exhibit 3 turns the three rates into rollout figures. It applies each rate to all 90,000 consented customers, an upper bound that assumes every reservation becomes a paying customer. The finance team's estimate of year-one contribution per customer differs by idea. The ₹4.2 lakh already spent on the three tests (₹2.4 lakh for subscription, ₹1.2 lakh for Match-my-set and ₹0.6 lakh for the reminder) is sunk and appears nowhere in the table.

Figure A sets out the calendar: Diwali falls on Sunday, 8 November, and the wedding season opens in the third week of November.

4. The people

Mitali Sanghvi, founder and chief executive, Pune. She proposed a subscription two years ago and sees recurring revenue as the route to a valuation story. She wants the ₹45 lakh subscription build and points out that it won the vote.

Mansi Suchak, senior designer, Berlin. She drew the Match-my-set sketch that became a cluster of 11, and wants it built, but warns that colour-matching needs a swatch service the ₹30 lakh may not cover.

Malhar Sapra, data scientist, Toronto. He insists the test says what it says and no more: three of five ideas were measured, reservations are not purchases, and no one should claim a ranking of the five.

Madhusudan Surve, customer-success lead, Singapore. He keeps returning to the 19 people who said they simply did not need another set. In his reading, none of the three tested ideas speaks to them. Marisha Sanyal, sales head in New Jersey, adds that her diaspora customers buy linen mostly as gifts for families in India, which is why she wants the gifting idea kept alive.

5. The options

Option A: build Match-my-set now. It led the test and leaves the most value after its ₹30 lakh build, ₹23.82 lakh against ₹8.52 lakh for the reminder; its value-to-build-cost ratio of 1.79 is close to the reminder's 1.71. A four-week build launches on 23 November, in time for the wedding season. The cost is commitment on one test of one metric, with the 19 "did not need another set" customers unaddressed.

Option B: build the subscription. It took the most dots and carries the highest contribution per customer, ₹3,200. It costs ₹45 lakh, nearly the whole allocation, takes six weeks, launches on 7 December and clears its build cost by only ₹1.08 lakh on the optimistic assumptions of Exhibit 3.

Option C: pause the build for a second round of ideation. Spend ₹4 lakh and eight working days on a new "how might we" session aimed at the 19 non-need customers, test its best two ideas, and decide on 6 November. It moves the launch of any build from 23 November to 7 December and gives up the first two weeks of the wedding season.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What did the 48 interviews and the 48 sketches each tell the team, and which of the five reasons in Exhibit 1 does the shortlist leave without a direct answer?
  2. The vote and the test ranked the ideas differently. What does each measure, and which is better evidence of future purchases?
  3. Using Exhibit 3, which of the three tested ideas should be preferred, and why must value be divided by rollout cost rather than by test cost?
  4. Have enough alternatives been generated? If you would diverge again, what would you ask the team to do, and what would the decision rule be?

7. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. Ideation asks whether enough distinct alternatives were generated before converging. Here the answer is mixed. The team started from a validated problem, a repeat rate to date of 9.0 per cent with interview evidence behind it, and it diverged, producing 48 sketches in five real clusters. The founder's own idea drew only 9 of them. But breadth is not coverage. Set against Exhibit 1, the shortlist answers 27 of the 48 reasons directly and the 19 largest only partly.

What a well-reasoned answer does. It separates what was measured from what was merely ranked. Only three ideas were tested, so the only supportable ranking is among them: Match-my-set first on reservations, with subscription and the reminder behind it and the latter two not separable. Nothing can be said about where the gifting bundle or the price-match guarantee would fall. It also compares like with like. Exhibit 3 divides rollout value by rollout build cost. It treats a reservation as an upper bound on demand, not a sale.

One defensible path. Choose Option A, with a bounded addition. Build Match-my-set for ₹30 lakh, because it is the best-evidenced idea, it launches inside the wedding season, and it keeps ₹20 lakh of the allocation free. In parallel, ring-fence the ₹4 lakh and eight working days of Option C for the non-need customers, with Madhusudan and Marisha leading, and judge the output by the same rule: reservations in a random cell of equal size, then value divided by rollout cost. Treat the subscription as a hypothesis not yet beaten: at 1.02 on optimistic assumptions it needs a cheaper first version. It commits where evidence exists and keeps divergence alive where it is thin. Its weak point is a single test, so the launch should be staged and measured against real payments.
exp20v2-sol.feedback.loop:
Concept, feedback, iterate

Running demo, feedback and revision rounds so that at the end you know what changed, why, and whether to build.

1. Opening: three Thursdays and a Monday

On Monday, 3 August 2026, Dhanya Chawla, head of product at Tijarat Ledger in Pune, was given a number and a deadline. Tijarat sells a phone-based credit book to neighbourhood grocers, known as kirana owners: a digital replacement for the notebook in which a shopkeeper records what each regular customer owes, called udhaar. The chief executive wanted to add automatic WhatsApp payment reminders. Engineering estimated ten weeks and ₹24 lakh. If the feature failed to change how shopkeepers behaved, that money, and a quarter of the roadmap, would be gone.

Dhanya did not doubt the idea. She doubted the evidence for it. A survey of 180 shopkeepers had found that most "liked" reminders; liking costs nothing. She proposed three demonstration rounds, two weeks apart, on Thursday 13 August, Thursday 27 August and Thursday 10 September, with a go or no-go meeting on Monday 14 September. Each round would show eight different shopkeepers an artefact, and each would be followed by a revision before the next. She would spend ₹4.2 lakh to avoid risking ₹24 lakh.

Her colleagues were Dipti Chakravarty, a design researcher in Bengaluru, and Dhanesh Chougule, who ran field operations in Pune and booked the shopkeepers. The CEO's concern was practical: three rounds meant six weeks before a decision.

2. The idea

A feedback round is a scheduled session in which a team shows people a rough version of a proposed solution (the artefact), watches what they do and say, and records the result against a question fixed in advance. An iteration is the revision made because of that result. The loop is the repetition of both until a decision rule, written before the first round, says to build, to stop, or to go around again. The change log is the running record linking each observation to each revision.

The problem it solves is old. Software built in one pass from a specification met its users only at delivery, when errors were costliest to fix. Barry Boehm's spiral model (1986) put repeated risk-reduction cycles into engineering. Jakob Nielsen's work on iterative interface design (1993) showed that usability improved with each cycle of test and redesign. Eric Ries's The Lean Startup (2011) added the idea of a minimum viable product as a vehicle for learning rather than a smaller product: its job is to answer a question, with a stated rule for what answer counts.

The sentence Dhanya could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: each round buys one answer, and the log is how we know which one.

3. How it actually works

Before round one, Dhanya wrote three things down. The first was the question: "Will a shopkeeper switch on reminders for a named customer?" The second was the behavioural test: enabling reminders for a real customer on a test phone, as opposed to saying "good idea". The third was the decision rule: build if at least 5 of 8 shopkeepers (62.5 per cent) enable reminders in two consecutive rounds; stop if two consecutive rounds fall below 3 of 8 (37.5 per cent); otherwise revise and go again. The rule was in the project notes on 3 August, before anyone had seen a result.

Round one used a six-panel storyboard: a shopkeeper, a customer who owes ₹1,850, a WhatsApp message, a payment. A storyboard is a comic-strip sequence showing an idea in use, the cheapest honest artefact at that stage. Dhanesh recruited eight shopkeepers in Hadapsar and Kothrud. Dipti asked each to walk through the panels, then handed over a phone: "Pick a customer you would send this to." Two of the eight did.

The steps practitioners usually leave implicit matter most. Someone other than the presenter takes notes, because presenters hear what they hoped to hear. The team separates the observation ("four of six decliners said the message would shame the customer") from the inference ("tone is the barrier") and from the change ("replace the demand wording with a friendly note"). Declined requests are logged with a reason, so nobody reopens them without new evidence. Table 1 shows the log after three rounds.

Table 1. Change log, Tijarat Ledger reminders concept

1Thu 13 AugSix-panel storyboard8225.0%Shopkeeper approves each message; wording softened (two changes)
