Rate = shopkeepers who enabled, divided by the 8 new shopkeepers shown that round. Each round used a different set of eight.

Notice what the log does. Of the six who declined in round one, four named shame as the reason: 4 of 6, or 66.7 per cent. That denominator is the decliners, not all eight. In round two, two of the three decliners asked for a Marathi or Hindi message, which created the single change tested in round three. Both revisions trace to an observation (the shame reported in round one, the language requests in round two), and a reader who joins in week four can reconstruct the argument.

4. A worked example

Figure 2 plots the three results against the rule. The bar for "build" is the line at 62.5 per cent (5 of 8) and the line for "stop" sits at 37.5 per cent (3 of 8). Round one, at 25.0 per cent, fell below the stop line, but one round does not trigger the rule. Round two met the bar exactly and round three exceeded it: two consecutive rounds, so the rule said build.

The cost side is just as concrete. Table 2 prices one round and then the three together.

Table 2. Cost of one round, in rupees
Item₹
Prototype revision (design time)90,000
Incentives, 8 shopkeepers at ₹2,50020,000
Travel, venue, recording30,000
Total per round1,40,000

Three rounds cost 3 × ₹1.4 lakh = ₹4.2 lakh, which is 17.5 per cent of the ₹24 lakh build (4.2 ÷ 24). That buys a test of the riskiest assumption before the other 82.5 per cent is committed.

Second pass: change one input. Suppose the CEO had insisted on a stricter bar of 6 of 8 (75.0 per cent) in two consecutive rounds. Round two (5 of 8) would not count and round three (6 of 8) would be the first qualifying round. A fourth round would be needed, so the loop would cost at least 4 × ₹1.4 lakh = ₹5.6 lakh, or 23.3 per cent of the build, and more if round four fell short. The first three rounds' evidence is identical; if a fourth round also reached 6 of 8, the decision arrives a fortnight later and ₹1.4 lakh dearer. A rule is a price, and should be argued over before the data exists.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Behaviour outweighs opinion

Dhanya's survey found approval, while the rounds counted enabling. People are generous in conversation and honest in action.

One change per round, if you can afford it

Round two altered two things at once, approval and wording, so the jump from 25.0 to 62.5 per cent, 37.5 points, cannot be split between them. Combined changes are acceptable when speed matters; they merely limit what you can claim.

Fresh participants, or declared carry-over

Someone who has seen version one is no longer a naive viewer of version two, so Tijarat used 24 different shopkeepers over three rounds. Re-using participants can be deliberate, to test a fix with the person who raised the problem, but should be declared.

Small samples are signals, not proofs

With 5 of 8, the proportion is 0.625 and the standard error is the square root of (0.625 × 0.375 ÷ 8), about 0.171, or 17.1 points. The true rate could plausibly sit far from 62.5 per cent. This is why the rule demanded two consecutive rounds. The method detects large effects and cannot adjudicate small ones.

Fidelity should match the question

A storyboard can test whether the premise is wanted. A clickable prototype tests whether the flow works. A polished build shown too early invites comments on button colour. Pick the roughest artefact that can still produce the behaviour you are counting.

A decision rule is not a verdict machine

The rule says when to stop arguing. It does not say the concept is good; judgement still decides whether the number matters commercially.

Distinguish a feedback round from a concept test

A concept test, as in solution interviews, asks whether an idea appeals. A feedback round is a concept test repeated, with a changed artefact and a log joining the repetitions: a snapshot becomes a trajectory.

What it cannot tell you

None of the 24 shopkeepers' customers saw the reminder, though they receive it. Enabling a reminder in a prototype is also not sending one, and sending one is not collecting money. The loop shows the shopkeeper's willingness. It says nothing about whether customers pay sooner.

6. How it differs by context

The mechanics hold everywhere; who must be in the room changes (Table 3).

Table 3. Where the loop bends
SettingWho gives feedbackWhat is different
ConsumerIndividual users, easily recruitedRounds are fast and cheap; the risk is mistaking politeness for intent.
B2BBuyer, user and approverFew participants per round, so one signed pilot letter can weigh more than eight reactions.
MarketplaceBoth sides, and both must be testedTijarat is close to this: the customer who receives the reminder is a second side no round has met.
Early-stage companyFounder runs everythingInformal logs are enough; speed beats ceremony.
Large companyMany stakeholdersThe change log is also a defence in governance reviews; rules are written down because people will dispute them.

Dhanya's company sits between the last two rows: she needed the log mainly so that engineering, sales and the CEO would accept one account of what had changed.

7. Common mistakes

Collecting reactions, not behaviour. From outside, the team reports that "everyone loved it" and nothing changes between rounds. The misunderstanding is that approval is evidence. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask, for each round, what number of people did something that cost them effort.

Pooling the rounds. A team averages everything. For Tijarat that would be 13 of 24, or 54.2 per cent, below the 62.5 per cent bar and so a false suggestion of failure, which hides the 25.0, 62.5, 75.0 trajectory. The misunderstanding is that more data is always better; the diagnostic is to ask whether the artefact changed between the observations being averaged.

Moving the bar after the results. The symptom is a decision rule that appears in the deck after the data does. The diagnostic is the file date on the rule.

Treating every comment as a requirement. The symptom is a revision list that grows weekly; the misunderstanding is that the loudest participant represents the market. Count how many of the eight raised the point.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the question, the behaviour and the rule sit on one page on 3 August. Within two days of each round the team publishes a one-page change log where every revision names its observation and every declined suggestion its reason. A sceptical colleague who did not attend can read the log, disagree, and still see how the team reached its recommendation. By 14 September the meeting is about what to do, not whether to trust the evidence.

9. Closing

At the meeting on Monday 14 September, Dhanya recommended building, but not the whole feature. The rule had been met, so she asked for the ₹24 lakh, with one condition: release to 40 shops first, and measure how much money shopkeepers actually recovered in 14 days. The prototype showed willingness; only a shipped version could show recovery, so the first release was itself the next round, with a decision rule attached. The ten-week build began that day.

To go further, study storyboarding, to see what is worth showing in round one, and the design of solution interviews and concept tests, because every round here was one.

Two questions to sit with. First, if the rule had needed 6 of 8 and round three had come back 5 of 8, what would you have changed, and what would you have been unable to say about why? Second, what is the cheapest way to put the customers who receive the reminder into your next round, and what would you do if they disliked it while shopkeepers loved it?
exp40v2-sol.feedback.loop:
Concept → feedback → iterate

What a round buys, what the record must say, and how two managers using one method reached opposite conclusions in one week.

1. Opening: two freezes, one instrument

On Thursday 8 October 2026 Dhriti Chennupati laid six round summaries across a table in Bengaluru. She is VP Product at Tarvana Treasury Works, which sells cash-forecasting and collections software to 310 mid-market manufacturers at a median ₹7.2 lakh a year. The question was whether to build a module predicting which invoices would be paid late: 22 engineer-weeks at a loaded ₹1.4 lakh a week, so ₹30.8 lakh of build, against a plan closing on Monday 12 October.

She had evidence. Between Tuesday 14 April and Thursday 25 June she ran six demo–feedback–revise rounds, from a six-frame storyboard to a prototype wired to two customers' real ledgers. Then, from Thursday 3 September to Tuesday 22 September, a commitment round against a rule written in April: fifteen controllers recruited; build if at least seven of those asked would route month-end collections through the tool without a parallel spreadsheet, kill if three or fewer would. Three never sat down, so twelve were asked and five said yes — 41.7 per cent of the twelve asked, in neither branch of her own rule. Her ML lead read the five as a mandate and Devendu Chivate, who facilitated, read the seven refusals as a verdict; Chirasmita Chakrapani, who coded the transcripts, said it was the wrong question.

Eight hundred kilometres north-west, Devaki Chimote of Thalir Agri Devices in Nashik was holding a purchase order. Thalir makes a solar pump controller with soil-moisture probes, sold to farmers through producer organisations under NABARD-refinanced loans. The hard steel mould for the enclosure cost ₹41.00 lakh and had to be ordered by Thursday 19 November 2026 to reach dealers before the June 2027 kharif season. An eight-week trial of 240 controllers across nine FPO clusters closed on Tuesday 6 October; logs pulled on Thursday 8 October returned usable data from 212 of the 240 units, whose mean pump time fell from a pre-fit 11.4 hours per acre per week to 8.6. Chetanya Chikodi, on firmware, pointed at nineteen failed valve-position sensors; Darshan Chhadva wanted the order signed anyway.

Two decisions, one structure: what is the next round worth, and what does the record say?

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A feedback round is a bounded episode in which a team spends a known amount on an artefact of chosen fidelity to answer one question written down before the artefact was made, and closes with a recorded change, refusal to change, or decision. An iteration is the revision a round causes. The decision rule states in advance what result would make the team build, stop or go round again, including its denominator. The change log records observation, inference, change and prediction; the carry-forward list holds objections heard and not acted on. This is an instrument with a stated read-out, not "showing things to users".

It exists because of the cost asymmetry of late discovery: an error found in a sketch costs a conversation, the same error after tooling costs a mould. The lineage is long: Shewhart's plan–do–study–act cycle, carried into management by Deming; Simon (1969) on design as generate-and-test; Schön (1983) on the situation talking back; Boehm's risk-driven spiral (1986); Nielsen and Landauer (1993) on how many participants a round needs; Thomke (2003) on the economics of one experiment; and Ries's minimum viable product, a learning vehicle with a decision rule rather than a small product.

Five schools share the vocabulary and disagree on substance. Craft and critique signs "five fresh participants, then revise" and refuses "the participants decide". Experimentation signs "no claim about value without a pre-registered quantitative test". Lean discovery signs "the artefact is an instrument with a kill branch" and refuses "wait for statistical power". Stage-gate and systems, which owns regulated and hardware work, signs "iterate freely before the freeze, not after" and refuses "requirements emerge from rounds". Vision-led signs "feedback measures comprehension, never the value of the unfamiliar". Dhriti's room held three of these.

3. Mechanics: what experts actually do

The question and its denominator

Question and rule come before the artefact, because an artefact built first rewrites the question to one it answers well. A rule names a numerator, a denominator and a kill branch. Tarvana's said "of those asked": hence 41.7 per cent (5 of 12) rather than 33.3 per cent (5 of 15).

The fidelity ladder

Fidelity is not progress but a dial selecting which feedback is available: a storyboard invites "why would I do this at all", while a finished unit draws interaction findings and few structural ones, because participants read finish as commitment. Thalir's ladder is therefore a price list for questions: find the cheapest rung that answers the question deciding the next commitment.

RungArtefactLead timeUnitsCost per roundWhat it can be asked
1Six-frame storyboard and a printed dial card1 day1₹4,000Comprehension; is the job worth doing
23D-printed shell, app driven by hand from the next room9 days12₹16,800Placement, reach, labelling, first use
3Soft aluminium tool, 300-unit pilot batch26 days300₹2.27 lakhDealer installation; dust, heat, wiring
4Hard steel tool, production enclosure62 days20,000₹9.00 lakhNothing: a commitment, not a question

Rung 2 is 12 units × ₹1,400 = ₹16,800; rung 3 spreads the ₹6.80 lakh soft tool over the three rounds it survives, ₹6,80,000 ÷ 3 = ₹2.27 lakh; rung 4's figure is one cavity change after the freeze, ₹9.00 lakh and 34 days, not the ₹41.00 lakh tool; rung 1 is one designer-day at ₹4,000. The four bases differ — units × unit cost, tooling ÷ rounds, one cavity change — so each is the price of a question, not a series.

The log

A log of observations and changes is a diary. What makes it an instrument is the prediction column: what the team expects next round if the inference was right. Without it no round disconfirms anything, since any outcome can be narrated as progress. The second column amateurs omit is the refusal.

The two return arrows are the real choice: improve this artefact, or buy a different question.

The arithmetic of how many

Nielsen and Landauer's result is the treatment practitioners half-remember: if a problem is present for a proportion λ of the population and participants are independent, a round of n surfaces it with probability 1 − (1 − λ)n. At λ = 0.30, five give 1 − 0.705 = 1 − 0.16807 = 83.2 per cent; at λ = 0.15 even eight reach only 1 − 0.858 = 1 − 0.27249 = 72.8 per cent. The famous recommendation is that line and no more.

The ledger, and the exit signal

R1Tue 14 AprStoryboard611341.83
R2Thu 30 AprStoryboard, revised77461.00
R3Wed 13 MayClickable mock64250.67

The last column is a ratio, not a sum: 11 ÷ 6 = 1.83 in R1, 2 ÷ 6 = 0.33 in R6, 31 ÷ 40 = 0.78 overall. Engineer-days cost ₹1.4 lakh ÷ 5 = ₹28,000.

This curve, not the calendar, is the exit signal. By R5 the rung yielded one finding per three participants, near the rate at which a team invents objections by itself. Three moves are then defensible: escalate a rung, stop because the rule is met, or change the instrument because the rule has proved unanswerable by demonstration — Dhriti's case, since no demo shows a forecast accurate over a quarter.

The economics, done properly

Thirty-seven engineer-days at ₹28,000 is ₹10.36 lakh of engineer cost alone, against a build of ₹30.8 lakh: the loop cost 33.6 per cent of what it protected, and at that ratio the naive justification fails. Say the module had a 35 per cent chance of being wrong before the rounds and 10 per cent after — Dhriti's judgement, not a measurement: avoided waste is 0.25 × ₹30.8 lakh = ₹7.70 lakh, less than the rounds cost by ₹2.66 lakh.

The missing term is opportunity. Those 22 engineer-weeks were the plan year's only uncommitted capacity; counting the slot at half the module's cost, 0.5 × ₹30.8 lakh = ₹15.4 lakh, exposure is ₹30.8 lakh + ₹15.4 lakh = ₹46.2 lakh and avoided waste becomes 0.25 × ₹46.2 lakh = ₹11.55 lakh, ₹1.19 lakh more than the loop cost. Rounds are cheap against opportunity, not against build.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be tested rather than assumed. A commitment point exists inside the horizon: Thalir's tool order on 19 November, Tarvana's plan closing on 12 October; without one the decisions never arrive. A rough artefact can elicit the behaviour in question: true for Tarvana's workflow, false for its forecast accuracy; true for Thalir's mounting, false for its water saving. Participants can be recruited at the cadence's rate: Tarvana's fifteen-day median gap held because controllers take a video call, while Thalir ran three weeks apart: twelve farmers need an FPO secretary and a cooperative crop stage. The round is cheap against the exposure: ₹10.36 lakh against ₹46.2 lakh.

It misleads in three situations. Where value lives in a quantity no artefact can carry — accuracy over a quarter, liquidity on both sides, trust built over years, latency under load — rounds yield confident feedback about everything except what decides the outcome, and the confidence is the danger. Where the room cannot contain the people who choose, they measure enthusiasm without authority. And where a concept is unfamiliar, preference is constructed in the session.

5. Hard edges

In multi-product companies two lines run rounds against one shared object and each log records changes the other does not know about; the fix is one log per shared object. In two-sided businesses a round on one side is a misleading whole experiment, because the rule that matters is joint: supply listed and demand booked.

In regulated products the log becomes evidence: a device team keeps a design history file, and a diagnostic instrument faces a Bureau of Indian Standards certification fixed by a drawing. Iteration before the freeze is free and after it costs a re-validation, so gates state the cost curve rather than obstruct it.

In hardware plus software there are two clocks, a fortnight and 62 days plus 34 for a change, so software rounds that inform a tooling question come before drawing release. In AI-native products the artefact is non-deterministic, so a demo is a sample rather than a specification, and the cheap rung of a human answering from the next room gives feedback on a capability the team may never reach.

What mature companies do differs from what they describe. They say continuous discovery and run a gated cadence tied to planning quarters; they say fresh participants and keep a standing panel, because recruiting binds. The better ones rotate the panel in thirds, so a third of each round is naive; the weaker ones also drop the record.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A round is bought with a question, not a slot in the calendar. The sign is an invitation with an agenda, a participant list and no sentence beginning "we will change our mind if". Cadence looks like discipline and is not: a round with no question is a meeting with guests.

Fidelity is a filter, not a score. The sign is a critique log changing character in the week the prototype acquires real typography: structural objections stop, alignment complaints start. The obvious reading is that structural problems are gone; in fact participants have turned polite about premises, so experts keep a low-fidelity rung in reserve.

Freshness is arithmetic, not etiquette. The sign is an agreement rate climbing while nothing in the product improves. A participant on her fourth round adds a fraction of a person to detection and a whole person's confidence to the room.

One change per round is a budgeting rule, not a purity rule. The sign of misapplication is eleven weeks spent on four independent fixes. Attribution matters only where effects interact: changes touching different screens and users can be batched; changes touching one decision cannot.

Record the refusals, or re-litigate them. The sign is a carry-forward list that is missing or has never shrunk, and a round-five discussion indistinguishable from round two. What outlasts a loop is the log, not the artefact.

A rule without a kill branch and a named base is not a rule. The sign is "we'll see how it goes", or a denominator drifting between the writing and the reading. Experts write the kill branch first: a rule with only a build branch will always be read as met.

Two observers do not see the same round, and the gap is measurable. After round four, Chirasmita Chakrapani and Devendu Chivate coded the same 58 moments independently.

Coding of the same 58 momentsCount
Both called it blocking18
Only Chirasmita called it blocking5
Only Devendu called it blocking4
Neither called it blocking31
Total58

Raw agreement is (18 + 31) ÷ 58 = 49 of the 58 moments, or 84.5 per cent. Chance agreement uses the marginals — Chirasmita called 18 + 5 = 23 blocking, Devendu 18 + 4 = 22 — giving [(23 × 22) + (35 × 36)] ÷ 582 = (506 + 1,260) ÷ 3,364 = 0.5250, so κ = (0.8448 − 0.5250) ÷ (1 − 0.5250) = 0.3199 ÷ 0.4750 = 0.67.

On nine of 58 moments two trained colleagues disagreed about whether a user was blocked, so κ = 0.67 calibrates every tally the loop produces — and high agreement is suspect when the note-taker heard the facilitator's summary first.

The strongest evidence in a round is what nobody asked for. The sign is a participant reaching for something of her own: the controller who opened her own spreadsheet to check the prototype's number, the farmer who had fitted a hand-made sunshade over the dial. A round with none of it failed to get out of the way.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

Four differences are real. In consumer products the constraint is recruiting breadth, because λ varies sharply across devices, languages and data plans. In business and enterprise software it is authority: the loop runs twice, with users for workability and the buyer for willingness, and Tarvana's rule was written for the second. In platforms and marketplaces the rule is a joint condition, so rounds come in pairs. In hardware lead time dominates, which is why the ladder has prices on it.

Two differences are smaller than claimed. AI products need the model's variance in the log and a frozen evaluation set behind the demo, but the round structure is unchanged. And stage changes the cost of a round far less than the cost of being wrong: both a seed-stage team and a listed company show artefacts to six people, but only one carries a wrong answer into a release train.

8. Three worked examples

Tarvana, the module never built. Six rounds, 40 participants asked, 31 problems first seen, 19 decisions recorded, 37 engineer-days. R6, the first on real ledgers, produced two new problems, one of which reframed everything: controllers kept a parallel spreadsheet because the forecast could not show its working. The rule then returned 5 of the 12 asked — a good rule meeting an ill-posed question.

Thalir, the ladder used properly. Rungs 1 to 3 settled dial placement, labels and dealer installation before the hard steel tool was cut. The trial then ran 240 rung-3 units across nine clusters for eight weeks to Tuesday 6 October 2026. Logs returned from 212 units; of the 28 silent ones, 19 had a failed valve-position sensor and 9 lacked mobile coverage. The pre-fit mean was 11.4 hours per acre per week on all 240 holdings and on the 212 alike. On the 212 it fell to 8.6 — 2.8 hours, or 24.6 per cent of baseline. Devaki also priced the silent units at no change: the mean over 240 is then [(212 × 8.6) + (28 × 11.4)] ÷ 240 = 2,142.4 ÷ 240 = 8.93 hours, a fall of 2.47 hours, or 21.7 per cent of 11.4. That is a no-effect-on-silent figure, not a bound — a failed sensor could as easily mean more pumping — and it is what she put in the dealer deck.

Tulvaa Slot Exchange, where the loop failed. Dhanush Chintalapati ran seven rounds between January and March 2026 on his Hyderabad marketplace for diagnostic-test slots, with lab managers in every round and patients in none. It launched on Monday 13 April 2026 and in the first thirty days, to Wednesday 13 May, 204 of the 1,480 slots listed were booked, or 13.8 per cent. The recovery was alternating rounds — four with labs, four with patients, to Friday 10 July — which established that patients wanted a two-hour home-collection window, not a laboratory chair. Relaunched on Monday 20 July, it booked 437 of the 1,180 slots listed in the thirty days to Wednesday 19 August, or 37.0 per cent.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Friendly-room drift. Tarvana's collections rework, released earlier the same year, ran nine rounds in eleven weeks with the same four design partners. In round two, 13 of 25 scripted prompts drew agreement, or 52.0 per cent; by round nine, 32 of 34 did, or 94.1 per cent, read as convergence. It had converged on four people: after the release of Monday 2 March 2026, by Friday 10 April only 3 of 41 trial accounts had converted — 7.3 per cent. Diagnostic: how many people here sat in an earlier round?

The unanswerable rule. Early sign: the rule is quietly rewritten after each round. Diagnostic: what would we see in this room if the forecast were twenty points less accurate? If the answer is "nothing", more rounds are a tax and the late cost is a build justified by the wrong evidence.

Fidelity creep. Early sign: nobody has asked "why would I do this at all" since round three. Diagnostic: what is the lowest-fidelity artefact we showed anyone this month? Late cost: a mould frozen around an unexamined premise, ₹9.00 lakh a change.

Log rot. Early sign: nobody can say what changed between two rounds without searching chat histories. Diagnostic: show me the row for last Thursday's change. Late cost: rounds repeated and dropped features quietly reintroduced.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Can a round be evidence of value, or only of workability? The experimentation school holds that desirability claims need a pre-registered quantitative test on real behaviour at real stakes, its evidence being the gap between concept-test scores and launch outcomes across portfolios. The discovery school replies that most decisions are not statistically decidable in the time available, and that a written rule over a dozen chosen buyers is a decision procedure, not a measurement. The first would concede if concept tests predicted launch outcomes well, the second if cheap rounds did not beat the team's prior.

Does the loop under-rate the unfamiliar? The vision-led position is not romanticism: preference for a new habit is constructed through use, so a session measures comprehension and the comfort of the familiar, and products that tested poorly and then succeeded are its evidence. Opponents note that this excuses every failure unless the team says in advance which feedback it will disregard and why — a settlement, not an agreement.

Is the record worth its cost? A lightweight school argues the artefact is the record, that writing a prediction column costs rounds, and that speed dominates. A governance school replies that an unlogged loop cannot tell learning from drift. Nobody has measured the price.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this writes the kill branch before the artefact and names the denominator unprompted. She declines rounds — the clearest mark of all — when no commitment hangs on the answer. She escalates fidelity only for a question the cheaper rung cannot hold, reports the conservative figure when the base is incomplete, and can say which round proved her wrong.

12. Closing: what each of them decided

On Monday 12 October 2026 Dhriti neither built nor killed. Her rule had landed in its ambiguous middle, and she treated that as a finding about the instrument rather than the market: the module's value turned on forecast accuracy, which no demonstration can show. She took the one thing all five willing controllers had said — a number must be defensible upward — and committed 4 engineer-weeks at ₹1.4 lakh, or ₹5.6 lakh, to an explanation panel on the existing forecast, under a rule written that day: if fewer than 15 of the 30 pilot accounts open it at two consecutive month-ends, the module dies.

Devaki did not sign on Thursday 19 November 2026. A sensor that failed in 19 of 240 units, or 7.9 per cent, is a mould problem: the valve-position sensor seats in a moulded boss, and the failures traced to that seat. She spent ₹2.40 lakh on a soft-tool revision of the boss, re-trialled 60 units through the rabi season and moved the ₹41.00 lakh tool order to Thursday 7 January 2027 — costing the June 2027 kharif window and roughly a season of volume, logged as a decision with a stated price.

Discussion questions. (1) Dhriti's rule was well written and returned an answer she could not act on: was the error in the rule, the instrument or the question? (2) Devaki reported 21.7 rather than 24.6 per cent from one trial — must she print both? (3) At which round should Tulvaa's single-sided rounds have been stopped, and on what signal?

13. Going deeper

Solution interviews and concept tests — the round as a unit of research. Storyboarding — the rung-1 artefact. Writing a solution hypothesis — the sentence a round tests. Ideation: brainstorming, Crazy 8s, HMW — where the alternatives come from, so a round chooses rather than approves. Concept and elevator pitch — the wording shown, itself a variable. Value Proposition Canvas — which questions bear on value. Value proposition statement — what a kill branch kills. Wireframes, mockups, prototypes — the ladder in software.
case20v1-sol.feedback.loop:
Dastkar Ledger: Three Rounds and a Rule

A teaching case on concept, feedback and iteration

1. Opening

At 9:30 on Monday, 30 March 2026, Kavya Parchure, head of product at Dastkar Ledger, sat in a rented meeting room in Pune's Baner district with a printed page she had signed on Friday, 30 January. It held two lines. Dastkar would commit its Bengaluru engineers to a full build only if, in the latest round of shopkeeper testing, at least 70 per cent of shopkeepers completed the core task unaided and at least 50 per cent said they would pay ₹199 a month.

Three rounds of testing had now finished. The first condition had been met. The second had been missed by one shopkeeper. At 4:00 p.m. India time, which was 12:30 in Berlin because Europe had moved its clocks the day before, she would present to the chief executive and two colleagues. The Bengaluru squad would be free on Monday, 6 April and needed an answer by Tuesday, 31 March.

2. Company background

Dastkar Ledger, founded in Pune in 2021, sells a billing and stock app to small retailers. It has about 6,200 active shops, mostly kirana and stationery stores in Maharashtra and Gujarat, and a paid tier at ₹149 a month. It competes with Vyapar and Zoho Books on invoicing, and with Khatabook and OkCredit on the notebook of credit sales, the udhaar ledger that every kirana owner keeps. Customers pay by UPI, but collecting an old balance is still a phone call or an awkward word at the counter.

Management had spotted a gap in that last step: a tool that turns a ledger entry into a polite, timed WhatsApp reminder with a UPI payment link. Any such tool must also respect the DPDP Act, 2023, since the customer never signed up to Dastkar. On 1 March the company held ₹5.2 crore (₹520 lakh) in the bank and spent about ₹40 lakh a month net, which is thirteen months of runway from that date.

3. The situation

Parchure ran the work as a sequence of rounds, each changing the thing shown and each recorded in a shared log. She wrote the decision rule down before the first round, having watched earlier projects drift toward "one more round". Exhibit 1 sets out the rounds and Exhibit 4 places them on a calendar.

Exhibit 1. The three rounds

Each percentage uses that round's own shop count as denominator. "Would pay" is stated intent, not payment. Returning shops had seen an earlier version. The three rounds covered 29 different shops.

Kabir Prabhune, who leads field research from Nashik, ran the sessions. Kshama Palshikar, the designer in Berlin, drew the Round 1 storyboard. The task in later rounds was fixed: add a credit sale for a named customer, then send that customer a reminder. A shopkeeper "completed unaided" if Prabhune did not need to touch the phone or give a spoken hint.

For every round Prabhune counted how many shopkeepers raised each issue without being asked, then recorded what the team did about it. Exhibit 2 reproduces it. Entry speed complaints fell from 7 of 14 shopkeepers to 1 of 15 after the v3 fix, tone complaints from 6 of 14 to 3 of 15, and language complaints from 5 of 14 to 2 of 15.

Exhibit 2. Change log: shopkeepers raising each issue unprompted

IssueR1 (of 12)R2 (of 14)R3 (of 15)What changed for v3
A. Ledger entry takes too many tapsn/a71Entry cut to two taps

"n/a" means the version shown could not produce the issue. Counts are shopkeepers, not mentions; one shopkeeper can raise several issues.

Two rows trouble her. Issue E is a regression the team made. To get entry down to two taps, Palshikar and the Bengaluru engineering lead, Kedar Pitale, had removed the step that asks the shopkeeper to confirm the customer's phone number. Four of fifteen shopkeepers then sent a reminder to the wrong person. Issue D is different: as a share of each round's shops it rose every time, from 25.0 per cent to 35.7 to 40.0, and it is the one request the team had refused to act on. A GST invoice is a different product, already well served by Vyapar and Zoho Books.

Round 3 also generated outcome data. Nine of the fifteen shops sent at least one real reminder between Monday 16 and Friday 20 March. Exhibit 3 compares those nine shops with their own manual reminders in the week before, as recalled from notebooks at follow-up visits on 23 to 25 March. A reminder counts as successful if the customer paid within seven days, so the last window closed on Friday, 27 March, three days before the meeting.

Exhibit 3. Reminder outcomes in the nine sending shops

Same nine shops in both weeks. The manual week is recalled, not logged. Gudi Padwa fell on Thursday, 19 March, inside the second week.

Prabhune is cautious. Shopkeepers chose whom to remind, the festival week may have put money in households, and nine shops is nine shops. The gap of roughly thirteen points is encouraging, but the study cannot say how much of it the product caused.

4. The people

Kavya Parchure, head of product in Pune, owns the decision and the rule. She does not want to be the person who moved the goalposts after seeing the score.

Kedar Pitale, engineering lead in Bengaluru, wants a firm scope and a start date. Idle weeks are costly, and he regards issue D as a trap that would double the build.

Kshama Palshikar, designer in Berlin, wants one more round. She believes the wrong-customer error is the kind of flaw that destroys trust and that two taps was the wrong fix.

Kabir Prabhune, field researcher in Nashik, sits with shopkeepers every day. He thinks the word "reminder" is the problem, since shopkeepers say they wish to "request payment gently", and he is unsure the pay figure means anything until money moves.

5. Exhibit 4: the calendar

Exhibit 4 places the rounds, the baseline week and the payment window against the meeting.

Exhibit 4. Timeline, 1 February to 6 April 2026 (10 px per day)

Scale: x = 40 + 10 × (days since 1 February); bars span whole working days, from the start of the first day to the end of the last.

6. The options

Option A: build the reminder MVP now. Ten weeks at a blended ₹8.6 lakh a week, or ₹86 lakh, would put a reminder product in front of the 6,200 existing shops by mid-June. The upside is speed, and the completion condition is met. The cost is that the payment condition was missed and issue E is unfixed.

Option B: hold the decision for a short Round 4. Three weeks at ₹3 lakh a week, or ₹9 lakh, from Monday, 6 April would repair issue E and rename the feature, then test twenty new shops from Monday, 20 April to Friday, 24 April, with the same rule and a decision on Monday, 27 April. The upside is a cleaner reading on price. The cost is three weeks of idle engineers and a habit of "one more round".

Option C: widen the product to include GST invoicing. Eighteen weeks at ₹8 lakh a week is ₹144 lakh, or ₹1.44 crore. It answers issue D. The cost is direct competition with Vyapar and Zoho Books, over a quarter of the 1 March cash balance, and no shopkeeper has ever been shown it.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What did each round teach that the previous one could not, and which row of Exhibit 2 shows that learning most clearly?
  2. Exhibit 3 shows 21.7 per cent against 35.1 per cent. What would you want to know before treating the difference as the product's effect?
  3. Is missing the pay threshold by one shop a failure of the rule or a failure of the measurement? Who should be allowed to say?
  4. Which of the three options would you take on Tuesday, 31 March, and what would make you change your mind in April?

8. A note for the learner

This topic frames the decision as a question of what each round was designed to find out. Each round shows something real to real users, records what they said and did, changes the artefact, and logs the change so the next round can tell whether it worked. A minimum viable product is a learning vehicle with a decision rule, not a small product, and Parchure's best asset is the page she signed in January.

A well-reasoned answer starts by reading the log honestly. Entry speed, language and tone improved after specific fixes, and the log ties each to a change. The wrong-customer error is a regression from one of those fixes, found only because v3 worked. Issue D is the real signal, but it points at a different product and has never been tested.

One defensible path is Option B, run tightly. The rule was set in advance, and one shop short of eight of fifteen is a close miss on a stated-intent measure with a small sample. Changing the threshold afterwards would destroy the rule's value, yet building on so narrow a miss would be poor judgement too. Round 4 should therefore fix issue E, keep both thresholds exactly as written, use twenty fresh shops, and be the last round before a decision. The cost, ₹9 lakh, is under two per cent of the ₹520 lakh cash balance of 1 March. Option C would be a bet on an untested need; Option A would ignore the one condition the team itself chose.

Purvai Technologies: Six Rounds and No Record

Pune, October 2026. A pharmacy-software company has spent ₹4.00 crore showing a new module to chemists and changing it in response. On the eve of a board meeting its product head cannot say what changed, or why.

1. The night before

At a quarter past nine on the night of Sunday, 18 October 2026, the third floor of Purvai's office on Baner Road in Pune held four people and the smell of reheated upma. Diwali was three weeks away. Yamini Dongre, the vice-president of product, had the board pack open on one screen and, on the other, a folder of her own making called rounds: six subfolders, 1,104 files, eight months of showing something to chemists and watching their faces.

The board met at 9.30 the next morning. Item four read: Dispense Advisor — general release decision. Three slides were blank: what six rounds of demonstration and revision had established, what the module would earn, and her recommendation.

She had written the first four times, and each version made a claim the folder could not support. The module had been shown to chemists six times since February and revised between rounds four times that anyone had written down — and the record of what changed, and on whose evidence, sat scattered across an expired Slack workspace, nine Jira tickets, a Figma file, two notebooks and the memory of an engineer in Bengaluru who was asleep. Her chief executive wanted a number; her sales head had one; her data scientist in Toronto had sent, on 7 October, a note arguing it was going the wrong way.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Purvai was founded in Pune in 2017 by Yogesh Dhaygude, a pharmacist's son, and sold one thing: billing and inventory software for independent chemists. By October 2026 it had 11,400 paying counters across five states, 214 employees, and revenue of ₹58.4 crore in the year ended 31 March 2026 against ₹44.9 crore before — growth of 30.1 per cent. It competed for the chemist's ₹2,400-a-month software budget with Tally, Marg ERP and GoFrugal, and for his attention with Tata 1mg, Apollo Pharmacy and Netmeds.

The decision that still binds Purvai was taken on Monday, 14 June 2021: build offline-first, a Windows application with a local database, syncing overnight. A chemist in Jalna could not bill during a power cut, and Purvai won three thousand counters from cloud-only rivals on that argument alone.

Five years later it meant Purvai could not watch its own product being used. Telemetry arrived nightly, and only from counters whose sync completed. Shipping a change meant persuading a chemist to accept an update, so the field ran fourteen builds at once and only 2,180 of the 11,400 counters (19.1 per cent) could run the module at all. Nor could two versions run side by side. Feedback had to run in series — show, listen, change, show again — the one method that makes a record of what changed indispensable, and the one Purvai had never had to keep.

3. The industry

Dispense Advisor was conceived against a real squeeze. A chemist's margin turns on the difference between a branded formulation and an equivalent one, bounded by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority's ceiling prices on one side and the Janaushadhi kendras on the other. ONDC has begun to list pharmacy catalogues, which cuts both ways.

The premise: when a prescription line item is out of stock, slow-moving or needlessly expensive, the software should propose a same-molecule alternative, the customer's saving and the counter's margin side by side. The legal ground is narrow. Substitution is governed by the Pharmacy Practice Regulations, and Schedule H1 molecules carry their own register and inspection risk from the state Food and Drug Administration.

Purvai's exposure was no longer only Indian: success in Singapore, design in Berlin, analytics in Toronto, sales in New Jersey. In 2023 it signed its largest contract, a single-tenant, data-resident deployment for Pearl Crescent Pharmacies, a 96-store chain in Dubai, worth ₹11.7 crore over 36 months — ₹32.5 lakh a month, ₹3.90 crore a year, equal to 6.7 per cent of FY26 revenue. It was a code fork: anything built for India had to be built twice.

4. What happened, and what has since come apart

Exhibit 1 and Figure 1 set out the six rounds, and on paper the pattern is orderly. In February, Yashodhara Dandavate's storyboards showed the suggestion appearing after the bill was totalled. Fourteen chemists in Pune and Nagpur were walked through them and eleven said they would use it; the team recorded that as evidence chemists wanted the advisory. What the storyboards chiefly tested, it now seems, was placement: the first complaint in Round 1 was that after the bill was too late, and that fix was one of three changes made at once before Round 2 (Exhibit 2, rows 1 to 3).

Round 3 widened the trigger from 180 fast-movers to the full 4,100-SKU catalogue and removed the confirmation tap, and the headline number rose again. On that basis, on Thursday 9 July — two working days before the Round 4 window opened — Yatin Dharwadkar and Yamini wrote the programme's only advance decision rule: proceed to general release if acceptance at the payment step exceeds 65 per cent across at least 20 stores over 60 days. Round 4 ran from Monday 13 July to Thursday 10 September across 26 stores and returned 71.0 per cent. By its own rule, the module passed.

Four things have since undermined that sentence. First, the denominator moved with the product. Yuvraj Darbari's roll-up (Exhibit 3) divides acceptances by the suggestions a chemist saw having already reached the payment step; Yohan Dalaya's re-derivation (Exhibit 4) prints the fuller counts, and on the wider base — every suggestion surfaced — the series rises from Round 1 to Round 2, then falls through Rounds 3 and 4. Between Rounds 2 and 3 the two measures move about six points in opposite directions. Neither is wrong; only one was written into the rule.

Second, attribution: three changes landed before Round 2 and two before Round 3, so no round isolates a change. Third, the sample: 17 of the 26 Round 4 stores (65.4 per cent) had taken part in Round 2, the stores that had enjoyed it — and Round 4 delivered 1,322 of the 1,560 scheduled store-days (84.7 per cent), six stores on weak evening connections accounting for most of the missing 238. Fourth, Round 5 ran on the Pearl Crescent fork, from which the advisory had been removed because UAE rules place substitution elsewhere; what six Dubai stores liked was the reorder half, the half nobody has argued about.

5. The people

Yamini Dongre, 39, vice-president of product, Pune. Position: the programme produced activity, not knowledge; one instrumented round with the rule written first is cheap against shipping the wrong thing to 2,180 counters. Incentive: her variable pay rides on module adoption by 31 March 2027. Not saying: she removed the confirmation tap in Round 3 without recording a reason, and is not sure she had one.

Yogesh Dhaygude, 51, founder and chief executive, Pune. Position: general release this calendar year, as a defence of the chemist against online pharmacies. Incentive: a shipped module is a better Series C story in January than a disciplined experiment. Not saying: he reads every chemist complaint personally.

Yatin Dharwadkar, 44, head of platform engineering, Bengaluru. Position: the fork is the real problem; no sixth round until someone decides whether India and Dubai are one product. Incentive: his Q4 plan assumes the eleven-person squad returns to platform work. Not saying: he knows the nightly sync drops evening traffic, and said so once, in April.

Yashodhara Dandavate, 35, design lead, Berlin. Position: the advisory gives the counter's margin the same visual weight as the customer's saving, and no round has tested whether that changes what a chemist recommends. Incentive: she has argued this since May and the issue is now hers. Not saying: her own Round 1 revision cut the alternates from five to two, which raised acceptance and hid the cheapest option.

Yohan Dalaya, 33, senior data scientist, Toronto. Position: no round supports a causal claim; the module is used, and use has not been shown to help anyone. Incentive: he was hired to build a measurement practice. Not saying: his re-derivation rests on the same incomplete logs he criticises.

Yashika Dhuru, 41, head of customer success, Singapore. Position: ship the reorder half; the advisory generates her hardest tickets. Incentive: her cost-to-serve target. Not saying: 9 of the 26 Round 4 stores (34.6 per cent) switched the advisory off by the end, using a toggle shipped in that build.

Yuvraj Darbari, 47, head of global sales, Edison, New Jersey. Position: Pearl Crescent has waited two quarters and the Round 5 build is ready. Incentive: 38 per cent of his variable pay sits on the Dubai go-live. Not saying: his 28 September deck's series is the payment-step measure only, and he was told so on 7 October.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Slide 6 is not a claim about the module. It is a claim about the subset of suggestions that survive to the payment step, and that subset shrank from 44.9 per cent of surfaced suggestions in April to 30.8 per cent in the monsoon, because we widened the trigger. Usage went up a lot; the fraction a chemist takes went down.”

— Yohan Dalaya, memorandum to Yamini Dongre, 7 October 2026

“Yohan, with respect, 11,900 is what the chemist saw at the moment of decision. The rest were never in front of a human about to take money. I am not telling Pearl Crescent we became worse because we did more.”

— Yuvraj Darbari, reply-all, 7 October 2026, 11.52 p.m. IST

“We have never once shown a chemist the same screen twice. Round 3 changed the trigger and removed the confirmation tap in one build. I removed the tap, and I cannot tell you today what I expected it to do.”

— Yamini Dongre, product review, Friday 9 October 2026

“Tell me honestly, madam. If I suggest the other company's tablet and the patient's sugar goes up next month, who does the doctor shout at? The software shows me ₹18 margin. It does not show me the patient coming back.”

— Yogita Dabhade, owner-pharmacist, Nagpur, Round 4 exit interview, 10 September 2026

“Our pharmacists like the stock prompts very much. On substitution, kindly note we have not asked for it, and our regulator would not expect your software to offer it.”

— Yusuf Dalal, pharmacy operations, Pearl Crescent Pharmacies, Dubai, e-mail of Friday 2 October 2026

8. The options as Yamini sees them

She has written them as three (Exhibit 6). Option A: harden the Round 5 build, release in December, bank the Dubai contract, treat eight months of rounds as sufficient. Option B: a sixth round — ten weeks, eight engineers, ₹2.00 crore, a rule signed before the window opens, an outcome measure that is not acceptance; a further 50 per cent on the ₹4.00 crore already spent, and Dubai in late March. Option C: ship the out-of-stock and reorder half to all 2,180 eligible counters now, and hold the advisory.

Each option takes for granted that the question is release or not. Yamini has noticed three things outside that frame. She could not describe what Round 4 tested without first reading Exhibit 2, and Exhibit 2 did not exist until Wednesday. Every version has been judged on whether a chemist taps accept; nobody has measured whether the customer returned, whether stock turned faster, or whether the suggestion was right, and Yogita Dabhade's question has no column in the folder. And per Figure 2, the only people who have watched a Pearl Crescent counter work are paid on the go-live.

There is a fourth option she has not written down, because it does not sound like a decision: the 2,180 eligible counters are not the scarce resource; a round whose result can be read is.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 9.30 a.m. on Monday 19 October 2026. The Pearl Crescent amendment window closes on Saturday 31 October 2026; after that the go-live date of 15 January 2027 is fixed, and a slip costs ₹65 lakh. Purvai held ₹39.6 crore of cash on 30 September 2026 and from 1 October has been burning ₹2.4 crore a month, which is 16.5 months — comfortable, but Yashwant Dhond of Pashan Capital opens the Series C conversation in January and will ask what the ₹4.00 crore bought. Option B takes eight of the squad's eleven engineers for ten weeks, and with them the Q4 platform plan, including the migration that would reduce fourteen field builds to four. Compliance has one immovable line: the advisory may inform and may never instruct; any patient-linked suggestion needs consent under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act that no chemist is collecting. Pahunch Medicals — 180 stores at ₹2,900 a store a month, ₹5.22 lakh a month and ₹62.64 lakh a year — renews on 31 December.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Reading Exhibits 3 and 4 together, what did Round 4 establish? State the claim you would defend and the figures it rests on.
  2. The rule was written on 9 July and the module cleared it. Was it a decision rule? What would have had to be true of it for the board to rely on it now?
  3. Exhibit 2 shows three changes landing before Round 2 and two before Round 3. Design the minimum record Purvai should have kept, given the 2021 architecture. What does it cost?
  4. Round 4 drew 17 of its 26 stores from Round 2, and its logs cover 1,322 of 1,560 store-days. Which would you fix first, and what does that imply about what the rounds are for?
  5. Dandavate wants the margin display tested before release; Darbari wants the contract. Both are right about their own objective. Whose should Purvai's measure serve?
  6. It is Monday morning, 19 October. What does Yamini Dongre do before the meeting, what goes on the three slides, and what does she tell the board the ₹4.00 crore bought? If she asks for Option B, what must she commit to that she has not in any of the six rounds?

11. Sunday, 11.40 p.m.

The office had emptied. Yamini had the change log printed across two desks, and she kept returning to row 5: confirmation tap removed, R3, Dongre, none recorded, not recorded. It had taken an afternoon to establish that she had done it.

Her phone showed a message from Dhaygude, sent at 11.02: Just tell me if it works. One word is enough. Below it, the annexure with the clause removing the advisory, initialled by Yuvraj in July.

She thought about the fourteen chemists in February who had nodded at a storyboard, and about Yogita Dabhade asking who the doctor would shout at. Six times Purvai had shown chemists something, and the log recorded a revision before four of those six, and the honest summary of eight months was that the module was used more and taken less often, for reasons nobody had arranged to know. Whether that was a failure of the module or of the method was the question she had nine hours to answer, and the slide was still blank.

Barkat Retail Technologies: What Is the Smallest Thing We Can Put in Front of a Retailer?

A case for discussion · Chennai, October 2026

1. Sunday night

On Sunday, 18 October 2026, Jeevitha Ramanathan sat on the floor of her flat in Besant Nagar with four printouts fanned out before her. The board pre-read was due on Tuesday, 20 October; the board met on Friday, 30 October. Deepavali fell on 8 November, which meant the festive stocking orders — placed between 5 October and 2 November, the densest four weeks in the southern trade — were already half spent.

Jeevitha was co-founder and chief product officer of Barkat Retail Technologies, and for nine months she had been running what the team called, half-affectionately, the Desk: fourteen agents and two supervisors on a rented first floor in Madurai who answered calls from kirana retailers, listened to them order in Tamil, Telugu or Hindi, and typed it into Barkat's app for them. Begun as a two-intern hack in January, it was still the only part of the voice-ordering idea that existed.

Each printout argued for something different, and each used Barkat's own numbers. What she could not settle was simpler: what question the next build would answer, and what answer would stop it.

2. How Barkat got here

Barkat was founded in Chennai in 2019 by Jeevitha Ramanathan and Jaganmohan Rayudu to sell a GST-ready ledger and ordering app to the distributors who supply India's kirana trade, and for three years it grew one super-stockist at a time.

The decision that shaped everything afterwards was taken on 1 July 2022, when Barkat signed a five-year white-label master services agreement with Belavadi Trade Distribution, a Hyderabad-headquartered FMCG super-stockist network: Belavadi's retailers would use Barkat's software under Belavadi's name. It bought scale — 11,400 live retailers across Tamil Nadu, Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. Belavadi kept the retailer relationship, wrote in a 99.5 per cent uptime commitment with a penalty of ₹18 lakh per quarter breached, and established a change advisory board, the CAB, whose approval was needed for anything touching order data in the tenant — a review cycle that had never in four years run shorter than nine weeks.

The agreement also barred Barkat until 31 March 2027 from selling an ordering product to any distributor competing with Belavadi in those states. Independent wholesalers were permitted, and that line — ₹18.3 crore in the year to 31 March 2026 — was the second business. Of ₹74.0 crore of revenue, Belavadi was ₹46.6 crore, or 63 per cent, Dubai ₹3.2 crore annualised, everything else ₹5.9 crore.

So the only dense population of retailers Barkat could reach sat behind the CAB gate, and the only clean comparison population, rival distributors' retailers, was out of bounds until April.

3. The industry

India's kirana trade remained the spine of grocery, and by 2026 was pulled three ways. Quick commerce — Zepto, Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart — had taken the metros' top-up basket and was pushing into tier-two cities; ONDC had made catalogue interoperability a live policy question; and UPI, on NPCI's rails, had solved collection, which left ordering as the friction in the trade. A retailer in Madurai still restocked by WhatsApp voice note or by handing a slip to a van driver, so Barkat's competitors were the salesman's visit, the distributor's call centre and Udaan's app.

Two regulatory facts bore on the product. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 had made notice and consent operationally real: a recording in which a retailer names his nephew, his landlord and his competitor is personal data about three people who consented to nothing. Inside the Belavadi tenant Barkat was a processor for Belavadi; in the WhatsApp channel it was arguably a fiduciary in its own right — a question counsel in Chennai put in writing on 4 September 2026 and never answered.

Barkat was exposed abroad too: Burooj Grocers, a Dubai group with 61 stores, had signed a three-year, ₹9.6 crore contract from 1 April 2024, and its group digital commerce head, Jigna Ramineni, wanted voice in the renewal.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In December 2025 Jiya Renganathan, Barkat's principal designer in Berlin, sketched a flow in which a retailer pressed one button and spoke. Nobody could build it, so Janani Rayaprolu, who ran retail operations from Madurai, put two interns on a phone line to type what they heard. The pilot ran 12–30 January 2026 with 24 retailers in Madurai, Tiruppur and Coimbatore.

The January number that travelled — into the February board deck, into a fundraising conversation, into the team's own self-understanding — was 92 per cent, and Exhibit 1 shows where it came from: 247 of the 268 calls that reached a human within ninety seconds ended in a confirmed purchase order. The denominator nobody put on the slide was the 412 calls retailers actually placed; against that base, 247 of the 412 calls became orders, or 60 per cent. The 144 calls that never reached an agent within ninety seconds — 35 per cent of calls placed — were described, correctly and misleadingly, as a staffing issue.

In February a Hyderabad speech-technology vendor benchmarked its Indic models on a 2,000-utterance set and reported 88.2 per cent word accuracy. The team read that as “the model is ready” and planned an in-app module; on 24 April 2026 the CAB rejected it, a new write path into order data needing a fresh security review. Jothi Rangarajan's engineers took the fallback, a WhatsApp flow outside the tenant where retailers sent voice notes the Desk transcribed. It shipped in May, believed to raise no legal question, because a voice note was “just a message the retailer chose to send”.

In June, Bindhu Field Research surveyed 420 retailers in six cities (Exhibit 4); 71 per cent of the 398 who completed the instrument said they would use voice ordering daily. In July, Jahnavi Rachakonda, the data scientist in Toronto, re-ran the vendor's benchmark on 1,180 utterances from live Desk recordings (Exhibit 3). She also returned to the pilot's call logs: 148 of the 247 completed orders — 60 per cent — came from five of the 24 retailers, and in all five the log's caller name suggests a paid assistant rather than the owner.

By September the Desk served 310 retailers and its economics were legible for the first time (Exhibit 2); it had also produced something nobody planned, a log of every order line it could not fulfil as spoken.

5. Exhibits

6. The people

Jeevitha Ramanathan, co-founder and chief product officer, Chennai, holds that the company has never run a test that could fail. Her incentive is a Series C story with one line that is not Belavadi; she has not told the board she authorised the 92 per cent slide and never corrected it.

Jaganmohan Rayudu, co-founder and chief executive, Hyderabad, wants the cheapest option that yields a board-ready number by 30 October, and talks about “learning per rupee”. His incentive is the Belavadi renewal; he has not told the team that Belavadi's managing director asked him in September whether Barkat would still be independent.

Jothi Rangarajan, vice-president of engineering, Bengaluru, argues for Option C: build it once, in the tenant, where the retailers are, since A, B and D leave the production app untouched and test nothing that will ship. His team has shipped three throwaway prototypes in nine months and is starting to leave; he does not say that his 18-week estimate assumes the two engineers at Burooj come back.

Janani Rayaprolu, head of retail operations, Madurai, defends the Desk: retailers trust it, her agents know who substitutes which SKU, and it “pays for itself in retained GMV”. Her incentive is sixteen jobs and a lease; Barkat has never measured retention against a control, so the exhibits cannot settle her claim.

Jahnavi Rachakonda, staff data scientist, Toronto, has been right more often than she has been heeded: nothing measured so far, she holds, distinguishes “retailers want to speak their orders” from “retailers want someone else to do their ordering”. She has not said that she declined to produce the model forecast Jaganmohan asked for.

Jiya Renganathan, principal designer, Berlin, is three and a half hours behind Madurai, sees the Desk only as transcripts, and is drawn to the five outlier retailers: the assistant who places the order may be the real user. She has not mentioned showing the concept at a Berlin meet-up.

Jwala Ravichandran, customer success director, Singapore, owns Burooj and the renewal her variable pay rides on, and wants Option E, or at least a roadmap slide for Jigna Ramineni by mid-December. She has not said that Jigna has told her, informally, that Burooj's board will renew anyway.

Jayesh Rathinavelu, head of enterprise sales for North America, in Edison, New Jersey, has two Indian-diaspora grocery chains asking for voice and wants something demonstrable, not learnable. He does not say that both have asked for Gujarati, which appears nowhere in Exhibit 3.

7. Voices

“The February note said 92 per cent completion and asked how fast we could take the humans out. Please stop putting 92 on slides. 247 orders came out of 412 calls. Understaffed, the retailer does not experience 92 per cent of anything; he experiences a phone that rings.”

Jahnavi Rachakonda, comment on the February deck, reopened 7 October 2026

“Option D costs ₹3.70 lakh and Option C costs ₹135.50 lakh — more than thirty-six times as much. If both teach us one thing, D is the better buy.”

Jaganmohan Rayudu, leadership call, 15 October 2026

“They do not teach us one thing each. D tells us how many people dial a number printed on an invoice during Deepavali; C tells us whether retailers who already use the app keep ordering through it once it has been live a quarter. Not the same unit, so the ratio is not a number. And nobody has written down what result would make us stop.”

Jahnavi Rachakonda, reply on the same call

“Madam, the boy speaks and your Madurai people understand. Last week I asked for Britannia 50-50, two cartons, and they sent the small pack — but they called me back and asked. The app never asked me anything.”

Jagadish Ramalingam, retailer, Madurai, WhatsApp voice note transcribed by the Desk, 3 October 2026

“Of 14,160 order lines in September, 2,860 could not be fulfilled as spoken — 20.2 per cent. Of those 2,860, 1,173 were out of stock at the stockist — 41 per cent — and 1,687 were pack-size or brand-name ambiguity. If a fifth of what retailers ask for is not available or not nameable, is speech the bottleneck at all?”

Janani Rayaprolu, operations review, 10 October 2026

“Before we widen anything: who is being told what, when we record a shop assistant naming his employer's customers? I do not have an answer and will not have one soon.”

External counsel, Chennai, note of 4 September 2026, in Jothi Rangarajan's CAB file

8. The options as Jeevitha sees them

Jothi had costed all five on 14 October at ₹0.75 lakh per engineer-week, and writing them out had begun to bother her. Option A widened the Desk to 900 of Belavadi's retailers for what was left of the festive window: no code, no CAB, a first call in two weeks — and a multiplied loss that Exhibit 2's figures imply at ₹84.34 an order on September volumes. Option B put the speech model into the ungated WhatsApp channel for 66 engineer-weeks (6 × 11), or ₹49.50 lakh, reaching the 2,400 who had opted in. Option C built the real thing in the tenant and reached all 11,400: 162 engineer-weeks (9 × 18) at ₹121.50 lakh, plus ₹14.00 lakh for the CAB's security review, and twenty-seven weeks with that nine-week review after the build, so, counting from 19 October, no retailer before 26 April 2027. Option D printed a number on 4,000 invoices for the Desk to answer: 2 engineer-weeks at ₹1.50 lakh plus ₹2.20 lakh of print run and IVR — ₹3.70 lakh, one week. Option E built what Dubai specified for its 61 stores: 56 engineer-weeks (4 × 14) at ₹42.00 lakh plus ₹18.00 lakh for the Arabic pack and audit trail, fourteen weeks.

What bothered her was that all five answered the question “how do we ship voice ordering?” None answered Jahnavi's — whether what retailers valued was speech at all, or someone competent taking responsibility for the order; nor Jiya's, whether the user was the owner or the assistant; nor Janani's, whether the constraint sat in the catalogue and the warehouse rather than the microphone. A sixth option, a managed-ordering service with no speech in it, was never costed. And not one of the five said what result would make Barkat abandon it.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The pre-read was due on Tuesday, 20 October, the board met on Friday, 30 October, and Deepavali was on 8 November; the next comparable density was Pongal, in mid-January 2027. Cash was ₹778 lakh as at 1 November on plan, against a September net burn of ₹112 lakh a month, and Bharanya Capital's board partner held a revenue-growth milestone for the year to 31 March 2027. Of 48 people in product and engineering, Jothi could free nine without touching the Belavadi roadmap, and Option C needed exactly nine. Exclusivity held until 31 March 2027, the Belavadi agreement expired on 30 June 2027 with its notice window opening on 1 January, and Burooj's decision was due by 15 December. Counsel's question — whose notice, whose consent, for whose voice — was open, which meant the cheapest and fastest options put more unresolved recording in front of more people.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What, precisely, was learned in the January pilot? State the claim, its base and its date.
  2. Take each of the five options. What decision would its result change, and what result would make Barkat stop? Which fail that test entirely?
  3. Exhibits 3 and 4 appear to say opposite things about readiness and demand. What would have to be measured, on what sample, for them to be comparable?
  4. Janani's September log suggests the constraint may be assortment, not speech. Given exclusivity and the CAB, how would you separate the two before 31 March 2027, and at what cost?
  5. What is the smallest thing Barkat can legally and contractually put in front of a retailer before 8 November, given the open DPDP question, the uptime penalty and nine engineers?
  6. What should Jeevitha do on Monday morning, 19 October, and what should she say to the board on 30 October — including about the 92 per cent?

11. Still Sunday night

At about eleven Jeevitha wrote a line at the top of a fresh page: The smallest thing that would change our minds. Under it she wrote Option D, struck it out, then wrote it again with a question mark against it. Her phone showed a message from Jothi, timestamped 10.52 p.m.: the two engineers on the Burooj build wanted an answer by Monday. Below it, Jwala in Singapore, already into Monday, asking for the roadmap slide. Below that, nothing from Jahnavi, who had said on Friday she would send her note when she was sure of it.

Jeevitha put the printouts in order of cost, then of weeks, then of how much she would have to explain. The three orders were different, and she did not know which her board would use on Friday.
exp40v2-sol.mvp.definition:
What an MVP is

The smallest thing that produces validated learning, and why "smallest" is a property of the question rather than of the product

1. Two decisions, four weeks apart

On Monday, 9 February 2026, at a board meeting in Ahmedabad, Ishank Gharge was asked for an MVP in ten weeks. Gharge was co-founder and chief product officer of Wazan Cold Metrics, which made a battery-powered temperature logger and dashboard for pharmacy chains and vaccine cold-chain operators regulated under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules. A quotation made that impossible: enclosure tooling cost ₹38 lakh on a fourteen-week lead time, and firmware, WHO certification and a first run added ₹22 lakh. The first mouldings would land on Monday, 18 May 2026 — four weeks past the date Jinal Gokulnath, who led the investor syndicate, had named. If the board meant a small logger, no version was small enough.

On Monday, 9 March 2026, Jigisha Goradia met the same word in a different world. As director of product at Wasool Credit Cloud in Pune, which sold collections software to eleven non-banking financial companies and small finance banks, she had a proposal for an AI voice agent placing first-reminder calls in Marathi and Gujarati: ₹140 lakh and sixteen weeks, so a 9 March start meant delivery on Monday, 29 June 2026. Idhant Gundewar, the chief executive, wanted it signed. Ikshita Gholap, who ran data science, had run the model over 180 archived calls; it gave the correct next utterance in 144 of 180, which is 80 per cent, against a bar she put at 95, a wrong utterance on a recovery call being a compliance event under Reserve Bank of India rules.

Goradia proposed ₹9.6 lakh over seven weeks, to Monday, 27 April 2026, to buy an answer; Gharge, ₹6.4 lakh over the board's ten weeks on forty hand-built units in off-the-shelf cases. Neither was building a small product.

2. The idea, and the propositions that divide it

A minimum viable product is the smallest construction that can be put before real people and produces evidence capable of changing a decision the team has already named and costed. Minimum refers to the effort needed to get that evidence, not the feature count. Viable means people behave as they would with a genuine offer: money moves, or reputation, or an hour of a working day. Product misleads, because the construction may be a video, a payment screen, a WhatsApp number with two people behind it, or forty circuit boards in boxes.

Frank Robinson used the phrase around 2001 for a narrower idea: the version that is both the smallest a customer will buy and the smallest the firm can profit from. Steve Blank's customer development method told founders their guesses were guesses, to be tested outside. Eric Ries fused the two from about 2009: the version yielding maximum validated learning for the least effort.

Four schools hold incompatible positions. The Lean orthodoxy will sign "a screen-recorded video with no software behind it can be an MVP" — Drew Houston's 2007 Dropbox video — and not "an MVP must be shippable and sellable". The minimum-lovable school will sign "anything bearing your name before a customer is your brand, permanently" and not "a deliberately poor version produces trustworthy learning". The process school, including Ash Maurya's work, will sign "the loop is the unit, not the artefact" and not "an MVP is a release". The abolitionists, whose clearest voice is Marty Cagan, will sign "the word product has cost the industry a decade" and not "therefore cheap testing is impossible". None disputes what makes a thing an MVP rather than a first release: a named decision, and a rule written before the data.

3. Mechanics: the rule is derived, not chosen

Expert practice has five steps; competent practice skips the first and the third.

Step one names and prices the decision: Goradia's binary ₹140 lakh, Gharge's ₹60 lakh with fourteen weeks of irreversibility in the tooling. A test that cannot move a named, priced decision is not an MVP. Step two states the hypothesis so it can fail — Wasool's, that an automated reminder call in the borrower's language lifts the share paying within seven days; Wazan's, that a manager receiving an excursion alert logs a corrective action within two hours, a claim about human response.

Step three derives the threshold. Across Wasool's eleven lenders in the quarter to 31 December 2025, 4,40,000 accounts were one to thirty days overdue and 96,800 paid in full within seven days of the first reminder: 22 per cent, the base being every such account, not only those who answered. An average lender carries 40,000 a quarter, so 1,60,000 a year. At ₹430 of value per account brought forward (₹310 of collection cost avoided, ₹120 of reduced credit loss), one point of lift is worth 0.01 × 1,60,000 × ₹430 = ₹6.88 lakh a year per lender. Wasool means to charge ₹18 lakh, and no finance committee signs for less than twice that in value: ₹36 lakh needs 36 ÷ 6.88 = 5.2 points, so 22 per cent must become 27.

The sample follows. For two proportions at 5 per cent significance and 80 per cent power, the size per arm is (1.96 + 0.8416)2 × [0.22 × 0.78 + 0.27 × 0.73] ÷ 0.052. The bracket is 0.1716 + 0.1971 = 0.3687; over 0.0025 that is 147.48; times 7.849 it is 1,158. So 1,158 per arm, 2,316 in all, of whom only the 1,158 treated are called: at sixty calls a day, twenty caller-days and ₹24,000 at ₹1,200 a day.

Step four picks the vehicle, cheapest gate first. Gholap's objection was precise: a human reading the script tests the script and the channel, not the model. So the model runs over 1,400 archived calls against a 95 per cent bar for ₹1.26 lakh — ending the project, if need be, for 0.9 per cent of the build — and only if it clears does the live comparison follow.

Step five, acting on the answer, is claimed far more often than performed.

The formal treatment: what a test is actually worth

An MVP is a purchase of information, so it can be priced. Wasool's plan has the module at eleven lenders in year one (₹198 lakh), thirteen in year two (₹234 lakh) and fifteen in year three (₹270 lakh) at ₹18 lakh each: ₹702 lakh of licence revenue less ₹42 lakh of inference and support, so ₹660 lakh before the build. The agent is therefore worth ₹520 lakh if it clears the bar and costs ₹140 lakh if not, on Gundewar's prior of 45 per cent.

Building blind is worth 0.45 × 520 − 0.55 × 140 = 234 − 77 = ₹157 lakh: positive, which is the uncomfortable starting point. Perfect information would be worth 0.45 × 520 = ₹234 lakh, so its value is 234 − 157 = ₹77 lakh, exactly the avoided loss of 0.55 × 140. Suppose the test flags a good agent 80 per cent of the time (sensitivity) and stops a bad one 70 per cent of the time (specificity):

The test flags 360 of the 450 good worlds, which is 80 per cent, as assumed. Under "build only if the test says go" the firm earns ₹520 lakh in 360 worlds and loses ₹140 lakh in 165: (360 × 520 − 165 × 140) ÷ 1,000 = ₹164.1 lakh. So the test adds ₹7.1 lakh on ₹157 lakh and costs ₹9.6 lakh. At Gundewar's prior, Goradia's test is not worth running.
