Two things follow. The same weak test is worth running at Wazan and not at Wasool, because where the default is to build a test must overturn a profitable decision. And each accuracy's marginal value has a closed form: one unit of sensitivity is worth the probability the idea is good times the upside, one of specificity the probability it is bad times the downside.

Gholap's lower prior moves this generic design's value more than either single improvement in Exhibit 1. At 25 per cent, building blind is worth 0.25 × 520 − 0.75 × 140 = ₹25 lakh, and the same weak test yields (200 × 520 − 225 × 140) ÷ 1,000 = ₹72.5 lakh: a gain of ₹47.5 lakh, ₹37.9 lakh net.

4. When the idea applies, stated as claims you can test

Four conditions, each checkable in advance. One: the decision is reversible in money but not in time. True at Wasool, where the ₹140 lakh is lost if the agent fails but can be earned again in later quarters, while sixteen weeks of six engineers cannot; truer at Wazan, whose tooling is single-purpose steel.

Two: the dominant uncertainty is behavioural, not technical. True at Wazan, where thermometry is solved and the question is whether a manager acts; half true at Wasool, where accuracy is a feasibility question and lift a behavioural one.

Three: a cheap vehicle produces the same measure as the real thing. True at Wasool for the lift, false for the model, hence the archive gate. Wazan's units give genuine traces and alerts but not battery life or a cost of goods, both out of scope. Four: the test's gain exceeds its cost. Exhibit 1 shows this can fail; the condition is not that the test is cheap.

The idea is actively misleading in three places. Where being wrong means a safety event rather than lost money, expected value understates it. Where value appears only at scale, a small test measures the absence of scale and returns a false negative. And where the organisation will build regardless, it is a ritual.

5. Hard edges

Two-sided markets. The smallest honest test is not a small marketplace but one hand-matched transaction loop, because liquidity is what is under test and is non-linear.

Regulated products. A recovery call is a regulated act, so a test trivial elsewhere needed a ₹2.10 lakh compliance review: a fifth of the budget, and the largest line after staff time. Permission is the cost to plan around, and the expert books legal in week one.

Hardware plus software. Lead times do not yield to cleverness. Route each question to the cheapest medium: Wazan's behavioural question to forty hand-built units, its battery question to four units in a chamber, its cost question to a quotation.

AI-native products. A Wizard-of-Oz test, in which a person performs what the model will, measures demand for the outcome and says nothing about attainable capability; an offline evaluation on archived data measures capability and says nothing about demand. Both are necessary, neither sufficient, the cheap one first: Gholap's 144 of 180 is a capability reading no demand evidence rescues.

Organisational seams. The binding constraint is usually a function that never agreed to be minimum: support will not answer for a hand-run product; finance cannot book forty units. Mature firms say they run MVPs and mostly ship small first releases behind a feature flag, abandoning the stopping rule, because nobody deletes a shipped feature on a threshold nobody remembers agreeing to.

6. Eight things an expert sees

The minimum belongs to the question. Tell-tale: the expert asks what would change your mind before asking what to build. Cutting features off a roadmap item preserves the shape of the suspect product.

A rule that cannot stop anything is not a rule. Tell-tale: asked cold, the expert names the number at which they abandon their own idea. "We will look at the data" is not a weaker rule but no rule.

Viability lives in behaviour, not finish. Tell-tale: the expert asks what the participant gave up — money, an hour, reputational risk before a colleague. Costless admiration is courtesy, not evidence.

The denominator is fixed when the test is designed. Tell-tale: the plan names who is eligible and when eligibility closes. The commonest corruption is a base chosen after the data arrives.

Concierge economics never transfer; only the demand signal does. Tell-tale: the expert reads demand off a hand-run test but not unit economics, since per-order hand cost is a fact about two people with a phone.

Which error to pay for is arithmetic, not doctrine. Tell-tale: the expert asks for the prior and the payoff ratio before discussing method. At Wasool's 45 per cent prior detection is worth three times refutation while at Wazan it reverses, so a reflex for the conservative test is often wrong.

Cheap tests fail asymmetrically, usually as a false go. Tell-tale: the expert asks what the test would report if the idea were worthless. Landing pages and interest surveys over-detect, since interest is free.

Evidence has a shelf life. Tell-tale: the expert dates the finding and names what would expire it. Goradia's 22 per cent dates from the quarter to 31 December 2025, so the honest move is a concurrent control arm.

7. How it really differs by product type and stage

Consumer software runs the cheapest tests: large populations, one session as the unit. B2B and enterprise differ not because samples are smaller but because user and buyer are different people, so measuring user enthusiasm has poor specificity for purchase; Indrajeet Godse, who sold Wasool's modules, asked one question in every pilot: whose budget code pays. Platforms and marketplaces differ because the quantity of interest is non-linear in participation, so the test must be a whole loop at tiny scale. Hardware differs because lead time, not money, binds. AI products differ because behaviour depends on data the team may not hold, splitting the MVP into a capability gate and a demand gate.

One received difference is weaker than claimed. Enterprise products are said to need a complete product; they need one complete workflow for one named account. Stage inverts too: early-stage firms are told to run MVPs when building is their cheapest test, while mature firms are told they are too big and need them most.

8. Three completed tests, one of which lied

Wartalap Audio, Hyderabad: a real door, not a fake one. Jigar Gambhir asked whether listeners would pay ₹149 a month for offline downloads and no advertising: a ₹26 lakh build decision, tested for ₹1.9 lakh. Over fourteen days a one-in-twenty slice of daily actives saw a working payment screen, downloads pre-loaded by hand: 9,250 saw it and 203 paid, which is 203 of the 9,250 or 2.2 per cent, against a bar of 1.8 per cent. A second clause needed 70 per cent of payers to remain after thirty days; 151 of the 203 did, or 74 per cent.

Watan Agri Works, Nagpur: no software for six weeks. Ismaan Ganatra asked whether agri-input retailers in Vidarbha would replenish through one channel instead of three distributors. The vehicle was a WhatsApp number and two people placing orders by hand. Of 38 retailers invited, 19 of the 38, or 50 per cent, ordered four or more times, against a bar of 40 per cent. Across 214 orders, contribution was ₹1,040 an order against ₹1,860 of hand cost per order, so the test lost ₹1.75 lakh — which Ganatra declined to read as a verdict, since trucking arranged by phone is not the proposed delivery model. The six weeks cost ₹4.6 lakh including that loss, against a ₹74 lakh build decision.

Wajib Compliance Cloud, Bengaluru: the test that lied. Jashodhar Gogia's team asked whether finance teams would buy automated goods-and-services-tax reconciliation at ₹85,000 a year. They spent ₹3.2 lakh on a landing page and counted requests for early access: 1,240 of 4,000 visitors clicked, which is 31 per cent, a figure the team called overwhelming. Five months and ₹92 lakh later it launched to the 1,240, and 38 bought: 38 of the 1,240, or 3.1 per cent.

Two errors compounded. The test had no price in it, so a click cost nothing and could barely separate a good idea from a worthless one. And the base was wrong twice: the 4,000 came from an advertisement promising free reconciliation, and the 3.1 per cent was computed over clickers while the 31 per cent was computed over visitors — the like-for-like figure is 38 of the 4,000, or 0.95 per cent.

Ipshita Gurtu's recovery replaced the measurement, not the product. Ninety-six firms were approached with a priced letter of intent at the real ₹85,000, and 7 of the 96, or 7.3 per cent, signed: a smaller number and a far better one, since it measured the act the business depends on. Figure 4 sets each test's cost against what it had at stake.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The MVP that is really release one. Sign: a roadmap rather than a question. Diagnostic: what result would stop this? Late cost: the full build.

Intent read as behaviour. Sign: the metric is a click or a survey score. Diagnostic: what did the participant give up? Late cost: Wajib's ₹92 lakh.

A base chosen after the data. Sign: the analysis names an eligible population the plan did not. Diagnostic: who was eligible, and when did that close? Late cost: a rate wrong in a known direction, defended for a year.

Learning banked and ignored. Sign: the result appears in a deck while the build proceeds. Diagnostic: what did we do differently? Late cost: the next test's credibility.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether an MVP may carry the brand. The minimum-lovable position is that first impressions are unrecoverable where switching costs are low, so a rough release measures roughness; the Lean reply is that this confuses an experiment with a launch, which a small consenting sample avoids. It is wrong if early users are the more forgiving.

Whether the concept survives capital intensity and regulation. The abolitionist case is that where permission costs more than code the discipline is staged qualification against pre-agreed gates, and MVP vocabulary smuggles a consumer-software metaphor into boardrooms, as Gokulnath's did. The defence is that this is the same logic renamed, and fails if teams behave identically under both.

Who owns the prior. Exhibit 1 makes this concrete: the gap between Gundewar's 45 per cent and Gholap's 25 per cent is worth more than either single improvement in Exhibit 1. One camp would elicit and record priors; the other says written priors become anchors.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes an MVP plan; someone who has internalised it writes the decision first, and asks what it costs before asking what it does. They will conclude that no test is worth running, which the studied practitioner reads as a failure of nerve. They design against the expensive error, not the embarrassing one, and treat the stopping rule as a promise made in front of the people it will disappoint.

12. Closing: what Goradia and Gharge decided

Goradia authorised the ₹9.6 lakh, having redesigned the test first. Her arithmetic said she was buying detection, not refutation — at Gundewar's prior, ₹234 lakh a unit against ₹77 lakh — so the behavioural arm runs where the effect should be largest: Marathi-speaking borrowers one to fifteen days overdue at the most cooperative lender. A positive result will therefore not generalise, and she pre-registered the consequence: a null on the most favourable segment ends the project, a win buys only a second, representative test. She did not adopt Gholap's prior, and the restricted design's own sensitivity and specificity are unpriced, so Exhibit 1 does not price the test she authorised.

Gharge declined to build a small logger. He told the board that day that no tooling would be ordered, that forty hand-built units would go into pharmacy refrigerators across Ahmedabad and Rajkot, and that the question was whether anyone acted on the alert. His rule: build if 60 per cent or more of excursion alerts produce a logged corrective action within two hours. Four weeks in, on the day Goradia met Gundewar and Gholap, 19 of 58 alerts had done so, which is 33 per cent, with six weeks to run. The rule was written first, which is the only reason the reading is uncomfortable rather than interesting.

Discussion questions

  1. A test of this generic design is worth −₹2.5 lakh at Gundewar's prior and ₹37.9 lakh at Gholap's. Who should set the prior on which a ₹140 lakh decision rests?
  2. She tested the most favourable segment, raising sensitivity and destroying generalisability. Is her staged rule good design, or a way of never having to stop?
  3. Gokulnath asked for an MVP in ten weeks when tooling took fourteen. Was that incoherent, or sound instinct in the wrong vocabulary?

13. Going deeper

  • Writing a solution hypothesis — nothing is testable until it can fail; hence step three.
  • Hypothesis-driven product development — the loop that gives the MVP its meaning.
  • MVP types — concierge, Wizard of Oz, painted door, single feature: step four's catalogue.
  • Minimum lovable and minimum marketable products — the strongest alternative to this orthodoxy.
  • Zero to one — when no comparable market exists, so Exhibit 1 loses its inputs.
  • Ideation: brainstorming, Crazy 8s, HMW — generates the candidates an MVP prices.
  • Concept and elevator pitch — the shortest testable articulation, often the painted door.
  • Value Proposition Canvas — surfaces the job the hypothesis claims to do.
  • Value proposition statement — the claim as one priced sentence, as Gurtu's letters were.
  • Storyboarding — which frame of the behaviour the test must observe.
  • Wireframes, mockups, prototypes — the artefacts most often mistaken for MVPs.
exp20v2-sol.mvp.definition:
What an MVP is

The smallest thing that produces validated learning

1. A quote for ₹62 lakh

On Monday, 2 March 2026, Jaspal Girme, engineering lead at Wadiya Rations in Pune, sent a quote to the company's two senior colleagues. Wadiya sold monthly baskets of staples (dal, rice, atta, oil and spices) to households in gated housing societies, packed from a rented godown in Wakad and delivered to a single drop point in each society. Girme proposed a proper subscription app, with society dashboards, payment mandates and route planning. It would take fourteen weeks and cost ₹62 lakh.

Imtiyaz Garud, the chief executive, was inclined to approve. The company held ₹310 lakh in the bank and spent ₹38 lakh a month before any build. Paying ₹62 lakh at once would leave ₹248 lakh, or 6.5 months of that spending. Jivitesh Gangurde, the head of product, objected. Nobody had shown, he argued, that enough households would pay in advance for a fixed monthly basket, or that Wadiya could deliver it at a margin. The app would assume both. If either assumption was wrong, Wadiya would find out in the sixteenth week (fourteen weeks to build, two to launch), with the money spent.

Gangurde did not propose a smaller app. He proposed to find out whether an app was worth building, within six weeks and for a small fraction of the cost. The difference between those two ideas is the whole subject.

2. The idea

A minimum viable product, or MVP, is the smallest thing that can be put in front of real people and that produces evidence capable of changing a decision the team has already named. "Minimum" refers to the effort needed to obtain that evidence, not to the product's size. The word "viable" means that the thing works well enough for the people involved to behave as they would with a real offer.

The idea comes from the Lean Startup movement. Eric Ries, a Silicon Valley software entrepreneur, popularised it from about 2009 and set it out in his 2011 book, drawing on Steve Blank's "customer development" method, which told founders to test their guesses with customers outside the building. The phrase itself had earlier uses; the engineer Frank Robinson used it around 2001. Ries defined it as the version of a product that yields the maximum validated learning about customers for the least effort. "Validated learning" means knowledge that has been tested against what customers actually did, rather than against what they said or what the team believed.

The problem the idea was invented to solve is expensive certainty. Start-ups often spent a year building to a specification nobody outside had tested, and learned at launch that customers did not want it. Dropbox's Drew Houston, in 2007, tested demand with a short screen-recorded video rather than a working product. Zappos's founder photographed shoes in local stores and posted them online to see whether people would order. In each case the founders bought an answer before the product.

"We are not building a small product. We are buying one answer, and we have written down what we will do with each possible answer."

Gangurde could say that in a meeting without sounding glib. It contains the two features that separate an MVP from a rough first release: a specific question, and a decision rule fixed before the data arrives.

3. How it works

The mechanics have six steps; practitioners leave the first and last implicit. The first is to name the decision. Gangurde's was binary: commit ₹62 lakh, or not. A test that cannot move that choice is not an MVP.

The second step is to state the hypothesis as something that can fail. Wadiya's solution hypothesis was that households in gated societies will pay a deposit for a fixed monthly basket priced at ₹2,400, delivered to a drop point on a set day, and will pay again the following month. Third, he picked the cheapest vehicle that could test it. A concierge MVP, in which people do by hand what software will later automate, suited this case. Ishrita Gadekar, the operations lead, would pack baskets by hand and the team would take deposits by UPI, India's instant bank-transfer system.

Fourth, and most often skipped, he derived the decision rule from the economics instead of choosing it by feel. The next section shows the arithmetic. Fifth, the team ran the test and recorded results against the rule. Sixth came the step nobody likes: acting on the answer, even if it disappoints its proposer.

4. A worked example

Gangurde built the rule from a break-even calculation. Each basket sold for ₹2,400. Goods cost ₹1,980 and Gadekar's estimate for delivery was ₹120, leaving a contribution (revenue minus the variable costs of serving one household) of ₹300 a month. He assumed a household would stay twelve months, giving ₹3,600 over a customer's life. The assumption was untested. Dividing the ₹62 lakh build by ₹3,600 gives 1,722.2, so 1,723 households are needed just to repay the app. Wadiya's addressable market was 100 societies of 300 households, or 30,000 households. Break-even therefore required about 5.7 per cent of them (1,723 / 30,000 = 5.74 per cent). He rounded up and wrote the rule on 9 March:

Build only if, among the households offered a basket, at least 6 in 100 pay the ₹500 deposit, and at least 70 per cent of depositors pay for a second basket.

The offer went to 1,200 households, four societies of 300 each in Wakad and Hinjewadi, on 16 March. Both denominators matter. The deposit rate uses the 1,200 offered as its base; the repurchase rate uses the 78 depositors.

Table 1. First reading, 27 April 2026
MeasureBaseCountRateRuleResult
Paid ₹500 deposit1,200 households offered786.5%at least 6% (72)Pass
Paid for second basket78 depositors5671.8%at least 70% (55)Pass

On these figures the rule said build. But the test had also measured something the plan had only assumed. Delivering 134 baskets (78 in the first round and 56 in the second) had cost ₹21,440, so delivery was ₹160 a basket, not ₹120. The whole six-week test cost ₹3,71,440:

Table 2. What the test cost
Item₹
Two operations associates, six weeks1,80,000
Delivery, 134 baskets at ₹16021,440
Society stalls and printed cards60,000
Packaging, UPI and WhatsApp Business fees1,10,000
Total3,71,440

The second pass changes one input only. At ₹160 a basket the contribution is ₹2,400 minus ₹1,980 minus ₹160, or ₹260, and a twelve-month life yields ₹3,120. The ₹62 lakh build now needs 1,988 households (6,200,000 / 3,120 = 1,987.2, rounded up), or 6.6 per cent of 30,000. The unrounded requirement is 6.6 per cent, about 80 of 1,200 households. Rounding up as before, the team set 7 per cent (84) for headroom; 78 misses either figure. That threshold did not exist before launch. The 9 March rule was passed; a measured input its arithmetic depended on changed, so Gangurde re-derived the threshold from the same formula and said so openly. The rule should have said "re-derive if any input moves". Two cautions apply. A two-household miss is inside sampling noise (the standard error on 6.5 per cent of 1,200 is about 0.7 points), so the cost is a reason to test again, not proof of failure. And the 71.8 per cent repurchase rate is never scaled into the break-even, so the effective customer rate is below 6.5 per cent.

5. Nuances a learner must know

Minimum is not small

A small product that tests nothing is merely small. Wadiya's concierge test demanded more effort per household than an app would, because humans packed every basket. It was minimal only in the cost of reaching the decision.

Viable means behaviour is real

A survey asking whether people would buy is cheap and weak. A ₹500 deposit paid by UPI is stronger because the household gave up money.

Validated learning is not validation

A test that returns "no" can still succeed, because the team can act on it. An MVP whose every outcome leads to the same decision has taught nothing.

The sample is chosen, not random

Gadekar selected the four societies because they lay near the godown and had cooperative committee secretaries. Such societies may convert better than the other 96, so 6.5 per cent is probably generous.

Some questions the test cannot answer

Two baskets say little about a twelve-month life, which stayed an assumption in both passes. It also cannot say whether the app will be good, or how BigBasket and DMart will respond. An MVP answers the question it was designed to answer, and no other.

It is not a prototype, nor a pilot

A prototype shows how something might work, often without testing demand. A pilot rolls out a finished product to a limited group. An MVP is defined by its question.

The questions to ask before relying on it

What decision does this change? What number would make us stop? Who is not in the sample?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

The vehicle and the behaviour measured differ (Table 3).

Table 3. The same idea in different settings
SettingTypical vehicleBehaviour that counts
ConsumerLanding page, hand-run servicePayment, repeat use
B2BMock-up, manual pilot for one accountSigned paper, a named budget, use by the staff
MarketplaceSpreadsheet matching two sidesCompleted transactions on both sides

In business-to-business products, buyers rarely pay a deposit, so a signed letter of intent or a staffed trial is the nearest equivalent. In a marketplace, supply and demand must both appear, so the MVP often seeds one side by hand. Wadiya was a consumer business with a supply chain behind it, which explains why delivery cost, not interest, undid the first reading.

Size matters as well. An early-stage company has little to lose and should run many cheap tests. A large company has brand and regulatory exposure, so its "minimum" is usually a restricted release to employees or existing customers.

7. Common mistakes

Table 4. Four mistakes, how they look, and the cheapest check
MistakeSymptom from outsideMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Building "version one"Six-month roadmap labelled MVPMVP means a small productAsk what question it answers
No decision ruleTeam debates the numbers after seeing themData will speak for itselfFind the written threshold dated before launch
Measuring words"Everyone loved it" with no purchasesPraise is demandCount payments, not comments
Wrong baseRate looks excellentAny percentage will doState the denominator and when it was measured

The fourth deserves a note. Had Gangurde divided the 56 repeat buyers by the 1,200 households offered, he would have reported 4.7 per cent and wrongly failed the repeat rule; the correct base is the 78 depositors.

8. What good looks like

The handling of Wadiya's decision showed the habits worth copying. The question was named on 2 March, two weeks before the offer went out. The rule was dated 9 March, a week before the offer went out, and it was derived from a break-even, not from instinct. A cost the team had assumed turned out to be wrong, and the team said openly that it re-derived the threshold from the same formula.

9. Closing: what Gangurde decided

At the board meeting on Friday, 1 May 2026, Gangurde recommended against releasing the ₹62 lakh. At ₹160 a basket the deposit rate did not clear the re-derived threshold, by a margin inside sampling noise. Garud objected that the app might lower delivery costs; Gangurde replied that route planning helps only if households sit close together, which the test had not shown. The board approved a second six-week test: six societies inside one two-kilometre cluster, same offer, same rules, with delivery cost the thing under test.

Readers should next study MVP types (concierge, Wizard of Oz, landing page), minimum lovable and minimum marketable products, and the zero-to-one problem of finding the first proof of demand.

Two questions to sit with. First, write down one decision your team is about to fund, and the number that would make you stop. Does it exist? Second, which of your own assumptions would survive a test in which the sample was drawn from the people least inclined to agree with you?
case20v1-sol.mvp.definition:
Aruvi Fresh: The Smallest Test

A decision case on what a minimum viable product is for

1. Opening

At 7:40 on the morning of Tuesday 13 October 2026, Ishwarya Parthasarathy stood at the window of Aruvi Fresh's office on Avinashi Road in Coimbatore and watched the first delivery vans of the day pull out towards the city's kirana stores. She had until Friday 16 October to decide how the company would find out whether stores wanted to buy on seven days' credit.

Deepavali falls on Sunday 8 November, and the fortnight before it is the busiest of Aruvi's year. If a test were to run through the festival, field staff had to be briefed and stores signed up by Friday 23 October, so that it could start on Monday 26 October. Her chief technology officer and her head of store network disagreed, and she had to choose before the weekend.

2. Company background

Aruvi Fresh Supply Private Limited was founded in 2021 by Ishwarya and Inbaraj Pasupuleti, who had met while working at a Bengaluru software services firm. It buys vegetables and fruit from farmers' groups and wholesale markets in western Tamil Nadu and delivers them each morning to small retailers and street-side eateries. Orders arrive on WhatsApp and by phone; stores pay on delivery in cash or by UPI. Aruvi earns a gross margin of about 9 per cent of sales.

At the start of October 2026 it served 2,100 active stores in Coimbatore, Tiruppur and Erode, with weekly sales of ₹134.03 lakh (Exhibit 1), or about ₹70 crore at the current weekly run-rate. The 62 people on its payroll include a field team in Coimbatore, engineers in Bengaluru and Pune, a product designer in Berlin and a data scientist in Toronto.

The competition came from two directions. Larger business-to-business platforms such as Udaan and Jumbotail had courted kiranas with credit offers. Meanwhile quick-commerce players, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart among them, were pulling household shoppers away from neighbourhood stores.

3. The situation

In August and September, Ilavarasi Perumal's field team interviewed 60 store owners, every one of them a store that ordered at least twice a week. Forty-one said they would order more often if Aruvi allowed seven days to pay: 41 of 60, or 68.3 per cent. Ishwarya's solution hypothesis followed: stores offered seven-day credit will order at least 25 per cent more often, and will repay on time. It was a bet on two behaviours, and the interviews measured neither; they recorded only what owners said to the person who sold them vegetables.

Three ways of testing it were on the table (Exhibit 2). Inbaraj, in Bengaluru, wanted a finished feature: a credit limit engine, ordering screens and a lending partner. Ilavarasi wanted to offer credit by hand to a few dozen stores, with orders still arriving on WhatsApp and a ledger kept by two coordinators. A third idea, a survey, had come from the Berlin designer.

Ilakkiya Pichai, the data scientist in Toronto, added a caution on Monday night. A pilot in the festival weeks, she wrote, would look good whatever credit did, because every store orders more before Deepavali.

4. The people

Ishwarya Parthasarathy, co-founder and chief executive, Coimbatore. She wants evidence strong enough to take to her board and to a lending partner, without committing her engineers for five months to obtain it.

Inbaraj Pasupuleti, co-founder and chief technology officer, Bengaluru. He fears that a hand-run pilot will prove nothing about scale and that a spreadsheet credit process will be unsafe.

Ilavarasi Perumal, head of store network, Coimbatore. She knows which stores settle at the door without a reminder. She wants to start in days and believes that stores will tell Aruvi the truth only through what they do.

Ilakkiya Pichai, data scientist, Toronto. She asks what would count as a pass before anyone starts.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Aruvi Fresh at a glance, four weeks ended 9 October 2026
ClusterActive storesOrders per store per weekOrders per weekAverage order (₹)Weekly sales (₹ lakh)
Coimbatore9003.22,8802,40069.12
Tiruppur7002.81,9602,10041.16
Erode5002.51,2501,90023.75
Total / average2,1002.906,0902,201134.03

Orders per week = stores × orders per store. Weekly sales = orders × average order. The average order in the last row is the sales-weighted figure: ₹134.03 lakh ÷ 6,090 orders = ₹2,201. Orders per store in the last row is 6,090 ÷ 2,100 = 2.90.

Exhibit 2. The three ways to test the hypothesis
OptionTime to first evidenceCost (₹ lakh)What it can show
A. Build the full credit productAbout five months to launch (late March 2027); evidence from April96.0 buildWhether stores adopt a finished product
B. Hand-run credit pilot, 40 storesReadout Monday 7 December 202622.0 at riskWhether credit raises ordering and gets repaid
C. Survey of stated intentTwo weeks1.5What owners say they would do

A: 8 people × 5 months × ₹2.4 lakh a person-month = ₹96.0 lakh. B: ₹6.0 lakh of coordinator and ledger costs plus a maximum credit loss of 40 stores × ₹40,000 = ₹16.0 lakh, because a store missing a due date receives no further credit. Total at risk ₹22.0 lakh.

Exhibit 3. Timeline of the pilot (Option B)

Scale: 15 pixels per day from 26 October 2026 (x = 60 + 15 × days). Weekly ticks fall on Mondays. Deepavali is 13 days in (x = 255), the last credit order 32 days in (x = 540), repayments close 39 days in (x = 645) and the readout 42 days in (x = 690).

Exhibit 4. The decision rule proposed for Option B
Result, treated vs comparison storesDefaults (unpaid ÷ credit extended)Action
Orders per store per week at least 25 per cent higher2 per cent or lessBuild the product
Uplift below 15 per centAny, or above 4 per cent with any upliftStop
Anything betweenBetweenExtend three weeks and read again

Assumptions: 9 per cent gross margin; 60 per cent of treated-store sales on credit; funding cost 14 per cent a year for 7 days = 0.27 per cent. At 25 per cent uplift, ₹100 of treated-store sales contains ₹20.00 of new sales (100 × 0.25 ÷ 1.25), worth ₹1.80 of margin; credit costs 60 × (2% + 0.27%) = ₹1.36. Net ₹0.44 per ₹100. Break-even uplift at 2 per cent defaults is 17.8 per cent; at 3 per cent it is 27.9 per cent. The Stop and Extend bands are judgement margins around break-even, not break-even itself. The 60 per cent credit share is assumed and the pilot will record it; sales rise with orders only if average order size holds.

6. The options

Option A: build. Inbaraj's team would deliver a credit-limit engine, in-app ordering and a lending-partner integration for ₹96.0 lakh (Exhibit 2). The upside is a product that scales. The cost is that launch comes in late March 2027, with adoption evidence only from April, after both Deepavali and Pongal, and that a lending partner would bring RBI's digital lending rules into the design before anyone knows whether stores want the product.

Option B: a hand-run pilot. Forty Coimbatore stores, drawn at random from 80 willing participants who each order about 3.2 times a week, are offered seven-day credit with a limit of ₹40,000. The other 40 are told nothing and form the comparison group. Orders still come by WhatsApp, repayment by UPI. The upside is real behaviour in six weeks (Exhibit 3) at ₹22.0 lakh at most (Exhibit 2), judged by the Exhibit 4 rule. The cost is manual work, one city, and a sample of 40 a side that will give a noisy read.

Option C: a survey. A two-week WhatsApp poll to all 2,100 stores, costing ₹1.5 lakh. It is broad and fast, but repeats the interviews already held and says nothing about repayment.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. State Ishwarya's solution hypothesis in a form that could be proved wrong. Which parts of it do the 60 interviews test, and which do they leave untouched?
  2. Of the 60 owners interviewed, 41 said yes. What is the base, who is missing from it, and why is 68.3 per cent a weaker reason to build than it first sounds?
  3. Compare the three options on time to first evidence, money at risk and the specific question each answers. Which is the smallest thing that produces validated learning?
  4. Using Exhibit 4, what would you do if the pilot showed a 20 per cent uplift and 2 per cent defaults? Why is it better to fix the rule before the pilot than after?

8. A note for the learner

An MVP is not a small product. It is the cheapest experiment that can change a decision, and the test of one is whether a result could make you stop. Ishwarya's two behaviours, ordering more and repaying, are the riskiest assumptions in her hypothesis, so the right test observes them directly.

On that standard, one defensible path is Option B with the Exhibit 4 rule agreed in writing before Monday 26 October. Option A has no decision rule: it spends ₹96.0 lakh to start learning in April what B can reveal for up to ₹22.0 lakh in December. Option C and the interviews already held both ask what owners think; only B watches, within six weeks, what a randomly chosen group of stores does when offered credit.

Ilakkiya's caution is built into the design. Because the comparison stores trade through the same Deepavali weeks, the festival lifts both groups and drops out of the difference. Random assignment among similar stores guards against comparing eager stores with indifferent ones, though credit may matter more in festival weeks than in ordinary ones. The plan has limits, and the page should name them. Forty stores a side is thin, which is why a result near the thresholds triggers an extension rather than a verdict. Coimbatore is not Erode. Funding credit from Aruvi's own balance sheet is not the same as a lending partner's, and scaling would need review under RBI's digital lending directions. It argues for a pilot honest about what it cannot settle, and for Inbaraj to start designing the credit engine only if the rule says build.
case40v1-sol.valueprop:
Discovery & Design · Solution Design & Prototyping

Kurinji Technologies: One Sentence Before the Board

An Indian School of Business teaching case. The data are those available to the protagonist on the evening of Sunday, 8 November 2026.

1. Bengaluru, Sunday night

The Diwali lights were still strung along the compound wall when Tharini Devarakonda let herself into the HSR Layout office at twenty past nine on Sunday, 8 November 2026. On her desk lay three printed sheets, each carrying one sentence beginning with the same four words: Kurinji Desk helps the…

At nine the next morning the board of Kurinji Technologies Private Limited would meet by video, with Pune, Singapore, Berlin, Toronto and New Jersey dialling in. The one substantive item had been written by the chief executive, Thenmozhi Desikan: Agree the value proposition statement for FY2028 planning. Tharini, vice-president of product, was to present it.

Three clocks were running. Kuyil Capital's term sheet for a ₹55 crore Series B at a ₹240 crore pre-money valuation — about 10.8 times current annual recurring revenue of ₹22.14 crore — lapsed on Monday, 30 November 2026. Kinaara Trading FZE of Dubai wanted a signed statement of work by the same date. And the white-label agreement with Kanmani Finserve Limited, which carried 412 of Kurinji's 571 accounts, renewed automatically for three further years unless notice was served by Thursday, 31 December 2026.

Tharini had written the first sentence herself, in February, and believed it. The discovery since had made it harder to say out loud, not easier.

2. How Kurinji came to be constrained

Kurinji was founded in Chennai on 4 March 2019 by Thenmozhi Desikan, eleven years in the finance function of a forging business, and Tirumal Dhanasekaran, who had built reconciliation systems for a Bengaluru payments firm. Their first product matched a manufacturer's sales register against the invoices its customers filed on the GST portal. Mandatory e-invoicing was coming down the turnover thresholds; every mid-market plant would soon have a reconciliation problem.

Bengaluru followed in 2020, and a ₹58 crore Series A led by Kuyil Capital on 15 July 2021, raised on a deck promising “cash visibility for the mid-market promoter”. By 2023 it had ninety-odd direct accounts and a board that wanted distribution.

On 12 October 2023 Kurinji signed with Kanmani Finserve, a non-banking financial company lending working capital to engineering suppliers. Kanmani would embed a white-labelled Kurinji Desk with its borrowers at a price Kurinji could never charge directly. The three-year agreement, effective 1 April 2024, carries three clauses that now shape everything: no direct sale of a receivables product to any account Kanmani sourced; parity, so any module shipped to direct customers reaches the white-label build within 180 days; and no research with a Kanmani-sourced account without written consent, sought twice and refused.

That decision bought 412 accounts and made them unobservable (Figure A).

3. The industry

Kurinji sells into Indian mid-market manufacturing: firms turning over ₹100 crore to ₹500 crore in auto components and engineering goods, clustered around Pune, Coimbatore and Rajkot. Three forces define their receivables. GST e-invoicing puts every B2B invoice in a government record both parties can see, turning reconciliation into a negotiation with evidence. The MSMED Act's forty-five-day payment rule gives small suppliers a statutory claim that larger buyers routinely ignore. And the TReDS platforms licensed by the Reserve Bank of India — RXIL and M1xchange among them — let an approved invoice be discounted within days, which makes the gap between approved and disputed worth real money.

At the small end sits Tally, which almost every Kurinji customer runs, and Zoho Books; at the large end SAP, whose receivables module is largely unused. Kurinji competes less with software than with a spreadsheet kept by one person who is good at it.

Exposure abroad runs through exporters. Kinaara Trading re-exports Indian engineering goods across the Gulf and chases its suppliers' ICEGATE shipping bills and DGFT licences by email. Eleven Kurinji accounts use the export module built for its 2025 pilot. They pay well, and there are few of them.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

Through 2024 the statement looked settled: reconciliation was the job, the finance head the customer, growth would come from Kanmani. Two things then turned uncomfortable. White-label retention ran far below direct retention, a gap the FY2026 renewal data confirmed in April 2026 (Exhibit 1). And the Kinaara module, built in nine weeks for one client, had drawn ten more accounts at the worst payback in the book (Exhibit 5).

On Friday, 13 February 2026 Tharini ran a half-day workshop and wrote the February statement: Kurinji Desk helps the finance head of a mid-market Indian manufacturer who wants to know what cash will land next week, by removing the three-day scramble across Tally, bank statements and the GST portal, and enabling a weekly collections call that runs off one screen. It went on the website and the sales deck.

Between Tuesday, 5 May and Tuesday, 11 August 2026 — fourteen weeks — the team logged 243 customer conversations. The guide was revised on 10 June, which is why only 171 were ever asked to rank their pains; the other 72 were not. Among those asked, the answer did not match the February statement (Exhibit 2).

From Monday, 24 August to Friday, 2 October came prototype critique cycles: three differently framed statements, each with a walkthrough built by Tarulata Dantuluri in Berlin, each shown to a separate sample, under one rule set in advance — a paid pilot booked within twenty-one days. The last window closed on Friday, 23 October (Exhibit 3).

Tabish Divakaran then pulled September telemetry and the renewal notes from every FY2026 renewal; the two tell different stories about the same customers (Exhibit 4). On 16 October Thamarai Devanathan, who runs Kinaara's trade desk in Dubai, offered ₹180 lakh a year for three years for a productised export module, conditional on Arabic localisation and a Dubai-hosted data option. Turab Dommeti's estimate is Exhibit 6; two of its five lines are unestimated.

What has turned out to be wrong is narrow. The February statement is not false. It names the person who signs. It does not name the person who opens the product.

5. The people

Tharini Devarakonda, 36, vice-president of product, Bengaluru
Joined 2022. Holds that the statement must name one customer: naming three names none. Her promotion to chief product officer is unconfirmed, and she has not said aloud that her February statement named the buyer, not the user.
Thenmozhi Desikan, 44, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru
Wants the cash-forecast framing: the board and Kuyil's committee have seen it. Her incentive is a term sheet lapsing on 30 November. She has not told the team that the Kuyil paper calls Kurinji a CFO platform.
Tirumal Dhanasekaran, 47, co-founder and chief technology officer, Bengaluru
Argues the export module triggers parity and will eat the quarter; wants to rebuild the reconciliation engine, which he wrote. Has not circulated that counsel's opinion on whether parity covers it, sought on 22 October, has not come.
Turab Dommeti, 33, engineering manager, Pune
Says the module ships in a quarter if parity work is deferred. Measured on delivery and attrition. Two engineers resigned in early November; he has not said that one owns the dispute desk, nor that his ₹96 lakh line omits Arabic localisation.
Tasneem Dasari, 41, head of sales, New Jersey
Pushes the export framing: larger contracts, a Dubai reference, a story that travels. Her commission pays on new contract value, not retention, and Kinaara is her account. Her team writes the renewal notes in Exhibit 4.
Tapaswi Damerla, 38, customer success lead, Singapore
Insists the user is the accounts-receivable executive and that churn lives where disputes live. Measured on net revenue retention. Has not escalated that nine direct accounts are held together by an analyst matching books by hand, some ₹18 lakh a year never in cost of revenue.
Tabish Divakaran, 31, data scientist, Toronto
Holds that no evidence separates the options and wants one more cycle; he caught a base error in a September deck and has been careful since. He has not said that a second cycle cannot close before 30 November.
Tarulata Dantuluri, 35, principal designer on contract, Berlin
Argues the sentence is an output of prototype, critique and revision, not an input. Her contract renews in January and bills by the cycle. A fourth statement naming two users went to six accounts in August and was dropped unlogged.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Accounts, revenue and renewals by segment

Note 2. A fourth statement naming two users was shown to six prospect accounts on 20 and 21 August 2026 and withdrawn before the main run; no record of their responses was kept.

Exhibit 4. What customers use, and what their renewal notes say

It matches who signs, who renews and who the Kuyil paper describes, plus 53.3 per cent of renewal notes and 12.0 sessions per enabled account.

Statement B, the disputes sentence. It names a person with no budget, and exclusivity bars selling a receivables product directly to the Kanmani accounts where that person sits.

What Tharini has not written down is that the evidence behind all three comes from the 159 accounts she may study, and from prospects and partners, never from the other 412; that the January quarter has ten free engineer-months whichever wins; and that Tarulata objects not to any of the three but to the shape of all three.

Money. ₹940 lakh in the bank at the close of 31 October 2026. Net burn averaged ₹62 lakh a month over the quarter to 30 September 2026. The spending window opens on 1 November, so at that rate the balance funds 15.2 months and is exhausted in early February 2028, before which a Series B must close or the burn fall.

People. Eleven engineers; 33 engineer-months in the January to March 2027 quarter, 23 committed, ten free. Two Pune resignations are unreplaced; Tarulata's contract is a January decision.

Regulation. The DPDP Act governs the consent Kanmani will not give. Kinaara's Dubai residency request is unreviewed by counsel and sits against an India-only hosting clause in nine contracts.

Contracts. Kanmani: no direct receivables sale to its accounts, parity within 180 days, no research without consent, notice by 31 December 2026. Kinaara: signature by 30 November 2026. Kuyil: a term sheet lapsing 30 November 2026, drafted around a positioning already shown.

  1. Mark which of the February statement's four slots — customer, job, pain, gain — Exhibits 2, 3 and 4 support, and which they do not.
  2. Exhibit 4 shows that the most-used and the most-cited module differ. What would you measure to know which one is the reason an account renews?
  3. Tabish says the gap in Exhibit 3 cannot carry a decision. If a rule set in advance cannot separate the options, was the rule wrong, the sample, or the question?
  4. 412 accounts are 72.2 per cent of accounts, 27.9 per cent of ARR and none of the discovery. How should the statement treat a segment it is forbidden to study?
  5. Tarulata argues the sentence is an output of the cycles, not an input. If she is right, what has the company been doing since February, and what rule should the next cycle carry?
  6. It is nine o'clock on Monday, 9 November 2026. What does Tharini put on the screen, and what does she say when Tilakraj Donthineni asks which customer Kurinji is for?

At ten past eleven she laid the three sheets side by side and read them once more in order. Each was true about somebody. Beyond the wall a last string of crackers went off for a festival still ending. She turned the sheets face down, in the order she had read them, and did not choose.
case20v1-sol.valueprop:
Jodi Invoice: One Sentence for the Board

A decision case on the value proposition statement

1. Opening

On Monday 19 October 2026, Saranya Chidambaram sat at a corner desk in Jodi Invoice's Indiranagar office in Bengaluru, with eleven days left before the board met on Friday 30 October. She was Jodi's head of product, and the board had asked her for one thing: the opening sentence of the company's first product strategy document. The sentence had to say who Jodi helps, what job that person wants done, what pain Jodi removes and what gain it enables.

The sentence mattered because it would decide where between ₹35 lakh and ₹1.2 crore of engineering effort, depending on the sentence went. Jodi's engineers wanted to begin sprint planning before Diwali, which fell on Sunday 8 November. Saranya had three candidate sentences and no confidence that she could tell, from the evidence on her desk, which was the right one.

2. Company background

Jodi Invoice was founded in 2021 by Srikanth Chebrolu, a former bank relationship manager from Vijayawada. It sells GST e-invoicing and receivables tracking to small manufacturers. At 30 September 2026 it had 4,200 paying customers at ₹3,000 a year each, or ₹126 lakh of annual recurring revenue. Most customers are knitwear and garment makers in Tiruppur, with smaller clusters in Erode and Coimbatore. A seed round of ₹14 crore closed in 2024; cash at 30 September was ₹6.2 crore, against a net burn of ₹38 lakh a month, or roughly sixteen months of runway.

The market around it is crowded. Zoho Books, Vyapar and Khatabook cover billing and ledgers; ClearTax covers GST filing. Receivables finance sits elsewhere: the RBI-regulated TReDS platforms (RXIL, M1xchange and Invoicemart) let MSMEs sell invoices to financiers, and lenders such as Lendingkart and Indifi offer working capital. Jodi's current tagline, "Billing made simple", could belong to any of them.

3. The situation

Between 3 August and 18 September 2026, Saranya's team interviewed 96 owner-managers in Tiruppur, Erode and Coimbatore: 64 existing customers and 32 non-customers. Every one of the 96 was asked the same question: which single problem in your business costs you the most? Exhibit 1 shows the answers.

Exhibit 1. Costliest problem named by owner-managers, by customer status (counts of owners)

GST errors, notices, input-credit mismatch12102222.9%
No cash to buy yarn on time1451919.8%

Total643296100.0%

Source: Jodi product team interviews, 3 August to 18 September 2026. Each owner named one problem. Shares are of all 96 owners interviewed.

Late payment led in both groups, but not equally. Among customers it was named by 30 of 64 (46.9 per cent); among non-customers by 11 of 32 (34.4 per cent). Owners also told the team that cash was the real consequence: a Tiruppur knitter who waits past 60 days for a buyer often cannot pay the yarn dealer, and the yarn dealer wants cash. The MSME payment rule (formerly section 43B(h) of the Income Tax Act, 1961) denies a buyer a tax deduction on dues to an MSME left unpaid beyond the agreed period, capped at 45 days, yet owners said the rule had shortened few payment cycles they had seen.

The global team reads the numbers differently. Sowmya Chokkalingam, Jodi's customer-success lead in Singapore, spends her evenings on calls with owners and hears the same sentence repeatedly: "I do not need another app, I need my money." Sushmita Chitturi, the data scientist in Toronto, rebuilt Exhibit 1 from the raw notes and cautioned that the two groups were small. Swetha Chinnaswamy, the designer in Berlin, has drafted three homepage headlines, one per candidate sentence, and says she cannot make the second and third sound different from the competition. In New Jersey, sales head Sanjay Challa starts calls at 8:30 pm Indian time to reach the buying offices of US importers. Exhibit 2 places the dates on a timeline.

Exhibit 2. Decision timeline, 2026. Scale: 6 pixels per day from 3 August (x=40); 88 days to the board date, 97 days to Diwali.

4. The people

Srikanth Chebrolu, chief executive, Bengaluru. He wants a story investors can fund in the next round and leans toward financing, because it has the largest revenue potential of the three. He also remembers how little his bank ever risked on an MSME ledger.

Sowmya Chokkalingam, customer success, Singapore. She wants Jodi to stop promising "simple" and start fixing the thing owners complain about: waiting for money. She worries about promising advances Jodi cannot deliver.

Sanjay Challa, sales head, New Jersey. He has had 11 conversations with large buyers, three of which asked for a pilot, among them Shamiyana Knit Sourcing in Dubai, a buying house that wants a supplier-payables dashboard. He wants a product he can sell to buyers.

Sushmita Chitturi, data scientist, Toronto. She wants the statement tied to something that can be measured in ten weeks, not argued about for ten months.

5. The options

Saranya has framed three distinct courses, each tied to one candidate sentence. Option A helps owner-managers who want cash for delivered orders by reducing the wait on buyer payments and enabling early advances against invoices through regulated financier partners. Option B helps the same owners, and their accountants, who want a clean GST record by reducing notices and mismatches and enabling confident filing. Option C helps large buyers who want reliable suppliers by reducing payables friction and enabling a supplier-payment view. Exhibit 3 sets out the economics.

Exhibit 3. Three options compared (first 12 months after launch; ₹ lakh unless stated)
ItemA. Early cashB. GST clean-upC. Buyer view

Revenue is before credit-loss sharing and partner costs, which are unknown. The ₹40 lakh financed per user is an assumption: no interview data bears on it, and at 600 users it implies ₹240 crore financed in year one. All users are assumed to pay for the full 12 months, with no ramp. Option A users are 14.3% of the 4,200 current customers (600/4,200). Option C assumes four buyers live, one more than the three who have asked for a pilot.

Option A has the largest upside and depends most on regulated partners and on owners actually borrowing against invoices. If the 30-of-64 customer share held across all 4,200 customers, about 1,970 owners would name late payment as their costliest problem; the 600 users assumed in Exhibit 3 are roughly three in ten of those, a plausible but untested conversion rate, and the 64 customers interviewed are a sample of unknown selection. Option B is cheap and quick, but at 800 owners (19.0 per cent of the base) it does not repay its build cost in the first year, and it is the least differentiated. Option C breaks even only if all four buyers are live from launch, eight months after the build starts, and its customers are not the owners the interviews spoke to.

6. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, who is the customer, and what is the job? What does it mean that the answer differs between the 64 customers and the 32 non-customers, and what can groups of this size not tell you?

2. Draft each option as one sentence in the form "Helps [customer] who want [job] by reducing [pain] and enabling [gain]". Which sentence could a competitor not also say?

3. In Exhibit 3, which figures are evidence and which are assumptions? Does revenue less build cost compare the options fairly?

4. What would Saranya need to see, and by when, before committing the full build behind her chosen sentence?

7. A note for the learner

A value proposition statement forces a choice on four things at once. A team that cannot fill all four blanks with something specific does not yet have a proposition; it has a feature list. Here, option B fills the blanks weakly (the gain, "confident filing", is vague), and option C names a customer whom the research never examined. Only option A can be written in a form an owner would recognise as her own sentence:

Jodi helps Tiruppur-cluster garment owner-managers who want to turn a delivered order into cash by reducing the wait on buyer payments and enabling an advance against each invoice, so that yarn can be bought on time.

A careful answer also notices what the evidence does not show. Exhibit 1 supports late payment as the most-named problem, at 41 of 96 owners; it does not show that owners would borrow against invoices, nor that the 12.5-point gap between customers (46.9 per cent) and non-customers (34.4 per cent) is more than chance with only 32 non-customers. It was also an interview, not a purchase, and people who say a problem is costly do not always pay to solve it. The question the study can answer is who hurts most; the question it cannot answer is who will pay, and a value proposition statement is only as good as the second answer.

One defensible path is therefore to adopt the option A sentence, but to treat the build as a learning vehicle with a decision rule rather than a commitment. Saranya could spend about ₹12 lakh on a ten-week concierge pilot, in which a financier partner advances against real invoices for 25 customers, handled mostly by hand. The rule, set in advance: build option A in full only if at least 10 of the 25 (40 per cent) ask for a second advance within eight weeks; otherwise fall back to a cheaper variant. The pilot also tests Sowmya's fear about delivery, answers Sushmita's demand for a measurable test, and gives Srikanth a real number for the board. Option C stays alive through Sanjay's three pilot requests, but only as a later bet.
exp40v2-sol.valueprop:
The Value Proposition Statement

Helps [customer] who want [job] by reducing [pain] and enabling [gain] — a sentence that looks like marketing and behaves like a budget.

1. Two sentences, one pricing review

On Monday 5 October 2026, Revati Lohakare had two sentences on a whiteboard in Pune and a pricing review on 12 October. Mulaank Diagnostics Cloud sold reconciliation and claims software to diagnostic-lab chains: the layer turning yesterday's tests and the Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY submissions into money. It had 41 paying labs and a six-lab pilot closed on 11 September. One sentence promised a lab's operations head that yesterday's billing would close before the nine o'clock round; the other promised the owner thirteen fewer days of receivables. Rupinder Laturkar, her head of sales, wanted both.

Discovery ran from 11 May to 26 June: 146 labs in the frame, 92 operations heads interviewed, 53 describing a daily manual reconciliation over ninety minutes. Revati's draft deck said 53 of the 92 interviewees — 57.6 per cent — were working around the problem. Rishad Luktuke, who built the interview database, pointed out that the question was added only after the first 21 conversations, so 71 were ever asked it. The rate was 53 of 71, or 74.6 per cent. No operation was wrong; the denominator was.

Some six hundred kilometres north, Qasim Limbachiya faced the same choice in hardware. Mahaul Instruments, in Ahmedabad, made a reusable Bluetooth cold-chain logger and its dashboard, sold to dairy and vaccine logistics operators under FSSAI and CDSCO rules. Its June-quarter pilot — 1 April to 30 June 2026, three operators, 1,240 monitored consignments — flagged 38 temperature excursions, of which 22 were caught in time to re-ice or re-route. The hardware team's favoured sentence said no monitored consignment need ever spoil; Rudrani Langote, the firmware lead in Bengaluru, noted that 16 of 38 excursions, or 42.1 per cent, were missed. Qasim had until 7 October to choose between a spoilage sentence for a finance head and an audit sentence for a quality head.

2. The idea, and the quarrel inside it

A value proposition statement is a single testable sentence naming four things: the customer, the job that customer is trying to get done, the pain the product removes and the gain it makes possible. Its function is to be wrong in public: with all four slots filled it can be falsified; with any slot vague it cannot.

The term is younger than the practice. Michael Lanning and Edward Michaels coined it in a 1988 McKinsey staff paper: a business is a value delivery system, not a product factory. Behind it stand Rosser Reeves's unique selling proposition (1961), binding a claim to one benefit; Ries and Trout on positioning (1981), binding it to a competitor; Levitt's drill-and-hole argument, binding it to an outcome; and Geoffrey Moore's 1991 template, which made the competitive alternative a required field. Christensen and Tony Ulwick made the job measurable, Kano's 1984 model separated the must-be from the delighter, and Osterwalder's Value Proposition Design (2014) turned it into a canvas. The problem is specific: firms that could describe their product could not say whose problem it was, and so could not price or scope it.

Four schools disagree, most sharply about what they will sign. The outcome school (Ulwick, Christensen) signs only if the job has a trigger and a finish line; it signs "closes yesterday's billing before the nine o'clock round" and refuses "helps mid-sized chains digitise revenue operations". The positioning school (Ries and Trout, Moore, April Dunford) refuses any sentence without the displaced alternative in it, and would require "instead of the LIS export and two spreadsheets" — a demand the outcome school rejects, on the grounds that a comparator anchors a product to a category its customer may be leaving. The resonating-focus school (Anderson and Narus, Harvard Business Review, 2006) signs only resonating focus, as against all-benefits or points-of-difference claims: one or two differences quantified in the customer's own cost terms. The canvas school will not treat the sentence as the artefact at all; it compresses an evidence structure, and without that evidence it is theatre. A fifth position, commoner among practitioners, holds that no statement is tested until someone switches or pays.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Experts do not write the sentence first. They assemble the cells, choose a denominator, and let the sentence fall out. Mulaank's pilot measured reconciliation time over 30 trading days a lab.

Exhibit 1 — Daily reconciliation time, six pilot labs, 30 trading days
Pilot labMinutes a day, beforeMinutes a day, duringMinutes saved
Lab 1 (Pune)18254128
Lab 2 (Nashik)15144107
Lab 3 (Indore)963858
Lab 4 (Nagpur)21461153
Lab 5 (Surat)1334786
Lab 6 (Raipur)1184474
Total, six labs894288606

Means: 894 ÷ 6 = 149.0 minutes before, 288 ÷ 6 = 48.0 during, a saving of 101.0 minutes a day, which is 101 of 149 minutes or 67.8 per cent. Window: 3 August to 11 September 2026.

Minutes must then be translated into the customer's unit of account. The labs ran roughly 300 trading days, so 101 × 300 = 30,300 minutes, or 505 hours, and at a blended loaded cost of ₹300 an hour, ₹1,51,500 a lab a year. Claims gave a second cell: in the 30 trading days before the pilot the six labs submitted 4,850 claims and had 456 rejected on first pass, or 9.40 per cent; during the pilot, 274 of 4,912, or 5.58 per cent. The 3.82-point difference on 4,912 claims is 188 rejections avoided across six labs in those 30 trading days; at ₹420 of rework each, ₹78,960, or ₹13,160 a lab per 30 trading days. Thirty trading days is not a month: a 300-day year holds ten such windows, so the claims leg annualises × 10 to ₹1,31,600. Annual value per lab: ₹1,51,500 + ₹1,31,600 = ₹2,83,100.

That is not a price. Economic value estimation adds the reference value — what the next-best alternative costs — to the differentiation value. The labs paid ₹96,000 a year for the LIS module they would drop, so total economic value is ₹96,000 + ₹2,83,100 = ₹3,79,100. Mulaank proposed ₹1,32,000 a year: a capture ratio of 1,32,000 ÷ 3,79,100 = 34.8 per cent. As the customer sees it, the incremental price is ₹1,32,000 − ₹96,000 = ₹36,000 against ₹2,83,100 of value: a return of 7.9 times. The owner's sentence had its own number. Insurer billings ran about ₹68 lakh a lab a year and days-to-collect fell by 13, so at a 10 per cent cost of money the financing released is 68,00,000 × 0.10 × 13 ÷ 365 = ₹24,219 a year, 8.6 per cent of the operational figure — under a tenth of the pain the user feels.

The last instrument is Ulwick's opportunity score, computed on the same 71 heads, surveyed from 6 to 24 July 2026 on importance and satisfaction, both on ten-point scales, where opportunity = importance + max(importance − satisfaction, 0).

Exhibit 2 — Opportunity scores, 71 lab operations heads, July 2026
