Each of the five rows recomputes from its own cells: 9.1 + (9.1 − 4.2) = 14.0; 8.8 + (8.8 − 6.9) = 10.7; 6.4 + max(6.4 − 7.8, 0) = 6.4. The mean row averages the five scores — 55.1 ÷ 5 = 11.02 — and the formula does not apply to it. Importance 40.8 ÷ 5 = 8.16; satisfaction 27.9 ÷ 5 = 5.58.

Shortening collection days is the second most important outcome but only the third-highest opportunity, because insurers and the National Health Authority had already improved it; Rishad noted that rows three and four were tied at 10.7, so calling receivables "the third priority" was an artefact of row order. This is why the mechanical work matters: the sentence Revati signs becomes the roadmap's scope filter, the price anchor, the sales script and the selector of her rivals. Choose the owner's and Mulaank competes with lending products for ₹24,219; choose the operations head's and it competes with spreadsheets for ₹2,83,100.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be stated as testable claims. One: the pain is recurrent and has a clock. Mulaank passes; Mahaul awkwardly, because an excursion is rare per consignment but routine per fleet. Two: the customer slot can be sampled. Mulaank passes with 146 labs in a frame; Mahaul's is harder, because the people who feel the pain, drivers and loaders, are not the people surveyed. Three: the pain converts into the customer's unit of account. Mulaank converts through hours, Mahaul through spoiled stock. Four: a named alternative exists. Mulaank names the LIS export and two spreadsheets; Mahaul, chemical indicator strips and a signature on a manifest.

It misleads where the gain is not additive or not the customer's to receive. In new categories there is no incumbent to reference and no satisfaction score to subtract, so a canvas built from interviews describes the old job precisely and misses the product. In regulated purchases the pain is compulsory, so willingness to pay is set by the penalty. And in low-frequency, high-consequence purchases the arithmetic can be sound and the buyer still refuse, because what is bought is the absence of a career-ending event.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In multi-product firms there is no single proposition, only a portfolio plus a brand promise that contradicts none of them: two true propositions are jointly unsellable if the bundle price exceeds the sum of their values. Two-sided businesses are harder, because the supply side's gain is funded out of the demand side's price. If demand-side value is ₹2,83,100 and the firm captures a third, all that is promised to supply comes out of that ₹94,000-odd — two generous propositions becoming a take-rate crisis.

In regulated contexts the pain slot belongs to a regulator, which inverts the usual advice: the job becomes satisfying the auditor cheaply, and a product that cuts risk without cutting audit effort tests well and sells badly. Hardware-plus-software is Mahaul's case, where the proposition must survive a refresh cycle, a warranty rate and physics: the 42.1 per cent missed is not a defect to iterate away but the latency of a Bluetooth gateway on a moving truck. AI-native products are harder again, because the gain is probabilistic, so an honest sentence carries a hit rate and a fallback, and the pain of a confidently wrong answer belongs in it, not the footnotes. Nobody has settled how to write that; naming the gain and burying the hit rate is the error Mahaul's hardware team was about to make.

At the organisational seam, mature companies do not do what they say. The line is that one proposition governs the roadmap; in practice product writes a proposition, sales a battlecard and finance a value calculator, and the three diverge within two quarters. Firms that handle it well insist not on one document but on all three carrying the same cells.

6. The nuances that separate an expert

The customer slot is a sampling frame, not a demographic. The tell is that the team cannot name twenty people who fit it. "Mid-sized chains in tier-two cities" is a persona; "operations heads at NABL-accredited chains with four to fifteen centres" is a frame, because Revati could count 146. A tighter slot is not a smaller market: it makes the pain measurable, and unmeasurable pain is unpriceable.

A job has a trigger and a finish line; most statements name an activity. The tell is no clock in the sentence: "manage billing efficiently" has no trigger, "close yesterday's billing before the nine o'clock round" has both. Specificity seems to narrow the promise; it widens the evidence, because with a finish line every pilot crosses it or does not.

The gain is not the pain negated. The tell is a second half restating the first with a "no more" in front: "reduces reconciliation time and eliminates reconciliation pain" has an empty gain slot. Mulaank's real gain was a morning shift staffed for patients. Pain and gain are not one scale: Kano treats them as different attributes, and relieving a must-be rarely delights.

The quantified value is not the price, and the capture ratio is a decision. The tell is a team quoting value and price as though the ratio were given; Mulaank's 34.8 per cent and Mahaul's 35.3 per cent are choices, and not comparable ones — Mulaank's denominator includes the ₹96,000 reference value, Mahaul's numerator one-off hardware. Higher capture buys revenue now and a motivated competitor later, because value left with the customer deters switching.

The sentence selects your competitors, and therefore your churn. If the proposition changed last quarter and the competitor named in lost deals has not changed within two, nobody acted on it. Competitors follow from the slots, not the market — move the customer from owner to operations head and the rival moves from a lending product to a spreadsheet.

Buyer and user get two linked sentences, never one compromise. The tell is a sentence with two subjects. Mulaank's value sits in operations and the signature with the owner; the expert keeps the operations sentence and adds an owner translation stating the ₹24,219 as secondary. Aiming at whoever signs yields an untestable proposition, because the signer does not feel the pain.

The template hides a quantifier. "Helps customers who want X" conceals whether that means all of them, most, or the minority who hit the trigger weekly; the tell is the absent frequency. Mahaul flagged 38 excursions in 1,240 consignments, three per hundred shipments, so the proposition must be about the fleet's annual loss.

A proposition must say what you will not build. Ask a team to name three things the sentence forbids; silence means they wrote a description. Revati's forbade a treasury dashboard, a patient app and anything priced per test. Negative space does not follow the proposition; it is the test of it.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the four slots survive but the conversion to money does not: the gain is often affective, and a rupee figure is false precision, so the honest treatment substitutes behaviour — retention at day 30, sessions per trigger. In B2B the complication is the buyer-user split, which is why enterprise teams carry a value calculator, not a slogan. Platforms and marketplaces differ structurally: two propositions bound by one take rate. Hardware changes the slots least and the burden of proof most, because a claim is locked at manufacture and a returns rate turns an over-promise into cash.

Across stages the format does not change: the four slots are the same for a seed-stage team and a listed firm. What changes is the cost of being wrong. Pre-fit the sentence is a hypothesis, rewritten the moment the falsifier fires, at a cost of a week; at Mulaank's 41 labs it meant re-pricing, re-training two salespeople and re-cutting a quarter's roadmap. At a few hundred customers it also means renegotiating contracts, which is why large firms freeze propositions and call it brand consistency.

8. Three worked examples

The one that worked. Both sentences were field-tested before either was signed. The owner-facing version, pitched to 14 chains across the June quarter, converted 4; the operations sentence, pitched to 11 chains in the four weeks after the pilot closed, converted 9. The windows differ in length; the measure — share of chains pitched that signed — does not. Evidenced at ₹2,83,100 a lab a year, it told Rupinder whom to call first.

The one that is fine but smaller than it looks. Mahaul's three pilot operators had spent 96, 74 and 118 quality-team hours assembling temperature records for the previous year's audits, a total of 288 and a mean of 96.0. In September, after the pilot closed, each team reassembled the same twelve months of records through Mahaul's export: 12, 9 and 15 hours, a total of 36 and a mean of 12.0 — same scope, different method. That is 84 of 96 hours saved, or 87.5 per cent, and at ₹900 an hour, ₹75,600 an operator a year — 4.6 per cent of the spoilage figure below. It is also the sentence that gets the meeting.

The one that failed. Mahaul's first proposition, carried for two quarters from late 2025, promised that no monitored consignment would spoil. The arithmetic was sound: 22 saves at a mean consignment value of ₹1,85,000 and an average 30 per cent loss per excursion is ₹55,500 avoided per save, so 22 × ₹55,500 = ₹12,21,000 across three operators in the quarter, or ₹4,07,000 per operator per quarter, or ₹16,28,000 a year. The failure was the superlative. The device caught 22 of 38 excursions, and in July the first operator to lose a consignment under monitoring read the sentence back to Qasim. Recovery ran through the September quarter: the dashboard began showing missed excursions rather than hiding them, and the model moved to 180 devices at ₹2,950 plus ₹240 a device a year — ₹5,31,000 + ₹43,200 = ₹5,74,200 of first-year revenue per operator, 35.3 per cent of ₹16,28,000. The sentence itself was rewritten on 7 October to name the catch rate. All three operators stayed; what was recovered was the right to be believed.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

The capability sentence in disguise — "helps labs by providing an AI-powered reconciliation engine" — shows itself when the customer name can be swapped for any other and it still reads true; read it to an adjacent segment and see what breaks. Caught late, it costs a roadmap of features nobody asked for. Buyer-user conflation appears when the quantified value sits in one budget and the signature in another; ask whose profit and loss the pain lands in, then who signs. Caught late, it stalls every cycle where the champion must justify the spend. The unfalsifiable gain is an adjective where a number should be; ask what result within ninety days would force a rewrite, because without one nobody can tell a pivot from a bad quarter. The unnamed alternative surfaces as "no decision" heading the loss reasons; ask what the real rival — usually doing nothing — was costed at. Freezing shows as a sentence unchanged for four quarters while churn reasons rotate underneath it; ask when its cells were last re-measured.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether the sentence must carry a number. The resonating-focus position rests on field evidence that quantified, customer-specific claims win deals and survive procurement, while unquantified benefit lists are discounted to zero by professional buyers. It would be wrong if the decisive value were, for some products, non-monetisable — which the consumer case concedes.

Whether it is an output or an input. The canvas school treats it as a compression of evidence; the founder-vision school as a bet that precedes evidence, since a market that does not exist cannot be interviewed — strongest where a technology shift has moved the frontier, weakest as an excuse for not asking.

Whether pain and gain are a sound decomposition. Kano's classes hold that relief of a must-be and provision of a delighter are not commensurable, so adding them, as Mulaank's ₹2,83,100 does, is a category error. Prospect theory makes it worse: because losses loom larger, a pain-led sentence beats a gain-led one by construction, so the template's symmetry is false. Nobody has a replacement, which is why it survives.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes a good sentence and defends it. Someone who has internalised it writes the falsifier first, keeps the cells where a customer can see them, refuses to merge the buyer's sentence into the user's, treats the capture ratio as a choice, and names what it forbids. Challenged, they open the spreadsheet, not the slide.

12. The decisions

On 12 October Revati signed the operations sentence and refused the slide.

Mulaank: Helps operations heads at NABL-accredited diagnostic chains with four to fifteen centres who need yesterday's billing closed before the nine o'clock round, by cutting daily reconciliation from about 149 minutes to under 50 and first-pass claim rejections from 9.40 to 5.58 per cent, so the morning shift can be staffed for patients. Falsifier: if fewer than half of the next twelve pilots close inside 60 minutes by day 45, this sentence is wrong. Review 26 February 2027.

The ₹24,219 went into a separate owner-facing paragraph labelled secondary. Pricing held at ₹1,32,000, argued as 7.9 times the incremental ₹36,000.

On 7 October Qasim signed the spoilage proposition with the catch rate inside it, keeping the audit sentence as the way in, not the promise.

Mahaul: Helps cold-chain operations managers moving vaccines and chilled dairy who must prove an unbroken chain, by catching about 58 per cent of temperature excursions early enough to re-ice or re-route — 22 of 38 in the June quarter — and cutting audit assembly from about 96 hours a year to 12, so a lost consignment becomes an exception with a record. Falsifier: if the catch rate over the next 2,000 consignments falls below 50 per cent, the device, not the sentence, is wrong.

For discussion

  1. Mulaank's value is ₹2,83,100 against the owner's ₹24,219. If the owner signs the cheque, why write the sentence for someone else?
  2. Mahaul's sentence names a 58 per cent catch rate. Does admitting the bound cost more deals than the lost credibility did?
  3. Exhibit 2 ties two outcomes at 10.7. Write the sentence an expert would produce had the tie favoured receivables, and say which decisions change.

13. Going deeper

  • Value Proposition Canvas — the structure this compresses; build it first and the slots fill.
  • Writing a solution hypothesis — supplies the falsifier, without which nothing is tested.
  • Concept and elevator pitch — the outward compression, where the named alternative earns its keep.
  • Ideation: brainstorming, Crazy 8s, HMW — generates the pain relievers the statement chooses between.
  • Storyboarding — tests whether the job has the finish line claimed.
  • Wireframes, mockups, prototypes — the cheapest way to measure the pain figure pre-build.
  • AI-generated prototypes — collapses the critique-and-revise cycle, so the falsifier must come first.
  • The product strategy document — what this unlocks: strategy inherits the slots, and a vague proposition yields an unprioritisable backlog.
exp20v2-sol.valueprop:
Value proposition statement

Discovery and Design, Solution Design and Prototyping

1. A sentence worth ₹90 lakh

On Monday 3 August 2026, Rukhsana Lathkar, head of product at Mandvi Books, had seventeen days to settle one sentence. Mandvi, based in Pune, sells GST invoicing and ledger software to small businesses. On Thursday 20 August the leadership team would release ₹90 lakh for a four-month campaign, and whatever sentence Rukhsana brought would become its headline, its creative brief and its targeting rule.

Since January the company had collected 14,000 trial signups and converted 1,260 of them, or 9.0 per cent, to a ₹499-a-month plan. Raunak Laddha, head of growth, wanted a line that could reach all 14,000 again and more. Rukhsana had spent 6 to 24 July interviewing 60 customers and trial users, and she doubted the line would survive contact with her notes.

DraftWordingWho it quietly includes
GrowthInvoicing made simple for every small business.Anyone who issues a bill
ProductHelps wholesale distributors who want to get paid on time by cutting the weeks spent chasing invoices, and enabling them to extend credit to more retailers.Distributors who sell on credit

The two drafts differ in more than style. If the first wins, ₹90 lakh buys attention from people for whom invoicing is a chore but not a cost, and they will trial the product and leave, as most trials already do. If the second wins, the campaign reaches fewer people, but each has a reason to pay. This page follows how Rukhsana decided, and the tool she used.

2. The idea

A value proposition statement is a single sentence that names four things: the customer, the job that customer is trying to get done, the pain that obstructs the job, and the gain the customer would not otherwise have. In the template used here: Helps [customer] who want [job] by reducing [pain] and enabling [gain]. A job, in this vocabulary, is the progress someone is trying to make in a given circumstance; a pain is a cost, risk or frustration that stands in the way; a gain is a benefit the customer values beyond merely finishing the job.

The statement was invented to solve a familiar failure: teams describe a product by its features, and a feature list cannot be wrong. Its ancestry is two lines of work. Geoffrey Moore's positioning template in Crossing the Chasm (1991) forced a team to say, in one breath, for whom a product existed and against what. Alexander Osterwalder and Yves Pigneur's Value Proposition Canvas, published in Value Proposition Design (2014), separated a customer profile (jobs, pains, gains) from a value map (products, pain relievers, gain creators) and asked whether the two fit. The jobs idea came from Clayton Christensen and Anthony Ulwick. The statement is the canvas compressed into a sentence.

Rukhsana wrote the sentence she could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: we help wholesale distributors who want to get paid on time by cutting the weeks they spend chasing invoices, and by enabling them to extend credit to more retailers. Every phrase in it is a claim that evidence can contradict. That is its purpose.

3. How it works

The mechanics run in five steps, and the last is the one practitioners leave implicit. First, choose the customer narrowly enough that you could list ten of them by name. Second, state the job in the customer's own words, from interviews, not from your roadmap; distributors did not say “automate receivables”, they said “get my money in by the 30th”. Third, name the pain with a cost attached: what it takes in hours, rupees or risk. Fourth, name the gain, which is what the customer can do afterwards that was previously unwise or impossible. Fifth, test whether the product demonstrably causes the pain reduction and the gain.

Two implicit moves matter. The writer must rank: a customer has many pains, and the statement carries the one that costs most and that the product removes most directly. And the writer must delete: any slot that interviews cannot support is removed, not softened. Figure 2 shows why the loop returns to step 1. When a pain is too small to justify a price, the usual repair is a different customer, not a louder claim.

4. A worked example

Rukhsana’s first table counted interviews. All 60 interviewees were asked whether they issued invoices on credit; those who did were then asked whether any invoice was more than 30 days overdue. The rate in the last column is therefore computed over credit users, not over everyone interviewed.

SegmentInterviewedIssue credit invoicesHad one overdue >30 daysRate among credit users
Wholesale distributors24211781.0%
Retailers3615640.0%
Total (pooled)60362363.9%

Next she priced the pain. Distributors with an overdue invoice carried an average of ₹3.2 lakh overdue (the model assumes the whole balance stays overdue for the month); retailers, ₹0.6 lakh. Informal credit in their trade costs about 18 per cent a year, so each month of delay costs 1.5 per cent of the amount. For a distributor that is ₹3,20,000 × 1.5% = ₹4,800 a month; for a retailer, ₹60,000 × 1.5% = ₹900. These apply only to affected traders, so she weighted them by incidence: ₹4,800 × 17/21 = ₹3,886 per distributor who issues credit, and ₹900 × 6/15 = ₹360 per such retailer.

The product’s reminders might recover some of that carrying cost. She assumed 40 per cent and compared the gain with the ₹499 price, requiring a multiple of at least 3, the margin below which buyers rarely bother to switch.

SegmentCost per affected trader (₹/month)Cost per credit user (₹/month)Gain at 40% (₹)Multiple of ₹499Gain at 60% (₹)Multiple of ₹499
Distributors4,8003,8861,5543.12,3314.7
Retailers9003601440.292160.43

Gains are the per-credit-user cost times the recovery rate; multiples are gain divided by 499. Figures rounded to the nearest rupee.

The second pass changes one input. Raising the recovery rate from 40 to 60 per cent lifts the distributor multiple from 3.1 to 4.7, but that is the upside case. The 40 per cent assumption clears the 3 × rule only narrowly: break-even is 1,497 / 3,886 = 38.5 per cent, and at 25 per cent the multiple falls to 1.9. The distributor case therefore stands or falls on a recovery rate nobody has yet measured, an average of ₹3.2 lakh resting on at most 17 distributors, and an incidence of 17 in 21. The 60 per cent figure barely moves the retailer, who reaches 0.43. No plausible recovery rate rescues that segment at this price, because the pain itself is small. Her draft was the better bet, not a proven one, and the evidence for it was a base-and-rate table anyone could recompute. Note also that the multiples describe the average credit user; about 4 of the 21 distributors had no overdue invoice and would gain nothing under the model.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

The customer is defined by the job, not the demographic.

“Small business” describes a size. “Distributors who sell on credit” describes a circumstance in which the job arises. Retailers and distributors both invoice, yet only one group has a pain large enough to pay for; 6 of 15 retailers with credit invoices had an overdue one, but at only ₹360 a month.

Pains and gains are not symmetrical.

Customers act to escape pain far more readily than to acquire gains, so a gain claim without a pain beneath it is usually weaker. In this case the gain, wider credit, only matters because chasing has already been tamed.

A feature is not a pain reliever until it is tied to a pain.

“WhatsApp reminders” is a feature. “Fewer weeks chasing” is the effect.

The statement is not positioning.

It says nothing about alternatives such as a spreadsheet, a clerk, or an established package like Tally. Positioning adds the comparison; the statement supplies what is being compared.

It is not a tagline or a mission.

A tagline is written to be remembered; a statement is written to be wrong in a useful way.

Interview evidence has a base and a bias.

Sixty people is enough to see a pattern and too few to size a market. Interviewees also recall pain more than they predict payment. Always ask for the last time it happened.

What the statement cannot tell you.

It cannot say how many distributors exist, whether the reminders work, or whether a buyer will switch from existing habits. Those need sizing, a prototype and a pilot.

Questions to ask before relying on it.

Who said the pain was real, and how many were asked? Is the cost measured in rupees? Would the customer pay a stated price? Which slot would you delete first if challenged?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and large

The four slots stay the same, but the evidence for each changes with the kind of product and the age of the firm.

SettingWhat shiftsTypical trap
ConsumerPain is often emotional or social, hard to price; gains carry more weightClaiming a gain nobody pays for
B2BBuyer, user and payer differ; the pain can be costed in rupees, as aboveWriting for the user while the budget holder decides
MarketplaceTwo customers, so two statements that must each be true before the other side joinsOne sentence that serves neither side
Early-stageOne statement, held loosely, rewritten often as interviews arriveDefending the first draft
Large companyMany statements, one per segment, which must not contradict each otherA committee sentence that promises everything

For Mandvi, a start-up of this size, one sentence suffices.

7. Common mistakes

MistakeSymptom from outsideMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
The adjective statement“Simple, fast, affordable”; rivals say the sameAttributes treated as painsSwap the rival’s name in; if it still reads true, it is empty
The compound customerCampaign copy addressing five audiencesBreadth mistaken for opportunityAsk whom you would refuse as a customer
The invented painInterviewees nod, then do not payLeading questions produce agreement, not behaviourCount those with a specific last-time story, over those asked

Each diagnostic costs an afternoon. Raunak’s draft failed the first two on sight.

8. What good looks like

A good version of this decision has a statement short enough to repeat, a customer small enough to name, and a pain priced in rupees. It carries a base for every rate and a rule written before the data arrives: here, a gain of at least three times the price. It also records what would change the mind. Rukhsana wrote hers on one page.

Mandvi Books helps wholesale distributors who want to get paid on time by reducing the weeks spent chasing invoices, and enabling them to extend credit to more retailers. Evidence: 17 of 21 distributors with credit invoices had one overdue past 30 days; modelled gain ₹1,554 a month against a ₹499 price (3.1 times).

Note what is absent: no adjective, no retailer, no claim about simplicity. Each missing item was a deliberate exclusion.

9. The decision, and what comes next

On 20 August Rukhsana took the product statement to the leadership team. She did not ask for the whole ₹90 lakh; she proposed releasing a first tranche aimed only at distributors, with the 3 × price rule as the test. Raunak accepted, on condition that the retailer trials already running continue untouched. The reasoning was cheap to state: the broad line would have reached more people, but the narrow one reached people who were modelled to gain three times what they paid.

The next idea to learn is the product strategy document, because a statement says for whom and why, while strategy decides what to build first, what to leave out and how the company will defend its position.

Two questions to sit with. If the 40 per cent recovery assumption had been 25 per cent, which slot would you change, and what would you test first? And which part of your own product’s description would a customer find hardest to recognise?
exp40v2-sol.concept:
Discovery & Design › Solution Design & Prototyping · Exp40

Concept and elevator pitch

Who it is for, what changes for them, why that is newly possible — and nothing about how it is built. Nearly all the discipline lives in that exclusion.

1. Two rooms, a week apart

On Tuesday, 2 June 2026, in a bungalow off Baner Road in Pune, Arnav Belsare had sixty-four slides and ten days. Shrutilipi Clinical AI, where he ran product, was raising ₹52 crore, and the lead partner meeting was fixed for Friday, 12 June. The product listened to an outpatient consultation and wrote a structured note into the hospital's record system. Avanish Bhanot, the founder, wanted the deck's opening line to be the corridor line salespeople used; the engineering lead wanted the words on-device in it, because running the model inside the hospital was what made the product saleable to a compliance officer. Two of the three candidate openings, Apurva Bhujle had noticed, made sense only to someone who already knew the product.

A week later, on Tuesday, 9 June, in a shed on the Nashik–Dindori road, Amrisha Bhalekar faced the same question with a shorter fuse. Sanchalak Pump Controls made a retrofit controller that sat between a farmer's existing pump set and its power source, sequencing the pump against the hours the DISCOM actually supplied. Arnika Baldota needed a tooling decision — injection moulds at ₹1.9 crore, fourteen weeks — before the dealer conference on Monday, 6 July. Bhavit Bhokare, who ran 212 dealers across Nashik, Dhule and Jalgaon, wanted the pitch to lead with diesel savings, which dealers repeated without training. Baisakhi Bhutoria, the chief financial officer, had lived through the last time they did that.

Neither decision is about a feature. Both are about a concept: the mechanism-free statement of what the product does for whom, from which roadmap, pricing, demo and objection-handling follow. The argument here: a concept's value comes from what it refuses to contain.

2. What a concept is, and what it was invented to stop

A concept fixes four things and nothing else: the person it is for, by circumstance rather than demographic; the problem in that person's world, with its cost; the change if the product exists; and why that change is newly possible. An elevator pitch is those slots delivered aloud under a time constraint, which forces a choice about whose problem is primary — and a statement that has not made that choice is not a concept.

The idea exists to stop one pathology. New-product research through the 1960s and 1970s — Robert Cooper's stage-gate literature and the NewProd studies — kept finding teams who could not say what their product was for in terms a buyer would recognise, and who found out only after tooling. The concept gate was the cheap instrument inserted upstream; Theodore Levitt's quarter-inch hole is the same move in rhetorical form. It arrived twice more: Geoffrey Moore's template added the displaced alternative, and Steve Blank, Eric Ries and Ash Maurya demanded a threshold so the sentence could be wrong.

Practitioners who all use the word disagree, and five positions each sign something the others will not. The working-backwards school, from Amazon's press-release-and-FAQ practice, signs that nothing is designed before the customer-facing narrative is written and reviewed; it will not sign that the narrative be short, since the FAQ is long on purpose. The falsifiable-hypothesis school signs that a concept without a stated threshold is decoration, and will not sign that good writing is evidence. The jobs-to-be-done school, after Clayton Christensen and Anthony Ulwick, signs that you name a job and a circumstance, never a demographic, and will not sign a concept naming a category, which imports the incumbent's assumptions. The design-led school, clearest in Bill Buxton's work on sketching, signs that a concept lives in artefacts and a sentence merely indexes it, and will not sign that three sentences can carry one, since a verbal test rewards the articulate. The positioning school, in April Dunford's form, signs that a concept not implying the alternative it displaces cannot be evaluated, and will not sign the exclusion of implementation: where the mechanism is the differentiation, excluding it hides the only thing that matters — Arnav's argument about on-device, left unsettled in section 10.

3. Mechanics: how the sentence is actually built

The visible steps are: fill the four slots badly, cut, read aloud to strangers, cut again. The implicit step does the work — the word budget. Experts cut against a measured allocation, which diagnoses what the team believes. Arnav wrote four drafts between 9 and 24 March 2026, and Apurva coded every word into the four slots plus a fifth for anything describing how the product worked.

Exhibit 1 · Word allocation across four drafts
DraftWho it is forProblem and its costWhat changesWhy now possibleImplementationTotal wordsImplementation share
v1 (9 Mar)9141107811269.6%
v2 (14 Mar)1116140529355.9%
v3 (19 Mar)1317196227728.6%
v4 (24 Mar)14182180610.0%

Each total sums that row's five slots: v1, 9 + 14 + 11 + 0 + 78 = 112. Implementation share divides a row's implementation words by its own total: 78 of the 112 in v1, 69.6%; 52 of the 93 in v2, 55.9%; 22 of the 77 in v3, 28.6%; none of the 61 in v4.

The second-order effect matters more than the tidying. Because the implementation clause carried most of v1, deleting it forced the team to see they had never written down what changed for the doctor. Three words of v1's what changes slot said the note would be "accurate and complete". By v4 it said the doctor leaves the room with the note signed and does not reopen the record system that evening. A stranger can contradict that; "accurate and complete" cannot, which is why it survived three reviews.

The formal treatment concerns reliability, not demand. Whether a draft is a concept or a specification is a judgement, and a gate built on judgement needs an agreement statistic. On 17 February 2026 two reviewers independently classified 60 archived drafts.

Exhibit 3 · Two reviewers, 60 drafts, February 2026
Reviewer A ↓ / B →B: conceptB: specificationTotal
A: concept18725
A: specification53035
Total233760

Observed agreement is the two diagonal cells, 18 + 30 = 48 of the 60 drafts, or 80.0%. Chance agreement from the marginals — A called 25 of 60 a concept, B called 23 of 60 — is (25/60 × 23/60) + (35/60 × 37/60) = (575 + 1,295)/3,600 = 1,870/3,600 = 0.5194. Cohen's kappa = (0.8000 − 0.5194) / (1 − 0.5194) = 0.2806 / 0.4806 = 0.58.

A kappa of 0.58 is moderate: high enough to gate on, low enough that the gate must publish its rubric. That rubric became Exhibit 1 — a draft whose implementation share exceeds a quarter of its words goes back. Note the limit: it says the reviewers mean roughly the same thing by "concept", and nothing about whether any of the 60 drafts describes something a hospital would buy.

The last step is the playback test. The statement is read once, aloud, to someone outside the team, who is then asked what would change for them. Experts score two things separately: whether the listener reproduces the intended change, and whether they add a mechanism the statement never mentioned — the sign it left a hole.

4. When the discipline applies, and when it misleads

Claim one: the buyer recognises the problem untaught. True at Shrutilipi — a doctor finishing a 40-patient clinic needs no explanation of the documentation burden — and true at Sanchalak for unreliable supply hours. Where it is false the statement actively misleads: it tests badly for a reason unrelated to the product, the listener judging a solution to a problem they have not named. Use a problem interview instead.

Claim two: the change is observable within one usage cycle. True at Shrutilipi, where the cycle is one clinic. Contested at Sanchalak, where diesel and uptime effects show over a season — which is why the field evidence took 90 days. Where the change is visible only over years, experts substitute a narrative of the first year.

Claim three: no part of the mechanism is the thing being purchased. True at Shrutilipi for the model architecture, false for where the data sits: a compliance officer is buying the location. False at Sanchalak for retrofit — that the box fits the pump a farmer already owns is the change in his world, since the alternative is a new pump. The test is not "is this technical?" but "does the buyer's decision change if the word goes?"

5. Hard edges: platforms, two sides, regulation, tooling, models

In multi-product companies honest practice is one concept per product plus a statement of what they share — which mature firms largely do while claiming a single company concept. The portfolio sentence is an investor artefact; the product sentences gate work. Confusing them is how roadmaps acquire unasked-for features.

Two-sided products need two concepts and a consistency condition: the change promised each side must be producible by the other side's behaviour at the implied volumes. A marketplace promising buyers same-day delivery and sellers no inventory commitment is a contradiction written twice.

Regulated contexts constrain vocabulary before rhetoric. Avni Bhagane, Shrutilipi's clinical governance adviser, struck diagnosis from v2 in forty seconds: a product making a diagnostic claim is a different regulatory object in India, and the concept sentence is where that exposure is created or avoided. The same holds for advice in financial products and certified wherever BIS reaches.

Hardware plus software is Amrisha's case, and the asymmetry is brutal. A software concept can be revised fortnightly; one implying an enclosure cannot be, once the moulds are cut. Her ₹1.9 crore commitment at fourteen weeks freezes the concept just over three months before the product exists. Mature hardware firms separate the claim, frozen early, from the feature set, which keeps moving.

AI-native products add a slot the template lacks: what happens when the model is wrong. If the note is wrong once in twenty consultations, whether the doctor must read it before signing largely determines whether the promised change happens, so it is not implementation detail. The tell that a team has missed this is a sentence with no clause about the human in the loop.

At the organisational seams, concepts decay. Abhra Bhakuni, the enterprise sales lead, collected the 23 decks his team had presented in the previous quarter; 14 of the 23 carried a claim absent from the statement, or 60.9%. That is not indiscipline but evidence the statement left a question buyers reliably asked unanswered.

6. Eight things an expert notices

Implementation leakage hides a missing "so what". The tell: you can delete the mechanism clause and lose no meaning, so it occupied the space where the outcome belonged. The obvious reading — the team is showing off — is wrong. The team is hiding, and the mechanism is the only thing it is sure of.

An "and" in a concept is usually an "or". The tell: the clauses have different buyers. Sanchalak's draft promised lower diesel spend and fewer burnt-out motors — the first speaks to an owner's cash, the second to a tenant farmer's harvest risk. Two concepts in one sentence yield a roadmap satisfying neither, because every prioritisation call picks a side.

A concept names a change in the buyer's world, not a capability. The tell is grammatical: can you rewrite it with the buyer as subject of an ordinary verb? "The doctor leaves the room with the note signed" passes. "The platform generates structured documentation" never will.

A pitch only its author can deliver is not a concept. The tell: it tests well when the founder reads it and badly when anyone else does. That is usually treated as a delivery problem. It is not: the founder supplies context from outside the sentence, and the sentence is short by exactly that much.

Abstraction can be discipline or cowardice, and they look identical. "An AI-powered platform for Indian healthcare" contains no implementation and is not a concept. The tell is exclusion: a concept ruling nothing out carries no information, so ask what feature request the sentence lets the team refuse.

The first noun sets the comparison set, and therefore the price. Call the Sanchalak box a controller and it is compared with starters costing a few thousand rupees; call it a pump-management service and the comparison is a burnt motor. The tell: pricing arguments reopen with no new information, because the team is relitigating a category choice made in three words.

Concept tests measure comprehension reliably and demand unreliably. The tell is which number the team quotes. Playback accuracy is the instrument used correctly; purchase intent from the same session is a number the method cannot support, and section 8's third example is the price.

A concept is a dated object with a named owner. The tell: the question "who may change this sentence, and on what evidence?" produces silence. An undated, unowned concept is reinterpreted quarterly by whoever is presenting, and the drift is invisible because nobody can name what it drifted from.

7. How it changes by product type and company stage

In consumer products listener and buyer coincide, so playback testing approximates the real conversation. In B2B and enterprise there are three concepts — user, economic buyer, compliance function — and the expert move is to write the user's first and derive the others, because the reverse order yields a sentence no user recognises. Platforms and marketplaces need the two-sided check; hardware is frozen by the tooling calendar; AI products must carry the wrongness slot.

By stage the difference is smaller than commonly claimed: the instrument is identical at seed and at scale, and what changes is the cost of being wrong. One real difference — a pre-revenue concept is a hypothesis, while a company with revenue has customers whose renewal assumed the old sentence, a switching cost on the decision. Large companies do not need longer concepts.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Between Monday, 6 April and Friday, 24 April 2026, Shrutilipi took v4 to doctors at nine hospital outpatient departments.

Exhibit 5 · Shrutilipi concept test, 6–24 April 2026 — bases stated
StepCountBase usedRate on that base
Doctors approached140——
Agreed to a 20-minute session118140 approached84.3%
Read the statement, asked the playback question96118 who agreed81.4%
Reproduced the intended change unaided6596 asked67.7%
Said they would ask for a hospital trial5496 asked56.3%

The playback question was added only in the second week, so 22 of the 118 who agreed were never put it. The denominator for playback accuracy is therefore the 96 who were asked: 65 of the 96, or 67.7%. Over all 118 who agreed it reads 55.1%, failing the two-in-three threshold on a question most of those doctors never faced. On the correct base v4 cleared the gate; on the wrong base the team would have rewritten a working sentence.

Between Monday, 11 May and Friday, 29 May, Bhavit's team visited 164 dealers, split by dealer-code parity: 80 heard a three-sentence concept, 84 got the two-page specification sheet. The outcome measured was agreeing to stock two demo units.

Exhibit 6 · Concept arm versus specification arm, 164 dealers
ArmDealersAgreed to stock two unitsStocking rate
Three-sentence concept803240.0%
Two-page specification sheet842125.0%
Both arms1645332.3%

32 of the 80 is 40.0%; 21 of the 84 is 25.0%; the difference is 15.0 percentage points. Standard error of the difference = √(0.40 × 0.60 / 80 + 0.25 × 0.75 / 84) = √(0.003000 + 0.002232) = √0.005232 = 0.0723, i.e. 7.23 points. So z = 15.0 / 7.23 = 2.07, and the 95% interval is 15.0 ± 1.96 × 7.23 = 15.0 ± 14.2, or 0.8 to 29.2 points.

The failure. Sanchalak's previous generation was pitched as halving the diesel bill. The concept tested beautifully and dealers repeated it untrained. Then the company instrumented 46 units for the 90 days from 1 September to 29 November 2024. Median monthly diesel spend fell from ₹4,800 to ₹3,360 — a real saving of 30 per cent, not the half promised. Owners who did the arithmetic asked for their money back: of those 46 instrumented units, 11 came back under the buy-back, or 23.9%. Sales ran well beyond the 46; only that set was measured.

Exhibit 8 · Hard cost of the mis-stated claim
ItemWorkingCost (₹)
Buy-back refunds11 units × 26,0002,86,000
Reprinted pitch material212 dealers × 31065,720
Total3,51,720

Reading the telemetry Sanchalak already held would have cost about one analyst-week, ₹28,000. Catching the error after the channel had repeated it cost ₹3,51,720, about 12.6 times as much — and the channel-trust cost, which Bhavit says was larger, cannot honestly be priced.

The recovery was not a better sentence but a smaller claim: a saving of about a 30 per cent, plus never losing a night's irrigation to a motor that should have been serviced. Duller, and it survives the telemetry. It is what Baisakhi was defending in the June 2026 room.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The specification in disguise. Sign: the concept lengthens at every review. Diagnostic: what share of the words describe mechanism? Caught at the gate it costs an afternoon; after an engineering estimate it costs the estimate.

Promising more than the evidence supports. Sign: nobody can name the measurement behind the headline number. Diagnostic: from which dataset, over what window, on what base? Sanchalak's ₹3,51,720 is the price of skipping it.

Mistaking comprehension for demand. Sign: the team celebrates a playback result. Diagnostic: what would these people give up for it? Caught late it costs a build cycle aimed at a problem people understood and did not want.

Concept drift at the seams. Sign: two field decks disagree. Diagnostic: collect what was presented, as Abhra did, and count claims absent from the canonical statement. Caught late it costs a renewal: someone bought the field version.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

May the mechanism appear when the mechanism is the differentiation? The positioning position, steelmanned: where a capability is the only reason the outcome is credible, excluding it does not purify the concept — it makes it an unsupported boast. Shrutilipi's compliance buyers do not infer local processing from a promise about a doctor's evening; they ask, and a sentence with no answer invites the worst assumption. The exclusionist position: once a mechanism enters it becomes what the organisation defends, and teams have shipped architectures nobody wanted because the concept promised them. For that to be wrong you would have to find firms that name a mechanism and still kill it. They exist, and they are rare.

Do sentences or artefacts carry concepts? The design position: language tests fluency, so the highest-playback sentence is often the most conventional, and verbal testing selects against ideas lacking vocabulary. For that to be wrong, playback accuracy would have to predict adoption as well as artefact-based tests do; the comparative evidence is thin both ways. The verbal position: a concept that cannot be said cannot be delegated. Both sides accept the hedge in Exhibit 4 and neither thinks it settles anything.

Do concept tests predict anything? The sceptics have the Sanchalak example and the stated-versus-revealed-preference literature; the defenders claim comprehension screening, not prediction, and call that failure a false claim rather than a failed method. Whether teams respect the distinction is open.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this writes a good sentence. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They state the denominator before the rate — which is how Arnav's team caught the 96-versus-118 problem before it inverted their conclusion. They keep the concept dated and owned, and can name the evidence that would change it. They separate the mechanism the buyer is purchasing from the one the engineers are proud of, and let the first in. And they read field drift as information: the hole the field filled is the missing requirement.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Arnav kept on-device out of the concept and put it in the second sentence of the FAQ behind it. His reasoning was claim three of section 4: remove the word and the doctor's decision is unchanged, so it is not in the concept; remove it and the compliance officer's decision changes, so it must be answerable in the next breath. The two are artefacts for different rooms, and collapsing them had caused the argument.

Amrisha led with uptime, kept the word retrofit, and cut the diesel figure to "about 30 per cent" with the measurement window printed beneath it. She committed the ₹1.9 crore of tooling on 9 June, because the claim she had chosen depended on nothing the enclosure could change. Bhavit lost the argument he came in with and won the one that mattered: the dealer pitch is three sentences, and its diesel figure is the one the 2024 telemetry supports.

For discussion. First: if the compliance officer's question is predictable and material, why does it belong in the FAQ rather than the concept — and would that change if Shrutilipi sold to compliance directly? Second: the split test gives a 15.0-point advantage, 95% interval 0.8 to 29.2 points. What would you decide differently if the true effect sat at the bottom of it? Third: Abhra's decks carried claims the concept did not. Is that a failure of the sales team, the concept, or the gate?

13. Going deeper

  • Ideation: brainstorming, Crazy 8s, HMW — supplies the candidates; weak divergence caps everything after.
  • Writing a solution hypothesis — adds the decision rule the concept lacks.
  • Solution interviews and concept tests — the apparatus behind Exhibit 5.
  • Value proposition statement — the four slots compressed for a buyer.
  • Value Proposition Canvas — forces pains and gains apart first.
  • Storyboarding — the gate's other input, and the design school's preferred medium.
  • Wireframes, mockups, prototypes — the fidelity ladder once words run out.
  • Concept → feedback → iterate — the loop the returning arrow implies.
  • What an MVP is — the build-time counterpart: a learning vehicle with a rule.
  • AI-generated prototypes — cheapens visual testing, moving where the words-versus-artefacts dispute bites.
  • AI product design choices — where the wrongness slot gets specified.
  • Build, buy, partner or open source — the decision a mechanism-free concept leaves open.
  • Physical product concept development — tooling calendars and frozen claims.
  • Point solution vs platform trade-off — the seam where portfolio and product sentences get confused.
case20v1-sol.concept:
Cresset Books: Three Sentences Before Ninety-Six Lakh

A teaching case on concept and elevator pitch

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 19 October 2026, Jaideep Nadig, head of product at Cresset Books, opened a shared document in the company's Bengaluru office and typed a single heading: "Friday." The product committee would meet on Friday, 23 October, and he had to bring one recommendation. Engineering had a free squad of four from 2 November, six days before Diwali on Sunday, 8 November, the week in which shopkeepers do their heaviest trading and bookkeeping. Nothing could ship by then; the choice would decide what they saw in the new year.

The squad could build only one of three concepts tested in September. The leading one had scored well, but when Jaideep tried to explain it aloud to his sales head, it took ninety seconds and two diversions into message parsing. He suspected that was a bad sign.

2. Company background

Cresset Books, founded in 2019 and headquartered in Bengaluru with an engineering group in Pune, sells a ledger app to small shopkeepers, mostly kirana stores, chemists and neighbourhood wholesalers. The core product records sales and credit given to customers, which Indian shopkeepers call udhaar. It had about 1.85 lakh monthly active merchants at the end of September 2026, most paying ₹199 a month for the premium tier, which adds invoices that meet GST requirements and WhatsApp sharing.

The market is crowded. Khatabook and OkCredit own the free ledger habit; Vyapar and Zoho Books serve merchants who want invoices and tax filing; PhonePe for Business and Paytm's merchant app bundle a soundbox and a basic ledger with UPI acceptance. Cresset's advantage was a loyal base in tier-2 cities such as Nashik, Coimbatore and Indore, and a reputation for simple screens. Its weakness was that merchants opened the app mainly to write entries, then closed it.

3. The situation

In August a Crazy 8s round converged on three ideas, each written as a concept card with a name, a description and the ₹199 price. The three were:

A, Udhaar Reminder: polite, scheduled WhatsApp reminders sent to customers who owe the shop money. B, Stock Credit: fourteen days of credit from a wholesaler when the shopkeeper reorders through the app. C, Roz ka Hisaab ("the daily account"): a nightly summary of the day's money.

The survey was a between-subjects design: 600 merchants were drawn from Cresset's panel and split at random into three cells of 200, and each merchant saw exactly one concept. The question was purchase intent on a five-point scale, and the figure reported is the share answering "definitely" or "probably" would use, called top-two-box. Fielding ran from 1 to 7 September. Exhibit 1 gives the results; Exhibit 2 the timeline.

Exhibit 1. Wave 1 (1–7 September 2026): one concept per respondent, 200 respondents per cell
ConceptTop-two-box (of 200)Share95% interval, ± points
A, Udhaar Reminder6231.0%6.4
B, Stock Credit7839.0%6.8
C, Roz ka Hisaab (long card)9045.0%6.9
Wave 2 (28 Sep–4 Oct): C, Roz ka Hisaab (three-sentence card), a fresh sample of 20010452.0%6.9

Share = top-two-box divided by 200. Interval = 1.96 × √(p(1−p)/200), a simple binomial approximation. Wave 2 respondents were drawn separately from the same panel; none had seen any wave 1 card. Both cards for C carried the same ₹199 price. Fielding cost: ₹1,150 per completed response; 600 + 200 = 800 completes, so ₹9,20,000, or ₹9.2 lakh.

Wave 1 gave the team a front-runner: concept C led at 45.0 per cent. But the long card for C read, in part: "The app reads UPI credit alerts from the shopkeeper's phone with an on-device parser, matches them to ledger entries using a rules engine, and at 9 pm pushes a summary through the WhatsApp Business API." In the 200-person C cell, 17 merchants wrote in the open comment box some version of "is it safe to let it read my messages?" Jolene Nauman, the designer in Berlin, pushed for a rewrite in which the card said only what the shopkeeper gets. In wave 2 the card read:

"Every night at nine, Roz ka Hisaab tells you in one WhatsApp message how much money came in today, how much is still owed to you, and whom to call tomorrow. You do nothing to set it up except say yes. It replaces the notebook count at closing time."

That version scored 52.0 per cent in a fresh sample, the figure in the last row of Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 2. Scale: 11 pixels per day, 1 September at x = 40. Wave bars span the first to last day of fielding, inclusive.

The global team read the numbers differently. Jasmine Nene, the sales head in New Jersey, said she had been arguing all quarter that the long card was killing the idea, and that wave 2 proved it. Jibin Nedungadi, the data scientist in Toronto, answered that it proved nothing of the kind: 52.0 against 45.0 is a seven-point difference between two different sets of people, and the interval for that gap, 1.96 × √(0.45×0.55/200 + 0.52×0.48/200) = 9.8 points, is wider than the gap itself. Joydeep Nirula, who leads customer success from Singapore, offered a third observation that settled neither side: of the 40 merchants he had phoned, none could repeat the nightly summary back in their own words after hearing the long description.

4. The people

Jaideep Nadig (Bengaluru, head of product) wants a decision he can defend if the build misses. Jolene Nauman (Berlin, design lead) wants a concept she can draw on one screen. Jibin Nedungadi (Toronto, data scientist) wants no one to claim more than the survey shows. Jasmine Nene (New Jersey, sales head) wants a headline for the Diwali campaign and the large distributor accounts, including a Dubai-based trading group that supplies some 3,000 Indian kirana stores and has asked what Cresset will offer them. Joydeep Nirula (Singapore, customer success) wants something his team can explain on a phone call in under a minute.

5. Exhibits and what they show

Exhibit 1 supports two claims and no more. First, the gap between C's long card (45.0 per cent) and A (31.0 per cent) is 14.0 points against a gap interval of 9.4, so the data distinguishes them. Second, the other gaps do not clear the line: C against B is 6.0 points against 9.7, and B against A is 8.0 against 9.3. The wave 2 row does not change this, because it is a separate sample of different people. Jibin's point is that the page cannot say whether the shorter card caused the seven-point rise, whether it is sampling noise, or whether panel mood moved between September and October.

Exhibit 3. The three options for Friday
OptionCostElapsed timeWhat it settles
1. Build C now, from the long card₹96 lakh10 weeksNothing before launch; the learning comes after
2. Rewrite, then a paired retest₹2.76 lakh fielding3 weeksWhether the short card beats the long card with the same people
3. Fifteen solution interviews₹3.6 lakh2 weeksWhether merchants can repeat the idea and what they fear

Option 1 is a management estimate of the squad's fully loaded cost for ten weeks, including cloud, WhatsApp Business messaging and testing; it was not derived from salaries and is shown only to size the stakes. Option 2: 240 merchants × ₹1,150 = ₹2,76,000. Option 3: 15 interviews × ₹24,000 = ₹3,60,000.

6. The options

Option 1, build now. Begin the 10-week build on 2 November from the long card. Its upside is the best raw score. Its cost is ₹96 lakh and a launch that misses Diwali anyway, since ten weeks from 2 November is mid-January. It also commits the squad to an on-device message parser before any merchant has said they would allow one.

Option 2, rewrite and retest. Fix the pitch at three sentences, then show 240 merchants both versions of C in random order, so each respondent compares the two and the effect of wording is isolated from who answered. It costs ₹2.76 lakh and three weeks and would let the team choose the wording on evidence. The cost is time.

Option 3, interview first. Run fifteen solution interviews. The upside is depth: what merchants fear, what they repeat back. The cost is ₹3.6 lakh and two weeks, and fifteen merchants cannot rank anything.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What did the long card describe that the shopkeeper does not need to know?
  2. Using Exhibit 1, which differences are larger than noise? What would Jasmine need to know to support her claim about the long card?
  3. Is the idea ready to build when the team cannot say it in three sentences? What is the cost of discovering the answer after ₹96 lakh, rather than before?
  4. Which option should Jaideep take on Friday, and what decision rule would he attach to the next step?

8. A note for the learner

A concept is the idea that survived convergence, written in two or three sentences, with no implementation detail. The test is simple: can you pitch it without describing how it works? Cresset's long card failed that test, and the 17 comments about message safety were an early sign that detail the customer did not ask for was creating worry the idea did not deserve. Whether that worry lowered the score is a separate question the data cannot answer: the long card was shown to one group and the short card to another.

One defensible path is Option 2, with a piece of Option 3 inside it. Jaideep fixes the three-sentence pitch now, and the retest uses the same 240 merchants for both cards, so wording is the only thing that differs and the respondents are their own comparison. Two caveats: at 240 unpaired merchants per card the gap interval would still be about 8.9 points, and the paired design's advantage depends on a correlation the team has not measured; the order of the cards must also be randomised because the second card may inherit worry from the first. A paired comparison is more sensitive than two fresh samples of equal size, because the differences between people drop out. He writes the rule before the data arrives: proceed to a six-week learning build of C only if the short card holds at least the level of the long card and at least 8 of 15 interviewed merchants can repeat the pitch back unprompted. Such an MVP is a learning vehicle with a decision rule, not a small product; its cost would be set once the pitch is fixed.

Option 1 is the weakest, because speed has no value if the squad builds the wrong parser. Option 3 alone cannot choose between wordings. The Dubai distributor and the sales campaign can wait three weeks for a pitch that holds up.
exp20v2-sol.concept:
Concept and Elevator Pitch

Discovery & Design, Solution Design & Prototyping

1. Three proposals, no comparison

On the morning of Tuesday, 8 September 2026, Aditya Bagal, head of product at Samarth Kirana Cloud in Pune, opened a shared folder holding three build proposals and counted their pages: eleven, nine and fourteen. The company sold stock and ledger software to 2,400 kirana stores, the neighbourhood grocery shops. On Friday, 25 September, a steering committee chaired by the founder, Bina Baviskar, would commit ₹90 lakh and fourteen engineers for two quarters to exactly one of the three.

The trouble was not quality. Bhavya Brahmbhatt, who ran engineering from Bengaluru, had sized all three carefully. But each opened with architecture: data models, partner interfaces, phased rollout. When Aditya asked Bina which she found strongest, she said she could not tell, because every document explained how the thing would work before saying what it was for.

The cost was concrete. A committee that cannot compare ideas defaults to the most persuasive author. If the wrong proposal won, fourteen people would spend six months building something a grocer might admire and never pay for. Aditya decided each proposal would first become a concept: two or three sentences, no implementation, which he could say aloud and test on shop owners.

2. The idea

A product concept is a short statement, usually two or three sentences, of who a product is for, what need it meets, what the person gains, and what they do instead today. It deliberately omits how the product is built. An elevator pitch is the same content spoken aloud in roughly thirty seconds to someone who can say yes, such as a manager or investor. The written version shown to customers in research is a concept card.

The discipline exists because teams argue about implementation, which is concrete, while the choice that matters is about value. A proposal opening with a database diagram feels rigorous and is nearly impossible to compare with another. The commonly used template comes from Geoffrey Moore's Crossing the Chasm (1991): "For [target customer] who [need], the [product] is a [category] that [key benefit]. Unlike [alternative], our product [difference]." Marketing researchers had by then tested written product descriptions for decades.

Aditya's repeatable sentence: a concept is the promise, in the customer's terms, that remains true when every implementation detail is taken away.

3. How it actually works

Writing a concept is a sequence of subtractions and choices, and Aditya followed it for each proposal.

First, name one customer in one moment. "Small businesses" is not a customer; a grocer in Nashik on a Monday morning, with a wholesaler's truck at the gate and too little cash to pay, is. Second, state the need in that person's words, since a need phrased in the team's vocabulary usually smuggles the solution in, and state the benefit as a change in their situation, not a feature. Third, and usually left implicit, choose a category and name the real alternative, often a habit. The category decides what the listener compares the product with: a "credit line" invites thoughts of interest rates, a "ledger app" of free apps.

Fourth comes the deletion test, the step most often skipped. Ask whether each sentence would stay true if the technology were replaced; if not, it is implementation and comes out. Fifth, read it aloud: at about 150 words a minute, thirty seconds holds roughly 75 words. Sixth, put it on a concept card and test it with shops.

Applied to the proposal for a stock-purchase credit line, the exercise produced this, which Aditya called Concept C:

For neighbourhood grocers who run short of cash between wholesaler visits and leave shelves empty, Samarth Shelf Credit is a stock-purchase credit line that lets them restock the day they need to. Unlike waiting for customers to settle their ledgers or borrowing on a wholesaler's informal terms, it gives a limit that reflects how the shop actually trades. The shop repays as the stock sells.

The other two proposals became Concept A, Udhaar Radar, which reminds an owner which customers' khata balances (the record of what regular customers owe on credit) are overdue; and Concept B, Auto-Reorder, which proposes the day's wholesaler order before the owner thinks of it.

4. A worked example, line by line

Aditya commissioned a monadic concept test, in which each respondent sees exactly one card. Between Monday, 14 and Friday, 18 September, a research agency showed the cards to kirana owners, 120 per concept, 360 in all, asking whether they would "definitely" or "probably" try it. Top-two-box means the share choosing either positive answer.

Concept (n = 120 each)DefinitelyProbablyTop-two-box countTop-two-box %Top box %
A Udhaar Radar30427260.025.0
B Auto-Reorder24366050.020.0
C Shelf Credit42307260.035.0

At face value A and C tie at 60.0 per cent and B trails by ten points. But people overstate intent, and the company held evidence of how much. In a 2025 pilot of an earlier feature, 20 of the 50 owners who had said "definitely" went on to pay, a rate of 40 per cent, while 8 of the 80 who said "probably" did, a rate of 10 per cent. The pilot measured paying, a stricter and later act than trying, so applying its rates to "try" answers gives expected paying adopters, not a trial rate. Table 2 does this.

ConceptDefinitely × 40%Probably × 10%Expected adopters (of 120)Expected paying adopters %
A Udhaar Radar12.04.216.213.50
B Auto-Reorder9.63.613.211.00
C Shelf Credit16.83.019.816.50
C, rate disclosed (retest)10.83.314.111.75

The tie broke: C's 42 "definitely" answers, against A's 30, count for more once calibrated, so C led at 16.50 per cent to A's 13.50. The second pass changed one input. Bhavya pointed out that Concept C said nothing about cost, and that regulators expect lenders to state a loan's cost clearly. Aditya added the charge, "2 per cent a month on the amount used", and retested with a fresh 120 owners between Tuesday, 22 and Thursday, 24 September: 27 "definitely" and 33 "probably", so 60 in the top two boxes (50.0 per cent) and 11.75 per cent expected paying adopters.

The ranking now read A at 13.50, C at 11.75 and B at 11.00. C's figure fell by 4.75 points between two independent samples of 120. Price is the likely cause, not a proven one: "definitely" fell from 35.0 to 22.5 per cent, a 12.5-point drop with a standard error of about 5.8 points (z about 2.2), marginal evidence.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Concept, idea and specification differ

An idea is a seed ("help grocers with cash"). A concept is a testable statement of one person, one need and one benefit. A specification says how the system behaves.

Price and constraints are part of the promise, not implementation

Whatever a customer must pay, give up or consent to is a term of the promise, and survives the deletion test because it holds under any technology. What goes is the lending partner, the scoring method and the screens.

A concept is not a value proposition or positioning

A value proposition maps customer jobs, pains and gains in detail; positioning is written for the market after launch. The concept serves an earlier reader, the person deciding what to build.

Stated intent is not behaviour

The 40 and 10 per cent rates came from one pilot with 130 positive responders (50 plus 80), a thin base, and are an assumption to revisit, not a constant.

Small samples cannot separate close concepts

With 120 respondents, the standard error of a 60 per cent share is about 4.5 points, and the gap between A (60.0) and B (50.0) has a standard error near 6.4 points. The ratio, 10 divided by 6.4, is about 1.6, short of the roughly 2 usually demanded. B may be weaker, but the test does not prove it.

A clear pitch is evidence of clarity, not of demand

Polished sentences can flatter a weak idea. Only customers can say whether it is wanted.

What a concept cannot tell you

It cannot say whether the product is feasible, the economics work, the partner will sign, or the habit will last to the fourth week. Those need pilots, which is why the best programmes define a minimum viable product (MVP) as a vehicle for learning with a stated decision rule, not a small version of the final product.

Questions to ask before relying on a concept test

Were the respondents the stated customer? What alternative was named? What was left unsaid that the real product would force into the open, as price was here? How many respondents stand behind each number?

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace; early and large

In consumer products, buyer and user are one person and the concept can be tested quickly, but intent inflates because saying yes costs nothing. In B2B there are usually two audiences: the user who feels the pain and the economic buyer who signs. Samarth's shops are both; a hospital software vendor needs one pitch for the ward nurse and another, about cost and risk, for the finance head. A marketplace serves two sides at once: a farm-produce exchange needs a concept for the farmer ("a buyer at a fair price within a day") and another for the trader, and the two must be consistent, since each side's benefit depends on the other turning up.

Company stage changes the job. In an early-stage company the concept is a hypothesis, cheap to write and rewritten weekly. In a large company it must survive committees, and the temptation is to add clauses until all are satisfied; a concept of seven clauses is a compromise.

7. Common mistakes

Disguised implementation. The symptom is a pitch rich in nouns such as "AI engine" or "API". The misunderstanding is that technical specificity signals seriousness. The diagnostic is the deletion test.

A pitch for nobody in particular. The symptom is a room that nods, then asks, "For whom, exactly?" The misunderstanding is that a wide target means a large market. The diagnostic is to name one person on one Tuesday afternoon and read the pitch to them.

No alternative. The symptom is the claim that there are no competitors. The misunderstanding is that no rival product means no alternative; customers always have a habit. The diagnostic is to ask what they do today when the problem occurs.

Reading intent as forecast. The symptom is a business case that uses the 60.0 per cent top-two-box as an adoption rate. The misunderstanding is that a stated answer is a behaviour. The diagnostic is to apply conversion rates from your own earlier launch, as Table 2 does.

8. What good looks like

A good handling of Aditya's decision looks like this. Three concept cards, each under 75 words, name no technology. Each is tested monadically on the stated customer, with price shown wherever the real product would force one. Results appear with counts, bases and a calibration from the company's own history, so any member can recompute them. The ranking carries its uncertainty.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

On Friday, 25 September, Aditya presented the three cards and the revised ranking. He did not ask for ₹90 lakh. A gap of 1.75 points between A and C is well inside what 120 respondents can resolve, and the test said nothing about weekly use. He proposed instead a six-week pilot of Concept A with 40 shops and two engineers, with a written rule: proceed to full build if at least 10 of the 40 shops (25 per cent) used the reminder in at least four of the six weeks; otherwise stop and test Concept C against a real lending partner. The concept had made the choice comparable; the next unit of learning was behaviour, not opinion.

Next, learn solution interviews and concept tests, which deepen the testing used here; the Value Proposition Canvas, which structures the jobs, pains and gains behind a concept; and storyboarding, which turns a concept into a sequence a customer can react to.

Two questions to sit with. First, take a product you work on and write its concept in three sentences without a single technology word: which sentence was hardest, and what does that reveal about what you know? Second, in Aditya's retest one sentence about price coincided with a concept's fall from first to second of three: what is the equivalent sentence in your product, the fact you have not yet told customers?
case40v1-sol.concept:
Nepathya Technologies: Three Sentences and a Clause

A decision case on choosing what to build, and on what a concept has to be able to say

Discovery & Design · Solution Design & Prototyping

1. The night before

On the evening of Sunday, 18 October 2026, Vidisha Chandorkar sat in the Nepathya Technologies office on Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru with three concept cards face up. The investor review was on Tuesday, 20 October; her pre-read was due on Monday morning, and it had to name one concept, one squad and one decision rule. The platform squad came free on Monday, 26 October — seven engineers plus fractional design and data science, with no capacity again until February. Diwali fell on Sunday, 8 November, opening the heaviest three weeks of the service year.

The concept that tested best in September was the one her engineering head said he could not legally build for fourteen of eighteen brand accounts. The concept that addressed the largest measured loss in her customers' operations was the one nobody in the company could explain out loud. The one she could explain in eleven seconds was the one her sales head called a toy. At the top of the page she had written a sentence she had not crossed out: if I cannot say it in three sentences, is that a fact about the idea or a fact about me?

2. Nepathya Technologies, 2017–2026

Nepathya was founded in Bengaluru in 2017 by Vihang Chitnis, eleven years in after-sales operations at a white-goods maker, and Virendra Chokhani, who built the first dispatch engine in Pune. Nepathya Desk sits between a brand's warranty desk and the technicians who open the appliance: it takes the claim, decides whether a part is needed, routes the job and closes it. By September 2026 it carried sixty enterprise accounts across India, the Gulf and North America on ₹68.00 crore of annual recurring revenue for the year ended 31 March 2026 (Exhibit 1).

One decision from 2021 shaped what Vidisha could now choose. To win its first two large brand accounts, Nepathya accepted a single-tenant instance per brand and what the contracts call clause 7.4: brand inventory and parts data may not be used in any shared service, model or index. It cost nothing then — there was no shared service — and the template spread. Fourteen of the eighteen Indian brand accounts now carry clause 7.4, together ₹19.80 crore of the ₹24.60 crore of brand ARR; four, ₹4.80 crore, are free of it. Five of the fourteen renew before 31 March 2027 and nine after. Virendra tried to re-paper two in 2024; both legal teams declined.

3. The industry

Indian after-sales service is a business of promises that are hard to keep. A consumer buys an air conditioner at Croma or Reliance Digital, or on Flipkart or Amazon; the brand owns the warranty, and a third-party network performs the visit. The Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules have made marketplaces insistent about resolution clocks, and Urban Company has taught urban consumers what a tracked visit feels like. Competition comes from horizontal desks — Zoho Desk, Freshdesk, Salesforce Field Service — already inside many of them; from Nimbark Works, funded in 2025 on a technician-first mobile product at a third of Nepathya's price; and from brands who build in-house after a bad Diwali.

Two external facts bore on the decision. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act framework had pushed Indian panel vendors to re-consent their respondent lists, and the list Nepathya used in June expired on Monday, 31 August 2026. And the PLI scheme for white goods was improving parts availability unevenly across brands. Nepathya's exposure abroad was lopsided: seven Gulf and South-East Asian accounts produced ₹16.80 crore, more than the twenty-one Indian third-party networks together, and Nujoom Electronics of Dubai alone ₹9.20 crore.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

On Monday, 11 May 2026, Vidisha ran a two-day workshop in Bengaluru: thirty-one how-might-we statements, two rounds of Crazy 8s, a convergence vote, then three survivors, each written as a card with a name, two or three sentences and the price band.

A — Parts Promise. When a customer logs a warranty claim, Nepathya tells them the date the part will be at their door. The brand's warehouse stock and the service network's van stock are read together, so the date is a commitment and not an estimate.

B — One Visit. Nepathya works out what is actually wrong before anyone is dispatched, so the technician arrives with the right part and the job closes on the first visit.

C — Service Wallet. Every appliance a household owns has one record — warranty, visits, parts fitted — that the owner can see and can hand to the next owner when they sell it.

Wave 1, fielded Monday 8 to Monday 22 June, was monadic: 240 service-operations decision-makers, each shown exactly one card, eighty per cell, asked purchase intent on a seven-point scale. B led on top-two-box intent (Exhibit 2). On 1 July the product committee minuted that B was "the leading concept", and Virendra began a spike on triage.

Three things then went wrong with that belief. Vallari Chhibber, the principal designer in Berlin, read the cards in July and pointed out that B's card had been rewritten three times during the workshop, acquiring each time another clause about how the triage worked: what respondents read was not a concept but a compressed specification. On Thursday, 13 August, the Nujoom renewal added a resolution-time commitment, which made B urgent and harder to discuss calmly. And the June panel list expired at the end of August, so the retest could not re-contact the June respondents.

Vallari rewrote all three cards to strip implementation language, holding names and prices fixed, and Wave 2 ran on a freshly consented panel from Monday 7 to Friday 18 September — again monadic, eighty per cell, 240 new respondents. A came out ahead of B. Separately, from 21 to 25 September, forty-eight prospects heard all three concepts read aloud in rotated order and restated each in one sentence — and on that measure the order was different again.
