5. The people

Vidisha Chandorkar, vice-president of product, Bengaluru, has shipped two modules on time since 2023. Her bonus pays on a module reaching twenty paying accounts within two quarters, which quietly favours whatever is smallest. She is not saying that she no longer believes the June minute she drafted herself.

Vihang Chitnis, co-founder and chief executive, wants a story for Nilotpal Capital about the platform rather than about tickets, and treats the clause he signed in 2021 as solved history. He is not saying that he has had two conversations about a 2028 listing, in which a shared parts index is the asset.

Virendra Chokhani, head of engineering, Pune, is the constraint made flesh: Parts Promise cannot read brand stock for fourteen of eighteen accounts, and a version reading only van stock is a different product with the same name. His incentive is a re-architecture B's triage work would fund. He is not saying that his nineteen-week estimate has a range he has never written down.

Vallari Chhibber, principal designer, Berlin, rewrote the cards and has read all 144 restatements. Her position is that B is not a weak idea but an unsayable one: a concept needing its mechanism explained has not finished converging. She is not saying that she also changed the order of A's clauses in a way she cannot separate from content.

Viveka Chandhok, data scientist, Toronto, is the only person willing to say that September does not establish what the others want it to; her incentive is a reputation for being right about studies. She is not saying that she argued against a fresh panel in August and lost.

Vaishnavi Chellaram, customer-success lead, Singapore, owns renewals for the Gulf and South-East Asia on a target of ₹16.80 crore, and holds that first-visit fix is the only number a customer has raised in a renewal. She is not saying that Nujoom's employed technicians make its figure flattering, or that Indian accounts would carry the hard work.

Vikrant Cavale, head of sales for North America, circulated Exhibit 6 from New Jersey on Wednesday, 7 October. He wants Parts Promise because a date is something a buyer repeats back. He is not saying that his five accounts are ₹6.30 crore of a ₹68.00 crore book, or that his quota resets in January.

Vasumitra Chapekar, partner at Nilotpal Capital and board observer, told the board pre-call: "I am less interested in which one you pick than in what you have agreed to stop doing if it fails, and when you will know." He will not say which way he wants it to point, which Vidisha reads as a test. Vijayan Chemburkar, service operations at Nujoom in Dubai, has no vote but has asked twice for the resolution clock the renewal promised.

6. Voices

Vikrant Cavale, email to the product committee, 7 October

"Stop arguing about June. We changed the words and A went from forty-nine to sixty-five. That is what a clear concept does. Nine accounts have asked for a date, and about half the brand book is clean on the data question anyway."

Virendra Chokhani, reply, same thread

"Four of eighteen. Not half. ₹4.80 crore of ₹24.60 crore. For the other fourteen I can promise a date off van stock, which is a van-stock promise, and the first time we miss one in Lucknow during Diwali we own the anger and the brand owns the part."

Viveka Chandhok, comment on the Wave 2 deck

"Please do not write that the rewrite caused the swap. Different people, different mix, and in both waves the A-to-B gap is smaller than the interval on it. The only thing I would defend in a room is that A is not behind. To know what the wording did you must show one person both versions."

Vallari Chhibber, design review, 29 September

"Twenty-nine of forty-eight people, asked to say One Visit back, described the model. Four did that for Parts Promise. I am not claiming the market prefers A. I am claiming we have never once said B without saying how it works."

Vaishnavi Chellaram, chat to Vidisha, 9 October

"Twelve accounts have asked me for a date, not nine. Vijayan does not want a date; he wants the second visit to stop happening. If we ship a date and the clock still runs twice, June 2027 is a conversation I would rather not have."

7. The options as Vidisha sees them

Build A for the four clean accounts. Ten weeks, ₹90.0 lakh, a concept anyone can repeat. But what Virendra can build for the other fourteen is a van-stock estimate wearing a promise's name, and clause 7.4 does not move before March 2027.

Build B. Nineteen weeks, ₹171.0 lakh, the only option aimed at the 41.0 per cent of claims that do not close on the first visit, a floor given Exhibit 5's inferred closures — spent on a concept the company has never stated without its mechanism.

Build C. Seven weeks, ₹63.0 lakh, easy to say, last on intent in both waves, and the first Nepathya product to touch consumers directly, with the data-protection obligations that follow.

Build none of them for ten weeks. Show the same respondents both versions of each card, and prototype B's triage with three accounts. The cost is a visibly idle squad and a board that asked for a decision rule, not a study.

The framing has a seam in it. All four options assume the question is which concept to build. Vallari's reading of Exhibit 4 is that A and B may not be alternatives: a promised date is worthless without the triage that makes it keepable, and triage is invisible without a date to make it legible. If so, the May vote converged on the wrong axis.

8. The deadline and the hard constraints

The pre-read is due Monday, 19 October; the review is Tuesday, 20 October. The squad is free from Monday, 26 October, and the next capacity is February — nineteen weeks from the twenty-sixth ends 8 March 2027. Cash and equivalents stood at ₹41.00 crore on 30 September 2026, and net burn in the September quarter averaged ₹2.10 crore a month — 19.5 months at that rate, so no option is existential and none is free. Clause 7.4 binds fourteen of eighteen brand accounts, ₹19.80 crore of ARR. The Nujoom renewal carries a resolution-time commitment and ₹9.20 crore to June 2027. Data-protection obligations apply to any consumer-facing record, which is C's premise.

9. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 2 establish, and what does it not? Name the comparison you would defend to the board and the one you would refuse.
  2. Vikrant reads the June-to-September change as evidence the rewrite worked. Using Exhibit 3, say what measurement would have to exist for that to follow, and what Nepathya should have done in August.
  3. Exhibit 4 and Exhibit 5 point at different concepts. Can the two measures be traded off at all? If not, what should Vidisha do with the one she cannot use?
  4. Rewrite Exhibit 6 so that it could support a decision. What is the correct denominator, and what would make such a ratio mean anything before a build?
  5. Vallari argues that B is not weak but unsayable. Is that difficulty evidence about the idea, the team, or the buyer? What would distinguish the three, and could Nepathya test it in ten weeks?
  6. It is Monday morning, 19 October. What goes in the pre-read, what decision rule does Vidisha commit to in writing, and what does she say to Vasumitra when he asks what she has agreed to stop doing — in about three sentences?

10. Sunday night

At a quarter to eleven Vidisha turned the three cards face down and wrote the pitches out from memory. Parts Promise took two sentences. Service Wallet took two. One Visit took four, and the third was about the parts taxonomy; she crossed it out, tried again, and it came back. She thought about Vijayan Chemburkar asking for the clock to stop running twice, and about Viveka's line that the only defensible claim was that A was not behind. She opened a blank document, typed "Recommendation:", and looked at it. Outside, the road had thinned to nothing. The pre-read was due at nine.

Eeram Trade: Which Kind of MVP?

A decision case on choosing a minimum viable product to fit one assumption and one budget

1. Opening

On Monday, 12 October 2026, Madhavi Venkataraman sat in a corner of Eeram Trade's Guindy office in Chennai with two sheets of paper and a deadline. The first sheet was a build estimate of ₹55 lakh for a feature called Reorder List. The second was a calendar. Diwali fell on Sunday, 8 November, and the three weeks before it were when Tamil Nadu and Telangana kirana owners stocked up hardest. The leadership committee would meet on Friday, 16 October, and Madhavi, the company's head of product, had to tell it what kind of test to run, starting Monday, 19 October.

What she owed the committee was a choice about how to learn: build the feature, or find out first whether anyone wanted it.

2. Company background

Eeram Trade supplies packaged groceries, edible oils, staples and household goods to small neighbourhood stores in Tamil Nadu and Telangana. It was founded in 2019 in Chennai and today serves 14,200 active kirana stores, those that placed at least one order in the past 60 days, through 310 field representatives and a mobile app. Annual sales are about ₹420 crore. Eeram competes with Udaan and Jumbotail on price and range, and with Flipkart Wholesale and JioMart's kirana programme on reach. Its edge is local: Tamil-language support, credit terms set by field staff who know the shopkeeper, and payment through UPI.

Growth had slowed. Order frequency per store had been flat for three quarters, at roughly one order every nine days.

3. The situation

Murali Vaitheeswaran, the chief executive, had an idea in August. Field staff reported that the commonest call from a shopkeeper began, "What am I short of?" A weekly WhatsApp message, listing the fast-moving items a store was likely to run out of and letting the owner reorder with one tap, might raise order frequency and justify a ₹299 monthly subscription. He called it Reorder List.

The company's telephone team asked 220 active kirana owners about it in August and September. Every percentage in Exhibit 1 uses all 220 as its base. Seventy per cent said they ran out of at least one fast-moving item every week, and 60.9 per cent said they would use such a list. Only 21.4 per cent said they would pay ₹299 a month, and just 8.6 per cent had ever paid for any software or subscription. Madhavi read the gap between 60.9 and 21.4 as the real finding. Interest was cheap; payment was not.

The team was dispersed. Manikandan Vijayaraghavan, the data scientist in Toronto, worked nine and a half hours behind Chennai. He believed a reliable stock-out prediction needed eight months of order history per store, and for many stores Eeram had less. Mohana Vadlamudi, who ran field sales from Hyderabad, was worried in a different direction: a badly timed list might arrive just as her representatives were negotiating credit, and the shopkeeper would trust the phone over the person.

4. The people

Madhavi Venkataraman, head of product, Chennai, owns the recommendation. She wants a test whose result she can defend whichever way it falls.

Murali Vaitheeswaran, chief executive, Chennai, wants Reorder List in stores' hands for the festive season. He says speed matters more than polish and has already told investors about it.

Mohana Vadlamudi, head of field sales, Hyderabad, wants nothing that undermines her representatives' relationships. She would welcome any test that uses their knowledge.

Manikandan Vijayaraghavan, data scientist, Toronto, wants to avoid shipping predictions that are wrong for stores with thin history.

5. Exhibits and the economics

Exhibit 2 sets out the three courses of action Madhavi was weighing. Exhibit 3 shows what the ₹55 lakh build would have to earn.

The engineering estimate for a build was 14 weeks. Starting on 19 October, it would finish in the week of 18 January 2027, with results by 25 January, well after Diwali. The other two options could produce evidence while the festive season was still running.

Exhibit 2. The three options. Costs are Eeram's internal estimates; dates assume a start on Monday, 19 October 2026.

Madhavi read Exhibit 3 carefully. If every survey respondent who said yes actually paid, the build comfortably repaid itself. If half did, it fell 16 stores short of break-even, and it took no account of the uplift in orders that was the real commercial prize. The numbers did not say the feature was a bad idea. They said it was a bet whose outcome nobody yet knew.

6. The options

Option A, a smoke test. Eeram would advertise Reorder List on WhatsApp and Facebook to roughly 5,000 stores and ask owners to pre-book three months at ₹99 a month through UPI. Nothing would be built. The upside is speed and price: ₹6 lakh covers advertising, a landing page and analysis, and results arrive on 6 November. The price is also a mismatch: ₹99 is not the ₹299 on which the survey and Exhibit 3 rest, so even a strong result would not validate willingness to pay ₹299. The cost is what it cannot tell her. A click or a pre-booking says the offer sounded good. It says nothing about whether the list itself would be right, or whether a shopkeeper would use it in week five.

Option B, a concierge test. Two category associates would prepare each store's reorder list by hand from its order history, send it on WhatsApp every Monday, and take any resulting order. Forty stores would take part for six weeks, and from week two each owner would be asked to prepay ₹299. At ₹14 lakh, or ₹35,000 per store, it is the dearest way to learn per store tested. The upside is that it tests demand, accuracy and payment together, with real behaviour. The cost is that it does not scale, and Murali would have to go back to investors with a finding rather than a feature.

Option C, a single-feature build. Engineers in Bengaluru and Pune would build automated lists inside the app, with Manikandan's model behind them. If it works, Eeram has a product on the day it learns, not a decision to build one. The upside is a real asset. The cost is ₹55 lakh and fourteen weeks, and a launch that misses Diwali and tests every assumption at once.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 establish, and what does it leave unknown? Which of the four bars would you trust to predict behaviour, and why?
  2. Name the assumption that, if false, would kill Reorder List. How does each option in Exhibit 2 test that assumption, and which does so most directly for its cost?
  3. Using Exhibit 3, what share of stores must pay for the build to be justified? What result from a test would give Madhavi confidence that this share is reachable?
  4. What decision rule, set before the test starts, would you give the committee? What would you do if the result fell between "proceed" and "stop"?

8. A note for the learner

This topic frames an MVP as a learning vehicle with a decision rule, not a small product. The question is never "what is the least we can build?" It is "which assumption could end this idea, and what is the cheapest honest way to test it?" Types of MVP are different ways of being minimal, and each one tests different things.

A smoke test measures stated interest at a price, before a product exists. A concierge test delivers the service by hand and tests whether the value is real. A single-feature build tests delivery at scale. A pre-order, as in Option A, is a stronger signal than a survey answer because money has moved, but its weakness here is that it is still a promise about a product nobody has seen working.

One defensible path is Option B, with the sample and the rule fixed in advance. Take 40 stores, ten each from Chennai, Coimbatore, Hyderabad and Warangal, mixing high-frequency and low-frequency buyers, so that Mohana's representatives help select them and Manikandan sees which stores have thin history. Proceed to build if at least 16 of 40 stores (40 per cent) prepay ₹299 and at least half of the lists sent in weeks four to six produce an order within 24 hours. Stop if fewer than 8 stores (20 per cent) prepay.

The 40 per cent bar has a reason. Even if real conversion across all 14,200 stores were half of that, 20 per cent would still exceed the 10.8 per cent break-even in Exhibit 3. This assumes a one-month prepay converts to a year's subscription, and that fees alone, before WhatsApp, support and running costs, are a fair yardstick; both are simplifications. Results between 20 and 40 per cent should trigger a second, cheaper test, such as a price change, rather than a build.

The path has flaws, and a good answer names them. Diwali falls in week three and inflates ordering, so weeks four to six are the clean read. The 40 stores are chosen with the reps' help and agree to take part, so they are likelier to engage than average. And Option A is not wrong, only insufficient: a stronger answer might add a small smoke test later, to learn price sensitivity among the stores that were not in the pilot.

Ghadiyal Technologies: Ninety Days of Evidence

Pune, Tiruppur, Bengaluru, Toronto, Berlin, Singapore, New Jersey, Dubai · November 2026

1. The night before

On the evening of Sunday, 22 November 2026, Nithya Yelamanchili sat in the empty third-floor office of Ghadiyal Technologies Private Limited in Pune with three printouts and a board call at half past nine next morning. The investors wanted one line: which experiment Ghadiyal would run over the next ninety days, at what cost, and what it would know at the end that it did not know now.

The product did not exist. For seven years Ghadiyal had sold machine-uptime monitoring to Indian textile mills one way only: clamping a retrofit vibration sensor, the GY-2, onto spinning frames and knitting machines and streaming the readings to a dashboard. Ghadiyal Lite abandoned the sensor. Modern machines logged their own stoppages through their controllers; the mill's MIS recorded shift output. If those streams carried enough signal, Ghadiyal could predict a breakdown with no hardware in the shed, at a price mills that had never bought from it might pay.

Nandakumar Yemineni, the chief executive, had asked for something narrower than a plan. "Pick the cheapest honest test," he had said on Friday. Nithya had spent the weekend finding that honest did most of the work in that sentence, and that the five tests before her tested different things.

2. How Ghadiyal came to be shaped this way

Ghadiyal was founded in 2019 by Nandakumar, eleven years a commissioning engineer on ring-spinning frames, and Neelesh Yendluri, formerly of a Bengaluru telematics firm; the first customers were three Ichalkaranji mills that had lost a monsoon to spindle-drive failures.

One decision from that period still ran the company. On Tuesday, 14 March 2023, to hold the sensor's landed cost down, Nandakumar signed a five-year agreement with Gumti Microsystems in Pune: a take-or-pay minimum of 6,000 GY-2 modules a year at ₹1,850, or ₹1.11 crore a year, to 31 March 2028. Sales simultaneously began offering three-year prepaid contracts bundling sensors, since prepayment funded the modules. Both choices bought Ghadiyal its growth; both now press against Ghadiyal Lite.

In the year ended 31 March 2026 Ghadiyal served 268 mills and monitored 9,380 machines — 35 a mill — at ₹650 a machine a month. Subscription revenue was 9,380 × ₹650 × 12 = ₹7,31,64,000 (₹7.32 crore); hardware added 4,100 modules at ₹9,950 = ₹4,07,95,000 (₹4.08 crore); total ₹11,39,59,000 (₹11.40 crore). Having bought 6,000 modules and sold 4,100, Ghadiyal put 1,900 into stock; with 3,500 more received since and 1,560 shipped, Chinchwad held 5,240 on 31 October 2026, at 5,240 × ₹1,850 = ₹96.94 lakh.

The prepaid book was sharper. Forty-one mills, 2,980 machines, prepaid at ₹650: 2,980 × ₹650 × 12 = ₹2,32,44,000, or ₹2.32 crore — ₹2,32,44,000 ÷ ₹7,31,64,000 = 31.8 per cent of subscription revenue. Publish a ₹310 price those mills could use and each has a conversation to open.

3. The industry around the shed floor

India's spinning and knitting capacity sits in dense clusters — Tiruppur, Coimbatore, Erode, Surat, Ichalkaranji, Solapur, Ludhiana — mostly partnership firms running twenty to four hundred machines. The machines come from Lakshmi Machine Works, Rieter and Trützschler, and newer ones log their own stoppage reasons. CODISSIA, SIEMA and the Tiruppur Exporters' Association run the exhibitions where mill owners buy; ATUFS and the PM MITRA parks shape when they re-equip.

Two outside forces pressed. Exporters were losing price-sensitive programmes to Bangladesh and Vietnam, making delivery reliability, not cost alone, what buyers interrogated; and European and American buyers, under their own due-diligence regimes, wanted data on their suppliers' factories. Hence the letter from Gomedh Apparel Sourcing FZE, a Dubai buying house placing roughly ₹900 crore of Indian knitwear a year for European retailers. Pulling the other way, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governed anything in those logs identifying a supervisor or operator, and the exports were full of operator identifiers.

Ghadiyal's exposure ran through its payroll as much as its market. Of 68 employees, 31 sat in Pune, 19 in the Bengaluru platform team, 12 were field engineers in the clusters and 6 abroad. A Toronto salary was roughly 5.4 times a Pune one, so any experiment needing overnight effort burned the costliest hours (Figure A).

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Exhibit 1 lays out the year. In February 2026 Nagendra Yuvarajan circulated a slide, built from machine-maker brochures and a count of installed models, asserting that about 70 per cent of target mills had machines whose controllers could export stoppage logs. Nobody disputed it; it entered the business case and stayed.

In June a Coimbatore firm surveyed 212 mills (Exhibit 5). In July a concierge pilot opened: twelve mills were asked for monthly log dumps, nine agreed, and Nainika Yegnanarayanan's team in Toronto analysed them by hand, alerting over WhatsApp (Exhibit 3). In August, chasing missing files, field engineers audited 1,480 machines across 46 surveyed mills and found 562 — 562 ÷ 1,480 = 38.0 per cent — able to export a usable stoppage log; of those 562, only 194 had a network path out of the shed, which is 194 ÷ 562 = 34.5 per cent of eligible machines and 194 ÷ 1,480 = 13.1 per cent of all audited.

Nainika wrote a paragraph nobody forwarded to the board. "The February slide counted mills; the August audit counted machines. A mill with one eligible machine in ninety counts as a mill with exportable logs. Not the same measurement, and 70 did not fall to 38. The audit says the per-machine denominator we price against is far smaller than assumed — a different and worse problem."

In September came a landing-page smoke test with a pre-order attached (Exhibit 2), timed around a knitwear machinery exhibition at the CODISSIA Trade Fair Complex, Coimbatore, Friday 18 to Monday 21 September 2026. Ninety-seven mills paid a ₹25,000 refundable deposit. Nagendra called it the strongest demand signal in Ghadiyal's history; Exhibit 6 draws it three ways.

Two things have since complicated that reading. First, 61 of the 97 depositors were already GY-2 customers, leaving 36 new mills. Second, when the pilot closed on Saturday, 31 October 2026 it emerged that six of the nine pilot mills had GY-2 sensors fitted, and that Toronto had used those sensor streams because the controller files were late or malformed: of 153 alerts, 128 came from those six and 25 from the three sensor-free mills. The test meant to validate a sensor-free product had, for 128 of its 153 alerts, validated the sensor. On Monday, 9 November 2026 counsel added that the dumps carried operator identifiers, collected without the notices the Act requires.

5. The people

Nithya Yelamanchili, vice-president of product, Pune, owns the recommendation. Her appointment letter sets a target of 500 new mills by March 2028, which the sensor channel cannot deliver. She has not said she thinks the pilot contaminated beyond repair, or that re-running it would cost the ninety days.

Nandakumar Yemineni, co-founder and chief executive, Pune, signed the Gumti take-or-pay and must explain the ₹96.94 lakh of modules in Chinchwad. He argues for "whatever gets a number by March", not saying that Gavaksh Capital's term sheet is conditioned on a non-hardware motion.

Neelesh Yendluri, co-founder and chief technology officer, Bengaluru, wants the single-feature build, arguing anything else produces throwaway code. Unstated: two of his five senior platform engineers have said privately they will leave if the manual pulls continue.

Nainika Yegnanarayanan, lead data scientist, Toronto, has read every log file. She says the sensor-free signal is untested at scale and only a Wizard-of-Oz run on thirty mills tests value and feasibility together. She has not said it means a quarter of night shifts, or that she holds a Montreal offer.

Neerja Yadlapalli, design lead, Berlin, built the landing page and deposit flow in nine days and thinks the team is refusing good news. She has not mentioned that her pricing page called Ghadiyal Lite "available from January", language nobody approved.

Nilesh Yanamadala, customer-success lead, Singapore, carries the 41 prepaid mills and opposes any ₹310 price before March; his bonus rides on that book. He has not said three have already asked for Lite pricing.

Nagendra Yuvarajan, head of sales for North America, New Jersey, brought in Gomedh and wants the pre-order taken, it being the only option that produces cash. He has not disclosed that his plan pays commission on booked value at signature, nor that Gomedh's draft asks for mill-level data Ghadiyal cannot lawfully pass on unconsented.

Nallathambi Yezhumalai, managing partner of a 148-machine Tiruppur knitwear mill, the pilot's keenest participant and a bidder for a Gomedh programme, says the alerts beat the dashboard. He has not said his supervisor, not Ghadiyal, spotted roughly half the stoppages logged as avoided, or that his ₹7.20 lakh took ten minutes.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

"Ninety-seven mills put money on the table for a product that does not exist. Nineteen years in enterprise software and I have never seen it. Conversion is 13.9 per cent. Stop auditing and go build."

Nagendra Yuvarajan, product council call, Friday 13 November 2026

"13.9 per cent of what? Of those who filled a form, 378 of whom we never reached. Nought point seven seven of those who saw the page. Twenty point three five of those we spoke to. I will give the board any of them, but not one of them called the conversion."

Nainika Yegnanarayanan, same call, 23:15 in Toronto

"₹1,055 a machine-month of value against a ₹310 price is three point four times. That is the whole case."

Nandakumar Yemineni, internal note, Monday 16 November 2026

"₹1,055 is what seven supervisors wrote on a form about downtime that did not happen, 104 of the 122 alerts from those seven mills, five of them with sensors. On the two sensor-free mills that replied it is ₹657. And it is lost contribution, not cash: you cannot set it against the ₹797 they spend on maintenance and conclude they will pay from that budget. Different pockets."

Nainika Yegnanarayanan, reply, Tuesday 17 November 2026

"My engineers have pulled CSVs off a shared drive at two in the morning since July. Call it concierge if you like. It is four people doing a cron job's work, and I will not do it on thirty mills."

Neelesh Yendluri, chat thread, Wednesday 18 November 2026

"Three prepaid mills have seen the pricing page. One asks why he pays ₹650 for what you offer at ₹310. I have ₹2.32 crore a year on that book and no answer."

Nilesh Yanamadala, email to Nithya, Thursday 19 November 2026

"Don't take the sensors off. The messages were useful because a person had looked. If a machine sends it, my supervisor will ignore it as he ignores the dashboard."

Nallathambi Yezhumalai, to Nithya in Tiruppur, Friday 20 November 2026

8. The options as Nithya currently sees them

Her note listed the five tests of Exhibit 4 against what each left unknown. A, a smoke test away from any exhibition, would show whether September was an artefact of the fair — but a deposit is intent from a mill whose machines may not be eligible, and she has 97 of those. B, a concierge round on sensor-free mills only, tests what the first round did not, costing three of five field engineers and six weeks. C, the Wizard of Oz, puts a real app before thirty mills with alerts written by hand; Nainika's one design measuring value and feasibility together, at ₹97.10 lakh and a person who may resign. D shows whether mills open an automated digest, which is adoption and not prediction, and yields nothing inside ninety days. E brings cash.

In the margin Nithya had written three queries she could not place. Four options test the mill as buyer; the fifth changes the buyer to a Dubai buying house and sits under the same heading. If 38.0 per cent of machines can export a log and 13.1 per cent have a path out of the shed, what is the addressable machine base, and which of the five measures it? And is a sensor-free product a product, or a cheaper version of what Ghadiyal sells — in which case what is on test is a price, on a book worth Nilesh's ₹2.32 crore.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Cash and bank balances stood at ₹7.42 crore on 31 October 2026. Net burn was ₹54 lakh in August, ₹67 lakh in September and ₹53 lakh in October — ₹174 lakh in all, an average of ₹174 ÷ 3 = ₹58 lakh a month — so ₹742 lakh ÷ ₹58 lakh = 12.8 months of runway from 1 November 2026. The ₹742 lakh includes 97 × ₹25,000 = ₹24.25 lakh of refundable deposits; on ₹717.75 lakh it is ₹717.75 ÷ ₹58 = 12.4 months. But Nivriti Yedida of Gavaksh Capital has made the next round conditional on evidence, at the March 2027 board, that Ghadiyal can acquire mills without selling hardware — so the real deadline is four months out, not twelve.

The Gumti take-or-pay runs to 31 March 2028 at ₹1.11 crore a year whether modules ship or not, with 5,240 in stock; the 41 prepaid contracts cannot be repriced before renewal without a credit note. Gomedh's offer of Friday 6 November 2026 is US$ 240,000 for a twelve-month licence over 34 supplier mills; at ₹88.40 to the dollar that is ₹2,12,16,000, or ₹2.12 crore, half (₹1.06 crore) at signature. It lapses on Tuesday, 15 December 2026. Eleven of the 34 mills are Ghadiyal customers; the other 23 have no contract and no reason to supply data. Counsel's view is due in a fortnight. Three of the five senior field engineers can be released; two cannot. And Nainika's team is one person, ten and a half hours behind Tiruppur.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What assumption is each option in Exhibit 4 testing, and which, if false, most damages Ghadiyal Lite?
  2. Exhibit 2 supports three conversion figures. Which base should the board see, and what of the 378 forms never reached?
  3. Exhibit 3's ₹1,054.59 and Exhibit 5's ₹796.69 a machine-month appear to conflict. Do they? What must be measured for either to bear on the ₹310 price?
  4. Six of the nine pilot mills had sensors fitted. Does that make the concierge result worthless, partly informative, or informative about something other than its target?
  5. Gomedh's ₹2.12 crore covers more than three months of burn. When is a pre-order from a buying house a legitimate test of a product meant for mills, and when a change of company?
  6. It is Monday morning. What will Ghadiyal have learned by the March 2027 board, what decision rule will you state in advance for a pass or a fail, and what will you say when Nivriti Yedida asks what happens if it fails?

At a quarter past eleven Nithya wrote three words on the whiteboard — price, signal, base — drew a box around the third, and sat looking at it. The Gumti invoice schedule was open in one window and Nainika's unforwarded note in another, and she had not decided which the board would mind hearing more.
exp20v2-sol.mvp.types:
MVP types: which kind of experiment fits this assumption and this budget

1. A tiffin start-up with six lakh rupees

On Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Nayana Jorapur, head of product at Zivara Tiffins in Bengaluru, walked into a founders' meeting with a single slide. Zivara planned a subscription service that would deliver home-cooked lunches from neighbourhood cooks to office workers around Whitefield. Milan Jhangiani, the chief executive, had approved a learning budget of ₹6 lakh and eight weeks. Nikita Jagtap, the operations lead, wanted to start by recruiting thirty cooks. The engineering lead wanted to build the app.

Jorapur's slide said neither. It listed five ways to test the idea, from a landing page costing ₹0.60 lakh to a working single-feature app costing ₹5.40 lakh. The stakes were plain. A wrong choice would either burn most of the ₹6 lakh before anyone knew whether a stranger would pay ₹3,000 a month for lunch, or would test the wrong thing cheaply and leave the company confident for no reason. The decision was not whether to build a minimum viable product (MVP) but which kind.

The room was divided along familiar lines. Jhangiani distrusted anything that looked like delay; he had watched a competitor spend a year on cook onboarding before learning that office managers would not allow outside deliveries into their buildings. Jagtap argued that cooks, not customers, were the scarce resource, so supply should be tested first. Jorapur's reply was that both were assumptions, and that the company could afford to test only one at a time. Which one, and by what method, would set the next eight weeks.

2. The idea

An MVP, in the sense Eric Ries popularised from about 2008 in the lean start-up movement, is the smallest thing that can generate real evidence about a specific assumption. It is a learning vehicle with a decision rule attached, not a small product. An MVP type is a way of being minimal: each removes a different part of the finished product while keeping the part that carries the question.

Five types recur. A smoke test is a page or advertisement describing a product that does not exist, measuring whether people respond. A pre-order adds money: customers pay or deposit before anything is built. A concierge test delivers the service by hand, with the customer knowing it is manual. A Wizard of Oz test presents a working-looking interface while people operate it behind the curtain, and the customer does not know. A single-feature MVP really builds one function, and nothing else. The idea is older than the label. Early web entrepreneurs showed products that did not yet exist, and the 2007 explainer video that Dropbox used around 2007–08 to gather a waiting list before shipping is the best-known example of what became a smoke test. Zappos began with photographs of shoes taken in shops and fulfilled orders by hand, a Wizard of Oz in all but name, since shoppers believed they were using an ordinary store. Jorapur's sentence for the meeting was: "Pick the cheapest test whose result could change what we do next."

3. How it works

The mechanics have four steps, and practitioners usually leave the first and last implicit. First, name the riskiest assumption and its type. Desirability asks whether anyone wants this; willingness to pay asks whether they will part with money; deliverability asks whether the company can serve them at an acceptable cost; usability asks whether they can work the product. Second, write the decision rule before the test: a number and the action it triggers. Third, choose the type that removes the most cost while keeping that assumption exposed. Fourth, accept in advance what the result will not tell you.

Applied to Zivara, the steps run as follows. Jorapur named willingness to pay as the riskiest assumption, because she judged that cooks and kitchens could be found by a start-up while customers were the less certain quantity. She wrote the rule down with Jhangiani before any rupee was spent. She rejected the single-feature build, which would test far more than the question needed, and the Wizard of Oz, whose interface question was premature. Only then did she consider what the result could not say: whether the lunches would be good enough to keep subscribers.

Figure 1 shows why the choice matters. The smoke test costs ₹0.60 lakh: ₹0.40 lakh of advertising and ₹0.20 lakh for the page. The pre-order reuses that page and adds ₹0.30 lakh for payment and refund handling, reaching ₹0.90 lakh. Concierge costs about ₹0.56 lakh gross, before ₹36,000 of revenue: a coordinator at ₹30,000 for one four-week month (₹30,000), plus twelve customers receiving twenty lunches each at a food and delivery cost of ₹110 (12 × 20 × 110 = ₹26,400), which totals ₹56,400. Those twelve customers pay ₹150 a lunch (12 × 20 × 150), returning ₹36,000 and leaving a net outlay of ₹20,400. Wizard of Oz costs ₹3.10 lakh and the single-feature build ₹5.40 lakh.

Table 1. What each type tests, and what it cannot
TypeAssumption it exposesWhat it cannot tell you
Smoke testDesirability of the promiseWhether anyone will pay
Pre-orderWillingness to payWhether the product satisfies
ConciergeValue of the outcome, in depthWhether it works at scale
Wizard of OzUsability and behaviour of the interfaceCost of the hidden labour at volume
Single-featureTechnical feasibility and retentionDemand beyond the first feature

4. A worked example, and what moves it

Jorapur's riskiest assumption was willingness to pay, so she chose the pre-order. The page would run for fourteen days, from Monday 12 to Sunday 25 October, offering a ₹500 refundable deposit toward a ₹3,000 monthly plan. Her decision rule rested on economics. A subscriber at ₹3,000 a month with a 25 per cent contribution margin yields ₹750 a month. The company would tolerate a two-month payback, so the ceiling for acquiring one subscriber was 2 × ₹750 = ₹1,500. The rule assumed, generously, that every depositor becomes a subscriber; at any lower rate the true ceiling per depositor is smaller, so a pass is a necessary signal, not a sufficient one.

Table 2. Two passes of the same test. Conversion is deposits divided by visitors (paid clicks), not impressions.
LinePass 1 (planned)Pass 2 (cost per click rises)
Advertising budget₹40,000₹40,000
Cost per click₹20₹25
Visitors (budget ÷ cost per click)2,0001,600
Deposit conversion1.5%1.5%
Deposits (visitors × 1.5%)3024
Cost per deposit (budget ÷ deposits)₹1,333₹1,667
Against the ₹1,500 ceilingProceedStop, or change channel

Pass 1 gave 30 deposits at ₹1,333 each, inside the ceiling. In pass 2 only the click price moved, from ₹20 to ₹25, and the same 1.5 per cent conversion produced 24 deposits at ₹1,667 each, which breaches it. Nothing about customers changed; the channel became dearer. The lesson is that a pre-order measures a product and a channel together, and the decision rule must say which one it is judging.

5. Nuances that separate users from the vocabulary-fluent

Concierge and Wizard of Oz are not synonyms

In a concierge test the customer knows a person is serving them, which makes it the best instrument for learning what the service should be. In Wizard of Oz the customer believes the system is automated, which makes it the right instrument for testing whether the interface works. Choosing one for the other's job produces the wrong evidence.

Interest is not payment

Of the five, the pre-order is the type most directly designed around the customer risking money. A 4 per cent sign-up rate to a free list is a statement about curiosity. Treat it as ranking messages against each other, not as a forecast of revenue.

Fake doors have an ethical edge

A smoke test advertises something unavailable. Keep the claim honest, state that the service is launching soon, and refund every deposit promptly. Indian consumers who feel misled by a deposit page will not return, and the damage to a young brand outlives the experiment.

Hidden labour is a cost, not a trick

A Wizard of Oz test works because humans absorb complexity. At twelve users that costs little; at twelve hundred the labour is the business model. Record the minutes of human effort per transaction during the test, or the result flatters the economics.

A single-feature MVP is the only type that tests whether you can build

It is usually the slowest to build, and teams often reach for it because building feels like progress. Choose it only when the dominant risk is technical or when retention, which needs a real product to observe over weeks, is the question.

Small counts are noisy

Thirty deposits from 2,000 visitors is a reading, not a measurement; a repeat could plausibly land well on either side of it. Set the rule with margin, or run the test a second time before committing the larger sum. A rule that would flip on one additional deposit is not yet a rule.

The type changes the sample

Advertising reaches people who click; concierge reaches people you recruit personally. The second group is friendlier. Never compare a concierge satisfaction score with a smoke-test conversion rate as though both described the market.

What no type can tell you

None reveals whether customers will still be paying in month six, or whether supply can be recruited. For those, only a longer, more real product answers.

6. How the choice shifts by context

Table 3. Where the same five types lean
ContextNatural first typeWhy
ConsumerSmoke test or pre-orderTraffic is cheap to buy and the buyer decides alone.
B2BConciergeFew buyers; a signed pilot letter is the equivalent of a deposit.
MarketplaceConcierge on one side, smoke test on the otherHand-match the scarce side, and measure demand on the abundant one.
Early-stage companyCheapest type that fitsRunway is the constraint.
Large companyWizard of Oz or single-featureBrand risk makes fake pages harder; engineering capacity is cheap.

A large company's constraint is usually reputation and approvals rather than cash, so it tends to climb the ladder faster. A founder with six lakh rupees cannot afford to.

7. Common mistakes

Table 4. Symptoms, causes and cheap diagnostics
SymptomMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
The team debates the result after the testNo decision rule was written firstAsk for the dated document stating the number and action
A 12 per cent sign-up is celebrated, then nothing sellsInterest treated as willingness to payAsk what the customer risked
The prototype takes five monthsType chosen by what the team enjoysAsk which cheaper type could falsify the same assumption
Results swing between runsChannel and product were not separatedRerun with a different channel and compare

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Jorapur's slide would state the assumption (a Whitefield professional pays ₹3,000 a month), the type (pre-order, then concierge), the rule (cost per deposit no higher than ₹1,500), the dates, and the single thing the result cannot tell them. The team would agree, before launch, what each outcome triggers. The experiment would cost under ₹1 lakh and take two weeks. The team would also record who acts on the number and by when.

9. What Jorapur decided

She proposed the pre-order first, at ₹0.90 lakh, and read the result on Tuesday, 27 October. Her fallback was explicit: if cost per deposit exceeded ₹1,500, she would test a different channel before concluding anything, because Table 2 showed that price per click alone could flip the answer. If it passed, she would run the ₹0.56 lakh gross concierge with twelve depositors, four weeks from about 28 October and ending before 1 December, the close of the eight-week window to learn whether lunches satisfied, which no deposit can show. That left more than ₹4.5 lakh unspent and uncommitted (6 − 0.90 − 0.56 = 4.54, gross of concierge revenue), reserved for a Wizard of Oz or single-feature build in a second phase beyond the window, and only if both earlier tests held. Jhangiani accepted this, on one condition: that cook recruitment begin in parallel at a trickle, since a yes would otherwise cost a month.

To go further, study how to scope the MVP once its type is chosen, then how these ideas change for hardware, where a concierge cannot ship a prototype overnight. Two questions to sit with. Which of your own current assumptions is the riskiest, and what type exposes it for the least money? And what result would make you stop, and have you written it down?
exp40v2-sol.mvp.types:
MVP types

Which kind of minimal product fits this assumption and this budget.

1. Two rooms, one day apart

On Thursday, 15 October 2026, Nirmit Jalihal put one table in front of the board of Zanskar Coldchain Systems in Pune. Zanskar made a reusable cellular temperature logger and dashboard for distributors moving insulin and vaccines, cargo that must hold between 2 °C and 8 °C under its principals' Good Distribution Practice audits. Mausami Jhabak, the chief executive, had ring-fenced ₹48 lakh and sixteen weeks before a Series A talk in March 2027.

The arithmetic was the argument. Priced in early September, with the page reused where it could be, the five tests came to ₹49.38 lakh against ₹48 lakh of budget. By the board meeting one rung had been climbed: the smoke test closed on 2 October and its ₹1.80 lakh was spent, leaving ₹46.20 lakh against the ₹47.58 lakh the four remaining rungs would cost — the same ₹1.38 lakh short. Zanskar could not climb the ladder; it had to choose. Jhabak wanted it run again on a second list. Naila Jhurani, the seed investor, wanted a second pre-order round, a deposit being the one signal politeness cannot fake. Nabendu Jadwet, who owned the hardware, wanted to build.

In April and May 2026 Zanskar ran exactly the pre-order Jhurani now wanted: eleven distributors paid a refundable ₹25,000 each, ₹2,75,000 in all, for twenty loggers apiece. Zanskar read that as demand and built 120 units. Four took their twenty; seven asked for refunds. Forty units, ₹1,56,000 at ₹3,900 each, sat in a cupboard.

On Friday, 16 October 2026, Mandira Jatkar faced the mirror image at Zehen Credit Systems in Bengaluru. Zehen's product read a borrower's bank statements, GST returns and tax filings and drafted the credit memo an NBFC officer signs before approving an unsecured business loan. From 17 August to 25 September 2026 it ran a pilot that was in fact a Wizard of Oz: four design-partner NBFCs sent applications into an interface that looked automated, and four analysts wrote every memo by hand behind it. Mukesh Jogani, the chief executive, wanted to show investors 62.5 per cent; the largest partner's credit head read the same test as 53.1 per cent. With ₹94.5 lakh left of the ₹107 lakh it held before the pilot, at ₹13.5 lakh a month, the gap between those numbers was the company.

2. The idea, and the four camps that disagree

A minimum viable product is the smallest artefact that can produce evidence capable of changing a decision. An MVP type is a choice about which part of the finished product to remove while keeping the part that carries the question. Five recur. A smoke test advertises a product that does not exist and counts the response. A pre-order adds money. A concierge delivers the outcome by hand, openly; a Wizard of Oz behind an automated-looking surface, unknown to the customer. A single-feature MVP builds one function.

The lineage is older than the lean-start-up vocabulary suggests. Wizard of Oz comes from human-factors research, the canonical study being Gould, Conti and Hovanyecz's 1983 "listening typewriter" experiment, where a human typist sat next door. The term MVP is traced to Frank Robinson's practice around 2001; Steve Blank gave it a process and Eric Ries's writing from about 2008 its moral force.

Four camps disagree substantively. Validated learning will sign "a build that cannot change a decision is waste" and not "ship the smallest sellable thing". Demand-first will sign "work by hand until it hurts, and charge for it" and not "a landing-page rate forecasts revenue". The craft camp will sign "the quality floor is part of the hypothesis" and not "a fake door is free". The decision-analytic camp will sign "take the highest value of information net of cost" and not "those probabilities are knowable to one decimal place".

3. Mechanics: pricing a test against the cost of being wrong

Expert practice runs in five steps, the first and last usually implicit. Name the assumption and its failure cost — not its probability, its cost. Write the decision rule, with a number, an action and a date. Price each type, and choose. Then write down what the test cannot tell you, before it runs. Zanskar's failure cost is concrete: the full product means ₹22 lakh of tooling, ₹9 lakh of certification and firmware, nine months of an eight-person team at ₹8 lakh a month — ₹72 lakh — and ₹17 lakh of inventory: ₹120 lakh in all.

Table 1. The five candidates as priced in early September. The pre-order reuses the smoke test's page and advertising, so it adds ₹0.70 lakh; alone it costs ₹2.50 lakh. That rung is now climbed; its ₹1.80 lakh is sunk.

Pricing is the easy half. The formal treatment is the expected value of information: for a test t, V(t) = p(t) × L − C(t), where L is the failure cost avoided (₹120 lakh), C the stand-alone cost, and p the elicited probability that the result changes what gets built. The elicitation is the step that gets skipped and the one open to argument; Jalihal ran it with the three board members separately and took the median.

Two second-order effects follow, neither in the formula. First, the ₹0.20 lakh gap between the Wizard of Oz and the build sits inside the rounding of the board's own guesses: raise Jadwet's p from 0.60 to 0.61 and the build wins, since 0.61 × 120 − 30.04 = ₹43.16 lakh. The formalism localises the disagreement rather than settling it. Second, it ignores what a test does to the world: a Wizard of Oz creates a transcript that, for an AI product, is a training set, and a concierge creates the habit of working by hand.

The step most often skipped is the power calculation. Zanskar's smoke test went out on Monday, 21 September 2026 and closed on Friday, 2 October. To tell a quote-request rate of 1.5 per cent from one of 3.0 per cent at 80 per cent power and 5 per cent two-sided, the approximation is n ≈ 16 × p̄(1 − p̄) ÷ δ², with p̄ = 0.0225 and δ = 0.015: 16 × 0.0225 × 0.9775 ÷ 0.000225 = 0.35190 ÷ 0.000225 = 1,564 per arm, 3,128 in all. The reachable universe was 1,200 delivered emails — one arm larger than the market.

Jalihal corrected him: 220 addresses were never reached, so the meaningful rate is 18 over 1,200, which is 1.5 per cent. Thirteen of the eighteen enquiries volunteered that a principal's audit was why they asked: the test had found, by accident, a specifier Zanskar had never met.

4. The conditions, stated as claims that can fail

Table 4. Five conditions for the right instrument, applied to both. Row one is not like-for-like: Zanskar's failure cost is the ₹120 lakh build a test avoids, Zehen's the cash at risk.
ConditionZanskarZehen
Failure cost ≥ ten times the testPasses for Wizard of Oz: 120 ÷ 11.84 = 10.1Fails either way: 107 ÷ 12.50 = 8.6 pre-pilot, 94.5 ÷ 12.50 = 7.6 after
The outcomes lead to different actionsFailed in April: no stop rulePasses: a 24-minute kill threshold

The minimal version keeps the mechanismFails: a keyed sheet is no audit recordHolds for the memo, fails for the model

Two situations make the framework actively misleading. Where value lives in the tail rather than the median — medicine, payments, safety — a concierge proves the ordinary case and conceals the rare one. And where the technology risk is the product, as at Zehen, every type but the build avoids the unknown that matters.

5. Hard edges, and the organisational seam

A multi-product company cannot run a fake door on a surface paying customers log into; the cost is a withdrawal from a trust account. Mature firms handle this with unpublished rules: fake doors on acquisition surfaces only, a sunset date in every ticket, pre-approved refund language. In two-sided businesses neither side's response means anything alone, so hand-build the scarce side.

Regulation changes the type, not merely the paperwork. A dashboard fed by keyed-in readings can test whether an alert at 8.4 °C changes a depot's behaviour, but it can never be the audited record, which must be tamper-evident and machine-generated. At Zehen the human in the loop is no trick to be removed later: in regulated lending the officer of record signs, so assisting rather than deciding is permanent. Hardware deforms the ladder differently, its costs lumpy. Neither the ₹22 lakh of tooling nor the ₹9 lakh of certification and firmware can be bought in tenths, and Table 1 shows the consequence: the single-feature rung pays the ₹9 lakh, defers the tooling, and no rung reaches the ₹22 lakh at all. AI-native products deform it again — the Wizard of Oz is at once test, training-data factory and trap.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

Failure cost, not likelihood

Competent practitioners rank assumptions by how likely they are to be wrong; experts rank them by what being wrong costs. An assumption 90 per cent safe but costing ₹120 lakh deserves more instrumentation than a coin-flip costing ₹4 lakh. The tell is a grid with confidence on one axis and no money on either.

Who knows changes the bias you buy

A customer who knows a human is serving them forgives, explains and coaches, making concierge the instrument for discovering what the service should be, not for measuring unattended use. One who thinks it automated behaves honestly and tolerates little. The tell is a team that cannot say what the customer believes.

A Wizard of Oz hides the profit and loss

Hidden labour is not a cost of the experiment but a preview of the cost structure. Experts instrument minutes per transaction per step, so each step becomes a separately priced automation target. The tell is a pilot report rich in satisfaction scores and silent on minutes.

A pre-order's denominator is recruitment

Zanskar's eleven deposits looked like a market and were a social network: nine came through Jhurani's introductions and Jhabak's former colleagues. A rate over a recruited sample describes the recruiter, so experts log each respondent's introduction path. The tell is a funnel with no provenance column.

The signer is not the specifier

Thirteen of Zanskar's eighteen enquiries pointed at the principal's audit. The distributor holds the budget; the pharmaceutical company whose products it carries writes the specification. An MVP aimed at the budget-holder measures willingness to pay for something that buyer may not choose. The tell is a plan that never names the signer.

Smoke tests compare; they do not measure levels

A smoke test is a good relative instrument — this promise beats that one — and a weak absolute one, the level depending on channel, week and creative. Experts run two arms and quote the difference, or one arm and quote only presence or absence. The tell is a single-arm level read as a forecast rather than as evidence that anyone answered at all.

The unit of analysis is not what you counted

Zehen processed 544 applications, a comfortable-sounding sample. They arrived in four clusters, one per NBFC, each with its own credit policy and definition of a material edit. The effective sample is nearer four than 544. The tell is an interval over transactions when institutions decide.

Do not count a shared asset twice

Zanskar's pre-order reuses the smoke test's page and advertising: run after it, it adds ₹0.70 lakh, not ₹2.50 lakh. Teams double-count shared assets, then overstate the gap between a plan and its budget. The tell is a budget whose rungs sum to more than was bought.

7. Where product type and stage genuinely change the answer

Table 5. Where the five types lean, by product type.
ContextFirst instrumentWhy, and the catch
Consumer softwareSmoke test, then single-featurePurchased traffic is not demand
B2B and enterpriseConcierge, then a paid pilotA letter of intent is the deposit
Platform and marketplaceConcierge the scarce sideNeither side means anything alone
Hardware and physical goodsPre-order, then single-featureDefers tooling; ignores durability
AI-nativeWizard of Oz, instrumented per stepGives a training set; hides automation rate

Stage changes the constraint rather than the logic. A seed-stage company is rationed by cash, so it buys the cheapest test that could stop it; a listed incumbent by approvals and brand risk, whose MVPs are often scoped-down first versions with the rule written afterwards. What does not change: the rule precedes the test, the denominator precedes the numerator, and only a type that ships yields retention evidence.

8. Three worked cases, one a failure

The first is the smoke test in Table 3: ₹1.80 lakh, 18 enquiries over 1,200 delivered emails, underpowered for its stated question. It earned its money because 13 of the 18 pointed at the principal — a test that fails its stated purpose and redirects the company is a good one.

The second is Zehen's Wizard of Oz, which cost ₹12.50 lakh: ₹3.90 lakh of analyst time (six analyst-months at ₹65,000), ₹7.20 lakh of interface build, ₹1.40 lakh of partner legal and security review. Of the 544 applications it processed, 340 memos were accepted without material edit — 340 of 544 is 62.5 per cent. But 96 of the 640 received were returned as outside the pilot's segment, and those were the hardest files; against all 640, the same 340 is 53.1 per cent. As a labour measurement it gave a cleaner number: the four analysts averaged 45 minutes per memo, every step logged by Nishtha Jhavar's pod.

Table 6. Monthly economics at an assumed production volume of 3,200 memos. One analyst supplies 160 hours, or 9,600 minutes, so analysts = 3,200 × minutes ÷ 9,600 = minutes ÷ 3, at ₹65,000 each; revenue is 3,200 × ₹180 = ₹5.76 lakh.

The rows recompute from that rule. At 45 minutes, 45 ÷ 3 = 15 analysts at ₹65,000 is ₹9.75 lakh against ₹5.76 lakh of revenue, short by ₹3.99 lakh a month. Automating the dark segments leaves 28 minutes, 9.33 analysts, ten in practice, ₹6.50 lakh — still ₹0.74 lakh short. Break-even is where (minutes ÷ 3) × ₹65,000 equals ₹5.76 lakh, that is 26.6 minutes on continuous labour and 24 on whole analysts, so the 45 must fall by at least 40.9 per cent merely to stop losing money.

The third case is the April pre-order, which failed for a reason no experimental hygiene would catch. Eleven deposits, ₹2,75,000, 120 units built, four deliveries, seven refunds, ₹1,56,000 of stranded inventory, eleven weeks gone. The instrument was right: pre-orders test willingness to pay. The error was measuring it on a party who does not control the specification, from a sample nine-elevenths recruited through the company's own network. The recovery was a concierge with the principal's quality head present.

9. Failure modes and their early signs

Table 7. What goes wrong, and what late detection costs.

Each defect is in the test's design, not its execution, cheapest to find in the hour before launch.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether fake doors are legitimate. The case for them is that demand information is close to a public good: an honest launching-soon page with prompt refunds prevents the greater waste of building for a market that does not exist. The case against is market-specific: in a market of 1,420 distributors who meet at the same trade events, a vendor advertising a logger it cannot ship acquires a reputation before a customer. They differ about market thickness — the demand-first camp is wrong if willingness to engage falls measurably in thin markets, the sceptics wrong if it does not.

Whether a deposit predicts revenue. Jhurani holds the strongest form of the demand-first view: everything except money is politeness, and a refundable deposit is the cheapest contract a stranger will sign. The decision-analytic reply is that a deposit's informativeness depends on whether respondents came from a channel you can buy again at a price the business can carry. She is wrong if a paid-channel cohort converts materially lower, right if it converts the same — and Zanskar never ran that comparison.

Whether AI products should prove the workflow before the model. One camp holds the Wizard of Oz mandatory first, because the human transcript is at once specification and training data, and no model is worth building for a workflow nobody wants. The other holds this backwards: the test proves the outcome valuable while hiding the unknown that can kill you, and the firm finds the automation ceiling after hiring the operations team. Without the pilot nobody would know how the 45 minutes decompose; equally, it cost ₹12.50 lakh against the ₹107 lakh of cash at risk before it ran, a ratio of 8.6 — below the bar Jatkar applies to everyone else, as is the 7.6 on the ₹94.5 lakh left. That camp is wrong if capability closes the residual 28 minutes inside a pilot's window.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this can name the five types; someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They state the denominator before the numerator. They price the test against the cost of being wrong rather than against the budget. Before the test runs they circulate one document holding the number that proceeds, the number that stops, the date and the test's blind spot. And they refuse to run a test whose outcomes lead to the same action.

12. What each of them decided

Jalihal's recommendation on 15 October spent nothing more on smoke tests and skipped the pre-order, the two Figure 2 ranked lowest. He proposed the ₹5.00 lakh concierge in two depots of one principal, with that principal's quality head present, because the April failure showed the specifier absent from every earlier test. Conditional on the quality head signing a specification letter by 30 November 2026, Zanskar would spend ₹11.84 lakh on the Wizard of Oz to learn what alert latency a depot tolerates. That leaves ₹29.36 lakh of the ₹46.20 lakh — ₹0.68 lakh short of the ₹30.04 lakh build, which is what the sunk ₹1.80 lakh costs him. Absent the letter it stops.

Jatkar's decision on 16 October was to end the Wizard of Oz and restart the service as a declared concierge — openly human, at ₹180 a memo, for two of the four partners — while engineering built only the statement parser. Her kill rule was the 24-minute line, to be met by 31 January 2027: below it the product is a business, above it Zehen sells the parser. Jogani dropped the single-denominator slide.

  1. Zanskar's Wizard of Oz ranks ₹0.20 lakh above the build, inside the precision behind it. What should a board do with an analysis that cannot separate its top two options?
  2. Jatkar's pilot fails her own ten-times bar, at 8.6 on the cash at risk before it ran. Was running it a mistake, or does the training data belong in the numerator?
  3. If the principal specifies the logger, every number here was measured on the wrong population. What cheaper test would have shown that in April?

13. Going deeper

  • What an MVP is — the definition these five vary.
  • Concierge and Wizard of Oz tests — the pair turning on belief.
  • Landing-page and smoke tests — the pre-product instrument and its power limit.
  • Scoping the MVP — how much of the type to build.
  • MVPs for hardware and physical products — why lumpy costs reshape it.
  • Writing a solution hypothesis — what a type is chosen against.
  • Ideation: brainstorming, Crazy 8s, HMW — where candidates begin.
  • Concept and elevator pitch — what a smoke test tests.
  • Value Proposition Canvas — the job the minimum must do.
  • Value proposition statement — what a pre-order charges for.
  • Storyboarding — no build, and first to expose a missing specifier.

Dravya Retail Systems: Scoping Project Deepam

A case for class discussion. Dravya, Durrah, Dharohar, Devaraya and Deevena are fictional; the regulators, institutions and market participants named as context are real.

1. The night before

At twenty minutes to eleven on Sunday, 11 October 2026, Latha Tadepalli was at her dining table in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with four slides open and a fifth deleted twice. The board call was at nine next morning: half past five in Berlin, half past eleven on Sunday night in New Jersey and Toronto, half past seven in Dubai, half past eleven in Singapore. Dravya Retail Systems had 172 uncommitted engineer-weeks in the November release train — nearly sixteen engineers for its eleven weeks — and a product called Deepam that four people described four ways.

Latha had been Director of Product for nineteen months, and Deepam was hers. The title slide read: a valuation engine for old gold at the counter — transparent, consistent, logged. In notes she would not show sat the question she could not answer: what is the one thing we do not know, and what is the smallest thing that would tell us?

What made the night long was not that answers were missing. There were four, each resting on a number somebody trusted, and at least two could not both mean what their owners said.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Dravya was founded in Bengaluru in 2016 by Laxmikant Tummala, who had spent eleven years selling billing systems to family jewellers in Chennai, Coimbatore and Vijayawada. Its flagship, Dravya Counter, runs jewellery retail: karat-wise valuation, making-charge rules, BIS hallmarking identifiers, GST invoicing and the eleven-month savings-plan ledgers.

In February 2022 Dravya made the decision that governs everything on Latha's slides. Customers had refused to put stock data in a public cloud; a jeweller's inventory, owners said, is the most private thing about the business. Dravya chose a Windows-based on-premises architecture with a quarterly release train. It won the accounts, taking Dravya from 31 stores to 559, and cost two things it now needs. Cadence: scope freezes eleven weeks before a train reaches stores. And sight: telemetry exists only for stores on the optional 2024 connected build, which are not a random sample (Exhibit 1).

In March 2024 Dravya's Series B raised ₹88 crore led by Dharohar Capital, ₹44 crore of it primary; the CFO, Lalima Tirumalasetty, reckons ₹26 crore went into the connected build and the Gulf office. In May 2025 Dravya signed a five-year exclusive Gulf reseller agreement with Durrah Jewellery Group, a 26-store chain off the Deira gold souk. Clause 7.4 obliges delivery of any new module to Durrah within 90 days of Indian general availability, at no licence fee for twelve months. The 2025 board pack called it a distribution win.

3. The industry

Indian jewellery retail is consolidating without becoming concentrated. Tanishq, Kalyan Jewellers, Malabar Gold & Diamonds and Joyalukkas compete with tens of thousands of single-store family jewellers holding much of the market by value. Mandatory BIS hallmarking with HUID identifiers pushed record-keeping into software. Section 269ST caps cash receipts at ₹2 lakh, PAN is collected above that, and full KYC above ₹10 lakh under the anti-money-laundering rules for precious-metal dealers. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 makes the identity documents on 559 Windows machines a liability that did not exist in 2022.

Old gold is the industry's quiet engine. On Friday, 9 October 2026 the 22-carat quote in Chennai was ₹1,08,400 per 10 grams, and at that level many purchases are part-funded by jewellery the customer already owns. The valuation belongs to an appraiser: a touchstone or an XRF gun, a scale, a deduction for solder and stones, a negotiation. He is the most trusted and least documented person in the store. In the Gulf, Durrah works under UAE VAT at 5 per cent and Dubai Central Laboratory hallmarking, in Arabic and English.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Deepam was scoped in January 2026 on one premise: old-gold exchange is slow, slowness costs sales on festival weekends, and a rules engine would compress it. Field notes from Devaraya Jewellers, a 34-store chain in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, put a counter exchange at twenty to forty-five minutes. In April 2026 a thin version shipped — the Exchange Slip, a printable valuation breakup, in 23 stores with the connected build. Nobody designed a stopping rule for it.

Between Monday, 3 August and Sunday, 13 September 2026 two analysts observed nine stores in Chennai, Coimbatore, Vijayawada and Pune, recording 1,164 counter transactions. Of those, 412 involved an old-gold exchange, or 35.4 per cent, and in 318 of the 412 the appraiser's working was legible enough to re-value against Deepam's rules (Exhibit 2). The study broke the January premise: an exchange averaged 34 minutes — 9 on assay and valuation, 12 on KYC and documentation, 13 on discussion with the customer and the family who had come along. Deepam addresses the 9 minutes.

The study also produced the number that split the company. Re-valued against the engine, 131 of the 318 recorded exchanges — 41.2 per cent — would have paid the customer more than the appraiser did, by more than 2 per cent of the metal's gross value. Across all 318 the engine would have paid ₹8.4 lakh more on ₹486.0 lakh of gross value, or 1.73 per cent — set against what one sale earns a store in Exhibit 3.

On Saturday, 19 September Luv Thotakura demonstrated Deepam at the Chennai user meet, collecting 38 responses (Exhibit 5). On Wednesday, 23 September Lithika Thirumalai pulled the first extract of Exchange Slip telemetry, for 1 April to 31 August 2026 (Exhibit 4): where the software records an override, the appraiser overrides more than four slips in five. Four of the nine study stores were also Exchange Slip stores, so the two bodies of evidence are not independent.

5. The people

Latha Tadepalli, Director of Product, Bengaluru. For her the riskiest assumption is that an owner will let software set a number his appraiser now sets. Her incentive is a product that ships. She is not saying that she has no stopping rule for any of the four options.

Laxmikant Tummala, co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru. Has promised Dharohar Capital Indian general availability in February 2027. For him the risk is competitive: the largest chains will build this and the single-store base will expect it free. He is not saying that he has already sold Deepam into two 2027 contracts.

Lajwanti Tanikella, VP Engineering, Pune, runs the 54 engineers. Her riskiest assumption is the XRF integration: eleven device models, four with no documented protocol. She owns the HUID reconciliation promised to the large chains by 31 January 2027. She is not saying that her 318-engineer-week estimate carries an undefended contingency.

Lingaraj Tenneti, Principal Designer, Berlin, contracted to 31 March 2027. Having sat with appraisers twice, he thinks Deepam points at the wrong person: the customer wants the transparent valuation, and the store is asked to pay for it. He is not saying that he has sketched a consumer version and shown it to nobody.

Lithika Thirumalai, Data Scientist, Toronto, built the re-valuation of the 318 exchanges. She is the only person who writes down each statistic's denominator, and has twice been asked to stop. She is not saying that she thinks the study too small for the weight now on it.

Luv Thotakura, Head of Sales for the Americas and the Gulf, New Jersey, carries Durrah and a 2027 number, and wants Option D. He is not saying that Durrah has asked him informally whether Deepam could reach the UAE before India — in which case clause 7.4 never fires.

Lalima Tirumalasetty, CFO, Bengaluru. Cash was ₹1,842 lakh on 1 October 2026 and the plan shows ₹1,906 lakh on 31 March 2027. The constraint, she thinks, is not cash but one eleven-week train and four stories about what it is for. She is not saying that Dharohar's partner, Lalitesh Tangirala, has asked her privately whether February is real.
