  • Capacity: 54 engineers over eleven weeks is 594 engineer-weeks; 422 are committed (HUID 146, GST e-invoice 118, support and defects 158), leaving 172 of 594 free, or 29.0 per cent. C needs the 172 plus all 146 of HUID's; D needs 172 plus 74.
  • Incremental cash excludes salaries; B includes nine XRF adaptors at ₹1.9 lakh each, or ₹17.1 lakh.
  • No column states what each option would teach: no common unit; A and B are test costs, C and D builds, and Durrah's ₹3.20 crore is a three-year total.

7. Voices

“Seven in ten of our accounts said they would pay. I am not going to stand in front of a board and call that a question mark.”

Luv Thotakura, product review, 29 September

“Twenty-seven of thirty-eight said yes or probably, and sixteen of those said probably at a lower price. Eleven accepted the price we quoted. Three said nothing. Those are four sentences and the slip cannot tell them apart.”

Lithika Thirumalai, same review

“Eighty-six per cent of slips get overridden. The appraisers are telling us the answer and we keep running studies.”

Luv Thotakura, email to the CEO, 24 September

“Eighty-six per cent is fourteen stores. Nine of the twenty-three cannot record an override at all, so for 2,288 slips we know nothing. And eleven of the fourteen are large chains, where the appraiser is on salary and has least to lose — the opposite of the stores the risk sits in.”

Lithika Thirumalai, reply, same day

“Durrah is three crore twenty. That is thirteen per cent of the book, for a market where nobody expects us to win.”

Laxmikant Tummala, founders' call, 2 October

“It is ₹320 lakh over three years. Year one is ₹140 lakh, which is 5.9 per cent of this year's ₹2,374 lakh. I will argue for it, but not against a number of a different shape.”

Lalima Tirumalasetty, same call

“Madam, the rate I give is not in the scale. It is in the twelve years the family has been coming to me. Your machine can print what it likes; I will write my figure underneath.”

Lokendra Talluri, head appraiser, Devaraya Jewellers, field notes, 21 August

“We are building a fairness instrument and selling it to the party that benefits from the absence of one. Somebody should say that before we spend 318 engineer-weeks.”

Lingaraj Tenneti, design critique, Berlin, 7 October

“I will support whichever option has a number attached that would make you stop. I have not seen one.”

Lalitesh Tangirala, Dharohar Capital, to Latha Tadepalli, 8 October

8. The options as Latha has written them

Option A, the concierge desk. Two analysts sit in six stores for ten weeks and value old gold by hand against Deepam's rules, with the owner's consent. Nothing ships. It would show whether an owner tolerates an externally set rate in front of a customer — Latha's question — and nothing about eleven XRF models. Laxmikant calls it “a consulting project with a product name”.

Option B, the side-loaded tablet. A thin tablet application in nine stores, installed by hand outside the release train, logging every valuation and every override. Short of a full ship it is the only option that would produce an override rate on a base Lithika would defend. It also puts hardware in nine stores and asks nine owners about an untested price.

Option C, the full module. Deepam in the November train, reaching all 559 stores from 22 January 2027 and Indian general availability in February. It honours Laxmikant's commitment and triggers clause 7.4, obliging delivery to Durrah within 90 days of that date — 2 May 2027 if availability lands on 1 February — at no licence fee. It takes the whole 172 free engineer-weeks and all 146 of HUID's, so six large chains hear that their 31 January reconciliation moves to the next train.

Option D, Durrah first. A UAE-first build funded by Durrah at ₹320 lakh over three years. With no Indian general availability, clause 7.4 never fires and Durrah pays rather than receives. It needs 74 of HUID's engineer-weeks, moves the learning to 26 stores whose customers, regulator and language differ from the base of 559, and lands on Leander Tallapragada's four people in Singapore, none of whom has seen an Arabic interface.

Latha has not written down that all four, as Exhibit 6 costs them, lie along one axis: how much to build. A and B answer the same question at different fidelity; C and D build before answering anything. Lingaraj's sketch sits off the axis, and so does a possibility nobody has priced — that the engine's buyer might not be the store. None of the four answers Lalitesh's question: what number, on what base, in what window, would make Dravya stop.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board call is at nine on Monday, 12 October 2026. Scope for the November train freezes on Friday, 6 November 2026, and it reaches stores from Friday, 22 January 2027. Headcount is frozen until April 2027, so the 54 engineers are the 54 engineers. Salary bands make substitution a fiction: a senior engineer costs ₹42 lakh in Bengaluru and ₹31 lakh in Pune, while Lingaraj's €96,000 is ₹92.16 lakh and Lithika's CAD 1,45,000 is ₹91.35 lakh at the plan's ₹96 to the euro and ₹63 to the Canadian dollar.

Cash does not bind: ₹1,842 lakh on 1 October 2026, a plan reaching ₹1,906 lakh by 31 March 2027 before Deepam, and Option C's ₹96.40 lakh would leave ₹1,809.60 lakh at that window's close. Engineer-weeks bind, and clause 7.4 is the constraint nobody costed when they signed it. The DPDP Act makes any design holding identity documents on 559 store machines a question for counsel; and the HUID date of 31 January 2027 is not a regulator's deadline but, Lajwanti points out, a promise with six logos on it.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. List the assumptions Deepam rests on. Which does each named person treat as the riskiest, and what in their position explains the choice?
  2. For Exhibits 2, 4 and 5, state each headline figure's denominator and when it was measured. Where in the Voices is a base misused, and does that change a conclusion's direction or its size?
  3. Exhibit 3 puts the appraisal spread at 5.5 per cent of gross contribution in the large-chain column and 17.0 per cent in the single-store column. What does each imply about who will adopt Deepam, and what does the exhibit not contain?
  4. Write a decision rule for Option B: the measurement, its base, the window, and the value at which Dravya would stop. Then say what Option B cannot measure, and whether that matters more.
  5. The four options differ in how much is built. Construct a fifth that differs in what is learned, cost it in engineer-weeks against the 172 free, and say which exhibit it makes redundant.
  6. It is nine o'clock on Monday. What does Latha Tadepalli do, and what does she say to the board about Laxmikant's February date, clause 7.4, and the HUID promise with six logos on it?

11. Sunday night

At a quarter past eleven Latha deleted the fifth slide for the third time. It had held one line — we are not ready to choose — and she could not decide whether it was the most honest thing in the pack or the end of her credibility. On the table lay Lokendra Talluri's note about the figure he would write under whatever the machine printed. On her phone was a message from Luv in New Jersey: Lathangi Thandavarayan, Durrah's retail head, will ask tomorrow whether we can do UAE before India. What do I say? Latha had not replied. The gold-rate notification arrived at 11.22 p.m. She read it twice without taking it in, and began the deck again from the first slide.
case20v1-sol.mvp.scoping:
Cheran Ledger Technologies: Scoping the First Advance

A decision case on the minimum version that tests the riskiest assumption

1. The decision

On the morning of Monday, 19 October 2026, Karthik Sethuraman, head of product at Cheran Ledger Technologies, wrote one question at the top of a blank page in the company's Coimbatore office: what result would make us stop? The board would meet in Chennai on Friday, 23 October. Kamalesh Seshadri, the chief executive, wanted from him a scope for the first version of "Cheran Advance", a feature letting a small supplier draw cash against an unpaid invoice. The engineering plan in his inbox ran sixteen weeks. Karthik suspected that most of what it contained was not needed to learn whether anyone would use the feature at all.

2. Company background

Cheran sells GST invoicing and e-invoicing software to micro and small manufacturers. Founded in 2018 in Coimbatore, among pump and textile units, it has 12,500 paying customers at an average of ₹9,600 a year, which makes annual recurring revenue ₹12 crore. It competes with Zoho Books, Vyapar and Tally on invoicing, and its customers sometimes borrow from lenders such as Indifi or Lendingkart. The board wants a second product that earns more from existing customers.

3. The situation

The idea came from the customers. Since the 2023–24 financial year, Section 43B(h) of the Income Tax Act has denied a buyer a tax deduction on amounts owed to a micro or small supplier that stay unpaid beyond 45 days (15 where there is no written agreement). Large buyers have not become faster payers as a result, and suppliers remain short of cash, most sharply before Diwali, which falls on 8 November this year. The regulated remedy is invoice discounting on the TReDS platforms (among them RXIL, M1xchange and Invoicemart), but customers said onboarding there felt like a lender's process.

In September, Kuhan Sitaraman, who leads customer success from Singapore, interviewed 24 customers. Nineteen of the 24 had at least one invoice from a large buyer unpaid beyond 45 days in the previous quarter. Fifteen said they would "probably" take an advance against such an invoice. Only six had ever discounted an invoice, and two were doing so now. A Chennai non-banking finance company (NBFC) has agreed verbally to fund a pilot of up to ₹60 lakh of invoice value at no more than 1.5 per cent a month, paying Cheran a 0.6 per cent origination commission. Across the 4,000 customers who send at least ten invoices a month to large buyers (counted on 30 September), the average invoice is ₹3.5 lakh. Of five buyer finance heads Karthik approached, two agreed to confirm invoices within three working days. Any sharing of invoice data with the lender needs customer consent under the DPDP Act. Exhibit 1 lays out what is known and what is not.

Kalyani Srinivasan, the product designer in Berlin, had already produced a polished prototype of the supplier screens. Kesava Sunkara, the engineering lead in Pune, had a team free after the e-invoicing release and a sixteen-week plan ready. Both had done sound work, and both plans assumed Assumption 2 was true. Karthik noted the pattern: rows 2 to 4 of Exhibit 1 rest on what someone said, not on what anyone did.

4. The people

Kamalesh Seshadri (chief executive, Coimbatore) wants a clear recommendation on Friday and cash discipline. Kesava Sunkara (engineering lead, Pune) wants a real build, since a manual pilot is, in his words, scaffolding his team will throw away. Kalyani Srinivasan (designer, Berlin) wants customers to see a finished experience, because she believes a rough pilot will make suppliers distrust the offer; her working day starts as Bengaluru's lunch ends. Kuhan Sitaraman (customer success, Singapore) hears the cash pain every week and wants a decision quickly, but says suppliers repeatedly promise things they do not do.

5. The evidence on cost and time

Karthik priced three courses. An engineer in Bengaluru or Pune costs about ₹2.4 lakh a month fully loaded; the Berlin designer costs ₹6 lakh. Exhibit 2 sets out the totals and the weeks each takes to produce real evidence.

6. The options

Option A: build the full product. Supplier onboarding, consent, buyer confirmation, NBFC integration and repayment tracking, ₹80.0 lakh in all. Its upside is a finished product. Its cost is that nothing is learned about Assumption 2 until week 20, and a negative answer arrives after ₹80.0 lakh is spent.

Option B: a concierge pilot. Karthik would draw 40 customers at random from the 310 of those 4,000 who had open invoices to the two buyers that agreed to confirm (counted on 12 October). This is not a random draw from the 4,000, and it holds Assumption 4 steady so that the pilot tests Assumption 2 alone. Operations staff would handle each request by phone and spreadsheet, the NBFC would fund it, and the buyer would confirm by email. The NBFC's ₹60 lakh limit covers about 17 invoices at ₹3.5 lakh, so funding stops there; a customer who submits and accepts the offer counts as a success whether or not it is funded. It costs ₹10.4 lakh and observes real behaviour with real money by 4 December. The cost is manual effort, a rough experience, and a sample too small to give a precise rate. Each customer would sign a data-sharing consent form, and an analyst would call within a day of any upload so that drop-offs could be explained and counted.

Option C: a fake door. An in-app banner offering "Get paid today" to all 12,500 customers, with a click leading to a waitlist. It costs ₹5.7 lakh and reports within three weeks. But a click is closer to the 15-of-24 "probably" Cheran already holds than to a submitted invoice, so it adds little about Assumption 2.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Which of the five assumptions in Exhibit 1 would end the product if false, and which could Cheran fix afterwards? Which is riskiest, and why?
  2. For each option in Exhibits 2 and 3, what does the result tell Cheran about that assumption, and what can it not tell?
  3. If Cheran needs 1,000 of its 4,000 eligible customers to finance one invoice a month to repay an ₹80.0 lakh build, what pilot result should lead to a go decision?
  4. What should Karthik say to Kesava and Kalyani, and what exactly should he ask the board to approve on 23 October?

8. A note for the learner

An MVP is a learning vehicle with a decision rule, not a small product. Scoping starts from the riskiest assumption and includes only what is needed to test it. Here the riskiest is Assumption 2, because if suppliers will not act, the lender, the buyers and the build do not matter. The others can be repaired later: a lender can be replaced, and a slow buyer can be chased by hand.

One defensible path is Option B. The arithmetic below sets the rule. At 0.6 per cent of an average invoice of ₹3.5 lakh, Cheran earns ₹2,100 per financed invoice. Taking question 3's target of 1,000 customers each financing one invoice a month, that is ₹21 lakh a month, and ₹80.0 lakh is recovered in 3.8 months on commission revenue only, before cost to serve, credit losses and ongoing engineering. A longer payback could be defended, and the true break-even is about 3,810 financed invoices in total. 1,000 of 4,000 is 25 per cent. So the rule is: 12 or more of the 40 (30 per cent) submitting a real invoice and accepting the advance within the four-week window means build; 10 or 11 means run a second cohort; 9 or fewer (below 25 per cent) means shelve. The 30 per cent bar leaves margin because willing once is not willing monthly, but it is not statistically safe: if the true rate were exactly 25 per cent, 12 or more successes out of 40 would still occur about three times in ten. Karthik should also state what the pilot cannot show. With 40 customers, 12 successes is consistent with a true rate anywhere from roughly 16 to 44 per cent (normal approximation, 95 per cent), the pilot tests only these two buyers, and it assumes the 310 resemble the 4,000. It also straddles Diwali, when cash pain peaks, so the rate may flatter a normal month.

Option C is weaker because it repeats stated intent: a customer who clicks a banner has risked nothing, whereas a customer who uploads a ₹3.5 lakh invoice and accepts a fee has. Option A is defensible only after Option B returns a go. Kesava's team is not wasted: it can build the first slice in the winning case, and the manual process becomes its specification. The board is asked for ₹10.4 lakh now, with ₹80.0 lakh conditional on the rule.
exp20v2-sol.mvp.scoping:
Scoping the MVP

1. Monday, 5 October

Kamini Hirlekar, head of product at Yatnam Care, had one slide on the screen and two engineers waiting for her answer. Yatnam sold repeat medicines to patients with diabetes and hypertension in Nashik: nine partner pharmacies, about 12,000 patients on their customer lists, and a plan to deliver monthly refills to the door. Lohith Holla, the engineering lead, had priced the plan as a full Android app: fourteen team-weeks at ₹4.4 lakh a week, or ₹61.6 lakh, inside the ₹62 lakh the board had earmarked. If work began that morning, the app would ship on Monday, 11 January 2027.

Kamini doubted not the build but the behaviour: nobody knew whether a patient who had walked to the same chemist for ten years would photograph a prescription, send it to a stranger, and wait for a delivery. If it did not exist, the ₹61.6 lakh would be gone before anyone found out. Lavina Hirwani, who managed the pharmacy partners, wanted it built properly or not at all.

The decision was therefore not whether to build, but what to build first.

2. The idea

A minimum viable product (MVP) is the smallest thing you can put in front of real users that will produce a trustworthy answer to your most dangerous open question. Frank Robinson used the phrase in the early 2000s; it spread through Steve Blank's customer development work and Eric Ries's The Lean Startup (2011). It addressed a specific waste: teams built complete products and learned only at launch that a core belief was false.

Scoping is the act of deciding what goes in. It rests on two ideas from the neighbouring topics. First, an assumption is a belief your plan needs to be true but you have not yet seen evidence for. Second, the riskiest assumption is the one that, if false, ends the plan. An MVP type is the form the test takes: a landing page, a human-run service, a clickable prototype, a thin working product. Scoping chooses the type and then the minimum features that type needs.

Kamini's meeting sentence: “We are not building a small product; we are buying one answer, at the lowest price, before we spend the large sum.”

3. How it works

Practitioners leave several steps implicit, so here they are, using Yatnam.

Step one: list the assumptions the plan needs. Kamini's team wrote four. A1: patients will send a prescription photo on WhatsApp and accept home delivery instead of walking in. A2: pharmacists will confirm and pack an order within four hours. A3: patients will reorder every month. A4: patients will pay by UPI at the door.

Step two: score each by how likely it is to be false and how badly its falsity hurts. Likelihood is a written team judgement. Consequence is graded 3 for fatal, 2 for serious, 1 for minor. The score is the chance of being false multiplied by the grade.

AssumptionChance trueChance falseGradeScore
A1 Photo and delivery replace the walk-in40%60%31.8
A2 Pharmacist confirms within 4 hours70%30%20.6
A3 Monthly reorder60%40%31.2
A4 UPI at the door90%10%10.1
Score = chance false × grade. Chances are the team's own estimates, not measurements.

A1 scores 1.8, three times A2 and eighteen times A4. A3 is fatal if false, scoring 1.2, but cannot be tested first, because nobody reorders a service they never used once. So riskiest first is also dependency-first.

Step three: choose the MVP type. A1 concerns real behaviour with real money, so a landing page or clickable mock would not do; users say yes to pictures. The team chose a concierge MVP, in which humans do manually what software would later do, while the customer experiences the real service.

Step four: cut features by one question. For each feature ask, “If this is missing, can we still read the answer to A1?” The table below applies it.

FeatureFull build, weeksNeeded to read A1?MVP, weeksMVP treatment
Account and login2No0WhatsApp number is the identity
Prescription capture and OCR (automatic text reading)3Yes, the photo; no, the OCR0.5WhatsApp Business inbox, read by a person
Pharmacist dashboard3Yes1Shared sheet with order status
Inventory sync3No0Pharmacist checks the shelf by phone
Reminders and subscription2No (this serves A3)0Deferred
Payments and invoicing1Yes0.5UPI QR at the door, ledger in the sheet
Total142
Team-weeks, priced at ₹4.4 lakh each.

Figure 2 makes the cut visible. Three features survive, none in full; account, inventory and reminders disappear. The MVP costs 2 × ₹4.4 lakh = ₹8.8 lakh to build, one-seventh of ₹61.6 lakh.

Step five, usually skipped: write the decision rule before launch. A rule names who will be invited, what counts as success, the number that triggers each outcome, and the date.

4. A worked example, and a second pass

The success number comes from the economics. Yatnam estimated that each active patient orders twelve times a year and leaves ₹70 contribution per order after the pharmacy margin and delivery. That is 12 × ₹70 = ₹840 per patient-year. Running the Nashik cluster costs ₹25.2 lakh a year, which is ₹25,20,000. Break-even is therefore 25,20,000 ÷ 840 = 3,000 active patients. Against 12,000 listed patients, that is 3,000 ÷ 12,000 = 25 per cent. This treats the first-order rate as a ceiling on the active share, assuming every first-orderer becomes a twelve-order patient. A3 is untested, so a go means “proceed to a retention test”, not “break-even proven”.

The rule that followed: invite 400 patients drawn at random from the 12,000 on the lists, all of whom had consented to contact; run four weeks live; count patients who complete a first delivered order. Go at 25 per cent or more, which is 100 of 400. Stop below 15 per cent, which is 60 of 400, three-fifths of the go line, a recorded judgement. From 60 to 99, extend four weeks with a fresh cohort.

Build runs through Friday, 16 October; the service goes live on Monday, 19 October; four weeks end on Sunday, 15 November; the readout is Monday, 16 November, six weeks after the meeting. The full app would have answered on 8 February 2027, eighteen weeks out. Spend is the build ₹8.8 lakh, two coordinators at ₹0.40 lakh each for one month (₹0.8 lakh), and provisioned delivery for 300 orders at ₹60 (₹18,000, or ₹0.18 lakh): ₹9.78 lakh.

Now suppose the cohort returns 124 first orders out of 400, which is 31.0 per cent. Against the go line of 100, the rule says go.

Second pass, one input changed. Suppose that pharmacies negotiate a better margin for themselves and Yatnam's contribution falls from ₹70 to ₹56 per order. Per patient-year it is 12 × 56 = ₹672. Break-even is 25,20,000 ÷ 672 = 3,750 patients, or 3,750 ÷ 12,000 = 31.25 per cent, which is 125 of 400. The same 124 now falls one patient short.

With 400 patients and a rate near 31 per cent, the standard error is the square root of 0.31 × 0.69 ÷ 400, about 2.3 percentage points, roughly nine patients. A gap of one patient is noise, and even a go at exactly 100 (error about 2.2 points) is consistent with a true rate somewhat below 25 per cent. A go line is only as sharp as its inputs, and the rule should say what happens in the grey zone.

5. Nuances

Viable means viable for the test, not viable for sale

The Yatnam MVP is ugly and run by hand, yet a real patient with a real prescription can complete a real order.

Riskiest is not the same as hardest or most uncertain

Inventory sync is the hardest engineering and A4 the most boring, but neither decides survival.

The rule must exist before the data

Once 124 is on the table, people bend thresholds toward their hopes. Writing the lines first separates a test from a demonstration.

An MVP is not a prototype, a pilot or a beta

A prototype tests whether a design is understood; a pilot runs a finished product in a small area; a beta hardens software. An MVP tests whether a belief is true.

The quality floor can contaminate the answer

If deliveries arrive two days late because the coordinators were swamped, a low conversion may reflect the service rather than the demand.

Who you invite decides what you learn

Random invitation protects against asking only the enthusiasts.

What an MVP cannot tell you

It reads a first behaviour in one city in four weeks. It cannot show monthly retention (A3), pharmacy supply when volume is ten times higher, or whether the unit economics survive scale.

Questions to ask before relying on it

What result would change what we do? Who is missing from the sample? Would the best possible result still leave us unsure?

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace; early and large

Yatnam is a marketplace, a product with two sides that each need the other. The MVP above supplies the pharmacist side by hand: nine partners were already signed, so only patient demand was tested. Where both sides are unproven, fake one side manually and test the other.

A consumer MVP leans on volume and a conversion rate. A B2B MVP cannot, because a company has perhaps twenty candidate customers. There the evidence is five design partners, a signed letter of intent or a paid pilot fee, and the rule reads like “three of five commit budget by month-end”.

Early-stage firms scope under cash pressure and few approvals. In a large company the permission costs more than the engineering, so scoping must include what the test needs from legal, brand and compliance, and a ring-fenced budget so that a ₹9.78 lakh experiment does not wait in a ₹62 lakh queue.

7. Common mistakes

The small v1

Symptom: the “MVP” takes five months and has a login screen. Misunderstanding: scope is cut by size, not by assumption. Diagnostic: for each feature, name the assumption whose reading would change without it. If none, cut it.

The rule written afterwards

Symptom: the readout meeting argues about whether 31 per cent is good. Misunderstanding: results speak for themselves. Diagnostic: ask for the dated document that names the go line. If it is not older than the data, there is no rule.

The comfortable assumption

Symptom: rich findings on button placement and nothing on demand. Misunderstanding: testing what is easy to measure. Diagnostic: imagine the best possible result; if you would still hesitate to build, you tested the wrong thing.

The friendly sample

Symptom: conversion far above benchmarks. Misunderstanding: any user is a user. Diagnostic: compare invitees with the whole list on past ordering frequency.

8. What good looks like

By the end of Monday, 5 October, Kamini's scope brief fit one page: the assumption (A1) with its 1.8 score; the type (concierge); the three features and their 2 weeks; the invited 400, drawn at random; stop below 60, extend from 60 to 99, go from 100, with the arithmetic behind them; the ₹9.78 lakh budget; and the readout on 16 November. It also named what the test would not answer.

9. Closing

Kamini decided against the app. She asked Lohith for the 2-week build and Lavina for two coordinators. Her reasoning was that the cheaper path risks at most ₹9.78 lakh and six weeks, while the expensive one risks ₹61.6 lakh and eighteen weeks. A go on 16 November would release a retention test, not the full build.

Learn next what this topic unlocks. Feature and prioritisation rationale explains how to justify each cut to colleagues. Value versus effort gives a way to rank what survives. MVPs for enterprise products revisits the B2B case with realistic sample sizes.

Two questions to sit with. First, which assumption in your current plan would end it if false, and what is the cheapest honest way to read it? Second, what number would make you stop, and have you written it down where you cannot change it?
exp40v2-sol.mvp.scoping:
Scoping the MVP

The minimum feature set that tests the riskiest assumption

1. Two decisions, three days apart

On Friday, 9 October 2026, Keertana Haldipur sat with a one-page summary in the Pune office of Yagna Field Systems. Yagna made a retrofit pod that clamps onto a collection centre's bulk milk cooler and reports tank temperature over a mobile network. Its customer was a district co-operative milk union inside the National Dairy Development Board's network; its user, a supervisor with a feature phone and eleven other jobs. Over the six weeks from Monday, 1 June to Sunday, 12 July 2026, Yagna silently logged 40 centres of the Yelgaon District Milk Union: 1,042 excursions, of which 126 ended in a can rejected at the chilling plant, 12.1 per cent. The same centres then had alerts for the six weeks from Monday, 20 July to Sunday, 30 August.

The result was good enough to put to the board on Monday, 9 November, where Kuhu Hadimani, Yagna's chief executive, would ask ₹169 lakh for tooling and a 2,000-unit run. But the test answered one question and left a second standing: the economic case assumed a supervisor who responded in time prevented a rejection four times out of five, and nobody had measured that. In four weeks Keertana could scope a second vehicle, or argue none was needed.

Three days later, on Monday, 12 October, Lalatendu Hirekerur faced the same problem in another shape in Bengaluru. Yojit Claims Cloud sold health insurers an assistant that read a pre-authorisation request, checked policy terms and exclusions, and proposed approve, query or decline. Yamuna Health Assurance had run it for fifteen working days in its Chennai hub, Monday, 31 August to Friday, 18 September 2026, and its committee would meet on Friday, 23 October to sign a ₹2.9 crore three-year contract or ask for a second pilot. Keshini Havaldar, Yamuna's head of claims operations, liked the tool and distrusted the business case. Lalatendu had to choose: six hubs thinly, or one hub across every specialty.

Both are scoping decisions, and both are usually got wrong the same way: by asking what a good first product contains rather than what question the next four weeks must answer.

2. The idea, and the fork in its history

Scoping an MVP is choosing the smallest set of built and unbuilt things that will produce evidence capable of moving a decision already named and given a threshold. Minimum refers to effort, not feature count. Viable means real enough that people behave as they would with the finished product: a supervisor who ignores an alert written in English has told you about your translation, not his behaviour. Tests means the result can come out either way, and the team has pre-committed to each.

Its history holds a fork that still shapes arguments. Frank Robinson, an American consultant, used "minimum viable product" from the late 1990s to mean the smallest product a segment would actually buy: a revenue instrument, sized by the market. Steve Blank's customer development and Eric Ries's The Lean Startup (2011) repurposed it as a learning instrument, sized by the question. Both meanings live in most companies at once, which is why two competent people can agree a team needs an MVP and disagree violently about its contents. The learning version was invented against expensive certainty: a year building to an untested specification, and a founding belief found false at launch.

Three schools disagree. The experiment school signs: scope is whatever the decision rule requires and not one feature more; a concierge or a spreadsheet counts. Not: the MVP is the first thing customers pay for. The complete-product school, lineage of "simple, lovable, complete", signs: a broken artefact measures tolerance for brokenness, not demand; ship something small and whole. Not: embarrassment proves you shipped early enough. The field and procurement school signs: the floor is what the buyer can legally run, and the learning goal cannot shrink scope below it. Not: scope follows the question alone.

3. Mechanics in depth

Experts run four steps; the middle two, usually left implicit, are where scoping is decided.

Step one: a register, not a list

An assumption register names each belief the plan requires, the consequence if false, and—the part teams skip—the evidence that would settle it. Keertana's held four. A1: a supervisor who receives an alert acts within 45 minutes. A2: acting in time prevents the rejection four times out of five. A3: the union pays ₹700 per device-month. A4: pods survive a monsoon on a shed roof. Ranking is by consequence times residual uncertainty. A1 won because A3 and A4 were recoverable—a price can change, an enclosure be re-moulded—while if supervisors did not act, nothing worked.

Step two: the decision rule, written before the scope

This step separates scoping from estimating. The rule has four parts: statistic, denominator, window, threshold. In the baseline window, 126 rejections across 40 centres over 42 days is 56 centre-months, so 126÷56 = 2.25 rejections per centre-month. A rejected can is 40 litres at ₹38 a litre, or ₹1,520. With prevention efficacy assumed at 0.8, the avoided loss per centre-month at response rate r is 2.25×0.8×1,520×r, or ₹2,736×r. Against a ₹700 fee, break-even is 700÷2,736 = 25.6 per cent; the union wanted two rupees avoided per rupee of fee, 1,400÷2,736 = 51.2 per cent. Yagna pre-registered 55 per cent, leaving margin for novelty wearing off.

Two rates, not one. The alert window produced 1,118 excursions; 1,039 alerts were delivered, 79 lost to network outages; 656 drew a response inside 45 minutes. Kalpesh Honakeri, Yagna's analyst, reported 58.7 per cent, dividing 656 by 1,118; Keertana corrected its meaning, not its operations. The behavioural question—will a supervisor act?—is conditional on his having been told, so its denominator is the 1,039 delivered alerts: 63.1 per cent. The economic question is indifferent to why milk spoiled, so its base is all 1,118 excursions: 58.7 per cent. The threshold belongs to the economic one: at the assumed efficacy of 0.8, ₹2,736×0.587 = ₹1,606 per centre-month against a ₹700 fee, a ratio of 2.3. The chain uses the rounded 0.587; unrounded it gives ₹1,605. Reporting only 63.1 per cent would have carried a telemetry defect into production as a behavioural success.

Step three: choose the instrument, then build down to it

Feature choice begins only now, and it is subtraction: strike every line the rule does not require, and record what replaces it.

The Pune voice desk substitutes a human for the untested part, so behaviour is measured against a prompt the supervisor certainly received. The line Yagna refused to cut is instructive: installation had to be real, because a pod a technician cannot mount in twenty minutes yields a response rate that measures the bracket.

Step four: price the information

The test cost 14 engineer-weeks at ₹65,000, or ₹9.10 lakh, plus 40 pods at ₹7,400, or ₹2.96 lakh, plus twelve weeks of field work across both six-week windows at ₹85,000, or ₹10.20 lakh: ₹22.26 lakh. A perfectly informative test returns 58.93÷22.26 = 2.65 times its cost; one half informative, the half being a second judgement, returns 1.32 times. The second figure goes to the board.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions, as testable claims. One: the decision is reversible only at material cost. Yagna passes; tooling is ₹46 lakh, unrecoverable. Two: the riskiest assumption concerns behaviour observable inside the window. Yagna passes; Yojit passes for acceptance and fails for renewal, which needs a year. Three: a smaller artefact can produce the same behaviour. Yagna passes, because a supervisor's response does not depend on the dashboard; Yojit partly fails, because an examiner's trust depends on the trail that justifies a recommendation. Four: the threshold is knowable in advance. Both pass, and both needed arithmetic to get there.

The idea actively misleads in three situations. Where the risk is craft rather than demand—a game, a typeface—a thin artefact measures the thinness. Where value is a network, a single-user test measures loneliness. Where switching costs are the point, as in payroll, a pilot measures politeness. The answer is not "scope smaller" but "this is not answerable by scoping".

5. Hard edge cases

In regulated products the floor is immovable, the sharpest qualification above. Yojit could cut single sign-on, the admin console and the ingestion adapters, but not the audit trail an IRDAI inspection would ask for, nor the security review for deployment inside Yamuna's cloud. Those two took 14 of its 30 learning-scope engineer-weeks.

Exhibit 3. Yojit's build-down, in engineer-weeks: the four-specialty pilot Yamuna ran, not the all-specialty scope Lalatendu later chose. With five engineers, 30÷5 = 6 calendar weeks against 81÷5 = 16.2. Estimated the same way as Exhibit 1, so the shares are comparable.

Thirty of 81 engineer-weeks is 37 per cent, against Yagna's 18 per cent: just over twice as much, on the same measure over the same kind of estimate. Compressibility is a property of context, not a constant.

In two-sided products scope is geography: one pin code with both sides thick beats ten with one side thin. In hardware plus software the asymmetry is tooling, so the expert splits the MVP in two, testing behaviour on hand-built units and manufacturability separately. In multi-product companies the shared platform team binds, so a scope small to a product team is large to the organisation. In AI-native products the variable is the field set.

At the organisational seams, mature companies diverge from what they say. They call the MVP a learning vehicle and run two tracks: a protected one with its own threshold, and a roadmap promised to sales last quarter and not truly contingent on it. The tell is a pilot whose end date falls after the availability date already in the sales deck.

6. Eight nuances that separate the expert

The denominator is the decision. An expert asks "over what?" before "how much?". The tell is a percentage with no base beside it; Yagna's 63.1 and 58.7 came from the same 656 responses. The obvious reading—that one must be the real number—is wrong, and a scope that retires the behavioural question while leaving a telemetry defect unpriced has retired the cheaper risk of the two.

Acceptance is not time saved. Yojit's panel accepted 1,132 of 1,886 recommendations unchanged, 60.0 per cent, which the sales deck turned into 60 per cent less examiner work. The tell is a benefit quoted in the model's units rather than the user's day. It fails because rejected recommendations made cases slower: the examiner read the file and the machine's reasoning.

The rule proposes, the floor disposes. Section 3 says the learning goal fixes scope; section 5 says compliance does. Both hold, in that sequence. The expert buys the floor once and reuses it across tests in that account, rather than arguing with an officer who cannot grant exceptions.

Substitute humans for the untested, never for the tested. A concierge desk is legitimate where it stands in for machinery nobody doubts, illegitimate where the doubt is whether machinery can do the work. The tell is a pilot in which the humans make the hard judgements; what it measures is the staff.

Write the threshold before the instrument. Teams that pick the instrument first find it cannot produce the statistic the rule needs. The tell is a rule stated in adjectives—"good engagement", "strong interest"—almost always written after the data was seen.

Retiring the riskiest assumption promotes the second. A scope does not make a plan safe; it changes which risk is largest. Keertana's pilot retired A1 and promoted A2, the 0.8 efficacy figure, from second in the register to the binding uncertainty. The related trap is sizing by money: a ₹46 lakh mould and a ₹46 lakh campaign are the same cash, not the same risk.

Novelty inflates pilot behaviour. Supervisors under observation respond faster than supervisors in March, which is why Yagna's rule was 55 and not 51.2. The tell is a rate highest early; the diagnostic compares first and last fortnight before any average is quoted. Yagna's three fortnights held 371, 369 and 378 excursions against 231, 219 and 206 responses, so the economic rate ran 231÷371 = 62.3, then 219÷369 = 59.3, then 206÷378 = 54.5 per cent. The 58.7 average clears the rule by 3.7 points; the closing fortnight misses it.

The unit of trust is not the unit of accuracy. Section 8's second example shows it: 89.0 per cent per field yielded only 43.0 per cent of contracts needing no re-reading. The tell is a quality metric at a finer grain than the user's decision, and the expert's first move is to scope down the field set, not the feature set.

7. Across product types and stages

In consumer products the scarce input is attention, so the question is which moment to build well; fake doors work because intent is cheap to observe. In B2B it is one workflow for one role at one design partner, and the risk is an unrepresentative partner. In enterprise the minimum includes the procurement floor, so the honest MVP is a paid pilot with an exit clause. In platforms and marketplaces it is a bounded market, with liquidity as the statistic. Hardware and AI products are section 5's cases.

By stage the differences are smaller than claimed. A seed-stage company and a listed one both benefit from a written threshold, and both find the floor set by their buyers. What changes is the cost of the alternative: a seed-stage team that wastes eleven months may not get a twelfth, while a large company loses a quarter to distraction and must get a test past legal and brand review.

8. Three worked examples

Yashomati Tiffin Works, Indore, consumer. Kanaka Hiremallur believed office workers would pre-pay weekly for a rotating regional lunch menu. An app had been quoted at ₹34 lakh. She instead ran five weeks from Monday, 9 February 2026 in one office park with a poster, a messaging number and three kitchens, for ₹2.4 lakh. Of 1,180 workers there, 214 scanned the code, and 96 of those 214 pre-paid ₹1,050 for five lunches, 44.9 per cent. The pre-registered rule was week-four renewal of the week-one cohort at 40 per cent. The cohort ran 96, 71, 59, 52, 44, so week four was 52 of 96, or 54.2 per cent. She built.

Yavanika Docs, Gurugram, AI-native B2B. Komalika Hazarimal's team extracted twelve fields from vendor contracts for a manufacturer's legal team. No product was built: two engineers ran a batch over 300 contracts in four weeks and delivered spreadsheets. Of 3,600 extractions, 3,204 were correct, 89.0 per cent. But 171 of the 300 contracts held at least one wrong field, 57.0 per cent, so only 129 of 300, 43.0 per cent, needed no re-reading, and lawyer time barely moved. Re-scoped to five fields: of 1,500 extractions, 1,452 were correct, 96.8 per cent, and 259 of 300 contracts were clean, 86.3 per cent. It shipped with five.

Yugmaya Mobility, Jaipur, hardware plus platform: the failure. Lohitaksh Hangal raised ₹6.2 crore in January 2025 for rickshaw battery swapping, and spent ₹4.1 crore by December 2025. He scoped the MVP around the assumption that drivers would swap rather than charge overnight, and built three stations to find out. They would. The assumption that killed the plan went untested: whether one station could reach the utilisation that pays for its batteries. Each held 24 batteries at ₹41,000, or ₹9.84 lakh, depreciating over 30 months at ₹32,800 a month, plus ₹26,000 rent, ₹19,000 for an attendant and ₹13,000 for power and chargers: ₹90,800 a month. At ₹32 of margin per swap, break-even is 90,800÷32 = 2,837.5 swaps a month, or 94.6 a day. In October 2025 the three recorded 3,726 swaps over 30 days, which across 90 station-days is 41.4 a day, 44 per cent of break-even. Three thin stations had answered a question nobody doubted. The recovery closed two and sold their 48 batteries rather than moving them, so the surviving station kept its own 24, its ₹90,800 a month and its 94.6-a-day break-even; density came from driver referrals on one corridor. By April 2026 it did 2,961 swaps in 30 days, or 98.7 a day.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Thin everywhere. Sign: a scope touching every feature area at 30 per cent. Diagnostic: "which assumption does this retire?" Late cost: a build cycle, as Yugmaya's ₹4.1 crore shows.

The scope that grew. Sign: the fourth week's standup adds "while we are in there" items. Diagnostic: "does the rule change if we cut this?" Late cost: a test arriving after the decision.

Wrong denominator. Sign: a rate quoted without its base. Diagnostic: "who was excluded, and when was this measured?" Late cost: a production defect disguised as a success.

Pilot purgatory. Sign: a second pilot with no new assumption named. Diagnostic: "what will we know in March that we do not know now?" Late cost: a year of pilots, no product.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is whether an incomplete artefact can measure demand at all. Steelmanned: users in 2026 have abundant substitutes, so a rough artefact's rejection is uninformative, and the only valid minimum is something small and whole. Its evidence is the products that tested badly and succeeded once finished. It would be wrong if rough tests predicted finished outcomes in the same category—the comparison nobody runs, because teams that kill a product do not then build it.

The second is whether the enterprise floor should be bought or avoided. The field school: it is a one-time cost that unlocks every later test in that account, so pay it. The experiment school replies that paying it biases the portfolio towards accounts that already said yes. Resolution turns on an unmeasured quantity: how much of the floor transfers to the next buyer.

The third is whether to scope for a number or for a conversation. One camp holds that an MVP without a pre-registered threshold is theatre. The other holds that thresholds borrowed from consumer A/B testing give false precision at the sample sizes B2B teams have—Yojit's panel was nine examiners—and that the real output is an informed judgement. It would be wrong if teams without thresholds reached the same decisions as teams with them; both sides say they do not.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this writes the decision rule, with its denominator and window, before anyone estimates anything, and treats the feature list as that rule's output, not its input. They name what becomes riskiest if the test passes, and know which parts of their scope are incompressible. They can say what result would stop the project, and price the test against expected loss rather than budget. Someone who has merely studied it builds a small product, calls it an MVP, and learns at the readout that nobody had agreed on the number.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Keertana Haldipur chose not to run a second pilot, and the page's own arithmetic shows what that rests on. At a response rate of 0.587 the exposure is 2.25×1,520×0.587 = ₹2,008 per centre-month, so an efficacy of 700÷2,008 = 0.35 covers the fee and 1,400÷2,008 = 0.70 clears the union's 2× test. At 0.6 the avoided loss is 2.25×0.6×1,520×0.587 = ₹1,205: above the fee, below the test. Her decision stands only if efficacy is at least 0.70, which nobody had measured, and the closing fortnight's 54.5 per cent offered no comfort. Her scope added one line to the production build — a logged outcome for every alert — so both are measured on the first 2,000 units rather than bought separately.

Lalatendu Hirekerur chose depth over breadth: all specialties in the Chennai hub rather than four specialties in six hubs. His reason: 430 of the 2,480 requests had been excluded as out of scope and the model abstained on 164 of the 2,050 remaining, so Yamuna's committee could not yet see the whole desk's economics, while the breadth variant answered a question nobody at Yamuna had raised.

Three questions. First: Keertana folded a measurement into a production commitment. When is that legitimate scoping rather than avoidance of a test? Second: Yojit's 60.0 per cent acceptance and 23.7 per cent time saving come from one pilot. Which belongs in the contract's success clause, and in what words? Third: Yugmaya tested breadth when depth was at risk. What in its January 2025 register would have caught that, and who was placed to notice?

13. Going deeper

MVP types—the instruments a scope chooses from. Riskiest assumption first—what supplies the question; without it, guesswork. Feature and prioritisation rationale—how struck-out lines re-enter the plan. Value vs effort—Exhibits 1 and 3 as a roadmap. MVPs for enterprise products—the procurement floor, paid pilots, exit clauses. Writing a solution hypothesis—the sentence a rule attaches to. Ideation: brainstorming, Crazy 8s, HMW—where candidates come from. Concept and elevator pitch—the compression test a scope must survive. Value Proposition Canvas and Value proposition statement—what keeps a shrinking scope attached to a testable claim. Storyboarding—finding the moments a scope cannot omit.

AI Product Design Choices: Autonomy, Error, and the Shape of Trust

How much should the machine be allowed to do on its own, what kind of wrong should it be allowed to be, and what stops it from doing damage while it learns?

1. A Tuesday in March, Ledgerline Inc.

Maya Chen, vice president of product at Ledgerline, a Series B company that automates accounts-payable workflows for mid-sized manufacturers, spent the second week of March 2024 staring at a single slider in a design mockup. The slider controlled a confidence threshold. Below a certain number, an invoice would be routed to a human reviewer; above it, Ledgerline's new feature, internally called Auto-Match, would approve the invoice and release payment without anyone looking at it first.

The stakes were not abstract. Ledgerline's 40,000 monthly invoices were currently reviewed by a team of fourteen analysts at a fully loaded cost of roughly $1.20 per invoice, a number the CFO, Priya Nair, wanted to cut by at least half before the next board meeting. Her counterpart in finance operations at a competitor, Vellum Systems, had quietly disclosed over a conference dinner that an over-eager automation rollout there had auto-approved a fabricated $85,000 invoice the previous autumn. The vendor did not exist. The invoice looked, to the algorithm, exactly like a normal one. Vellum's auditors found it during a routine SOX control review, and the finding cost the head of finance operations his job and Vellum three months of remediation work.

Maya's CEO, Daniel Osei, did not want a repeat of that story at Ledgerline, but he also did not want to ship a feature so cautious that it saved nobody any time, since the entire pitch to the board rested on reducing the review team's workload by 50 percent within two quarters. Maya had, in other words, inherited a decision that could not be resolved by enthusiasm for AI or by caution about AI. It required a specific, technical vocabulary for talking about how wrong a system is allowed to be, how much it is allowed to do by itself, and what rails keep it from leaving the track entirely. That vocabulary is the subject of this case.

2. The idea, defined plainly

Four design choices sit at the centre of every AI-powered product feature, and they are logically separate even though teams often blur them into one conversation. The first is the error trade-off, usually discussed through two numbers borrowed from information retrieval research: precision, the share of the system's positive calls that are actually correct, and recall, the share of the actually-correct cases that the system manages to catch. These terms were formalised by researchers including Cyril Cleverdon in the Cranfield experiments of the 1960s, which tested how well early document-retrieval systems found relevant material in a library without burying the user in irrelevant results. The second choice is autonomy: how much of the decision loop — propose, decide, act — the system is allowed to complete without a person. The third is guardrails: hard limits placed around the system's behaviour that hold regardless of what the model's confidence score says. The fourth, less technical but equally consequential, is personality: the tone, hedging style, and disclosure behaviour the system presents to the people who interact with it, which shapes how much trust users extend to it and whether that trust is well calibrated.

The sentence Maya could say in a board meeting without sounding either glib or evasive is this: "Before we talk about how smart the model is, we need to agree what kind of mistake we are willing to make more of, and who is positioned to catch the other kind." That sentence does real work. It forces the room to accept that there is no error-free option, only a choice about which error costs the company more, and it makes explicit that a human reviewer is a design component, not a stopgap for an unfinished model.

3. How it actually works, mechanically

Every classification-style AI feature — and Auto-Match is a classification feature, sorting invoices into "approve" and "review" — produces a confidence score between 0 and 1 for each item. A threshold converts that continuous score into a binary action. The mechanics practitioners often skip over are not the model training itself but the five steps around it that determine whether the feature is safe and useful.

First, the team must build a labelled validation set: a sample of past invoices where the true outcome — fraudulent, mismatched, or clean — is already known, ideally several hundred to a few thousand cases, refreshed periodically as the business changes. Second, the team must price the two kinds of error in the currency the business actually cares about, typically dollars: what does it cost when the system wrongly approves a bad invoice (a false negative) versus when it wrongly flags a good one for human review (a false positive)? Third, the threshold is chosen using that cost ratio, not by maximising accuracy, because accuracy treats both error types as equally bad, which they almost never are. Fourth, the team assigns an autonomy tier to each confidence band — not a single on/off switch but a graded set of permissions, for example "suggest only," "act but allow override within 24 hours," and "act silently." Fifth, guardrails are written as absolute rules that override the confidence score entirely, such as "no invoice above $10,000 is ever auto-approved regardless of model confidence," because some risks are too asymmetric to leave to a probabilistic judgment. A sixth step, frequently skipped and expensive to skip, is instrumenting the live system so that the validation-set numbers can be checked against reality on an ongoing basis, since the population of invoices in production drifts away from the population used to build the validation set.

Precision = 30 / (30+10) = 75%. Recall = 30 / (30+20) = 60%. 20 real problems are auto-approved unseen.

4. The arithmetic, worked twice

At a threshold of 0.80, Auto-Match flags 40 of the 1,000 validation invoices for human review. Of those 40, 30 are genuine problems and 10 are false alarms, giving precision of 30/40 = 75% and recall of 30/50 = 60%. The 20 real problems that slip through at this threshold are auto-approved with no human ever seeing them. If Priya's finance team estimates that a missed problem costs, on average, $5,000 once rework, vendor disputes, and audit exposure are counted, and that a false alarm costs only the $1.20 of an analyst's time to clear it, the expected cost of running at threshold 0.80 is (20 × $5,000) + (10 × $1.20) = $100,000 + $12 = $100,012 against this 1,000-invoice sample.

Now lower the threshold to 0.50, which makes the system more willing to flag borderline cases. Auto-Match now flags 120 invoices, catching 45 of the 50 real problems: precision falls to 45/120 = 37.5% and recall rises to 45/50 = 90%. Only 5 real problems are missed. The expected cost becomes (5 × $5,000) + (120 × $1.20) = $25,000 + $144 = $25,144. The lower threshold looks, by the crude measure of precision, like a worse model — three out of five flags are now false alarms rather than one out of four — yet it is roughly four times cheaper for the business, because the cost of a missed fraud so outweighs the cost of an analyst glancing at a clean invoice. This is the calculation a team skips when it reports "our model is 94% accurate" (achieved trivially here by flagging nothing at all, since 950 of 1,000 invoices are already clean) without ever pricing the asymmetry between the two kinds of mistake.

A tighter threshold looks more "precise" but costs four times as much once errors are priced correctly.

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

Accuracy is not the metric; the cost-weighted matrix is

Accuracy counts every mistake as equally bad, which disguises the fact that a system can be 95% accurate purely by predicting the majority class. The question that matters is never "how often is it right?" but "when it is wrong, which kind of wrong, and what does that kind cost?"

Autonomy is a spectrum, not a switch

Teams frequently argue about whether a feature "should be automated," as if that were one decision. In practice there are at least four workable tiers: suggest only (human initiates every action), assist (system drafts, human approves), act-with-override (system acts, human can reverse within a window), and act-silently (system acts, no review unless flagged by monitoring). Each confidence band can sit at a different tier.

Each confidence band of a feature can be assigned a different point on this spectrum.

Guardrails bound the worst case, not the average case

A guardrail such as "never auto-approve above $10,000" does nothing to improve the model's everyday precision or recall. Its job is to cap the damage of the rare, catastrophic miss, the Vellum scenario, regardless of how the statistics usually behave.

Personality is a trust-calibration decision, not a cosmetic one

A system that always sounds confident trains users to stop checking its work, even on the cases where its confidence score is low. Whether the interface visibly hedges — "I'm 55% sure this matches" versus a flat "Approved" — changes how much independent scrutiny a human reviewer applies, and therefore changes the effective error rate of the whole human-plus-machine system.

The confidence score is a self-report, not ground truth

A model can be miscalibrated: it might say "90% confident" on cases that are right only 60% of the time. Threshold decisions are only as good as the calibration underneath them, which is a separate piece of engineering work from building the model itself.

Human-in-the-loop can decay into rubber-stamping

If reviewers see the model agree with their judgment 98% of the time, they stop reading carefully, a phenomenon called automation complacency. Recall numbers measured in a lab do not capture this; they must be re-measured against what reviewers actually do once bored.

This framework cannot tell you whether the feature should exist

Precision, recall, autonomy, and guardrails are downstream questions. They presuppose problem–model fit: that an AI model is actually capable of distinguishing good invoices from bad ones well enough to be useful at all. If the underlying signal is too weak, no threshold or guardrail rescues the feature; the team is only arranging deck chairs.

6. How this looks different by context

ContextTypical error priorityTypical autonomy defaultGuardrail style
Consumer (e.g. a recommendation feed)Recall-leaning: missing a good match is worse than an occasional bad one, since cost per error is lowHigh, often act-silentlyLoose, brand-safety focused
B2B (e.g. Ledgerline)Precision-leaning on high-stakes items, recall-leaning on low-stakes ones, split by dollar exposureLow to medium, act-with-overrideExplicit, auditable, tied to compliance
Marketplace (two-sided)Must be set separately for each side; a false positive harms the seller, a false negative harms the buyerMedium, varies by sideDual guardrails, one per side

Stage matters as much as context. An early-stage company like Ledgerline at Series B has perhaps a few thousand labelled examples and no dedicated data-science function, so thresholds are set partly by statistics and partly by informed judgment, revisited every few weeks as a prototype-critique-revise cycle rather than fixed in a specification document. A large incumbent with years of transaction history can run proper randomised experiments to find the threshold that minimises cost, but moves more slowly because legal and compliance review sits in front of every change, and because a threshold change at that scale touches enough volume that mistakes are expensive in absolute terms even when the rate of mistakes is unchanged.

7. Common mistakes

Mistake one: reporting accuracy instead of cost. Symptom: a dashboard proudly shows "94% accurate" while complaints from the field keep arriving. Underlying error: accuracy hides which class is being missed. Cheapest diagnostic: build the confusion matrix and multiply each cell by its dollar cost before trusting any single summary percentage.

Mistake two: treating autonomy as binary. Symptom: the team spends a meeting debating "should this be automated, yes or no" and gets stuck. Underlying error: autonomy has at least four workable settings, and different confidence bands can sit at different settings simultaneously. Cheapest diagnostic: draw the autonomy spectrum on a whiteboard and make someone place a dot on it for each confidence band.

Mistake three: bolting guardrails on after launch. Symptom: a growing, ad hoc list of "if X, then don't do Y" exceptions accumulating in the codebase after each incident. Underlying error: guardrails were never derived from a risk register up front; they are scar tissue. Cheapest diagnostic: ask whether anyone can show the risk register that guardrails were written against before the feature shipped.

Mistake four: designing personality separately from error strategy. Symptom: the assistant sounds equally confident whether its underlying score is 0.95 or 0.55, and users over-trust it on the weak cases. Underlying error: personality was handed to a copywriter without reference to the confidence distribution. Cheapest diagnostic: pull ten transcripts at the lowest confidence decile and check whether the tone of the response signals uncertainty at all.

8. What good looks like

Six months later, a well-run version of this decision at a company like Ledgerline looks like this. Maya's team built a 1,000-invoice labelled validation set refreshed quarterly. Working with Priya, they priced a missed problem at $5,000 and a false alarm at $1.20, and chose a threshold of 0.65 after testing several points on the curve, explicitly favouring recall because the cost asymmetry demanded it. They defined three confidence bands rather than one cutoff: above 0.85, auto-approve; between 0.40 and 0.85, auto-flag with mandatory human review; below 0.40, auto-hold and escalate to a senior analyst. Independently of any of those scores, a guardrail fixed in policy required human sign-off on any invoice above $10,000 regardless of confidence, closing off the Vellum scenario by rule rather than by probability. The interface showed reviewers the model's confidence number rather than hiding it, so that a 0.42 case was visibly treated with more scepticism than a 0.83 case. A monthly job compared live outcomes against the validation-set assumptions, catching when invoice patterns drifted as Ledgerline signed new customers in unfamiliar industries.

9. The decision, and what comes next

Maya recommended a threshold of 0.65 with the $10,000 guardrail, a one-quarter pilot before expanding auto-approval further, and a dashboard that reported expected dollar cost rather than accuracy at every weekly review. Her reasoning: the cost asymmetry between a missed fraud and a wasted analyst-minute was roughly 4,000 to 1, which made recall the dominant consideration everywhere except the highest-dollar invoices, where the guardrail did the work that no threshold could safely do. Daniel approved the pilot; Priya got her cost reduction, roughly 35% in the first quarter rather than the hoped-for 50%, with the gap explained honestly as the price of keeping recall high enough to sleep at night.

The natural next topics are human-in-the-loop versus autonomy in more depth, which examines how review tiers interact with reviewer behaviour over time, and the idea of the prototype as the new specification, which explains why teams like Maya's treat each threshold and guardrail choice as a hypothesis to be revised through prototype-critique-revise cycles rather than a decision to be finalised once and documented.

Two questions worth sitting with:

What is the actual dollar cost ratio between a false positive and a false negative in a feature you currently own — and have you ever asked the finance or risk function for that number directly, rather than assuming it?

If you raised your product's confidence threshold by ten points tomorrow, would you know within a week whether that change helped or hurt, or would you only find out the way Vellum did?
